topic_knowledge.topic: Inter-hospital transfer communication in mental health
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Transfer letters are often missing: none in 8 transfers [3172], 17–40% [3267]. SBAR handover not documented in 62% [3486]. Physical health is the weak point: complete notes 7/12 [3365], NEWS charts sent 17 of 42, oral intake 13 [3453]. Legal paperwork is good: MHA paperwork 36/36 [3453].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Raising the need for a transfer letter at governance and management meetings: transfer or discharge letter 0% to 88% [3172]. Samples were small (8) and differed between cycles.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: A structured preadmission checklist made no difference to information sought (n=5 to 2); physical, mental health and safeguarding updates were still needed [3433].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Samples here are tiny and few loops closed. Legal paperwork is already done. Measure physical health handover, such as NEWS charts, allergies and medication, and whether issues on arrival led to return or delayed actions.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Maintenance fluids are rarely prescribed to guideline. Recommended fluid 16% [2286]; correct composition 0% [2384]; none to NICE [2460]. Too much sodium and too little potassium: 295% excess sodium, 82% less potassium [2054]. U&Es pre-checked in 10% [2351]. Fluid balance recorded 38% [2754].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: An electronic TrakCare review proforma plus teaching: fluid balance 38% to 78%, heart rate 35% to 96% [2754]. Targeted teaching: optimal resuscitation 43% to 83%, sodium met 66% to 91.7% [2686]. Teaching and posters: maintenance when indicated 52% to 84% [2384].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Teaching and posters leave composition poor. Correct composition 0% to 15% [2384]; glucose met in 24% and potassium in 16% [2477]. Posters and emails: recommended fluid 16% to 38% [2286]. Appropriate fluid types 36% to 45.5% [2686]. Tutorial and algorithm gave only 'some improvement' [2147].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Overdone in surgical juniors, with the same finding each time. Teaching raises volumes but not potassium or glucose content. More useful to audit electrolyte harm, such as hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia, or build a review template into the electronic record.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Renal and thyroid tests are usually done (78–94%); lithium levels, calcium and weight lag. 3-monthly levels 10% [3273], 44.4% [3503], 78% [3131]. Calcium 61.1–64% [3503][3372]; full compliance 12% with no calcium or BMI [3632]. Annual ECG 26% [3165]. Pre-lithium TFTs 4.2% and weight 0% in one unit [3591].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Nurse-led or dedicated clinics and teams: all parameters over 85% [3705]; average 57% to 94% with levels, renal and calcium 100% [3328]; 12% to 68% fully compliant [3632]. A clinic proforma raised safety netting from 11.1% to 75% [3386]. Teaching lifted pre-lithium TFTs 4.2% to 61.6% and ECG 19.4% to 67.4% [3591].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Without a set intervention, 3-monthly levels moved only 10% to 17.5% and clinic documentation fell 67.5% to 62.5% [3273]. After a clinic and stickers, calcium stayed 8% and BMI 0% [3632]. Weight stayed below 40% after teaching [3591]. Weight/BMI and action on out-of-range results stayed weak [3328].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Overdone, with 16 audits and the same answer. A lithium clinic or nurse-led system works; reminders and teaching help less. Don't re-audit blood tests. Audit whether abnormal results are acted on [3503][3540], plus calcium, weight and urine ACR, which stay poor even after clinics.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Oakland scoring is rarely used: 7.1% as a discharge criterion [2254]. Unstable patients seldom get CT angiography (0% [2248]; 4 of 6 with Shock Index >1 missed it [2654]). Inpatient endoscopy was 14.9% [2248]; 62.1% of major bleeds had no colonoscopy [2009]. Some unnecessary admissions and transfusions occur (14% and 7%) [2654].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Teaching and BSG posters raised inpatient endoscopy from 14.9% to 66.7% and CT angiography in unstable patients from 0% to 50% [2248]. Posters and email raised DRE from 79% to 91% [2779]. Integrating BSG guidance cut 28-day readmission from 23.1% to 8.3%, with all discharges scoped [2500].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Oakland score documentation did not improve after posters and email; TXA use fell from 44% to 38% and CT-A from 29% to 19% [2779]. Oakland compliance improved minimally [2500]. After national guideline publication alone, Oakland use rose only to 14.6% [2254].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Oakland score uptake stays low whatever the teaching. More useful is measuring safe discharge of minor bleeds, CT angiography in unstable patients and readmission. One site judged the Oakland score not accurate enough for safe discharge [2866], so pair scoring with outcome data.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Lower GI bleeding risk stratification (Oakland score)
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: The Oakland score is almost never documented: 0–10% in most units, 36% at best. Shock index is recorded in 0–27%. Many clinicians do not know the score (61.8% unaware in one survey). Only 35% of patients were managed appropriately in one unit.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Education alone gave large gains. Teaching with a summary sheet and e-calculator link: documentation 10% to 42% [2381]. Posters and a teaching session: 4.8% to 48.8% [2849]. A targeted educational intervention: Oakland score 36% to 79%, shock index 27% to 82%, admission rate 53% to 38% [2864].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: No failed fix reported in these audits. Even after teaching, over half of patients still had no documented score in two units [2381] [2849].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Documentation audits here all show the same thing. More useful is whether the score changed decisions: avoidable admissions, safe discharges and unnecessary CT angiograms. Build the score into the clerking proforma rather than relying on teaching, as gains after teaching reached only 42–49% in two units.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: A capacity assessment is usually recorded (85–100%), but the detail is weak. The specific decision is named in only 37% [3665]. Functional tests lack evidence in 40–50% [3665]. Best interests are covered in 53% [3584]. In Section 3 patients, admission assessment was 46.2% and three-month review 7.7% [3574].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A 30-minute teaching session on the MCA template, reinforced at MDT and handover: diagnostic test 77.5% to 95%, functional parts 70% to 90–100%, reasoning 60% to 92.5% [3555].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: No failed fix reported in these audits
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Only one of five audits closed the loop. Checking that capacity was mentioned adds little; it usually is. Audit the quality of the four functional tests and whether the decision is specific, or three-month Section 3 reassessment, which was almost never done.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Mental Health Act consent to treatment documentation
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Forms usually exist but the paperwork around them is weak. Consent to treatment form 52% and capacity form 71% [3178]; T3 discussed with patient 11% [3182]; CTT list on the drug chart 24/31 [3164]. Community forms uploaded 99.8%, but letters referencing forms only 14% [3553].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Whiteboard above the drug trolley flagging patients on T3, plus teaching using real incidents: off-T3 incidents fell from four to zero for four months; staff knowledge 58% to 71% [3557].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Re-audit with no reported intervention showed no change: capacity still 80% at admission and 60% at 3 months; SOAD request recorded 56% to 25%; T3 not documented for any patient [3182].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Checking forms exist is not useful; they usually do. Audit whether every drug given is covered by the T2 or T3, with a visual prompt at the drug trolley. Capacity at three months is the item that stays poor.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Usually well under the 20% benchmark in UK units: 3.05–14.3%, with 4.67% and 5% typical. One cohort was 29%, and 43.5% in women of child-bearing age [2156]. Rates are higher in women (18.1% vs 11.1%) and those aged 16–25 (11.54%).
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: More preoperative cross-sectional imaging, 69% to 88%, went with a fall from 10.3% to 3% [2690].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: An undescribed action plan left the overall rate at 25% and 37% in women of child-bearing age [2156]. One trust drifted from 2.04% to 4.67% despite universal imaging (not significant) [2872].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Most units now sit far below 20%, so a simple rate audit rarely shows a problem. If you must, study young women and imaging-negative versus imaging-positive cases, or the other side: missed appendicitis and perforation from avoiding surgery, which none of these measured.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: NELA data entry and case ascertainment
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Case ascertainment is usually half to two-thirds: 50%, 66%, 45 of 68 entered, and 21% in one earlier period. Entries are often incomplete (only 1 of 45 complete) and late (average delay 206 days, 13% met the deadline). The NELA section of the CEPOD form was completed in 42.7%. Formal risk assessment on NELA was 11.7%.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Presentations, NELA log-ins at induction and a QR code on the CEPOD form: risk assessment 11.7% to 86.2% [2675]. Emails, discussions and posters: CEPOD NELA section 42.7% to 87.5% [2485]. Targeted interventions: registration 50% to 84% then 95%, all by deadline [2605]. Unstated QI: all entries complete, ascertainment 54% [2173].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Adding registrars to the NELA team and a redesigned booking form: entry 66% to 71%, with only 14 cases at re-audit [2603].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Small topic, and simple prompts at booking work well. The recurring problem is new rotating doctors, so re-audit after each changeover. Check completeness and timeliness of entries, not just whether a case was registered.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Full BOAST compliance 8.8% [1375]. Antibiotics within 1 hour: 13.3% [1274], 27% [1620], 41.7% [1601]. High-energy debridement within 12 hours 25% [1681] and 41.7% [1601]. Soft tissue cover within 72 hours 56.4% [1545]. Joint orthoplastic consultants at debridement 10% [1224] to 33.3% [1545]. Tetanus prophylaxis 48.8% [1274].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A second weekly orthoplastics list halved missed 7-day soft tissue cover from 11% to 5% [1224]. Teaching, posters and a clerking proforma raised STAT antibiotic prescriptions from 15.4% to 51.7% and cut mean time from 271 to 233 minutes [1200]. Tracking antibiotic times with quarterly audits improved 1-hour order and administration [1597]. Soft tissue cover within 5 days rose from 50% to 100% [1407].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Education alone did not improve antibiotic timing [1597]. Mean time to antibiotics was still 233 minutes after improvement [1200]. Both consultants at initial debridement only reached 26% [1224].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Antibiotic timing matters: prehospital antibiotics within 1 hour were linked to lower infection [1681]. Audit time from injury to antibiotic and STAT prescribing, or joint orthoplastic debridement. Link process to infection rates, which were 13–24% [1681][1375].
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Core items (surgeon, date, procedure, findings) are near 100%. The same few items fail: blood loss 0–8% [2216, 2323, 2450, 2794], time of operation 0–9% [2216, 2319, 2524], elective/emergency 0–10% [1640, 2216, 2259], DVT prophylaxis 6% [2257]. Overall compliance about 50–72% [1600, 1276, 2319]; full compliance 4–7% [2274, 2844].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A typed or electronic template with mandatory or drop-down fields. Overall 50% to 92% [1600]; below 80% to above 98% [2280]; 37.5% to 83.3% [2577]; 67% to 94% [2827]; full compliance 7% to 85% of template notes [2844]; 35% to 89% in template notes [2514]. Easy online access plus induction: 69% to 96.6% [2762].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Teaching or presentation alone: all items stayed well below standard, time 3% to 6.67% [2619]; knee 71% to 74%, hip 68% to 64% [1227]. Blood loss stayed at 8% despite a template [1136]. Templates are bypassed: use fell 45% to 28% [2169]; tonsillectomy proforma 33% [2118]. Gains fell at 24 months as new staff missed the template [1366].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: One of the most overdone audits, with 65 here and the same answer. Don't audit RCS items again. Audit whether a template is still used a year on and by new staff, or procedure-specific GIRFT items and whether notes reach the ward on time.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Ottawa rules and radiograph request appropriateness
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: About half of requests meet the rules. Ottawa compliance 59.5% overall, ankle 33.1% [1676]; ankle 43%, foot 32% [1707]; OAR referenced in 37% [1734]. Knee criteria documented in 41% [1714]. GP knee films: 50% within RCR guidelines, 87% changed nothing [1788].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Multi-channel teaching with posters, leaflets and emails. Compliance 59.5% to 85%, ankle 33.1% to 75.8% [1676]. Knee criterion documented 41% to 91% [1714]. Foot documentation 48% to 78% [1707]. Radiographer briefings: OAR referenced 37% to 51% [1734].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Knee compliance 72.5% to 83.5%, not significant, below 95% target [1733]. Informing GPs left the knee X-ray referral rate unchanged [1788]. Foot and ankle request compliance only reached 54–57% [1707]. Under-55s lag behind [1676].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Done many times; teaching works but plateaus below target. Don't repeat an education-only cycle. Test an electronic request prompt or radiographer vetting, and measure negative X-ray rate, not just documentation.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: DNA rates vary: 7.5% [3421], 29% [3468], 35.3% in perinatal care [3484]. Letters go out (98.1%) but follow-up is weak. Risk assessment after a DNA 48.2–50.9%, updated in 25% [3311][3610]. After a DNA no contact in 57% [3468]. Risk plans 49.4% [3610].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: SMS reminders one working day before appointments cut the mean DNA rate from 7.5% to 5.0% [3421]. Staff awareness of the trust guideline raised risk documentation after DNA from 48.2% to 95% and repeat appointments offered from 77.6% to 92% [3610].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: In the same audit risk management plans rose only from 49.4% to 58% and MDT notification from 50.5% to 60%. Contacting patients after DNA fell from 81.1% to 74% and confirming appointments from 94.1% to 92% [3610].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Few audits and only two closed loops, so there is room here. Awareness fixes the risk entry but not the plan. Audit what happens after a DNA for high-risk patients, welfare checks and family contact [3311], and test reminders or home and remote options, as DNA was lower away from the centre [3484].

topic_knowledge.topic: Paediatric buckle and forearm fracture management
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Buckle fractures are over-treated: rigid casts in 22–100% [1271, 1765], 95.4% full cast in clinic [1692], fracture clinic follow-up in 43–58% [1307, 1765], and discharge at first visit in 7.7% [1692]. For displaced forearm fractures, national BOAST compliance is 63%, with post-manipulation neurovascular checks in 35% and consent in 38% [1758].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Guideline revision, leaflets and education cut plaster casts from 34% to 10% and clinic follow-up from 43% to 17% [1307]. Parent education and email reminders gave 62/64 direct ED discharges [1651]. Teaching raised NICE compliance from 56% to 80% at a DGH [1765]. A BOAST pathway raised ED manipulation from 23/72 to 73/87 [1648]. An ED SOP cut theatre need from 36.4% to 1.9% [1663].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: The same teaching reached only 31% compliance at an MIU, where rigid immobilisation stayed at 69% [1765]. After a new pathway, first-visit discharge was still only 44.8% and 47.1% kept a cast [1692]. Neurovascular documentation before discharge stayed at 64.36% and clinic within 7 days at 49.42% [1648].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Buckle fracture audits are common and the fix is well known. Check splint stock and cover minor injury units, where rigid casts persist. More useful is the forearm manipulation pathway: ED versus theatre reduction, failed reductions, consent and post-manipulation neurovascular checks, which national data show are weak [1758].

topic_knowledge.topic: Physical health assessment on psychiatric admission
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Examination within 24 hours is often done (60–98%) but ECG and bloods lag at 24–72%. The full set is rarely complete: 0% in one ward, 62.8% in another. Specific tests fall far lower: QRISK 2%, urine dip 15–28%, glucose 6–53%. Abnormal ECGs are rarely followed up (3 of 13).
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Checklists and proformas work best. An admission checklist raised bloods 52.9% to 100% and ECG 58.8% to 94.4% [3266]. A proforma took examination from 23% to 100% [3126]. A pre-filled blood request form: full tests 77% to 100% [3295]. Active handover to the physical health nurse: 62.4% to 96.6% [3546]. PDSA cycles on a rehab ward: 92% overall [1361].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: An A3 poster gave small gains: examination 34.5% to 47%, all three components 33% [3260]. Undescribed recommendations moved ECG within 24 hours only from 52% to 62% [3281]. Chaperone documentation stayed at 14%, with no choice of chaperone gender offered [3272].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Heavily overdone, with the same result across trusts. Don't repeat an admission-checks audit. Audit what happens to abnormal results instead: abnormal ECGs followed up, raised HbA1c acted on, vitamin D re-checked after loading. Transfers and duty-doctor admissions do worse and are worth targeting.

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Full protocol analgesia is uncommon: 0/27 [1529] and 34% [1321] after joint replacement. Pain was well managed in 30% [2453]. NSAIDs are under-used: 28% of eligible patients [2611], ibuprofen often omitted without a reason [1529]. IV paracetamol is used when oral would do [2611].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Electronic order sets work. A prescribing order set: total compliance 0% to 58% [1529]. An EPR powerplan: 34% to 61%, with 87% of compliant patients using it [1321]. Posters and teaching: 30% more regular oral opioids on day 0 [1298].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Teaching, leaflets and emails: WHO ladder compliance fell from 83.3% to 50.9% [2043]. A departmental talk: adequate pain control only 30% to 46%, anti-emetics down from 92% to 82% [2453]. Ibuprofen stayed at 58% despite an order set [1529].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Build the protocol into electronic prescribing and audit its use. Education alone has not held. More useful measures are NSAID omission without a reason and IV paracetamol when oral is possible, both simple to fix.

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Anaemia is common and rarely treated. 71% below Hb threshold but 6.7% given iron [2128]; 38% operated with Hb <130 and 7% treated [1387]; iron studies 8% and screening 6 weeks before surgery 3.95% [1590]; 18% of anaemic colorectal patients given IV iron [2046].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Governance presentation and a departmental plan to treat to Hb 130: operated with Hb <130 fell from 38% to 21%; anaemias investigated 11% to 80% [1387]. Education plus publicising a day-case iron pathway: IV iron 18% to 60%, transfusion 45% to 20% [2046][2174].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Actual treatment lagged investigation: attempted treatment rose only from 7% to 20%, not significant (p = 0.279) [1387].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Everyone finds untreated anaemia. Audit timing instead: whether Hb is checked early enough, at least 6 weeks before surgery, to treat it. Measure iron given and Hb reached, not just screening.

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Fasting is almost always too long: clear fluids mean 10.5 hours, solids 15.8 hours; 62% 'nil by mouth from midnight' [1655]. Only 39% got their usual medicines while fasting [1644]. Unnecessary tests are routine: 91% of ASA 1–2 abscess patients had bloods [2685]; 81% of coagulation screens inappropriate [2279].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Posters and dissemination: abscess bloods 91% to 27%, £2,151 to £406 [2685]. Coagulation appropriate 19% to 56% [2279]. Decision aid cut ASA 2 FBCs by 75.0% [2859]. Patient leaflets: clear fluid fasting median 10 to 3 hours [2380]. Drug trolley posters: correct medicines 39% to 61% [1644]. Liquid fasting 10% to 60% [2088].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: SipTilSend lapsed: fluid fasting rose from 3 h 45 min to 11.2 hours despite reinforcement [1191]. Solid fasting did not improve: 5% to 0% [2088], median 12.5 to 11 hours [2380].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Fasting audits are common and relapse fast, so measure sustainability months later rather than another baseline. Unnecessary bloods before minor surgery are a quick, cheap win with cost figures. Omitted critical medicines while nil by mouth are less audited and more important.

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Errors are widespread. One audit of 228 prescriptions found errors in every field except timings [3214]. Generic names in 40.6% and block letters in 17% [3403]. Missing dose, frequency, strength and dates in 156 charts [3462]. In a community team, 65% of prescriptions uploaded and 19% in the clinic register [3607].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: BNF guidance presented and copies placed at nursing counters: generic names 40.6% to 84.69%, block letters 17% to 71.42%, start date 82.8% to 99.18% [3403]. A faculty workshop and mandatory teaching gave improvement across all areas, but no figures were given [3462]; nor for [1797].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Presentation and re-training made things worse: GMC number errors up 20.33%, doctor's name up 16.87%, indication up 12.94% [3214]. The trust then issued stamps with GMC number and name.
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Common and easy, and several audits report no figures, which makes them useless. If you do it, report numbers per field. Stamps or electronic prescribing will fix identifiers better than teaching, so audit the fields that need clinical thought, such as indication.

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Indication and maximum 24-hour dose are near 100% [3340][3522][3636]. Review is the gap: review date 0/32 [3636], ward round review 3.2% [3522], reviewed in last 7 days 25% [3340]. Unused PRN not stopped: 0% [3522], 0/8 [3636], 5 of 21 still active [3664]. PRN protocol standards met in 53% [3096].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Induction teaching, weekly pharmacist discussion, chart prompts and weekly MDT PRN review: reviewed in last 7 days 25% to 56% [3340]. After a serious incident, ward round reviews rose from 3.2% to 64.5% and minimum dose interval from 64.5% to 93.5% [3522].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Stopping unused PRN only reached 22.2% and review of regularly used PRN 28.5% [3522]. Minimum dose documented rose only from 10.7% to 24%, and no item reached the 100% standard [3340].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Don't audit indication or maximum dose; they are nearly always met. Audit review and discontinuation. One Trust added an automatic 14-day review date in EPMA [3636]; re-auditing whether that works would be more useful than a new baseline.

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: About half are checked: 23.33% [3142], 41–52% [1363, 3379], 43–47% [3224, 3612], up to 80.6% [3381]. Baseline before starting is 43–44.4% [3191, 3224]; 12-week check 12% [3623]. Raised results are often not acted on: action 27.3% [3191], 41.7% [3381]; symptoms assessed 9.1% [3191].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Trust-wide recommendations after a 2021 audit (not described): monitoring 47% and 43% to 100% (n=160) [3612].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Re-audit with no described intervention: 41% to 51% [3379]; 69% to 76% on admission [3657]. Even at 100% testing, raised prolactin was managed in only 4 of 9 [3612]. Symptom documentation stayed poor [3657].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Testing rates are well documented and ten audits say the same. The real gap is what happens after a raised result: symptoms asked, action taken, repeat test. Audit that, with a named pathway or electronic prompt, and re-audit it.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Rationale is usually recorded (85–100%). Plans to reduce or stop are not: timescale for stopping 29% [3469], reduce/stop plan 10–17% [3709], no clear indication for 50.6% of antipsychotics [3608]. Monitoring and consent are weak: consent and monitoring under 10% [3216], metabolic monitoring 0% [3292]. One CAMHS service scored 98% [3383].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Repeated cycles in one ID team: metabolic monitoring 0% to 95%, risk assessment 68% to 100%, target behaviour described 74% to 100% [3292].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Side-effect discussion at initiation fell from 73% to 38% after criteria changed [3440]. Consent stayed low (19% to 46%), and single drug therapy 19% to 34% [3292]. Mental health evaluation fell from 87% to 60% [3292].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Thirteen audits, only two re-audited. Documenting a rationale is solved. Audit whether a reduce-or-stop plan with a timescale exists and is acted on, and count actual dose reductions, not just reviews.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Most patients are on medication: 81–96% [3067][3308][3312]. Antipsychotics over 4 weeks without psychosis 86% [3219]; 80% had no licensed indication, mean 36.79 months, with no physical review [3308]. Time-limited prescribing 39.4%, written information 4.2% [3312]. PRN over one week in 21 of 50 inpatients [3067].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A trust prescribing guidance for personality disorder [3219] raised documented reasons for antipsychotics from 43% to 69% and medication reviews from 90% to 100%.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: After the same guidance, antipsychotics over 4 weeks without psychosis rose from 86% to 91%, Z-hypnotics over 4 weeks from 13% to 37.5%, benzodiazepines over 4 weeks from 28% to 38%, and crisis plans fell from 87% to 79% [3219]. Review quality was unchanged.
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Only one loop is closed, and guidance alone did not cut long-term prescribing. Don't just count prescriptions. Audit whether antipsychotics are reviewed with a plan to stop, whether physical health checks happen, and whether patients get written information, which is almost never given.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Positioning standards are often missed. Calibration marker balls were present in 44–45% [1322, 1727]. Lateral ankle talar domes superimposed in 61% [1724]; wrist piso-scapho-capitate relationship 50% [1745]. 69/100 arthroplasty films were adequate [1633]. Only 23.09% of shoulder AP views met criteria and 21.17% had an axillary view [1667].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Posters plus teaching by an associate specialist raised talar dome superimposition from 61% to 85% [1724] and wrist relationship from 50% to 82% [1745]. Posters, a radiographer presentation and a mandatory checklist raised marker ball presence from 45% to 78% [1727]. A protocol and ordering rota raised timely templating films from 20% to 70% [1698]. Guidelines and feedback raised adequate arthroplasty films from 69/100 to 84/100 [1633].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Calibration marker compliance fell to 44% after an earlier improvement from 64% to 73% [1322]. Pubic symphysis centring reached only 47% and GT/LT level 43% [1633]. Overall marker compliance change was not significant (59% to 80%, p=0.132) [1727].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Radiograph positioning audits improve quickly with posters and joint teaching of radiographers and doctors, but gains fade [1322]. Involve the radiography team from the start and build checks into the request or checklist. More useful is measuring whether poor films led to repeat exposure or missed injury, which none of these assessed.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Choice and dose of drug are usually right. Documentation around it is weak. Protocol steps followed in 60%; indication documented in 50%; reasons for IM medication and side-effect monitoring 25.42%. Post-RT monitoring is the most common failure: full observations in 33%, or not evident at all. Junior doctors often do not know the protocol.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A structured pre-RT checklist with staff education: pre-RT workup 47% to 85%, reassessment before repeat dosing 42% to 92%, de-escalation 71% to 92% [3590]. At re-audit in older patients, indication documented rose from 50% to 88.8% [3407].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Post-RT monitoring stayed poor at re-audit: still not evident in older patients [3407], and below standard with debriefing, medication review and incident reporting in an acute ward [3656]. Advance directives were absent in both audits [3656].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Don't just audit drug choice; it is usually correct. Audit post-RT physical observations and debriefing, which stay poor after re-audit. On medical and older people's wards, check junior doctors' knowledge of the protocol, which was limited [3382].

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Many transfusions fall outside threshold. Only 21.4% met NICE thresholds and targets [1254]; 73.5% were inappropriate [1294]; 40.2% of units followed NICE [2539]; 34% used a threshold below 70 g/L in critical care [2967]. Back-to-back units without reassessment were 20.5% [2539]. Out-of-hours units were appropriate in 70.6% [2638].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Teaching and ward posters of thresholds: back-to-back units 20.5% to 4.51%, reactions 2 to none, saving about £5493 a year [2539]. Teaching and an induction booklet: TACO assessment 58.8% to 90.9% [1294].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: After teaching, 45.5% of transfusions were still inappropriate [1294], and only 50.4% of units followed NICE [2539]. Both re-audits were small.
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Worth doing but the finding is well known. Measure single-unit prescribing and reassessment between units, and reasons for higher thresholds, such as a loosely defined 'coronary history' with no ACS [1254]. Pre-operative iron treatment was 7% and is a better target.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: CT KUB within target is usually good, 93–100% [2383][2464][2495][2691], but not everywhere (335 of 705 within 14 hours [2273]). Serum calcium 21–51% [2691][2464][2624], urate 2.6–4%, NSAIDs 52–55% [2464][2495], dietary advice 8.7–17% [2495][2624].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Renal order-set and stone diet leaflet: calcium 77.9% to 94.7%, NSAIDs 54.5% to 71.9%, dietary advice 8.7% to 39.4% [2495]. Email reminders and a handover-sheet note: calcium 21% to 72% [2691]. Hot URS theatre: treatment within 48 hours 35% to 53%, dietary advice 17% to 72% [2624].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Updated NSAID dosing and pathway: NSAIDs fell 87% to 50% on six patients [2383]. After teaching, only 26.4% were seen in clinic within 4 weeks [2049]. Dietary advice stayed low at 39.4% [2495].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: CT timing is done and usually met; don't audit it again. Audit what happens after the ED: time to definitive treatment, stent use without indication, and follow-up clinic waits. Use an order-set for calcium.

topic_knowledge.topic: Resuscitation and physical health equipment on psychiatric wards
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Equipment is usually partly available: 66–90% of standards met. Missing or expired adrenaline, suction and masks in 7/10 locations [3380]; 70% of weekly checklists wrong. One learning disability unit had no trolley [3070]. Small items such as testing pins, Snellen charts and ophthalmoscopes are borrowed between wards [3671].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Equipment boxes in clinic rooms: availability 66% to 73.5% [3093]. Weekly checks, maintenance registration and complete sets: resuscitation equipment 94.2% to 99.2% [3244]. An updated local protocol left trolleys better stocked [3070].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Physical health equipment fell from 83.8% to 76.6% despite the same interventions [3244]. Secure wards still lagged controls [3093]. Items added to trolleys were hard to find [3070].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: A quick audit, but resuscitation kit tends to improve once weekly checks are enforced. Physical health kit is the neglected side. Measure whether it is working and used, with a named checker, rather than just counting items.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Risk assessment documentation in mental health
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Risk to self and others is usually recorded, but depth is poor. Junior clerking included risk in 40–70%. Absconding, historical risk and risk to the opposite sex are often missed. Structured suicide assessment was near zero: C-SSRS 0.8%, safety plan 0.8%. Service user involvement 16%. Annual review 81.8%, lower for doctors than nurses.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Staff education, ward checklists and ward-round reminders: risk assessment within 24 hours 64% to 92%, review before discharge 40% to 84%, update before discharge 40% to 80% [3691]. An email with updated guidance: annual CRAFT 81.8% to 86.4%, medical 77.6% to 83.6% [3642].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: No failed fix reported in these audits
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Checking that a risk assessment exists is overdone. Audit its quality: structured suicide assessment, safety planning, historical risk and whether the patient took part. Samples here are often small (10–37), so aim for more.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Rationale and timing of review usually above 90%. Medical review within 1 hour is poor: 20% [3297], 34% [3212][3305], 39% [3483], 44% [3404]. Content gaps: medication side effects 0% [3651], risk to self 5% [3404]. No review met all eight criteria [3651]. Independent reviews by an Approved Clinician often missing [3280].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A seclusion review template in the documentation plus teaching: 95–100% [3152]. An integrated care pathway: MHC rule compliance from 3–100% to 69–100% [3064]. Education in secure LD wards: review within 1 hour 34% to 66%, medications 20% to 72% [3212]. Huddles and weekly meetings: consultant review within 24 hours from under 70% to over 90%, average seclusion 30 to 20 hours [3129].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Four PDSA cycles of proforma, email and teaching: 75% to 83%, minimal change on the SPC chart [3576]. Teaching and posters: side effects 0% to 19%, steps to end seclusion 25% to 23% [3651]. A previous audit led to no change [3297]. Just under half still monitored per guidelines [3129].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Medical review documentation has been audited many times. Teaching alone gives small gains; a mandatory template works better. More useful: audit out-of-hours timing, Approved Clinician independent review [3280], seclusion room standards [3485], or seclusion duration.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Acute care is mostly done: pre- and post-reduction x-rays 88–97% [1212, 1713], MUA successful 98% [1713]. Follow-up is weaker: appropriate imaging 40–43.3% [1212, 1240], shoulder specialist 40.3–50% [1212, 1240]. Post-reduction views adequate in only 22.7% [1729]. Triage to reduction x-ray 2 hours 25 min [1571]; mean time to reduction 152 minutes [1713].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A Shoulder Reduction Bench with nurse practitioner training, a written protocol and an online video: triage to reduction x-ray 2 h 25 min to 1 h 54 min, triage to discharge 3 h 22 min to 2 h 30 min, sedation 57% to 18% [1571].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: No failed fix reported in these audits
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Only one loop is closed here. Pre- and post-reduction x-ray rates are high, so don't re-audit them. Audit whether post-reduction films are truly orthogonal, and whether first-time dislocations reach a shoulder surgeon with the right imaging.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Early CT is good: 88–98.3% [2348][2561]. Water-soluble contrast is patchy: 12% [2348], 37% [2402], 64% [2170], 80% [2092]. Delays to surgery are long: 4 days [2402], 2.4 days [2561]. Operative mortality 14% [2417][2561].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Flowchart plus a theatre slot within 72 hours: SBO operative mortality 14% to 5% [2417]. Presenting NASBO recommendations at governance: water-soluble contrast 12% to 44%, no oral intake >5 days 44% to 17% [2348].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Nutritional assessment did not improve after governance presentation: malnourished identified 6% then 5% [2348].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: CT timing is already good and not worth auditing. Measure water-soluble contrast use, time to theatre after failed conservative care, and nutrition. Guaranteed theatre access is the fix with an outcome to show for it.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Smoking cessation in mental health inpatients
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Status is usually asked (66.7–92%, but 31% on older adult wards [3650]); treatment lags. NRT offered 20–25% [3582][3692]; dual NRT 0% [3451]; NRT within 30 minutes 0% [3650]; side-effect monitoring 0% [3582]. Detailed assessment under 10% [3205]. Cessation in discharge letters: one of 219 [3707], 3.3% [3582].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Staff education and clerking reminders [3692]: status 66.7% to 93.3%, brief advice 33.3% to 84.6%, NRT 25% to 76.9%, referral 8.3% to 53.8%. A ward poster cut incorrect NRT prescribing from 22% to 0% [3148]. A standard smoking and vaping checklist gave full histories in both new admissions [3698].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: A re-audit with no intervention fell from 71.88% to 36.84% assessed; after a shared presentation it reached only 57.14%, with under 40% assessed in detail, blamed on doctor rotation [3205].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Many baselines; asking about smoking is mostly fine. The gaps are prompt and adequate NRT, dual NRT, vaping and plans at discharge. Audit time to first NRT, dose adequacy, and whether the discharge letter carries a cessation plan and medication adjustment [3707].
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Substance misuse screening in mental health patients
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: About half to two-thirds of patients are asked about substance use: 69% [3115], 7/12 [3333], nearly half not asked [3238]. Older people, women and ward referrals are asked least (over 80s 0%) [3115]. Drug screening was documented in 57.5% and offered to 52.5% [3473]. Specialist service involvement is weakest (62.06% on admission, 42.8% at discharge) [3514].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A training session on results and NICE recommendations raised screening from 69% to 93%, over 80s from 0% to 60% and ward referrals from 33.3% to 85% [3115]. At re-audit, 78% were asked about alcohol and 77% about drugs, with documented advice up 21% [3238].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: No intervention was followed by no improvement. Items that stayed poor: at re-audit, 27% with identified misuse had no intervention documented [3238]. Over 80s reached only 60% after training [3115].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Asking the question is easy to improve with teaching. The gap lies in what happens next: advice, brief intervention and specialist referral, and reasons for refused drug tests [3473]. Audit the action taken for positive screens, and include older patients and women.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Supracondylar fracture nerve and vessel documentation
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Under half fully documented: 36–46% in most units. Individual nerves are worst, anterior interosseous as low as 10%. Many notes say only 'NV intact'. Post-operative nerve checks were 9.7% in one unit. After manipulation in ED, 63.2% had no documentation.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A proforma, best built into clerking. Electronic pro forma: 86–95% across nerves, sustained at 12 months [1142]. Simple proforma: under 40% to 70% [583] [1270]. Proforma plus teaching: 45.8% to 76.5% [578]; ED nerve function 37.9% to 72.7% [1654]. Consultant-led joint ED and orthopaedic teaching: ED specific documentation 38.9% to 82.9% [1628].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: A single awareness talk: detailed neurological findings 38.8% to 54.2%, not significant [1747]. With no stated fix, 36% only reached 45% [1211]. Pre-op nerve documentation stayed at 50% [1654], and post-manipulation documentation stayed poor, 31.8% still with none [1628].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Heavily overdone, with the same finding and fix. Don't repeat it unless your unit has no proforma. Audit whether the proforma is still used a year on, or audit documentation after manipulation and after surgery, which stay poor even when admission notes improve.

topic_knowledge.revises_seed_card: Supracondylar fracture nerve and vessel documentation

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Prophylaxis is almost always given. Duration and choice fail. Full compliance ranged 23.7% [2316] to 74.1% [1333]. Correct agent 43.5–65.4% [2316, 1712]. Duration too long in 21–25% [2074, 2316]. Postprocedural doses were appropriate in 48.3% [1591]. Post-incision dosing ran 18.9% [2445] and 26% in appendicectomy [1594].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Changes built into theatre routine work. Posters and stickers: correct MRSA-unknown agent 18% to 94% [1541]. A new protocol with posters: courses cut to 24 hours, stay 3.33 to 2.04 days, no SSI [1607]. Sign-in/time-out edits and a duration sticker: mean duration 70.4 to 28.2 hours, correct agent 43.5% to 65.3% [2445].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: MRSA eradication stickers: 1% to only 8% [1541]. Presenting at governance: appropriate prophylaxis 78% to 83%, with more incomplete courses [1255]. Full compliance stayed at 39.8% after a year of QI [2445]. Administration time stayed poorly documented [2887].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Don't audit whether prophylaxis was given; it nearly always is. Audit duration after surgery and choice of agent, and add a prompt to the WHO time-out or drug chart. Recording SSI and dosing errors, as one large audit did [1333], adds more value.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: SSI rates vary widely: 6.76% in emergency general surgery [2512], 14.5% across a district hospital [1267], 29% in elective colorectal surgery [2535], deep infection 3.6% after hip fracture [1404]. Prevention steps patchy: perioperative showering 44%, intra-op antibiotics 14.29% [2512].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Changing gloves and instruments before abdominal closure, then team education: 29% to 23% to 15%, sustained 6 months [2535]. Fixing infection-policy shortfalls: deep infection 3.6% to 1.1% [1404]. Antibiotic flow-chart for diabetics: 7/14 to 16/19 given prophylaxis, 0 diabetic infections [2335].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: No failed fix reported in these audits
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Active follow-up matters: 38 SSIs were found only by telephone call [1267], so ward-based counts undercount. Pick one specialty, follow patients after discharge, and test one specific measure such as glove and instrument change.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.topic: Suspected cauda equina time to MRI
topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Request-to-scan often meets targets, but presentation-to-MRI is long: mean 12.5 hours [1660], median 5.9 hours [1704], 438 minutes [1318]. Only 15% referred with an MRI done [1279]. CES confirmed in only 7–18% of referrals or scans. Documentation of perianal sensation 72% and spinal plan 20% [1621].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: An orthopaedic middle grade in ED: mean MRI wait 12.5 to 8 hours, same-day discharge 29% to 58% [1660]. Referral 176 to 60.8 minutes, MRI 438 to 185 minutes [1318]. Teaching and SBAR template: perianal sensation 72% to 97% [1621]. SOP and triage work: unnecessary MRIs 38% to 18% [1704].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Three PDSA cycles left median presentation-to-MRI at 5.7 hours; scanners closing at 20:00 blocked it [1704]. Senior ED discussion fell 61.9% to 9% and documented spinal plan 20% to 0% [1621].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Time to MRI depends on scanner hours and staffing more than on trainees. Audit the whole pathway from arrival, not just request-to-scan, which usually passes. The yield of scans and discharge safety are more useful than another timing audit.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Time and pressure are usually recorded (time 56–95%, pressure 20.5–88%). Skin condition, isolation and exsanguination are almost never recorded: 0–43%. Pressures often exceed BOAST limits: within standard in only 24–35% in two audits, over in 47.5–70% in another. Fixed 250 mmHg used in 95.3% [2626]. Time over 120 minutes is rare.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A mandatory electronic op note template: skin 37% to 69%, pressure documented 71% to 94%, within limit 25% to 75% [1664]. EPR auto-text: skin 0% to 64.3%, exsanguination 5.6% to 42.9% [1665]. A smart phrase with automatic SBP calculation: 17% to 62% [1677]. A template and laminated reminders: skin isolation 80% to 100% [2764].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Education alone gave little change: exsanguination 9.8%, skin 5.2% [1665]. EPR roll-out without a template dropped compliance to 17% [1677]. Teaching, checklist and posters left most items under 50%; time stayed at 56% [1759]. Pressures within standard did not improve with the proforma (13.0% lower limb) [1665].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Well audited, with a known fix: a mandatory electronic template. Don't repeat the documentation audit. Audit the pressures actually used, cuff sizing and paediatric pressures, which stay poor even when documentation improves.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Senior ownership and ward round checks. Regular frailty consultant review: 58% to 83% [2697]. Local pathway letting F1s complete TEPs plus post-take ward round reminders: 69.5% to 88.2% [1661]. Ward round check, SHO completion at clerking and training: 40.47% to 64.86% [2220]. Education and handover reminders: 0% to 40% [2278].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Email: 6.18% to 5% [2718]. Departmental presentation and a target: 15% to 17% [2600]. Posters: 39.6 to 34.6 hours, not significant [2658]. Take-list column then poster and teaching: 31% to 33% [2343]. Correct TELP 11.1% to 16.7% [2106]. Completion within 48 hours fell from 47.82% to 35.29% [1661].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Heavily overdone in surgery, with emails and posters failing again and again. Don't repeat a completion count. Audit form quality, such as capacity and discussion, or test senior review on the post-take ward round and whether it lasts.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Documentation is very poor. ARAF completed in 3% [3220], 0% dual-signed [3680]; 4/25 on the programme [3139]. Teratogenicity discussed in 3% [3442]; full counselling 24.5% [3622]. Contraception advice 0% [3442], 15% [3680]. Men are worst: risk discussion 17%, contraception 3% [3680].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Structured outpatient reviews, MHRA materials, a live ARAF tracker and education: men's risk discussion 17% to 87%, contraception 3% to 83%, consent 20% to 87% [3680]. Phoning and emailing teams: ARAF 3% to 54% [3220]. Teaching: teratogenicity 3% to 47.6%, pregnancy test 65.6% to 90% [3442].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: After teaching, discussion of benefits barely moved (21% to 23.8%) and contraception education reached only 38.1% [3442]. ARAF completion still reached only 54% [3220].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Baselines are uniformly poor, so another snapshot adds little. The 2024 guidance covering men is barely audited and gave the biggest gains. Audit a tracker-led system, or whether patients were switched to alternatives.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Doses and level timing are mostly right: correct starting dose 100% [2972][2982], levels at correct time 87–90%. Levels are often out of range: first levels in range 7–33% [2996][2972][3012]. Abnormal levels are not always acted on: 3 of 4 low levels ignored [2982].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Continuous infusion in neonates: levels in range 28% to 62% [2980]. New paediatric guideline with pharmacist input: in range at 48 hours 7% to 40%; out-of-range levels reviewed 40%, 80% with pharmacist [2996].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Electronic prescribing templates and recirculated guideline improved dose frequency (75.9% to 92.6%) but therapeutic first concentration fell from 24.1% to 19.2% [3012]. Still over 80% not in range.
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Prescribing compliance is not the problem. The dosing regimen itself often misses range. Audit first-level attainment and the response to out-of-range levels, and test continuous infusion or pharmacist-led adjustment.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Testing is patchy: 0% [3345], 56% [3007], 56.4% [3123], 89% [3183]. Deficiency is common: 64% insufficient [1159]; only 25% adequate [3183]; 68.18% deficient or inadequate [3345]. Dosing is often wrong: correct dose 21.4%, 41.4% no dose when indicated [1360]. Prophylaxis prescribed 16% [3472], 1 of 10 [3497].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: A pre-populated admission blood form including vitamin D: testing 0% to 86.67%, then 90% sustained in round three [3345]. Psychoeducation and a clinic room poster: supplementation 1 of 10 to 9 of 10 [3497]. A simplified poster and flow chart: prophylaxis 16% to 31% [3472].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Policy update and education in a frailty ED changed nothing: 65% to 61% [1826]. In the CAMHS unit, level monitoring stayed at 5 of 10 over three cycles [3497].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Mostly single-cycle audits across very different settings. The default test on the admission form is the fix that sticks. Audit whether deficient patients get the correct dose and a repeat level, not just whether a test was sent.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Initial assessment is often fair, but reassessment is almost absent: 0% [1206] and 0.13% within 24 hours [1690]. Risk assessment for immobilised lower limbs was 32–45% [1358, 1228]. Operation notes lacked any VTE plan in 42% [1642]. Psychiatric wards did worst: 13% [3109], 0–8% [3176].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: An automated EPMA prompt raised 24-hour reassessment from 0.13% to 74% [1690]. A redesigned pathway with an electronic discharge block raised ED risk assessment from 32% to 93.1% [1358]. A teaching half-day and written policy raised discharge chemoprophylaxis from 57% to 98% [1642]. A discharge letter template reached 95% [1207]. A proforma on drug charts reached 100% [3109].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Teaching, posters and an EPR dropdown raised reassessment only to 3% within 24 hours [1206]. Teaching did not change prophylaxis after long arthroscopy (50% to 55%, p=1.0) [1718]. An aspirin policy reached 93% but symptomatic VTE stayed at 6.4% [1520]. Compliance dipped to 86% after rotation [1524].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: VTE assessment audits are very common. Initial assessment is usually fine because it is mandatory; target the gaps instead: reassessment at 24 hours, the plan in the operation note, and discharge prescriptions. Electronic prompts and templates beat teaching. Where possible, record VTE events, not just forms completed [1520].
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Completion of risk assessment varies widely, from 0–39% to over 90%. Completion is not accuracy: one trust had 72.1% completed but 15.4% accurate. Re-assessment at 48 hours is poor (36.1%). Mechanical prophylaxis is the weakest item: TEDs given to 5% of eligible ENT patients, appropriate in under 40% elsewhere.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: Changes to the system work best. Electronic assessment, mandatory teaching and clerking prompts: completion 16.67% to 100% [2416]. Drug chart checkboxes for weight and renal function: correct doses 29/36 to 37/38 [2219]. A handover checkbox and posters with forms attached: form use 0% to 70% [2475]. Mandatory junior doctor training: prescribing accuracy 41.2% to 79.5% [2195].
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: Posters and reinforcement: insufficient prophylaxis rose from 40% to 50%, stocking non-compliance 37.4% to 46.4% [2158]. Five years of teaching and reminders: documentation fell from 92% to 53% [2172]. Teaching did not reduce omitted doses (9.3%) [2549] and delayed assessments rose 16.3% to 35.7% [2676]. Assessment accuracy stayed at 34.5% [2195].
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: Heavily overdone. Completion alone is not worth auditing again. Audit accuracy instead: correct risk category, correct dose for weight and renal function, and stockings actually worn. Re-assessment at 48 hours and over-prescribing, as in plastic and breast surgery, are measured far less often.
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

topic_knowledge.usual_baseline: Hip fractures are nearly always allowed to weight-bear (95.7–98.5%) [1247, 1286]. Other fractures are not: 32.3% of non-hip fragility fractures [1630], 57% after femoral fixation [1767], 21% after ankle fixation [1562]. Operation note documentation against BOAST is poor: 6% [1309] and 0–14% [1323]. Restrictions rarely give reason or duration.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_works: No successful fix with re-audit numbers is reported in these audits.
topic_knowledge.fix_that_fails: No failed fix reported in these audits
topic_knowledge.consultant_advice: None of nine audits closed the loop, so the gap is known but no fix is tested. Test a fix, such as an operation note template or a default weight-bearing-as-tolerated pathway, and re-audit it [1309, 1736]. Also measure the outcome: non-weight-bearing patients were less often discharged home (21% vs 56%) [1767].
topic_knowledge.evidence: Detailed records in this library; judgement written by Claude from them

paper.title: Elevating orthopedic documentation: a clinical audit of orthopaedic operative note quality against RCSE and BOA standards.
paper.abstract: Background The main aim of this audit was to measure the performance of the orthopedic Operating Theatre (OT) notes as compared to the standards laid down by the Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCSE), British Orthopedic Association (BOA) and their collaborators. Methods This single-cycle audit was conducted in the Department of Orthopaedics of a tertiary care hospital. One hundred randomly selected orthopaedic operative theatre notes from January-June 2023 were assessed against RCSE and BOA documentation standards. Following identification of deficiencies, targeted interventions were implemented between July-October 2023, comprising a standardised documentation template and a staff training programme. A re-audit of 100 notes was subsequently performed from October 2023-March 2024 to evaluate the impact of these interventions. Domain-specific compliance rates were compared between cycles using the chi-square test. Results Baseline audit identified deficiencies across four documentation domains: patient identification (72%), intraoperative findings (65%), postoperative plan (58%), and surgeon details (70%). Following the intervention programme, re-audit demonstrated significant improvements in all domains: patient identification (95%, p p p p p Conclusion A single audit cycle with targeted training and a standardised template produced statistically significant improvements across all RCSE/BOA documentation domains. Incorporating operative note training into routine induction programmes for rotating staff is recommended to sustain these gains.
paper.citation: Kamat A, Pillai AA, Ajmani U, Pasya S. Elevating orthopedic documentation: a clinical audit of orthopaedic operative note quality against RCSE and BOA standards. Front Surg. 2026;13:1704348. doi:10.3389/fsurg.2026.1704348. PMID: 42344576.

paper.title: Adequacy of Operative Notes for Orthopaedic Procedures: A Quality Improvement Project.
paper.abstract: Introduction High-quality operative documentation is fundamental to safe patient care, supporting communication, guiding postoperative management, and serving as a medico-legal record. Despite its importance, variability in the quality and completeness of operative notes remains common. Methods A closed-loop audit was performed at University Hospital Crosshouse, United Kingdom. The first cycle reviewed 82 operative notes, assessing compliance with set standards. Interventions included encouragement to use typed instead of written operation notes, display of posters in theatres, and introduction of a structured post-operative checklist. A second cycle reviewed 84 notes post-intervention. Results between audit cycles were compared and analysed using chi-squared tests to evaluate the statistical significance of improvements. Results In Cycle 1, typed notes accounted for 25 (30%), with documentation of operative diagnosis in 53 (65%), operative findings in 60 (73%), closure technique in 73 (89%), and signature completion in 78 (95%). Estimated blood loss was recorded in only five (6%) notes, and prosthesis identification (where applicable) in 60 of 69 (87%). In Cycle 2, following the intervention, typed notes increased significantly to 55 (65%). Closure technique documentation improved to 84 (100%) and signature completion to 84 (100%). Modest improvements were found in documentation of operative diagnosis (n=62, 74%) and intra-operative findings (n=68, 81%). Prosthesis identification remained at 87% between audit cycles, and estimated blood loss documentation fell to 2 (2%). Conclusion Simple, low-cost interventions such as visible documentation standards, typed templates, and postoperative checklists produced meaningful improvements in legibility and completion of key operative note parameters. Sustaining and expanding these measures, particularly through electronic templates with mandatory data fields and ongoing audit cycles, could further enhance the accuracy, completeness, and medicolegal robustness of operative documentation within surgical practice.
paper.citation: Jan AA, Imtiaz H, Ahmed T, Alkhatib O, Rahim AK, Kouklidis G. Adequacy of Operative Notes for Orthopaedic Procedures: A Quality Improvement Project. Cureus. 2025;17(11):e96179. doi:10.7759/cureus.96179. PMID: 41211261.

paper.title: A Clinical Audit of Orthopaedic Operation Note Documentation and Digitalization of the Operative Note Template: A Quality Improvement Project.
paper.abstract: Background Good communication between a surgical team and other colleagues is vital, and the medium of communication is often the operative note. It is essential to ensure continuity of care between the operating team and other colleagues; also, it provides a medicolegal record of patient care. It checks all the four main domains of good surgical practice guidelines set by the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) of England. The aims of this project were to evaluate the quality of operation notes against the set parameters by the RCS and to improve quality of the operative notes using information technology (IT) service software update to provide operative note digitalization. Methods This was a retrospective and prospective closed-loop audit, in which the operative notes were analysed for the Trauma and Orthopaedics speciality. Three separate cycles of audits were completed. In the the first cycle, data were collected retrospectively from all the operative notes, from June 1, 2020, to June 15, 2020; then, data were collected prospectively after making interventions to establish digitalization of the operative notes. The second cycle was completed from February 14 to 21, 2021, and from March 1 to 7, 2021. The third cycle was completed from August 1 to 31, 2021. All data were collected in Excel using a checklist that evaluated 34 parameters. These parameters were based on the recommendations of RCS Good Surgical Practice guidelines. All trauma and orthopaedic patients were included regardless of the type of procedure. There were no exclusion criteria in place. Results An overall increase from 9.5% to 66.7% in typed operative notes was achieved with the introduction of the templated operative note documentation service. There was a 40% reduction in the use of handwritten operative notes. Concerns regarding legibility were reduced in view of the digitalization of the operative notes. The first cycle of the audit, in terms of the parameters yielded, found that the operative notes were missing 10 important parameters, independent of the author grade; these were recorded in less than 10% of the operative notes. The second cycle, in terms of the parameters yielded, found that the operative notes were missing four important parameters, independent of the author grade; these were recorded in less than 10% of the operative notes. The third cycle of the audit, in terms of the parameters yielded, found that the operative notes were missing three important parameters. Specific documentation for 12 different parameters improved over the course of the three Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles. Conclusion Royal College of Surgeons guidelines and integration with IT services significantly improved the quality and legibility of operative notes that were being documented in the trauma and orthopaedics department. Structured document standards and good integration with a computer-based IT service help prompt surgeons to document in a better and easy way, thereby leading to improved clinical documentation.
paper.citation: Nasim O, Durrani A, Eskander B, Pantelias C, Gallagher K. A Clinical Audit of Orthopaedic Operation Note Documentation and Digitalization of the Operative Note Template: A Quality Improvement Project. Cureus. 2022;14(12):e33171. doi:10.7759/cureus.33171. PMID: 36601195.

paper.title: Audit of Orthopaedic Surgical Documentation.
paper.abstract: Introduction. The Royal College of Surgeons in England published guidelines in 2008 outlining the information that should be documented at each surgery. St. James's Hospital uses a standard operation sheet for all surgical procedures and these were examined to assess documentation standards. Objectives. To retrospectively audit the hand written orthopaedic operative notes according to established guidelines. Methods. A total of 63 operation notes over seven months were audited in terms of date and time of surgery, surgeon, procedure, elective or emergency indication, operative diagnosis, incision details, signature, closure details, tourniquet time, postop instructions, complications, prosthesis, and serial numbers. Results. A consultant performed 71.4% of procedures; however, 85.7% of the operative notes were written by the registrar. The date and time of surgery, name of surgeon, procedure name, and signature were documented in all cases. The operative diagnosis and postoperative instructions were frequently not documented in the designated location. Incision details were included in 81.7% and prosthesis details in only 30% while the tourniquet time was not documented in any. Conclusion. Completion and documentation of operative procedures were excellent in some areas; improvement is needed in documenting tourniquet time, prosthesis and incision details, and the location of operative diagnosis and postoperative instructions.

paper.title: Improving Compliance With the British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma and Orthopaedics (BOAST) Guidelines for Early Weight Bearing Following Ankle Fracture Fixation: A Closed-Loop Audit From a UK District General Hospital.
paper.abstract: Background Ankle fractures are common injuries, and in many cases, operative treatment is required. While the indications for surgical fixation are well established, the optimal timing for weight bearing after open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) remains controversial. Some surgeons continue to favour a conservative approach involving delayed weight bearing, whereas others encourage early mobilisation. The recent guidelines recommend early weight bearing unless there is a documented concern regarding fixation stability or soft tissue condition. Adherence to these guidelines promotes patient satisfaction and reduces strain on healthcare services. This closed-loop audit aimed to compare our department's practice at Royal Cornwall Hospital against the British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma and Orthopaedics (BOAST) standard for postoperative mobilisation after ankle fracture fixation. Methods This closed-loop audit involved both retrospective and prospective analysis of postoperative weight-bearing status in patients undergoing ORIF for isolated, closed ankle fractures at a single UK centre. Two audit cycles were performed. The first cycle (November 2023 to May 2024) retrospectively analysed patients' postoperative instructions. Following an educational intervention, including departmental emails and posters, a second cycle was prospectively conducted between July and November 2024. Inclusion criteria included skeletally mature patients (>18 years old) who underwent surgical treatment for isolated, closed ankle fractures. Exclusion criteria included open fractures, associated injuries, conservative management, or treatment with hindfoot nails. Results In the first cycle, 112 patients met the inclusion criteria. Of these, 56 patients (50%) were advised against early weight bearing, while 56 patients (50%) were advised to commence early weight bearing in a cast or boot. In the second cycle, 58 patients were assessed; 18 patients (31%) were advised against early weight bearing, and 40 patients (69%) were advised to commence early weight bearing, indicating significant improvement following intervention. Conclusion A targeted educational approach, including the distribution of BOAST guidelines and departmental discussions, led to improved compliance with early weight-bearing protocols. This audit highlights the value of team-based education and proactive audit cycles in enhancing adherence to national standards and improving service provision.
paper.citation: Mohamed A, Fuad U, Zahed M, Shyam M, Elasad A, Aqeel A. Improving Compliance With the British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma and Orthopaedics (BOAST) Guidelines for Early Weight Bearing Following Ankle Fracture Fixation: A Closed-Loop Audit From a UK District General Hospital. Cureus. 2025;17(7):e88092. doi:10.7759/cureus.88092. PMID: 40821226.

paper.title: Clinical Audit to Assess Orthogeriatrician Input to the Management of Elderly Trauma Patients.
paper.abstract: Objective The primary objective of this study is to assess the adherence of our department to the British Orthopaedic Association's Standards for Trauma and Orthopaedics (BOAST) guidelines for "the care of the older or frail orthopaedic trauma patient" and the results of this adherence on clinical patient outcome measures. Methods This was a clinical audit. All ≥65-year-olds admitted to the orthopaedic department with a fragility fracture between 8 September 2022 and 8 March 2023 with a length of stay (LOS) of >72 hours were included. Patients were stratified into hip fracture (HF) and non-hip fracture (NHF) patients. A further similar cohort of NHF admissions between 8 March and 8 May 2023 was added to the data. The adherence of both cohorts to the national guidelines was recorded. Primary outcome measures of each cohort were recorded such as LOS and patient mortality. Results Data from 70 patients was collected. HF patients adhered to the guideline 79.4% of the time (31/39 patients) compared to NHF patients at only 19.3% of the time (6/31 patients) (p Conclusion Medical orthogeriatric care is unequal despite similar LOS and mortality between both cohorts; thus, increasing orthogeriatrician input in NHF patients may lead to better patient outcomes for these patients.

paper.title: Improving Identification and Management of Modifiable Risk Factors in Hip and Knee Osteoarthritis: A Quality Improvement Project in an NHS Orthopaedic Interface Service.
paper.abstract: Background Hip and knee osteoarthritis are highly prevalent conditions associated with pain, disability and increasing demand on orthopaedic services. Best practice guidance emphasises early identification and optimisation of modifiable risk factors to improve outcomes following joint replacement, yet these are often inconsistently addressed in routine musculoskeletal care. This quality improvement project aimed to improve the consistency with which clinicians identified and acted on key modifiable risk factors during orthopaedic interface consultations. Methods The project was conducted in an NHS Orthopaedic Interface Service using the Model for Improvement. A retrospective audit of 291 consultations demonstrated low rates of documented action despite a high prevalence of modifiable risk factors. Four domains were prioritised: excess body weight, smoking, diabetes optimisation and psychosocial factors. A bundle of low-burden interventions was introduced through sequential plan-do-study-act cycles. Prospective monthly sampling of 180 consultations over six months assessed change over time. Results Across 180 prospective consultations, documented action increased from 30% to 78% among consultations where at least one targeted modifiable factor was present. Improvement was clearest for weight-related advice and signposting. Smoking, diabetes and psychosocial findings were limited by small denominators or variable documentation and were interpreted descriptively. The largest increase was observed following introduction of embedded workflow supports, although attribution to any single component is limited by the sequential QI design. Conclusion A simple quality improvement bundle was associated with improved documentation of action on modifiable risk factors during routine osteoarthritis consultations, particularly for weight-related advice and signposting. Embedded documentation prompts may support more reliable care processes, but further work is needed to assess sustainability, patient-level outcomes and transferability to other settings.

paper.title: Avoiding never events in orthopaedics theatres: a quality improvement project.
paper.abstract: Never events in the operating room are a surgeon's nightmare, with an incidence rate of 54%. These events are highly stressful for theatre staff and significantly compromise patient safety. The aim of this project is to avoid never events in trauma and orthopaedic theatres by ensuring that theatre staff adhere to the surgical pause and imaging pause protocols through regular audits.This prospective study was conducted in both trauma and elective orthopaedic theatres. It involved theatre staff members who were not part of the surgical team. The study was designed to take place on random days across different theatres, with the operating team unaware of the audit to ensure genuine behaviour and compliance.The audits focused on observing whether the surgical and imaging pause protocols were followed correctly. These protocols are critical for verifying patient identity, the surgical site, and the specific procedure and confirming the correct imaging is available and reviewed before proceeding. Data collected and corrective actions were implemented when non-compliance was observed, and data on compliance rates were systematically collected and analysed.Preliminary results indicate a substantial increase in compliance with both the surgical and imaging pause protocols, corresponding with a reduction in the occurrence of never events. Theatre staff reported improved understanding and confidence in performing these safety checks The use of external auditors who were not part of the surgical team provided an unbiased assessment of compliance, enhancing the reliability of the findings.In conclusion, the project demonstrates that regular audits, and data collected by non-surgical team staff, significantly improve adherence to surgical and imaging pause protocols, thereby reducing the incidence of never events in trauma and orthopaedic theatres. This approach highlights the importance of continuous monitoring and education in fostering a culture of safety and precision in surgical practice.

paper.title: Enhancing Documentation Standards of Complications in Informed Consent for Neck of Femur Fracture Surgery.
paper.abstract: Background Neck of femur (NOF) fractures are a major cause of morbidity in the United Kingdom. Operative management is the standard of care, and informed consent is essential to ensure patients understand potential benefits and complications arising during the surgical management of NOF fractures. This study aimed to assess and enhance the quality of Consent Form 1 documentation of complications of NOF fracture surgery as per the British Orthopaedic Association (BOA) and to assess improvements following focused interventions. Methodology A closed-loop audit was conducted in the Trauma and Orthopaedic Department, Heartlands Hospital, Birmingham, from February to October 2024. In the first cycle, we analyzed the Consent Form 1 retrospectively for the documentation of complications. Interventions for improvement were performed, including teaching sessions and posters on consent documentation. The second cycle assessed post-intervention practice. The study encompassed patients with capacity who underwent fixation, hemiarthroplasty, or total hip replacement (THR). Documentation was considered complete if it included all common, less common, and rare complications. Results The initial documentation rates were modest, with fewer than 50% of forms recording pain, catheterization, avascular necrosis, hip stiffness, limb length discrepancy, and mortality. Post-intervention improvements were observed, including pain, avascular necrosis, and death for NOF fixation, alongside better values of infection, altered wound healing, pulmonary embolism, and bone damage for hemiarthroplasty. For THR, improvements were seen in the documentation of bleeding, dislocation, blood clots, prosthetic wear, infections, altered wound healing, bone damage, and death. Conclusions Targeted teaching and visual reminders improved documentation, but there are persistent gaps. Further strategies are required to standardize consent practices and ensure complete patient information in line with BOA guidance.
paper.citation: Shahbaz A, Shahbaz R, Dinesh Y, Imami F, Akbar R, Bose D. Enhancing Documentation Standards of Complications in Informed Consent for Neck of Femur Fracture Surgery. Cureus. 2025;17(11):e96220. doi:10.7759/cureus.96220. PMID: 41211270.
