audits.title: 666 Audit of Tip-Apex Distance in Dynamic Hip Screw Fixation of Proximal Femoral Fractures
audits.standard: Tip-apex distance <25mm
audits.finding: Mean TAD 22.85mm (range 15–36mm); TAD >25mm in 13 cases (26%).
audits.change: Posters on TAD recommendations displayed in theatre and a weekly departmental metalwork meeting reviewing imaging from all surgeries.

paper.title: 666 Audit of Tip-Apex Distance in Dynamic Hip Screw Fixation of Proximal Femoral Fractures
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Lag screw cutout is the commonest mechanical failure in dynamic hip screw (DHS) fixation of proximal femoral fractures. Tip-apex distance (TAD), the combined distance from the tip of the lag screw to the apex of the femoral head on AP and lateral views, is the most important predictive factor for cutout. TAD >25mm is associated with a high risk of cutout. The aim was to determine the proportion of DHS fixations performed in our department with ‘acceptable’ TAD (<25mm) and assess the impact of weekly departmental metalwork meetings. Method Retrospective data was collected of all DHS fixations performed in our department in a 6-month period. Intraoperative imaging was reviewed to determine TAD. Posters illustrating TAD recommendations were displayed in theatre, and a weekly departmental metalwork meeting was introduced, reviewing imaging from all surgeries performed. Post-intervention, a further audit cycle over a 6-month period was performed. Results 50 patients underwent DHS fixation during the initial audit cycle. Mean TAD was 22.85mm (range 15mm – 36mm); TAD exceeded 25mm in 13 cases (26%). In the second cycle (n=53), mean TAD reduced to 14.95mm (range 8.5mm – 29.4mm), with 1 case exceeding 25mm (2%). Conclusions The introduction of a weekly departmental metalwork meeting has significantly reduced the mean tip-apex distance of DHS fixations in our department, as well as the proportion of fixations with an unacceptable TAD. This should reduce the risk of lag screw cutout in these patients.

audits.title: 973 Managing Primary Endocrine Treatment (PET) in Breast Cancer Patients: An Audit of Resource Utilisation and Risks
audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: 5 patients (10%) had a DEXA scan and 16 (33%) were on bone protection; 3 had fractures on PET.

paper.title: 973 Managing Primary Endocrine Treatment (PET) in Breast Cancer Patients: An Audit of Resource Utilisation and Risks
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Primary endocrine treatment (PET) is considered in patients with oestrogen receptor (ER) positive breast cancer who decline or are deemed unfit for surgery. This treatment can affect bone density resulting in osteoporosis and risk of fractures. With increasing demand on resources, our aim was to examine clinical practices in this vulnerable patient group, balancing risks whilst ensuring good patient selection for treatments. Method We reviewed patients who had PET for ER positive breast cancer from a single consultant database in a district general hospital in South Wales between May 2018 and March 2023. We examined use of bone density (DEXA) scans, bone protection medications, outcomes, and complications. Results 48 patients were included, aged 50-95 years (median 80) and male: female (1:47). All were ER positive, excepting 2 with limited prognosis empirically started on treatment. Reasons for PET included patient choice (15%), palliative treatment (8%), co-morbidities (65%), late stage (4%) and other (8%). There were 27 deaths (54%), with mean time from diagnosis to death 14 months (range 1-50 months). 5 patients (10%) had DEXA scan and 16 (33%) were on bone protection. 3 patients had fractures whilst on PET, likely due to pre-existing conditions. Conclusions The frail breast cancer patient population has limited life expectancy and should not be over-investigated unnecessarily. It could be debated as to how much benefit bone protection provides, given the low fracture rate. Further studies are required to determine benefits of empirical bone protection in PET patients.

audits.title: 343 Distal Radius Fracture Emergency Analgaesia and Management Audit
audits.standard: 2018 BSSH guidelines: intravenous regional anaesthesia and haematoma blocks for manipulation of distal radius fractures
audits.finding: 87.88% received methoxyflurane (Penthrox) and the remainder lidocaine haematoma block; guidelines not being followed.

paper.title: 343 Distal Radius Fracture Emergency Analgaesia and Management Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To audit analgesia used in the initial management of patients with Distal Radius Fractures (DRFs) that require manipulation against the current standards. Method Standards used were 2018 British Society for Surgery to the Hand (BSSH) guidelines, which recommend intravenous regional anaesthesia and haematoma blocks when manipulating DRFs. Data collection using survey dissemination at 2 tertiary centres included adult patients presenting between 13/08/2022 and 26/11/2022 with DRFs. Exclusion criteria were open fractures, multiple fractures and major trauma. Patient factors and management, with corresponding pain Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) before, during and post manipulation were recorded. Imaging was reviewed to determine radiographic measurements on presentation and in clinic. Data was recorded using REDCap database. Results There were 33 mostly female (F:M 29:4) patients included. Only 24.24% had no co-morbidities. Comorbidities included Hypertension (42.42%), Ischaemic Heart Disease (24.24%) and Asthma (21.21%). Most patients (87.88%) received Methoxyflurane (Penthrox), the remainder had Lidocaine haematoma block. Manipulations were mostly performed by staff from A+E (63.64%). Increased pain scores during manipulation were reported in 64.29% of patients, with a median increase of 7 points. Decreased post manipulation scores were reported in 87.10% with a median decrease of 16 points. Further manipulation was required in 27.27%. Operative fixation was required in 21.21%. Conclusions In conclusion the current guidelines are not being followed in the centres we audited. Methoxyflurane was used for the majority of patients, with good outcomes. Further data is required from multiple centres across the UK to assess whether guidelines need to be updated.

audits.title: 489 Management of ACL Injuries and the Impact of the Coronavirus Pandemic: A Regional Audit
audits.standard: BOAST guidelines for management of ACL injury
audits.finding: 82% had timely clinic assessment; 37% had MRI within 14 days; 38% referred for prehabilitation; 84% had post-operative physiotherapy

paper.title: 489 Management of ACL Injuries and the Impact of the Coronavirus Pandemic: A Regional Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim 15,000 anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstructions are performed annually in the United Kingdom. The aim of this audit was to compare local management of ACL injury at the University Hospitals of Morecambe Bay NHS Foundation Trust (UHMBT) to current British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma (BOAST) guidelines. A secondary aim was to understand the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on the management of ACL reconstruction. Method The audit was registered with the local audit department. Lists of patients with ACL reconstructions were obtained across two time periods and data was extracted from the electronic patient record software and PACS. The pre-covid period, was defined between 1st of July 2018 and the 1st of July 2019. The post-covid period was defined between 1st of July 2021 and 1st of July 2022. Microsoft Excel software was used for analysis. Results Sixty cases were identified, with a mean age of 28. 37 patients were from the pre-covid period, and 23 patients from the post-covid period. 82% of patients underwent a timely clinic assessment following initial presentation, in accordance with guidelines. 37% of cases had an MRI scan completed within 14 days. 38% of cases were referred for prehabilitation. The average time to surgery was 230.5 days in the pre-covid period, increasing to 353.9 days in the post-covid period. 84% of patients had post-operative physiotherapy. Conclusions The results demonstrate poor compliance with current guidance. The COVID-19 pandemic had a significant impact on average time to surgery. An improved multidisciplinary approach is required to improve functional outcomes.

paper.title: 513 A Clinical Audit on the Use of Red Cell Transfusions in a DGH’s Trauma and Orthopaedics Ward
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To compare the practice of prescribing, administering, and monitoring transfusions, with the current local Trust guidelines in order to determine the proportion of inappropriate blood transfusions especially in times of regional and national shortage of blood products Method For a six-week period in 2022, numerous endpoints were measured, reflecting the specifications of the Trust guideline. Based on the results from this initial data, a teaching session was conducted to create awareness of the Trust guideline amongst all rotational doctors. A subsequent re-audit was conducted to determine the effectiveness of the intervention. Following data analysis, further suggestions were discussed and implemented. Results Prior to intervention, 34 units were transfused across 16 patients with the mean age being 81.88 years. Post-teaching session, 11 units were transfused with the mean age being 79.58 years. 26.4% units were transfused for active haemorrhage, none were due to major haemorrhage, compared to 18.2% for active haemorrhage post-teaching session. 73.5% transfusions were inappropriate, defined as transfusions conducted in those who did not meet the haemoglobin level (Hb) threshold stated in the guideline. This significantly reduced post-teaching session to 45.5%. Transfusion-associated circulatory overload assessment was completed in 58.8%, improving to 90.9% post-intervention. Conclusions Simple measures such as an induction booklet highlighting the Trust’s blood transfusion guideline ensured rotational doctors were aware of the local protocol, preventing a significant proportion of inappropriate red cell transfusions.

paper.title: 530 Repatriation of Care for Ambulatory Orthopaedic Trauma Patients Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The safe repatriation of care for non-local ambulatory orthopaedic trauma patients to their local trust is vital. Poor documentation and communication between trusts leads to delayed treatment and poor outcomes. Thorough documentation is required to prove that a satisfactory referral has been made. This audit, with two-closed loop cycles, aimed to improve the repatriation process. Method At a London MTC, electronic patient records were reviewed over a one-month period, examining 6 areas to assess referral quality to local trusts (initial data collection, n=17). Interventions were implemented, followed by a re-audit over a further one-month period (n=25), which was then repeated (n=18) after secondary interventions. Initial interventions consisted of the development of new departmental guidelines (referral pathway, electronic repatriation letter template, patient information e-leaflet). Secondary interventions consisted of educational posters and a doctor tutorial. Audit standards: BOAST Fracture Clinic Services and trust recommendations. Results Documentation of: Named local trust in clerking, 65% to 96% to 89%; Evidence of phone referral, 94% to 96% to 100%; SHO/registrar’s name taking referral, 24% to 88% to 94%; Local trust Consultant on-call’s name, 6% to 48% to 83%; Repatriation letter sent to local trust, 0%* to 92% to 94%. Uploading of the repatriation letter to electronic record, 0%* to 40% to 89% (*letter only introduced during initial interventions). Conclusions Improvements have been made in all areas, increasing the quality and accountability in referrals to local trusts. We recommend the introduction of formal referral pathways for non-local ambulatory orthopaedic trauma patients to prevent miscommunication and treatment delays.

paper.title: 766 Audit of Stratified Treatment Escalation Plan Completion and DNACPR in Patients with Femoral Fractures – 4th Cycle
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Assess how many patients admitted on the fragility fractures ward (including hip, shaft, distal, periprosthetic fractures) had escalation (STEP) forms completed. We audited whether this was done in a timely fashion, which specialties and grades filled in the forms, if was there a weekend effect in form completion, and if the decisions were communicated with patients or relatives. Method In this 4th cycle of the audit, notes of patients admitted on the fragility fracture ward in the period 14/09/23 - 25/10/23 were examined prospectively. Paper and electronic notes were assessed for presence of escalation and DNACPR forms completion, and for evidence of discussion. Standards were set as internally as 100% for all measures: evidence of STEP form completion, completion done within 24 hours, and evidence of escalation plan discussion. Results 30 patients were audited. STEP form completion was 100% however 13% contained minor errors, needing correction; STEP completed within 24 hours of admission to the ward = 77%; documentation of discussion if for less than full escalation 58% (cognitively intact) and 64% (cognitively impaired). Conclusions All patients audited had a STEP form completed. STEP form completion within 24 hours improved from cycle 3. Documentation of discussions did not meet the standard for cognitively intact and cognitively impaired patients for less than full escalation. To improve future care, posters will be displayed, audit mentioned in junior doctors' inductions, and email reminders sent to all grades. Further cycles are being planned, and e-documentation system utilisation for improvement is under consideration.

audits.standard: NICE guidelines for complex fractures and the Vascular Society guidance for major amputations

paper.title: 802 Assessing the Below Knee Amputation Service in a London Major Trauma Centre: An Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim For certain complex orthoplastic patients, a below knee amputation (BKA) is the best form of reconstruction. An audit was carried out to assess whether orthoplastic patients undergoing BKAs at a major trauma centre in London were being managed according to best practice guidance set out by NICE and the Vascular Society. Method A retrospective review was carried out to analyse all BKAs that were performed on orthoplastic patients at the Royal London Hospital between 2020-2022. Patients were found by manually searching through the plastic surgery departmental inpatient database, and their electronic medical notes were reviewed for information specifically related to the recommendations set out by NICE guidelines for complex fractures and the Vascular Society’s guidance for major amputations. Results 19 cases were identified. The average age of patients was 45.8 years. 11 amputations were emergencies, 8 were planned. The average time to surgery once a decision was made to amputate was 1.75 days. Compliance was 100% with having an MDT discussion pre-operatively, recording the decision to amputate in the patient’s notes, and making a formal referral to the amputee rehabilitation team for prosthetics. Areas of lower compliance included giving written counselling to families, naming a discharge co-ordinator pre-operatively, and review by the pain team within 24 hours post operation. Conclusions This audit has identified specific areas for improvement and will help to develop a written pathway for lower limb amputations in the trust, ensuring that patients undergoing BKAs receive the best care possible.

paper.title: 858 Post Operative Opioid Prescribing in Patients Undergoing Primary Elective Total Hip Replacement (THR): A Closed-Loop Clinical Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess departmental performance versus NICE NG180 recommendations for post operative analgesia in patients undergoing primary THR. Method Local databases were reviewed, and patients selected based on the following inclusion criteria:Elective patients undergoing Total Primary Hip ReplacementNo contraindications to oral intake.Aged 60+ The extracted data were as follows:Immediate post operative regular opioid prescribed on Day 0 (D0).Regular post operative opioid prescribed on D0?How many hours from end of surgery to receiving 1st oral opioid dose?Pain reported on D0 post operative.Pain reported on Day 1 (D1) post operatively. The initial loop involved data from May 2023-July 2023, with the second cycle reauditing based on data from collected from September 2023-November 2023 following implementation of printed posters of NICE NG180 and face to face education on post operative analgesia. Results In comparison to the first cycle of the audit, there has been a 30% increase in the number of purely regular oral opioid prescriptions on D0. A 10% increase in the number of patients receiving their oral opioid dose within 2 hours post operatively is seen between cycles in those with a regular opioid prescription. Whilst the 2-8 hour and >8-hour prescriptions remained at similar percentages for comparative patient sizes. Conclusions The interventions implemented after the first cycle have shown improvement in departmental performance. To better this further, we propose creating an electronic prescription order set to help clinicians appropriately manage post operative analgesia requirements in this patient group.

paper.title: 964 Intra-Operative Tourniquet Use in Lower Limb Orthopedic Surgery: A BOAST Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Surgical tourniquets reduce operative time and blood loss and improve visualisation of the surgical field. However, risks include pain, neurovascular and local tissue damage. Operative tourniquet pressure should be baseline systolic pressure plus 70-130mmHg. Ischaemic tourniquet time should be less than 120 minutes. We aim to audit the use and documentation of surgical tourniquets of lower limbs surgery undertaken at a single DGH over a 6-month period against BOAST guidelines. Method Retrospective data collected on torniquet use, torniquet time, pressure and patient demographics recorded collected from operation notes and theatre logbooks. Results 66 patients were included, mean age 55 (7-92) years. 95.4% (62/66) of lower limb procedures had recorded use of tourniquet. 78.5% (51/66) had the total tourniquet time recorded. Mean tourniquet time was 82.4 (15-130) minutes. 58.7% (37/62) had inflation pressure recorded. Mean inflation pressure was 265.7mmHg (150-300). 5 patients (7.6%) exceeded the maximum recommended tourniquet time without deflation. Conclusions Our results indicated that level of documentation of tourniquet use fell below the standards set out in BOAST guidelines. A second cycle will determine whether implemented changes in the theatre documentation system has conferred change.

audits.standard: NICE guidelines on neurovascular assessment and documentation; poor compliance defined as <75%
audits.finding: Basic mention of neurovascular status 911/959 (95%); gross sensation 492/959 (51%); named nerve assessment 143/959 (15%); MRC motor assessment 71/959 (7%); pulse assessment with pulses documented 367/959 (38%).

paper.title: 79 Neurovascular Status Documentation in Complex Limb Fractures: First Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Assessing neurovascular status post-fracture is vital to detect complications and guide medical actions. Fractures can cause neurovascular problems and timely recognition prevents long-term damage. Neurovascular status should be recorded on admission to establish a baseline and identify those that need urgent surgery, and the findings should be well documented. Method Neurovascular documentation for patients with fractures of the tibia or femur was audited over the period of one year at a major trauma centre according to NICE guidelines. 885 patients met the inclusion criteria, giving a total of 959 fractures. Results Poor compliance was defined as <75% of guidelines followed. 911/959 (95%) of all fractures had a basic mention of neurovascular status in patient notes. 492/959 (51%) had gross sensation documented, 143/959 (15%) had a named nerve assessment, 71/959 (7%) had motility assessed using the MRC scale and 367/959 (38%) had a pulse assessment, with the pulses assessed documented. We recommend a pre-written template for clinicians detailing the different aspects of the neurovascular examination and documentation. This template will remind clinicians of examination and documentation, enabling ongoing monitoring, facilitating prompt detection of issues, thus improving outcomes, and reducing long-term complications. Conclusions Inadequate documentation of neurovascular status in patient records poses a risk to those requiring urgent surgery or experiencing neurovascular compromise, potentially leading to long-term complications. Ensuring an error-free documentation process is crucial and a primary goal for the trauma and orthopaedic department.

paper.title: 649 Retrospective Audit into Management of Periprosthetic Joint Infections as per National and International Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The main aim of this quality improvement project is to improve care of patients with peri-prosthetic joint infections (PJI), by assuring appropriate diagnostics are sent and antibiotics recommended are as per Pro-Implant and British Orthopaedic association (BOA) guidelines, which are international and national guidelines. Method Retrospective analysis of all tissue samples received for patients with periprosthetic joint infections during August 2022 and August 2023 from patients across Manchester. There were 68 samples (17 patients) in total with peri-prosthetic joint infections out of 197 samples (62 patients). These were all compared to standards set by the Pro-Implant and BOA. Multiple criteria were compared by analysing clinic letters and Labcentre documentation. Results The results show a 100% compliance in discussion of PJI diagnosis with microbiologists, correctly labelling samples, and CRP analysis. However, we struggled with making diagnosis as per guidelines, sending more than 5 samples and discussing discharge antibiotic plans with microbiologists. Furthermore, we didn’t utilise sonification, PCR and histology to aid diagnosis. We also struggled with meeting the appropriate interval time between stages of two stage exchanges. Conclusions In conclusion, there is room for improvement in certain criteria’s’ as per the guidelines:Engagement with orthopaedic stakeholder to explore barriers to compliance.Dedicated MDT compromising of orthopaedic surgeons, infection doctors.Creation of an intraoperative pro-forma for suspected PJIs’ to act as a reminder to surgeons and allow clear documentation.Availability and awareness of guidelines to orthopaedic teamFunding for PCR, sonification and histopathologyJoint follow up clinic with microbiologist to improve patient follow up plans.

paper.title: 150 Audit in Post-Operative Documentation in Trauma and Orthopaedic
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Post operative surgical documentation is a critical component of patient care and ensures seamless communication among health care providers. In this audit we evaluated the quality of orthopaedic operative notes against the RCS-England guidelines aiming to improve adherence to these guidelines. Method We prospectively included 50 orthopaedic post-operative patients from July 20th till July 30th 2023. Adult trauma and elective procedures were included regardless of the type of the procedure. We compared the operative notes included in the audit to the RCS good surgical practice guidelines and collected data using a checklist including the parameters in the RCS guidelines. Areas with deficient documentation were highlighted for auditing. Results The first Audit cycle identified poor areas in post operative notes as the documentation of ‘emergency/elective procedure’ (25%), ‘weight bearing status following procedure’ (25%), ‘VTE instructions’ (75%), ‘follow up instructions’ (35%), ‘investigations required after procedure’ (25%), ‘instructions regarding post operative wound care’ (50%). We created a mnemonic to aid memorising the necessary post operative instructions. We’re presenting this audit in the orthopaedic department monthly M&M meeting in November and aiming to do a second Audit cycle to compare the quality of post operative documentation following the interventions implemented following the first cycle. Conclusions Post operative surgical documentation plays a pivotal role in ensuring effective patient care, enhancing patient safety, shortens their hospital stay and provides a legal protection for healthcare providers.

paper.title: 776 Retrospective Audit of CPIP and Hip Surveillance Compliance in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim CPIP (Cerebral Palsy Integrated Pathway) is a national pathway used to assess whether children with cerebral palsy show signs of hip migration based on regular pelvic x-rays. This allows Clinicians to determine if early surgical intervention is required. The aim of this audit is to determine if we are adhering to the CPIP at Torbay Hospital. Method Data was collected on the children who are under CPIP in the Devon area. Adherence to this pathway was assessed based on whether children were receiving their hip x-rays at the appropriate time based on their Gross Motor Function Classification System Score (GMFCS). Furthermore, we will be distributing a questionnaire to determine patient satisfaction with CPIP. Results Based on our analysis 64 children were identified, with 83% having a recent CPIP assessment and 68% of patients receiving their x-rays in an appropriate timeframe. Additionally, it was found that 72% of hip x-rays requested were reported. Conclusions It can be concluded that the Trust is adherent to CPIP, however some improvements could be made to increase adherence. To increase adherence, actions such as monthly meetings between the radiography and physiotherapy department will take place. Following these improvements, a repeat analysis will be carried out to determine adherence to CPIP.

audits.standard: BOAST: if CT brain is needed for head injury it should include CT cervical spine

paper.title: 994 Enhancing Compliance with BOAST Guidelines: A Closed-Loop Audit on Cervical Clearance in Head Injury Patients
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to evaluate the compliance of cervical spine clearance in head injury patients according to BOAST guidelines following the implementation of a novel intervention, a single request tab, suggested after the previous audits. Method BOAST guidelines state that if brain CT is necessary for a head injury, this should include the CT cervical spine. Previous audits (June/Nov 2021 and Aug/Sept 2022) highlighted a persistent lack of adequate cervical spine clearance in head injury patients at Queen Alexandra Hospital. In response, a solution was proposed and implemented on May 5, 2023, introducing a single request tab within the Imaging requesting software (ICE) for CT Brain and CT C-spine. Data collected from July/Aug 2023 assessed the adherence to BOAST guidelines for all admitted head injury patients. Results The data encompassed 36 head injury patients, primarily diagnosed with subdural hematoma (55%), followed by skull fractures (14%). The audits in 2021 and 2022 revealed suboptimal compliance (23% and 37% respectively) despite interventions. The new implementation showcased a significant improvement, with a 53% compliance rate. This contrasts with the previous audits, suggesting enhanced adherence to BOAST guidelines. Conclusions Ensuring cervical spine clearance in head injury patients aligns with BOAST guidelines, emphasizing patient safety. Our audit demonstrated substantial progress in compliance, signifying improved adherence to guidelines and elevated patient care standards. The implementation of the single request tab streamlined the workflow, enhancing efficiency for clinicians to request scans promptly. We recommend widespread education initiatives for Emergency Department staff and the adoption of the single request tab across all trusts to optimize patient care.

audits.standard: BOAST guidelines for distal radius fracture management
audits.finding: Requirement for operative reduction in theatre 45% (2018) and 24.1% (2020).
audits.change: Three training sessions for ED staff on BOAST standards, including finger-trap manipulation and three-point moulded plaster.

paper.title: 1073 Optimising the Acute Management of Distal Radius Fractures: Re-Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Distal radius fractures are a common presentation and early management is often in the emergency department (ED). Good, early management in the ED has been shown to reduce the number of people requiring operative treatment. We aimed to evaluate the impact of a staff training programme intervention on the number of patients requiring theatre. Method Three training sessions were held, training ED staff on fracture management standards according to BOAST guidelines. These included manipulation with finger traps (instead of in-line traction) and application of effective three-point moulded plaster. We assessed reduction from radiographs pre- and post-reduction. Data on patients’ requirement for further management were collected and compared to previous years. Results Satisfactory reduction in ED was achieved in 42.8% of patients. Requirement for eventual operative reduction in theatre was reduced to 17.3% from 45% and 24.1% in 2018 and 2020 respectively. This may be attributable to adoption of reduction with finger traps after training sessions, although no patients received a three-point moulded plaster in the ED. Conclusions This study found that the staff training sessions improved the quality of reduction of distal radius fractures. This lowered the operative intervention rate (17.3%), which is still higher than seen in the literature (10%). This could be improved by further interventions to standardise application of appropriately moulded plaster.

paper.title: SP7.7 - A 6-month retrospective re-audit of “Code Red” trauma requiring surgical intervention in a regional major trauma centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Major trauma (MT) is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in the United Kingdom, with an estimated incidence of 20,000 cases annually in England. A certain proportion of patients presenting following MT require immediate operative intervention. This study is a re-audit of the process for managing these patients in order to assess the impact of introduction of a Damage Control Surgery (DCS) pathway. Methods Data were reviewed for all patients presenting as Code Red MT and requiring immediate operative intervention from May to November 2023. This accounts for all patients since the implementation of the DCS pathway. Patient details were taken from a MT database, Electronic Care Records were used to determine aetiologies of trauma and outcomes, and Theatre Management System software was used to determine timings. Results 9 patients were identified, with a median age of 30.33. 89% of patients underwent preoperative CT imaging, with an average time to CT of 15 minutes (range 5 to 57 minutes). Median time to theatre was 88 minutes (range 39 to 325 minutes). Specialties involved included General Surgery, Vascular, Cardiothoracics and Trauma and Orthopaedics, with multispecialty involvement in some cases. Overall mortality was 22%. Seven cases were the result of road traffic collisions. Conclusions MT remains a significant cause of mortality in our cohort, but implementation of a DCS pathway has led to significant improvements in both time to CT and time to theatre compared with our initial audit cycle (32 minutes/144.5 minutes).

audits.title: 1015 Improving the Management of Buckle Fractures at a District General Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project Based on Evidence from the FORCE Trial
audits.standard: FORCE trial evidence: buckle fractures managed with soft bandage or nothing and discharged without follow-up
audits.finding: Plaster cast 34%; removable splint 66%; soft bandage or nothing 0%; fracture clinic follow-up 43%.
audits.change: Revised paediatric wrist fracture guideline, updated virtual fracture clinic leaflets and staff education.

paper.title: 1015 Improving the Management of Buckle Fractures at a District General Hospital: A Quality Improvement Project Based on Evidence from the FORCE Trial
paper.abstract: Abstract Buckle fractures (BF) are common paediatric injuries, and the FORCE (Fracture Observational Research in Children Evaluation) trial demonstrated that BF can be safely and effectively managed with a soft bandage (SB) or nothing, and discharged without follow up. This quality improvement project audited BF management at a District General Hospital and implemented interventions to align with these findings and de-escalate treatment. The study aimed to reduce plaster casts (PC) in BF management. Patients were identified during separate 3-month cycles (aged 1-15 years) pre and post interventions; 41 patients in cycle one versus 42 patients in cycle two. Interventions included revising paediatric wrist fracture guidelines, updating virtual fracture clinic leaflets, and staff education. Pre versus post-intervention findings showed: PC 34% versus 10%; removable splints 66% versus 68%; SB or nothing 0% versus 22%. Fracture clinic follow up reduced from 43% to 17%. Interventions resulted in a 24% reduction in treatment with PC and a 26% reduction in fracture clinic follow up. The EQ-5D-Y questionnaire collected patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) 6 weeks post-injury. No complications were reported, and the average health outcome score was 96/100 (100 being the best health imaginable). These findings highlight the effectiveness of targeted educational and guideline-driven interventions in improving adherence to evidence-based BF management. Adoption of FORCE trial recommendations significantly reduced the use of restrictive PC treatment without compromising patient outcomes, promoting comfort and convenience for children and families while saving time and money for both the patients and the trust.

audits.title: 242 Audit of Postoperative Laboratory Tests Following Elective Lower Limb Arthroplasty. Do They Influence Treatment?
audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: Four (3.8%) patients had no post-operative blood tests; mean haemoglobin drop 22.5 g/L; no transfusions or iron given; seven patients given IV fluids (one AKI, six hyponatraemia)

paper.title: 242 Audit of Postoperative Laboratory Tests Following Elective Lower Limb Arthroplasty. Do They Influence Treatment?
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Orthopaedic departments are moving towards reducing patient length of stay and day case arthroplasty. We aimed in our departmentTo determine if all elective hip and knee arthroplasty patients have routine postoperative laboratory tests (i.e. full blood count and renal function), andTo determine if the results of these investigations influence post-operative care. Method Retrospective chart review of 104 consecutive arthroplasty patients in one hospital between 3/4/24 and 5/6/24; 54 total knee replacements and 50 total hip replacements. Results Average age was 68.2 years (38 – 82). 60 patients were female. Mean ASA was 2.2. Mean length of stay was 3 days, median was 2 days. Two patients were discharged on the day of surgery (day zero). Four (3.8%) patients had no post-operative blood tests. Mean drop in haemoglobin was 22.5 g/L. Mean post-operative haemoglobin was 113.3 g/L (86 – 157). No patients received a blood transfusion or post-operative iron supplementation. Mean pre-operative and post-operative creatinine were 78.5 and 78.3 µmol/dL, respectively. Mean pre-operative and post-operative eGFR were 76.1 and 75.2 mL/min/1.73m2, respectively. Seven patients were prescribed post-operative intravenous fluids; one for an acute kidney injury and six for hyponatraemia. Conclusions The results raise the question as to whether we need to perform routine postoperative blood tests on this patient population. Postoperative blood tests could potentially be targeted at higher risk populations. A larger sample is needed to determine this. This could allow for potential cost saving for routine postoperative bloods and of clinician and laboratory technicians’ time.

audits.title: 100 Weightbearing Status Documentation in Orthopaedic Operation Notes – A Snapshot Audit
audits.standard: BOAST guidance on weight-bearing terminology and documentation; target 80% compliance
audits.finding: 6% compliance (non-weightbearing cases only); no rationale given for limited or non-weightbearing status; functional and duration limitations given in 60% and 86% respectively.
audits.change: After consultation with physiotherapists: theatre posters, template training and reminder messages via WhatsApp groups for surgeons.

paper.title: 100 Weightbearing Status Documentation in Orthopaedic Operation Notes – A Snapshot Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim A snapshot audit was performed to assess current compliance with the most recent guidelines on weightbearing documentation in accordance with British Orthopaedic Association Standards (BOAST). Weight-bearing terminology has been shown to be ambiguous and is often understood variably by both healthcare professionals and patients. Standardisation of terms has been suggested to reduce confusion for patients and therapy teams during rehabilitation following surgery. Method A single-centre retrospective audit of 50 lower-limb operation notes (25 trauma; 25 elective) from electronic patient records to correct weightbearing terminology use and documentation of mobilisation limitations following surgery in accordance with BOAST guidelines. After baseline measurement and consultation with physiotherapists, educational interventions were implemented for surgeons including theatre posters, template training and reminder messages via WhatsApp groups. A target of 80% compliance was set. Results The baseline audit showed 6% compliance (for “non-weightbearing” cases only) with significant variability in terminology used. None of the cases in which patients were limited or non-weightbearing had rationale given for this. Functional and duration limitations were given for 60% and 86% of cases respectively. Conclusions It is evident that knowledge on the changes in recommended weightbearing terminology is severely lacking. Simple educational methods and use of a template can invariably improve compliance with this. This particular topic promotes interdisciplinary working among therapy colleagues who have a vested interest in the timely rehabilitation of postoperative patients, accurate to surgeon preferences. A series of rapid-cycle audits are currently underway to review the impact of these interventions.

audits.standard: BSCOS 2021 clubfoot consensus statement (casts changed every 4–7 days; tenotomy expected in 85–95%)
audits.finding: Casting started at 2–6 weeks in 63%; hip ultrasound screening 91%; Pirani score used 100%; casts changed every 4–7 days in 73%; tenotomy 91%.

paper.title: 180 Audit of the Ponseti Clinic & Management of Clubfoot Deformity at RHC, Glasgow
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim BSCOS published a consensus statement on clubfoot deformity in 2021 which prompted a clinical service change in 2023 with the development of a dedicated clubfoot clinic at RHC, Glasgow. This audit looked at a 12-month period following implementation of this weekly clinic. All cases of clubfoot in this institution had their treatment begin with Ponseti casting. Method BSCOS consensus statement on clubfoot was reviewed and auditable standards were identified. The clinic was audited starting June 2023 for 12 months. Results 48 new patients were reviewed, 22 of these had clubfoot (19 idiopathic, 3 secondary) and 26 had other foot and ankle presentations or were normal. 63% of patients had their Ponseti casting started between 2 and 6 weeks of age. 91% of babies received a screening US hip scan. In the clinic records folder, the Pirani scoring system was used 100% of the time. The number of casts required per patient ranged from 3 to 6 and the mean was 4.5. Ponseti casts should be changed every 4-7 days. [1] 73% of patients met this. BSCOS expected that a tenotomy will be required in 85 to 95% of cases. [1] Achilles tenotomy was performed for 91% of patients. The post-tenotomy cast was on for 90% of cases for 3 weeks and the remaining patients were in cast for 4 weeks. Conclusions This audit has highlighted overall good clinical practice, and that the clinic meets nearly all the standards as expected for clubfoot management.

audits.standard: NICE guidelines: baseline DEXA and calcium and vitamin D supplementation for patients starting aromatase inhibitors
audits.finding: Baseline DEXA in 61% (280/458); follow-up DEXA at appropriate intervals in 35% (161/458); calcium and vitamin D prescribed in 52% (239/458).

paper.title: 209 Assessment of Bone Health in Postmenopausal Breast Cancer Patients Starting Adjuvant Aromatase Inhibitors: A Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are a cornerstone in the adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. However, AIs are associated with accelerated bone loss and an increased risk of fractures, necessitating proactive management of bone health. NICE guidelines recommend bone mineral density (BMD) assessment using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) scans and appropriate supplementation with calcium and vitamin D for patients at risk. Aim To evaluate the adherence to NICE guidelines regarding bone health assessment and management in postmenopausal breast cancer patients commencing adjuvant AI therapy. Method This retrospective audit included data from 1,137 breast cancer cases treated over three years at Charing Cross Hospital (CXH) and West Middlesex University Hospital (WMUH). Among these, 458 postmenopausal women receiving AIs were identified. Data were collected on the frequency of baseline DEXA scans. Results Of the 458 postmenopausal patients on AIs, only 61% (280/458) underwent a baseline DEXA scan prior to or shortly after starting therapy. Follow-up DEXA scans were conducted in 35% (161/458) of patients at appropriate intervals. Regarding supplementation, 52% (239/458) of patients were prescribed calcium and vitamin D during their treatment. These findings highlight significant gaps in adherence to guideline. In the Second cycle following intervention the results progress. Conclusions The audit underscores the need for improved compliance with national guidelines to enhance bone health care for postmenopausal breast cancer patients on AIs. Recommendations include implementing standardized pathways for DEXA scanning and supplementation, alongside education for oncology and breast clinic teams to ensure patients receive comprehensive follow-up care.

audits.standard: BOAST guidelines on neurovascular assessment documentation
audits.finding: Complete neurovascular documentation 29%; pulses documented 36%; 20% had no neurovascular documentation.
audits.change: Tick-box neurovascular sticker, plus local presentation of results and colleague education.

paper.title: 287 Neurovascular Status Assessment and Documentation in Long Bone Fractures Admitted to Orthopaedics in a Major Trauma Centre: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Acute fractures have the potential to disrupt neurovascular structures, which may be limb or life-threatening for patients. Recent case reviews highlighted the importance of documenting neurovascular status on admission. The current orthopaedic clerking booklet has been acknowledged to not provide suitable space for concise neurovascular documentation. Aim To improve the assessment and documentation of neurovascular status for all long bone fractures admitted to orthopaedics. The documentation was audited against BOAST (British Orthopaedic Association Standards for Trauma) guidelines. Method Retrospective review of clerking booklets of 70 inpatients with long bone fractures for documentation of neurovascular status on admission. This was audited and results presented locally, along with colleague education. An intervention was developed, consisting of a sticker with tick boxes for the correct neurovascular documentation. The neurovascular status documentation of 70 inpatient clerking booklets after this intervention was assessed to complete the cycle. Results The complete documentation of neurovascular status (including motor and sensory for each nerve and peripheral pulses) improved almost 3-fold from 29% before the intervention to 86% after. Documentation of pulses increased 2.5-fold, from 36% to 89%. 20% of patients had no neurovascular documentation at all prior to the intervention; this improved to no patients having absence of documentation. Conclusions This study has shown that a simple and cost-effective intervention can vastly improve documentation compliance. Locally, this intervention has provided scope to alter the clerking booklet to include the tick box proforma. This has knock-on benefits for patient safety and potential avoidance of medicolegal financial penalties.

paper.title: 314 Evaluation of Anaesthetic Practice for Total Knee Replacement - an Audit at the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Total knee replacement is a prevalent procedure that necessitates effective management of post-operative pain to enhance recovery. This study aims to evaluate the anaesthetic techniques utilised by anaesthetists and surgeons at the Royal Orthopaedic Hospital, focusing on their impact on opioid use, physiotherapy outcomes, and hospital length of stay. Method An audit and retrospective review were conducted on 30 patients who underwent total knee replacement from May 10 to June 2, 2023. Data collected included demographics, types of anaesthesia (spinal, general, and peripheral nerve blocks), post-operative opioid consumption, and timing of physiotherapy interventions. Results The median age of patients was 71 years, with a range of 48 to 89 years. A variety of anaesthetic techniques were employed, with 16 out of 26 patients receiving spinal anaesthesia without general anaesthesia, and 10 receiving a combination of spinal and general anaesthesia. The median oral morphine equivalent daily dose for postoperative opioid use was 30mg, with a range of 0-60mg. Patients receiving peripheral nerve blocks demonstrated a trend towards reduced opioid consumption and shorter hospital stays. The mean anaesthetic time was 19 minutes, and the mean recovery time was 51 minutes. Conclusions This evaluation highlights the variability in anaesthetic practices for total knee replacement at ROH. While no single technique emerged as superior, the use of peripheral nerve blocks appeared to correlate with reduced opioid requirements and shorter hospital stays. Further research is needed to establish best practices in anaesthetic management to improve patient outcomes and reduce reliance on opioids.

audits.title: 333 An Audit on New Cancer Diagnosis in Orthopaedic Inpatients
audits.standard: Scottish Cancer National Standards on wait times
audits.finding: 68% of patients met current cancer diagnosis standards.

paper.title: 333 An Audit on New Cancer Diagnosis in Orthopaedic Inpatients
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim New diagnosis of malignancy is a common finding in Orthopaedic departments. Patients present with atraumatic pain, fractures or Cauda Equina syndrome. Over 70% of malignant bone lesions are found to be metastatic and prompt investigation is required to identify the primary site and initiate appropriate management. This study aimed to identify the number of new cancer diagnosis in Orthopaedic inpatients and audit the time taken from diagnosis to investigation. Mortality at one year was used as a marker of outcome. Method A Retrospective study was conducted over a 3-year period from 2020-2023 in the Orthopaedics department at The Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, Glasgow. Keywords “CTTAP” were cross-referenced with consultant orthopaedic surgeon names in the online imaging system. This identified 267 cases. Scan results were reviewed to identify 47 cases of confirmed malignancy. Cases were analysed to compile indications for admission and pathology. Data was compared to The Scottish Cancer National Standards on wait times. 1 year mortality was assessed and compared to Scottish average. Results 47 patients had new malignancy confirmed whilst inpatients. Neck of femur fracture and atraumatic pain were the most common presenting complaints. 36% of patients had a cancer of unknown primary. 68% of patients met current cancer diagnosis standards. At one year, 55% of patients were deceased. Conclusions The number of patients receiving timely investigation was below the national average. Mortality at one year was higher than the Scottish average. A prospective study and further analysis are recommended to investigate how delay in investigation affects 1 year mortality.

paper.title: 380 Re-Audit of Documentation of Closed Hand Fractures Referred to Hand Therapy Trauma Clinic at Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The British Society for Surgery of the Hand (BSSH) guidelines for closed hand fractures outline that there should be clear documentation of the decision for non-operative management and factors that have influenced this, particularly if the decision for non-operative management is not the expected approach. At Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust, this cohort of patients are referred to a Hand Therapy Trauma Clinic (HTTC) for triage and appropriate non-operative management. Method A retrospective review was conducted of all closed hand fractures referred to HTTC over a two-week period in November 2024. The referral forms were assessed against objective criteria and outcomes were compared to data from the initial audit in March 2024 prior to intervention. Results There were 36 closed hand fracture referrals to HTTC, of which 21 (58%) were adults and 15 (42%) were children. The number of patients with electronic documentation of the referral to HTTC was improved when compared with initial data (17% vs 8%, p=0.45). There were 34 referrals (94%) with a specific diagnosis recorded and 32 (89%) had documented senior input (speciality registrar or consultant) in the decision for non-operative management. Only 64% of referrals had a detailed description of the mechanism of injury. Conclusions The HTTC referrals for closed hand fractures have clear diagnoses and senior involvement in the decision for non-operative management The number of referrals with electronic documentation has increased compared to the initial data but there remains significant improvement to be made.

audits.standard: BOAST Fracture Clinic Services: timely imaging to avoid delays to surgery
audits.finding: Mean time from imaging request to performance 4.51 days (range 0-30); imaging delays 29.5% of time from VFC review to surgery (9 surgical patients).
audits.change: Interdepartmental T&O-radiology imaging pathway with priority slots for VFC patients.

paper.title: 525 Reducing Cross-Sectional Imaging Delays from a Virtual Fracture Clinic: A Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Background A virtual fracture clinic (VFC) provides a safety net for orthopaedic injuries coming through a hospital. Cross-sectional imaging is sometimes necessary to guide surgical decision-making. The BOA Standards for Trauma (BOAST) Fracture Clinic Services recommend timely imaging to avoid undue delays to surgery. Aim To assess and improve VFC compliance to the BOAST guidelines. This was done by identifying and evaluating sources of delays between the date of VFC review and date of surgery before and after implementation of an interdepartmental imaging pathway. Method An initial retrospective audit was undertaken from January to June 2024. An imaging pathway between the T&O and radiology departments was introduced following this, which implemented priority slots for VFC patients. A prospective re-audit was performed from July to October 2024 post-pathway introduction. Data collected included demographics, timestamps of imaging, and details of surgical intervention. Results The pre-intervention period had 86 imaging requests (41 CT, 45 MRI). The mean time between imaging request and performance was 4.51 days (range 0-30 days). 9 patients required surgical management, with imaging delays accounting for 29.5% of the total time between VFC review and surgery. The post-intervention period had 86 imaging requests (36 CT, 50 MRI). The mean time between imaging request and performance was 3.56 days (range 0-24 days). 10 patients required surgical management, with imaging delays accounting for 21.0% of the total time between VFC review and surgery. Conclusions The introduction of an interdepartmental pathway has successfully reduced the imaging delay between request and performance by 21.1%.

audits.finding: Intra-articular fractures had surgery on average 6 days after injury; average casting and post-operative immobilisation 6 weeks.

paper.title: 760 Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) Following Distal Radius Fractures: An Audit to Improve Service Provision to the Distal Radius Fracture Patient Population
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), characterized by severe sensitivity to touch, skin changes, and joint stiffness, is a post-traumatic complication affecting the upper and lower extremities. This audit evaluated numerous clinical endpoints in the management of distal radius fracture (DRF) patients who developed CRPS, with the aim of improving service provision. Clinical endpoints were audited against the BSSH guidelines for DRF management. Method DRF patients with CRPS symptoms who underwent hand therapy between January 2023 to October 2024 were included. Clinical endpoints included duration from injury to definitive management and rehabilitation, type and duration of post-injury and post-operative immobilisation, and casting complications. Results Thirteen patients (100% female) were identified. Post-injury, all DRFs were immobilized in a backslab. Six patients (46%) were managed conservatively in a full cast for 6-weeks, on average 4-days from injury. Seven patients (54%), all with an intra-articular DRF, underwent surgery on average 6-days for injury, with six (46%) requiring an open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) and one (8%) managed with closed reduction and percutaneous pinning (CRPP) and full cast. Post-ORIF, Futura splint immobilization was used for five patients (86%) and backslab followed by Futura splint for one patient (14%), with 6-weeks of immobilization on average. Average duration from casting to physiotherapy was 54-days, in comparison to 35-days post-operatively. Conclusions Patients with intra-articular DRFs underwent surgery on average 6-days post-injury, while BSSH recommends surgery within 72hrs. The average duration of casting and post-operative immobilization was 6-weeks, whereas BSSH recommends 4-weeks. These findings aim to improve the management of DRFs.

paper.title: 1060 Audit on Compliance with GIRFT and WM RSN Standards for Management of Cauda Equina Syndrome Patients at UHNM
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit was to quantify the average time taken for a patient referred with suspicion of Cauda Equina Syndrome to receive an MRI and management outcome at UHNM; and compare that duration to national guidelines. Method This closed-loop quality improvement audit evaluated 25 patients referred to the Spinal Surgery department between February 2020 - March 2020 with clinical symptoms suggestive of Cauda Equina syndrome (CES). Time intervals from initial referral to specialist team review, MRI scan, MRI report, and final management decision were assessed. A second audit cycle was conducted on a subsequent cohort of 25 patients referred between November 2023 - December 2023. Results Of cohort one, 16 patients self-presented to A&E and 9 were GP referrals; of the second cohort, 22 were GP referral, 2 self-presented and 1 was an out-of-area transfer. The average time intervals of cohort one: from presentation to Spinal surgery referral was 176 minutes; 69 minutes for GP referrals and 242 minutes for self-referred. For cohort two: 60.8 minutes, 60.7 minutes and 161 minutes, respectively. Mean wait time from arrival to MRI scan was 438 minutes for cycle 1 and 185 minutes for cycle 2. MRI reporting intervals were on average: 254 minutes for the first cycle, and 95.75 minutes for the second cycle. Conclusions This QIP demonstrated an overall improvement in the investigation of suspected CES evidenced by a decreased in A&E referral time, decreased wait time for specialist review, decreased wait time for MRI scan and reporting.

audits.standard: NICE and local trauma call guidelines

paper.title: 1112 An Audit of Trauma Call Attendance and Documentation at a Major Trauma Centre in London: Improving Trauma Care
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Adherence to NICE and local guidelines of trauma calls significantly reduces mortality, morbidity, and healthcare costs. Accurate documentation of attendance and roles during trauma calls is crucial for guideline compliance, quality assurance, and medico-legal accountability. This audit aims to assess and enhance adherence to trauma call documentation. Method An audit was conducted over two weeks in November 2024 at St. Mary's Hospital London, a major trauma centre. Data were retrospectively collected via pre-alert forms (Signal App, Microsoft Teams) and electronic patient records. Data points included trauma type (code red/black), specialty attendance, sign-in sheet completion, role documentation, and admission details, comparing in-hours and out-of-hours performance. Results Of 103 trauma calls, 31% lacked completed sign-in sheets, and team roles were recorded in only 22%. 64 patients were admitted, 56 under surgical specialties. The admitting surgical specialty was present from the start of the trauma call in 55% of cases. Attendance for obligatorily attending specialties based on records varied considerably: Major Trauma/Neurosurgery (94%), Anaesthetics (64%), Trauma and Orthopaedics (50%), and General Surgery (40%). Identified barriers to accurate documentation included unfamiliarity with electronic systems, consecutive trauma calls, and resource issues (e.g., faulty computers). Documentation was poorer out-of-hours. Conclusions The audit highlights critical gaps in trauma call documentation, with incomplete records posing risks to care delivery, guideline adherence, and medico-legal safety. Proposed improvements include implementing a tap-in card system for automated sign-in, documentation templates, and identifying attendance barriers through staff surveys. These changes aim to enhance compliance with guidelines and improve multidisciplinary coordination in trauma care.

audits.title: 1132 The Impact of Time-to-Operation for Hand Trauma: A Local Audit
audits.standard: BSSH: surgery within 24 hours for open fractures and bites, 7 days for closed fractures, 4 days for other injuries
audits.finding: 24 (52%) did not meet criteria; 73% of open fractures and bites not operated within 24 hours; 1 of 3 closed fractures and 13 of 28 other injuries delayed.

paper.title: 1132 The Impact of Time-to-Operation for Hand Trauma: A Local Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction The British Society for Surgery on the Hand (BSSH) recommends time from injury to operative intervention is 24 hours for open fractures and bites, 7-days for closed fractures and 4-days for other injuries requiring surgery. Method We conducted a retrospective audit of hand trauma requiring operative management over 3-months and the time from injury to surgical intervention. Infection (diagnosed at the time of operation or at any presentation following surgery), surgeon grade, anaesthetic method and injury mechanism were recorded. Fishers exact and chi-squared tests were used to assess for differences in the rate of delay and the impact on outcomes. Results 46 cases were recorded with the primary surgeon recorded as a registrar in 100%. 5 of 46 cases (10.8%) were completed on the CEPOD list, with all other cases on a designated trauma list. 4 of 5 cases met BSSH guidelines. 24 cases (52%) did not meet these criteria. Of open fractures (7) and bites (8), 73% were not operated within 24 hours. 33% of closed fractures (1 of 3) were not operated within 7 days and 46% of other hand trauma (13 of 28) were not operated within 4 days of injury. Injury type did not affect the chance of delay (p=0.22). 6 were diagnosed with injury-related infection (13%) and the effect of delay was not statistically significant (p=0.90). Conclusions Small numbers have limited the ability to reveal this impact on outcomes however the potential impact and prevalence of delay has been highlighted. Future work and continuous audit will be undertaken.

audits.standard: Hospital perioperative arthroplasty protocol: regular opioids plus regular non-opioid analgesics plus PRN analgesia (score 3)
audits.finding: 34% achieved protocol-standard analgesia (score 3).
audits.change: Elective arthroplasty protocol powerplan implemented in the Surrey Safe Care electronic patient record.

paper.title: 501 Post-Operative Pain Management in Elective Arthroplasties – Results of a Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Effective pain management following elective arthroplasty influences early mobilisation, patient satisfaction and reduces hospital stay length. The hospital perioperative arthroplasty protocol highlights a combination of opioid and non-opioid analgesics to achieve this goal. In this second-cycle audit, the elective arthroplasty protocol powerplan was implemented within the Surrey Safe Care electronic patient record (EPR). Primary objectives Evaluate the adherence to the new elective arthroplasty protocol powerplan. To determine if the powerplan led to improved compliance with the standardised regimen. Method EPR drug charts were reviewed in the 24 hours from the operation. The data collection period spanned between June-July 2024. A non-validated, ad-hoc, protocol-based scale was used for data analysis: 0 = no analgesia; 1 = 1 regular non-opioid analgesic (NOA) + PRN analgesics; 2 = 1 regular weak opioid + regular NOAs + PRN analgesics; 3 = Regular opioids + regular NOAs + PRN analgesics(protocol standard). Results 51 drug charts were analysed (age range of 43-84 years) - 20 knee (39%) and 31 hip arthroplasties (61%). The proportion of patients achieving a Score 3 rose from 34% to 61%. Of those that adhered to the protocol, 87% of them utilised the powerplan. Conclusions This closed loop audit demonstrates an improvement in protocol compliance with EPR implementation. However, there remains a subset of patients who did not receive the recommended analgesia. Continued monitoring and education around the use of the powerplan will help sustain and improve these results, ultimately enhancing pain management and recovery outcomes for elective arthroplasty patients.

audits.title: 511 An Audit on the Use of a Calibration Marker in Neck of Femur Fracture X Rays
audits.standard: NICE: calibration marker on all X-rays for possible neck of femur fracture
audits.finding: Previous QIP improved compliance from 64% to 73%.

paper.title: 511 An Audit on the Use of a Calibration Marker in Neck of Femur Fracture X Rays
paper.abstract: Abstract Background In the UK, 75,000 hip fractures occur annually. Accurate radiographic and clinical assessment is required to inform timely and appropriate intervention for these patients. A ball calibration marker is used for templating of neck of femur fractures (NOF). As per NICE Guidelines, all patients receiving an X-ray for a possible NOF should have a calibration marker included on X-ray for operative planning. Aim To assess radiological investigations performed for NOFs in an MTC and compare with a previous QIP in the same trust in 2018, which showed an improvement from 64-73% compliance with this standard. Method Patients were identified who had NOF documented in the trauma database. For this repeat loop of the audit, patients with a NOF between 01/05/24 – 31/8/24 were identified. Online records were assessed to see if calibration markers were used at the time of the original radiograph. Basic statistical analysis was completed on an anonymised spreadsheet. Results From May - August 2024, 144 patients were admitted with NOFs. Only 44% of these patients had a ball calibration marker used in original X-ray. Conclusions Following the first loop in 2018, most patients who had a confirmed NOF had a ball calibration marker used. However, there has been a reduction in concordance, with less than half of the patients having an appropriate ball calibration marker on the initial X-Ray. A re-audit will be done to improve this compliance and shows the importance of regular interventions to maintain the efficacy of QIPs in busy departments.

paper.title: 997 An Audit into Compliance with Boast Standards for Mobilisation and Weightbearing After Orthopaedic Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess compliance within our department to the new BOAST Standards for documentation of mobilisation and weightbearing status after orthopaedic surgery. Method This audit identified all orthopaedic operations which had occurred over a two-month period from August 1st 2024 to September 30th 2024. Scanned operation notes were then obtained for each operation and compliance with the BOAST Standards was assessed. Results In total, 159 patients who underwent orthopaedic surgery during the specified time period were identified, with 11 operation notes being compliant with BOAST standards. Identified patients were further separated into three groups: upper limb surgery, lower limb surgery (excluding neck of femur fractures) and neck of femur fractures. Of these, lower limb surgeries showed highest compliance of 14% (7 of the 50), compared to 7% of upper limb surgeries (4 out of 59) and 0% of neck of femur fractures (0 out of 50). All but one of the neck of femur fractures had ticked the “full weightbearing” box on the operation note, making them technically non-compliant with the updated nomenclature of “unrestricted weightbearing”. Conclusions This audit has shown there is currently poor compliance with the BOAST standards within our department, leading to potential confusion in patients’ rehabilitation pathways. If compliance is to be improved then simple structural changes such as reformatting the operation note, which encourages incorrect documentation, should lead to a marked increase. Further education and awareness into the new standards will also likely be required.

paper.title: SRS99 - An audit assessing the surgical outcomes of Major Lower Limb Amputation (MLLA) in south tyneside and Sunderland NHS foundation trust
paper.abstract: Abstract This audit evaluates peri-operative care and outcomes for patients undergoing major lower limb amputation (MLLA) at Sunderland Royal Hospital between August 2024 and March 2025. MLLA, defined as any amputation above the ankle, is a critical intervention primarily for patients with chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) and diabetic foot infections (DFI). The audit assessed compliance with national standards from the Vascular Society of Great Britain and Ireland (VSGBI) and the National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD), focusing on consultant review timing, operative timing, prophylaxis, multidisciplinary team involvement, and patient outcomes. Data from 45 eligible MLLA cases revealed full compliance with consultant review within 24 h, antibiotic and venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis, and physiotherapy involvement during admission. However, only 67% of amputations occurred within 48 h of decision, and just 45% of diabetic patients received specialist diabetes team input. The below-knee to above-knee amputation ratio was 2:1, meeting best practice standards. Post-operative stump complications occurred in 20% of patients, with a 30-day mortality rate of 2.2%. The average hospital stay was prolonged at 34 days, with nearly half of patients remaining hospitalized beyond 30 days, highlighting potential inefficiencies in discharge planning and rehabilitation. The audit recommends improved diabetic specialist engagement through a blanket referral policy or weekly multidisciplinary ward rounds and enhanced physiotherapy input pre- and post-operatively to optimize rehabilitation and expedite discharge. These measures may reduce post-operative complications and length of stay, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare costs.

audits.title: 556 The Value of ‘check XRs’ Post Hemiarthroplasty- Challenging Whether Routine Post-Operative Pelvic Radiographs Are Clinically Important Following Hemiarthroplasties for Neck of Femur Fractures- a Retrospective Audit from a UK Major Trauma Centre

audits.finding: Post-operative pelvic radiographs performed in 98% at mean 2.71 days; only 8.2% had a documented clinical indication; positive findings in 3.1% (one dislocation, two leg-length discrepancies).

paper.title: 556 The Value of ‘check XRs’ Post Hemiarthroplasty- Challenging Whether Routine Post-Operative Pelvic Radiographs Are Clinically Important Following Hemiarthroplasties for Neck of Femur Fractures- a Retrospective Audit from a UK Major Trauma Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Currently, there is no national guideline regarding routine pelvic X-rays in the post-operative period following hemiarthroplasties for NOF fractures. Practice varies locally, and increasing evidence suggests that routine imaging may be unnecessary unless clinically indicated. This audit assessed the current practice at our Major Trauma Centre- University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire (UHCW)- and evaluated the value of routine post-operative radiography. Method A retrospective review was conducted of all hemiarthroplasties performed for NOF fractures between May and October 2025 (n = 100). Data collected included whether a check pelvic x-ray was performed post-operatively, timing, documented clinical indication, mobilisation status before imaging, radiological findings, imaging reviewer documentation, and resultant intervention. Results Post-operative pelvic radiographs were performed in 98% of patients, with a mean timing of 2.71 days post-surgery. 90.8% of patients mobilised successfully with physiotherapy before imaging. Only 8.2% had a documented clinical indication (pain, fall, failure to mobilise, or suspected dislocation). Positive findings were identified in 3.1%: one dislocation and two leg-length discrepancies. The only clinically significant finding (dislocation) occurred in a patient unable to mobilise, appropriately prompting imaging and subsequent revision to THR. 32% of documentation lacked reviewer attribution. Conclusions Routine post-operative pelvic radiographs following hemiarthroplasty demonstrate a low diagnostic yield and limited impact on management. The only clinically significant case was associated with clear clinical indications. We recommend reserving post-operative imaging for clinically indicated cases. Implementation of an electronic proforma may support targeted imaging, enhance documentation, reduce radiation exposure, provide cost savings, improve patient comfort, and potentially shorten hospital stay.

paper.title: 134 Audit of Implant Selection for Simple Proximal Femoral Fractures at North Manchester General Hospital: Sliding Hip Screws Versus Short Intramedullary Nails
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Sliding hip screws (SHS) and short intramedullary nails (IMN) achieve equivalent clinical outcomes for AO A1/A2 proximal femoral fractures. The NHFD confirms the majority of these simple fracture patterns are treated with SHS in the UK however some centres almost exclusively utilise IMN with no proven benefit. We investigated current practice at North Manchester General Hospital using a retrospective consecutive case series analysis. Method 106 patients with proximal femoral hip fractures were identified from the NHFD records treated Jan-Dec 2024. 55 patients treated with short IMN and 51 treated with SHS. Case notes, blood results and images from the electronic patient record were analysed using the consensus of parametric non-parametric tests. Results There were no statistical differences between the two techniques regarding age, gender, ASA status, preoperative hemoglobin, perioperative delay, methods of anaesthesia and post-operative mobility. 120-day mortality (12%) and revision surgery rates (0%) were the same for both groups. SHS performed statistically better (p<0.05) in relation to post-operative hemoglobin levels (101 vs 91 g/dl), surgical time (29 minutes faster) and length of hospital stay (16 vs 23 days). 28 of 55 fractures treated with short IMN could have been treated with SHS (AO A1/A2). Conclusion NICE UK recommend SHS for AO type A1/A2 hip fractures, the implant is non inferior and more cost effective than short IMN. Our study revealed that over half of patients treated with short IMN could have been treated with SHS. SHS demonstrated modest clinical and cost benefits over the IMN implants despite a small sample size.

paper.title: 428 An Audit of Inappropriate Referrals to the Virtual Fracture Clinic at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The virtual fracture clinic (VFC) at the Queen Elizabeth University Hospital works with the accident and emergency department (A&E) to streamline patients and reduce face-to-face appointments. Patients meeting criteria can be discharged and reviewed remotely by an orthopaedic consultant. However, referrals are often varied and inconsistent with guidelines. This work analysed VFC referrals to identify safety issues and resolve problems within the referral system. First round Inappropriate referrals over a four-month period (4/9/23-4/1/24) were identified by VFC nursing staff and reviewed. Referrals were categorised based on the reason for the inappropriate referral, and data on fracture type, referral origin, and VFC outcomes were collected. 80 inappropriate referrals were identified: 52.5% presented with injuries not requiring follow-up after discharge, and 30% had no identifiable fracture. 3 patients required urgent inpatient orthopaedic assessment and were admitted after VFC review. Second round Assessment of guidance showed a discrepancy between A&E and orthopaedic protocols. Updated guidelines were therefore developed jointly with A&E and a second data collection (4/10/24–4/2/25) was carried out three months after the implementation of the new guidelines. 24 inappropriate referrals were identified: 70.8% involved injuries normally discharged from A&E, 8.3% had no fracture, and none required inpatient assessment. Conclusions This closed-loop audit demonstrates a clear reduction in inappropriate referrals and improved patient safety, with no patients requiring inpatient assessment being mis-referred. Remaining inappropriate referrals may reflect a need for additional reassurance for clinicians or patients, or a delay in the full uptake of the updated guidelines.

paper.title: 614 Necrotising Fasciitis in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To determine the incidence of necrotising fasciitis at a busy urban district general hospital and to assess departmental compliance against recently published BOAST guidelines for management of musculoskeletal soft tissue infections. Method All referrals to the orthopaedic service for suspected soft-tissue infection between April and September 2025 were retrospectively identified. Analysis identified confirmed cases of necrotising fasciitis. Clinical timelines, operative intervention and microbiological investigations were assessed for compliance with BOAST guidelines. Results Of 20 referrals, 3 (15%) were confirmed as necrotising fasciitis, all affecting the lower limb. All patients were clinically septic on admission and received the sepsis six within one hour, meeting BOAST guidelines. All cases underwent emergency operative management, with a mean decision-to-incision time of 2 hours (range 1-3), meeting the BOAST guidance for prompt surgical debridement. Intra-operative sampling was performed in all cases, median 1 specimen per procedure (range 1-3), and histology was obtained in 2/3. Polymicrobial growth (Pseudomonas and Staphylococcus species) was seen in two cases; Serratia Marcesecens was isolated in the third. One patient died within 72 hours; the remaining two required multiple returns to theatre (3 and 7 respectively) with a mean hospital stay of 50 days (34-66). Conclusions Necrotising Fasciitis remains an uncommon but rapidly fatal and costly condition presenting to the acute orthopaedic take. We demonstrate high local compliance with BOAST guidelines, particularly regarding early recognition, sepsis management and urgent debridement. Improvements will be driven through focussed teaching and workshops with relevant healthcare professionals, structured pathway reinforcement and planned re-audit to ensure sustained, measurable progress.

paper.title: 615 Septic Arthritis in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To determine the incidence of septic arthritis at a busy urban district general hospital and to assess compliance against the BOAST guidelines for management of musculoskeletal soft tissue infections. Method All referrals to the orthopaedic service for suspected soft-tissue infection between April and September 2025 were retrospectively identified. Analysis identified confirmed cases of septic arthritis. Clinical pathways, operative management and sampling were assessed against BOAST guidelines. Results Of 86 referrals, 7 cases (8.1%) were confirmed as septic arthritis. The median age was 67 years (16-89). The knee accounted for 57% of cases, the shoulder 29% and elbow 14%. Two patients had pre-antibiotic joint fluid cultures, and only 2 patients had pre-antibiotic blood cultures, indicating a key area for improvement. All cases had a sample sent for microscopy in line with guidelines. Six cases proceeded to operative management, all by arthroscopic washout. Microbiology cultures were obtained in five cases, although histological sampling was performed in only one case. Streptococcus species accounted for five infections; Staphylococcus aureus and Neisseria meningitidis were isolated in the others. Thirty-day mortality was zero; the median length of stay was 16 days (10-44). Conclusions Septic Arthritis represents an uncommon but debilitating condition which presents on the acute orthopaedic take. Our findings show strong local compliance with BOAST guidelines, while also highlighting targeted areas for improvement, notably consistent pre-antibiotic culture collection and increased intra-operative sampling. These gaps will be addressed through a teaching series and workshop with relevant healthcare professionals, pathway optimisation and re-audit to ensure sustained improvement.
