audits.standard: NICE secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease (smoking cessation, lipid modification, antiplatelet therapy, blood pressure control, diabetes risk assessment); target 100%
audits.finding: Smoking cessation 40.5%, lipid modification 18.8%, blood pressure control 29.5%, diabetes risk assessment 21.1%, antiplatelet therapy 38.9%.

paper.title: 401 Cardiovascular Risk Factor Optimisation Amongst Inpatients with Peripheral Artery Disease – a Single-Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Patients with symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD) are highly co-morbid and thus may benefit from cardiovascular disease risk factors optimisation at the time of admission. This audit aimed at reviewing adherence to NICE guidelines for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease amongst hospital in patients with critical limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) or intermittent claudication (IC). Method A retrospective review of all CLTI or IC inpatient admissions to a tertiary referral vascular surgery centre, over 9 months, was performed. We assessed adherence to five NICE recommendations for cardiovascular risk factor optimisation: 1) smoking cessation 2) lipid modification 3) antiplatelet therapy 4) blood pressure control 5) diabetes risk assessment, with target adherence of 100%. Results 97 admissions for PAD were recorded (CLTI n=87, 89.7%; IC n=10, 10.3%). The average age was 70.8±11.7 years, and 68.4% were male. Smoking cessation service was provided to 40.5% of eligible patients, lipid modification to 18.8%, blood pressure control to 29.5%, diabetes risk assessment to 21.1%, and antiplatelet therapy to 38.9%. Admissions longer than 10 days had a significantly higher rate of adherence (>10 days 35.5% vs ≤10 days 19.8%, p=0.017). Conclusions There are gaps in risk factor optimisation amongst PAD inpatients, with risk factors either not documented, or addressed appropriately. Shorter, elective hospital admissions were associated with worse risk factor optimisation. A dedicated review of risk factors should be offered to all PAD inpatients early during their admission. To achieve the best long-term adherence, multidisciplinary engagement of geriatrics, smoking cessation, diabetes, and primary care is essential.

audits.standard: BSDS and BSH perioperative antithrombotic guidelines
audits.finding: Postoperative bleeding 8.6%; aspirin monotherapy not stopped 80%; pre-op INR for warfarin 75%.
audits.change: Poster 'cheat sheet' of antithrombotic advice displayed in the department.

paper.title: 432 Perioperative Antithrombotic Agent Use in Cutaneous Surgery: A Complete Audit Cycle
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Management of antithrombotic therapy prior to cutaneous surgery is a contentious topic with mixed opinions. The primary of this audit was to analyse the incidence of post-operative bleeding following cutaneous surgery in our minor operations theatre over two audit cycles. Secondary aims included measuring the standards outlined by BSDS and BSH peri-operative antithrombotic guidelines and assessing bleeding by risk. Method A single centre retrospective review of all patients undergoing cutaneous surgery on established antithrombotic therapy between 8/9/22 - 31/10/22 (cycle 1) and 10/7/2023 to 15/09/2023 (cycle 2) was conducted. A poster 'cheat sheet' containing antithrombotic agent advice was displayed in the department, forming the intervention. Results A total of 165 patients underwent cutaneous surgery with continuation of their antithrombotic agent. A reduction in post-operative bleeding from 8.6% to 7.4% in the second cycle was observed. The most common agent associated with bleeding in both cohorts was a DOAC, 33.3% and 42.9%, respectively. Overall, high risk operations had a proportionally higher incidence of post-op bleed compared with lower risk; 26.7% versus 4.6%, respectively. We recommended aspirin monthotherapy was not ceased before surgery, this improved from 80% to 71.4%. Equally we saw an increase in pre-op INR from 75% to 100% for warfarin users. Conclusions Patient factors, indication for antithrombotic agent and risk of the procedure should be all considered when listing for surgery, to help determine how the antithrombotic agent should be managed. Postoperative bleeding increases the risk of delayed wound healing, graft/flap failure and wound infection, and therefore should be considered.

audits.title: 458 Post-COVID-19 Regularisation of Emergency Laparoscopic Cholecystectomies: A Single-Centred Multi-Cycle Audit
audits.standard: AUGIS advice: emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of diagnosing acute cholecystitis
audits.finding: Median admission to theatre 106.5 hours; median length of stay 7.5 days.

paper.title: 458 Post-COVID-19 Regularisation of Emergency Laparoscopic Cholecystectomies: A Single-Centred Multi-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The COVID-19 pandemic has increased the number of emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomies due to elective surgery cancellations. However, the impact of COVID-19 on the timing of surgery remains unclear. The Association of Upper Gastrointestinal Surgery (AUGIS) advised to perform an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of diagnosing acute cholecystitis. This audit aims to evaluate the impact of the post-COVID-19 period on the timing of emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomies. Method A retrospective analysis of patients who underwent an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy, in the post-pandemic period, between January and December 2022 was conducted. Primary outcomes include admission to imaging time, admission to theatre time, length of hospital stay, intra- and post-operative complications. Outcomes were audited against AUGIS guidelines and compared with previous audit cycles during the pre-pandemic (2019) and pandemic (2021) periods. Results In 2022, 411 patients underwent an emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Median admission to imaging time was 11 hours (IQR 4.6-21.9). Median admission to theatre time was 70.7 hours (IQR 48.4-107.7), compared to 106.5 hours in 2019 and 76.7 hours in 2021. Median length of hospital stay was 5.6 days (IQR 4.0-8.1), compared to 7.5 days in 2019 and 5.3 days in 2021. There were 38 (9.2%) subtotal cholecystectomies, 112 (27.3%) on-table cholangiograms, and 57 (13.9%) CBD explorations performed. 61(14.8%) patients had post-op complications including 9 (2.2%) bile leaks, 5 (1.2%) retained stones, and 7(1.7%) collections. Conclusions Timings to emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomies continue to improve in the post-COVID-19 period and is consistent with AUGIS recommendations.

paper.abstract: Abstract Background Operation notes are vital as part of patient care in-line with Good Medical Practice to provide excellent continuity of care and for medicolegal purposes. This also to raise awareness on existing guidelines and accuracy of operation note documentation. Aim To assess compliance of op-notes documentation against Royal College of Surgeons (England) Good Surgical Practice Guidelines “1.3 Record your work clearly, accurately and legibly” in ENT Department Imperial College NHS. Method This is a retrospective 2-cycles audit (n=27) analysing October 2023 theatre list for first cycle and November 2023 theatre list for second cycle. Inclusion and exclusion criteria applied to ensure uniformity of data collected based on type of operations. Data documentation analysed against domains in RCS guidelines. Results Results are compared for both cycles, for which the results of first cycle were presented in a regional meeting. Almost all domains achieved 100% compliance of documentation except deep vein thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis (10%), blood loss (5%), antibiotic prophylaxis (85%) and anaesthetists name (50%). Part of the discussion is that blood loss should be documented even in minor cases with minor bleeding risk. DVT prophylaxis might be overlooked in some cases (e.g., hemithyroidectomy which require only overnight inpatient). Conclusions Surgical teams are responsible in documenting clear plans and instructions peri-operatively to provide optimum level of patient care, reduce perioperative complications, improve patient satisfaction and ensuring patient safety.

paper.title: 581 A Standard Base Audit Regarding Documentation of Urinary Catheterization of the Patients Who Had a Urinary Catheter Inserted in a General Surgical Ward at Sri Jayewardenepura General Hospital, Sri Lanka
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the documentation of urinary catheterization of patients who had a urinary catheter inserted in the ward and to achieve good documentation following urinary catheterization Method We performed a standard base audit on documentation of urinary catheterization of the patients who had a urinary catheter inserted in the ward. We collected the initial retrospective data from the patient's notes and observed any documentation of urinary catheterization. The data was analysed and then a printed document was introduced to the ward to be filled following urinary catheterization. After 5 months we have carried out the re-audit to check for the improvement of documentation. Results A total of 50 patients were included. Before the implementation of the printed form for the documentation of catheterization, only 2% of patients had complete documentation following a urinary catheterization. After the implementation of the form, the documentation following urinary catheterization has improved to 88%. Conclusions The documentation of urinary catheterization has been recommended in the guidelines to ensure patients’ safety. The documentation of the indication, pre-insertion examinations and observations, catheter details, the volume of water instilled in the balloon, characteristics of the initial urine drained, and last but not least the removal plan is important for patient management and safety. These domains have been entered in the form and introduced to the ward to be filled and pasted on the patients' notes following a urinary catheterisation.

paper.title: 582 A Re- Audit of the Metabolic Screening for Patients with Urinary Tract Calculi and the Implementation of an Electronic Requesting Bundle
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Renal colic is one of the commonest elective and emergency Urological presentations. As highlighted in NICE and EAU guidelines, serum calcium and uric acid levels should be measured in such patients as part of a metabolic screening. This audit aims to reassess the compliance of this at a local DGH. Method All patients diagnosed with a urinary tract calculus between 1/5/2023 and 31/7/2023 were included and retrospective data was collected which included the serum calcium and uric acid levels. The results were compared with a previous audit in 2022. Results 65 patients were eligible for inclusion. 46% of patients had their serum calcium level measures in the current audit compared to 65% in 2022. 37% of patients had their uric acid level measured in the current audit compared to 46% in 2022. Discussions Despite previous audits and interventions by means of education and posters, there has been a decline in the metabolic screening of patients with urinary tract stones. Via the trust electronic requesting system, we have implemented a “renal colic” bundle which includes the automatic selection of FBC, UEs, CRP, INR, Serum Calcium and Serum Uric acid levels for such patients. This convenient integrated IT feature will aim to improve the metabolic screening of these patients. Key stakeholders have been educated on the importance of metabolic screening and of the newly implemented bundle. We aim to re-audit in 6 months.

paper.title: 612 A Quality Improvement Project of Management of Acute Pancreatitis in a District General Hospital; How Well Are We Doing Against NICE Guidelines?
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Pancreatitis is a common condition with significant complications, and mortality in 5% of cases. We aimed to identify compliance to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines of pancreatitis management in our District General Hospital (DGH) to improve patient safety and outcomes. Method A retrospective analysis of first-time presentations of acute pancreatitis over a 12-month period, assessing the five domains addressed in NICE-NG104: identifying cause, antibiotic stewardship, nutrition, severity and complications, and lifestyle advice. Our data was compared to that of the PANC study, a UK-national cohort study. Results A total of 33 cases fit criteria –17 male and 16 female. Cause was identified in 55%, of which 86% were within 48 hours. 51% were prescribed antibiotics on admission, of which 23% had an indication recorded. 91% of patients were nil-by-mouth, only 20% of those cases had a reason recorded. Only 6% had severity documented. Four patients were discussed with a tertiary centre. Lifestyle advice was offered to 33% of patients on discharge. In comparison with the PANC Study, there were domains with significant differences. For example, the study reported that 56.4% of cases were offered oral nutrition vs 9% in our DGH, and antibiotics were prescribed in 34% vs 51% locally. Conclusions The audit highlighted need for improvement in NICE guideline compliance of acute pancreatitis management in our DGH. This is being tackled by cycles of quality improvement, including introduction of a ‘Pancreatitis Management Bundle’ and local clinical guidelines, increased staff awareness and patient education.

audits.standard: Valid group and save sample within 72 hours pre-operatively
audits.finding: 383/571 elective and 245/265 emergency patients had a valid G&S; no elective patient required transfusion and no patient needed intra-operative transfusion.

paper.title: 656 Is Routine Group and Save Required for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy? An Audit of a High Volume NHS Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Bleeding is a recognised complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC). Yet very few patients require blood transfusion in the perioperative phase. However, it is routine practice for patients undergoing LC to have a group and save (G&S) prior to surgery. This audit aims to assess number of LC patients at Northumbria Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust who required transfusions, and the number who had “valid” group and save (G&S) samples obtained within 72 hours pre-operatively. Method Records of patients who had either elective or emergency LC at Northumbria Healthcare NHS Trust between 1st January 2021 to 31st December 2022 were reviewed retrospectively using theatre and transfusion records. Results A total of 836 patients were included (557 female and 279 male, age ranges 19 to 90 years old). Out of 571 elective LC, none required transfusion. 383 had a “valid” G&S, despite 360 having at least one historical sample. Of 265 emergency LC, 245 patients had a “valid” G&S, despite 207 having at least one historical sample. No patients needed intra-operative transfusion. 2 emergency LC patients required non-urgent post-operative transfusion where G&S sampling could have been taken once transfusion decision was made. One patient had cirrhosis and anaemia secondary to liver metastases, and the other developed a post-operative liver haematoma. Conclusions This audit suggested that no patients required intra-operative transfusion, and very few patients required peri-operative transfusion for LC. Eradication of routine G&S sampling is likely to provide financial and environmental benefits without increasing the risk profile of this procedure.

paper.title: 686 National Audit Assessing the Imaging of Acute Pancreatitis at Mater Dei Hospital, Malta
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit is to assess the imaging of acute pancreatitis (AP) in patients admitted to Mater Dei Hospital, Malta using the Royal College of Radiologists (RCR) recommendations as standard. Method Retrospective data of patients admitted with AP between 1/1/22 and 31/12/22 was collected. Timing of initial CT (at least 72 hours after symptom onset), CT report inclusion of prognostic factors, and timing of ultrasonography (US) of the gallbladder (within 24 hours of diagnosis) were analysed. Results 187 patients were included in this study. 99 patients were investigated with a CT scan during their admission, with only 25.3% of these patients being scanned at least 72 hours after developing symptoms. 74.7% of CTs were done within 72 hours of symptom onset. 47.3% of patients who had an early CT received a further CT or MRCP scan in the same admission. 24.2% of CTs mentioned all 3 key prognostic factors outlined in the RCR recommendations: pancreatic necrosis, free intraperitoneal fluid, and peripancreatic fat stranding. Only 20.2% of patients had an US examining the gallbladder within 24 hours of diagnosis. Conclusions Results show that CT scans are being performed too early in the clinical course of AP, with little reliance on US as a quick, non-invasive, and inexpensive first-line scan. Early CTs in AP generally do not alter management and risk missing complications. Our aim is to improve local practices through multiple educational sessions addressed towards emergency doctors, general surgeons, and radiologists.

paper.title: 718 An Audit of Chaperone Documentation in the Breast Clinic
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The General Medical Council and the governing trust (NHS Lothian) for our local hospital provide clear guidance on the role of chaperones within the breast clinic; specifically for all intimate examinations, a chaperone should be offered regardless of the genders of practitioner and patient, and the patient’s response to this should be documented. This entitlement to a chaperone is important in protecting staff and patients. This two-cycle audit reviews the documentation of chaperones in the breast clinic at a single centre, and whether consent to intimate examination is documented. Method Documentation was assessed for all adults attending low-risk or new patient clinic in both cycles (from 04-10/07/23, then 13-16/11/23), reviewing the staff grade assessing the patient, whether consent was recorded, and whether a chaperone had been accepted, refused, or not documented. The second cycle was conducted after putting up posters to remind medics to document and remind nursing staff to check this data. Results Junior doctor documentation of offering a chaperone increased by 43.7%, although consultant and ANP documentation decreased, by 20% and 34% respectively. When accepted, the chaperone’s name is recorded in all cases, and their grade in 3% more cases following our intervention. Conclusions Following intervention to target the lack of documentation in clinic notes, a significant positive change has been affected in junior doctors’ records. This change has however not been seen among consultants and ANPs, highlighting the ongoing need to improve documentation standards, to keep in line with national and local guidelines, and to protect our staff and patients.

paper.title: 752 VTE Prophylaxis and VTE Assessment Form in Plastic Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Failure to conduct a risk assessment and administer suitable venous thromboprophylaxis in surgical patients is deemed as negligence. It was estimated that 25,000 deaths in the UK was due to VTE in 2004-2005. Seventy percentage of hospital acquired VTE is potentially preventable with appropriate VTE prophylaxis. The Trust published a form for risk assessment for VTE for surgical patient. Our aim was to examine the departments adherence to the trust guidelines. Method All plastic surgery inpatients with a stay longer than 24 h were reviewed for VTE prophylaxis prescription for a period of two weeks. This was followed by presenting the audit results in a departmental meeting and introducing a checkbox to the handover list with posters placed in the doctors’ office. VTE assessment forms were placed in a clear divider and attached to the poster to remind doctors. Two weeks later, a re-audit was undertaken. Results In first audit, 22 patients were eligible for VTE prophylaxis compared to 24 in the re-audit. VTE chemoprophylaxis prescribing improved after intervention from 69.5% to 95%. Mechanical prophylaxis increased by 15.8%. Most importantly, the use of the VTE risk assessment form improved from 0 to 70%. Inappropriate chemoprophylaxis prescription reduced from 18.8% to 8%. Conclusions Despite the improvement in results after educating doctors and introducing the checkbox, our goal to be 100% compliant has not yet been met. Given the nature of the rapid turnover of junior doctors, a more robust system incorporating VTE assessment in the electronic system and replacing the paper form is required.

audits.standard: RCPath dataset for pathology reporting of breast disease in surgical excision specimens: 90% of reports to include items

paper.title: 759 Lost in Translation: Breast Surgery Pathology Reporting Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate and consistent reporting of surgical specimens is essential to guide appropriate clinical decisions in management of patients with breast cancer. In 2017 NHS England consolidated pathology services with hub and spoke networks which aimed to improve efficiency and reduce variation in service delivery. Following a Serious Incident within our well-performing breast unit, it was clear that strengthening communication by standardised reporting in merged services improves patient safety. An audit was performed to review reporting consistency. Method The Royal College of Pathologists (RCPath) guideline 'Pathology reporting of breast disease in surgical excision specimens' describes a dataset that 90% of reports should include. We reviewed breast cancer operations from October to December 2021 at one unit and analysed reports for inclusion of guideline components. Margin and lymph node re-excisions were excluded. Results Of 126 reports 65 were included. Procedures were wide local excision (65%) and mastectomy (35%). Specimen type, histological grade, and presence of invasive disease were well reported but other items were inconsistently documented, including date of surgery (0%), core biopsy site identified (1.5%) and presence of microinvasion (4.3%). Conclusions There was variation in the pathology reporting of breast cancer. Multi-disciplinary team clinical decisions are based upon these results and error could arise if components are omitted or incomplete when reports are published. Investigating incidents drives change that makes services robust and enhances patient safety. Service improvement considerations need not be onerous or impact tight demand and capacity needs. We propose implementation of a streamlined reporting proforma that includes RCPath core dataset components.

paper.title: 760 Intravenous Maintenance Fluid Prescribing in Nil-by-Mouth Patients in General Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Inappropriate intravenous fluid prescribing in peri-operative nil-by-mouth patients increases the risk of electrolyte, metabolic imbalances, and starvation ketosis.(1) NICE guidelines offer recommendations for intravenous maintenance fluid prescribing in nil by mouth' patients. (2) This audit assessed the prescribing of maintenance intravenous fluids in nil-by-mouth patients in our General Surgery department. Method We retrospectively audited our practice over two randomized 14-day periods pre and post-intervention to check compliance with guidelines. Inclusion criteria included non-diabetic patients, no pre-existing electrolyte imbalances and nil-by-mouth for ≥24hrs. Interventions: We delivered teaching sessions to FY1/2 on General surgery highlighting NICE guidelines on correct IV fluids prescribing. Posters summarizing this were displayed around the surgical wards. Results Cycle 1 showed significant lack in the prescribing of potassium and glucose in our department. Cycle 2 revealed that 82% of patients met their daily water requirements, while 94% and 96% met their sodium and chloride requirements, respectively. This translates to 40%, 10% and 11% increase in adherence to recommended water, sodium, and chloride intake, respectively. Although a small percentage of patients met their glucose (24%) and potassium (16%) requirements, the department witnessed a 55% and 54% increase in prescribing of glucose-containing and supplemental potassium-containing bags, respectively. Conclusions This audit identified an area of miseducation in our department and created a positive impact in the correct prescribing of maintenance fluids, particularly in the prescribing of potassium and glucose in nil-by-mouth patients.

paper.title: WP2.13 - Local Audit based on MAGIC study to improve abscess management at Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess efficacy of current management approaches of subcutaneous abscess at the Royal Devon University Healthcare Trust (RD&E). Methods Our audit is based on the MAGIC (Management of Acute surGIcal absCesses) national audit which involved anonymous retrospective analysis of patient records at the RD&E during September – December 2022. We collected data on patient demographics, clinical characteristics and their management. Furthermore, we conducted a literature review to compare our results to the recommended practice. Results 31 patients records were analysed whereby 22 underwent surgical intervention (general anesthetic 17, local anesthetic 5) whereby the most common incision type was transverse (n=7). Nine patients were diabetic, two were immunosuppressed, 29 had hidradenitis suppurativa, while 19 had a past medical history of abscesses (n=31). The most common abscess type was pilonidal sinus (n=10). Eighteen patients received antibiotics prior to hospital admission, 12 of whom underwent surgery. Furthermore, 19 patients received antibiotics upon admission to hospital (n=31). Of the surgically treated cohort, 19 underwent packing and six were discharged with antibiotics. Conclusion Most subcutaneous abscess are approached surgically. However, postoperative care varies widely, with prolonged packing and frequent use of antibiotic postoperatively. Literature reviews have suggested no benefit of postoperative packing and specified certain circumstances of antibiotic use. Furthermore, clear communication with primary care providers detailing clear postoperative instructions is vital for patient safety and cost effectiveness.

audits.standard: Locally agreed guidance-based 3-monthly HbA1c monitoring
audits.finding: Appropriate HbA1c re-checks on indicated admissions 25%; repeat HbA1c required in 38%; mean staff knowledge score 56%.
audits.change: Educational teaching programme on diabetes management for clinical staff

paper.title: 893 Addressing the Potential Harms in Vascular Surgery Inpatients with Diabetes: A Double Audit and Intervention Project on HbA1c Monitoring and Diabetes Management
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Diabetes mellitus confers crucial prognostic consequences in vascular surgery patients. Derangements in long- and short-term glycaemic control predispose to increased risks of post-revascularisation amputation and overall cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. This project aims to address these potential risks by improving departmental HbA1c monitoring practice and diabetes management knowledge at a tertiary centre through a comprehensive educational intervention. Method A retrospective audit of HbA1c monitoring practice in vascular surgery admissions from August-September 2023 for peripheral arterial disease or diabetic foot infections was performed against a locally agreed guidance-based 3-monthly monitoring frequency. An educational audit on clinical staff’s knowledge of relevant practical and theoretical aspects to diabetes management was performed through a multiple-choice assessment. An educational teaching programme was subsequently designed and delivered. Post-intervention HbA1c monitoring was prospectively reassessed between October-November 2023, and a post-intervention knowledge assessment was performed. Results Mean pre-admission HbA1c values in the pre- and post-intervention admission cohorts were 78.6±18.4 mmol/mol (n=21) and 73.6±35.7 mmol/mol (n=12) respectively. Repeat HbA1cs were required in 38% of pre-intervention and 50% of post-intervention admissions. Appropriate HbA1c re-checks on indicated admissions increased from 25% to 86% post-intervention. Mean knowledge assessment performance increased from 56% to 77% with improved mean scores in all knowledge domains. Conclusions Gaps in departmental understanding of practical diabetes management and monitoring relevant to vascular surgery patients with diabetes were effectively addressed through the educational intervention. Referral practice for multidisciplinary diabetes optimisation and harm reduction should be a further area of focus given the patient cohort's highly elevated HbA1c measurements.

audits.standard: Centre for Perioperative Care: daily delirium screening with a validated tool such as the 4-AT in patients 65 and over
audits.finding: 4-AT screening in only 39.2% (n=20), on average 90 hours post-operatively; never documented in consultant-led post-operative review (100%, n=51).
audits.change: Recommended: stakeholder discussion, the mantra 'Post-op bloods and 4AT', and education on the 4-AT proforma.

paper.title: 929 An Audit of the Perioperative Clinical Assessment and Documentation of Delirium in Older Patients Following Vascular Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Guidelines established by the Centre for Perioperative Care recommend daily screening for delirium using a validated tool such as the 4-AT and proactively documenting delirium in patients aged 65 years and over. This audit evaluated the assessment and documentation of delirium in older patients following vascular surgery. Method Patients aged ≥ 65 years who had undergone vascular surgery in August 2023 were identified. Data was collected retrospectively with access to the Trust electronic patient record system on a bespoke Microsoft Excel spreadsheet and analysis was carried out using SPSS®. Results Of the 51 patients identified, delirium was screened using the 4-AT tool in only 39.2% (n=20) of patients and on average 90 hours post-operatively. The highest documented score was 7 (n=1), with 7.8% (n=4) of patients scoring 1, 2 or 3 and the majority scoring 0 (n=15). The 4-AT was never documented in a consultant-led surgical post-operative review (100%, n=51). Additionally, there were concerns of delirium documented in 7 instances in the post-operative period, with the 4-AT documented in 5 of those instances. Conclusions This audit demonstrates poor compliance with perioperative care standards on screening for delirium using the 4-AT and documenting delirium, highlighting the need to increase awareness and improve the perioperative clinical pathway for older people undergoing vascular surgery. Our recommendations include discussion with stakeholders to identify barriers to assessment and documentation of delirium, (2) use of the mantra: 'Post-op bloods and 4AT' during post-operative reviews, and (3) education of various healthcare professionals in completing the 4-AT proforma on the ward.

paper.title: 943 Audit of Endoscopy Service Safety in District General Hospital Rated ‘Inadequate’ by the CQC
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim In June 2021 the overall CQC rating of Weston General Hospital (WGH) was ‘inadequate’. A wave of changes including a merger of trusts between Bristol and Weston-Super-Mare has aimed at improving services across the board. The endoscopy service at WGH offers inpatient and outpatient investigations to thousands of patients every year. We aimed to evaluate the safety of the service offered over a 12-month period, using measures set out by the Joint Advisory Group on GI endoscopy and other published statistics. Method A retrospective review of periendoscopic complications in OGD, ERCP, flexible sigmoidoscopy and colonoscopy leading to re-admission within eight days of procedure or death within thirty days of procedure. Each case was analysed, using paper and digital case notes, for clinical course, outcomes and learning points. Results There were a total of 3428 cases between June 2021 and May 2022. There was an overall readmission rate within eight days of 0.002% (1 ERCP, 1 OGD, 4 colonoscopy). There was a mortality rate of 0.0003% (1 case of post-ERCP pancreatitis). A review of cases showed all complications were recognised complications of the given procedure and treated appropriately in a timely manner. Conclusions It was concluded that the endoscopy service at WGH was safe and viable. Numbers of readmissions and deaths related to endoscopy were similar to previous audits and well below the published rates of complications in literature.

audits.standard: ENT UK guidelines for SSNHL
audits.finding: not reported separately
audits.change: Data presented to the local department with updated SSNHL guidance and treatment pathway.

paper.title: 965 What Did You Say? a Completed Cycle SSNHL Management
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To compare the management of patients with SSNHL in a district general hospital to the ENT UK guidelines. Method Data encompassing the management of individuals presenting with (SSNHL) at an ENT centre in both 2022 and 2023 was collected. Data included: investigations, MRI and audiograms, and treatment: oral and intratympanic steroid (ITS) administration. Subsequently, the collected data underwent analysis and was presented to the respective local department for updated information on the SSNHL guidance and treatment pathway, a second cycle of an audit was then conducted. Results In an AUDIT involving 35 patients, 92% underwent same-day diagnostic audiograms, and 76% had MRI scans. All patients received oral steroids, with 80% concurrently receiving proton pump inhibitors in the second cycle. Additionally, 52% required intratympanic steroid (ITS) injections, all administered within six weeks. Subsequent audiograms showed that 66% experienced complete or partial resolution of sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL). Conclusions This centre's adherence to national guidelines was higher for same-day audiograms than including MRI in patient evaluations. Most patients received oral steroids, and 52% underwent intratympanic steroid (ITS) treatment, potentially contributing to observed improvements. Literature supports the benefits of successive ITS with oral steroids in sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SSNHL). The ongoing national STARFISH trial may further contribute to evidence on SSNHL management.

paper.title: 975 A Re-Audit on Bowel Preparation for Colonoscopy in a Surgical Unit of a Tertiary Care Hospital, Sri Lanka
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This re-audit assessed changes in colonoscopy preparation practices at a Sri Lankan tertiary care hospital, aligning with ESGE guidelines. The primary goal was to gauge adherence improvements after introducing a protocol and educational initiatives. Method Conducted from May to July 2023, the initial audit identified deficiencies, leading to protocol development based on ESGE guidelines. Educational initiatives for nursing and junior staff were implemented, adjusting split-dose timing, discontinuing enema use, and providing clear instructions. A re-audit from August to October 2023 assessed the impact, analysing records through descriptive statistics. Results The re-audit revealed substantial improvements in colonoscopy preparation adherence to ESGE recommendations. The total number of patients undergoing the procedure was 88 in the initial audit and 96 in the re-audit. Adherence to a low fibre diet rose from 22.72% (n=20) to 90.62% (n=87), and compliance with enhanced instructions improved from 14.7% (n=13) to 70.8% (n=69). Routine enema use was eliminated (0% to 100%). Compliance for split-dose preparation increased from 42.04% (n=37) to 81.25% (n=78), and last dose timing within 5 hours improved similarly. Specific instructions to patients and clinic staff significantly improved from 28.4% (n=25) to 97.9% (n=94). Conclusions In conclusion, the re-audit emphasizes significant improvements in colonoscopy preparation, highlighting the positive impact of introduced changes. These findings underscore the effectiveness of evidence-based guidelines, education, and continuous audits. Implementing a checklist, staff, and patient education has proven essential for transforming and enhancing bowel preparation quality. These simple yet focused measures are essential in transforming and streamlining the quality of bowel preparation.

paper.title: 980 Audit of the Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Pathway in Frimley Park Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To confirm the proportion of patients that stayed overnight in the hospital after their cholecystectomy. To determine the major causes of patients staying overnight in the hospital. To ensure Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy is being performed according to Get It Right First time (GIRFT) guideline GIRFT recommendation Anticipated day case rate of 90%. Standard positioning of patient, with slight head up, table rotation towards surgeon. Use intermittent pneumatic compression for DVT prophylaxis. Local anaesthetic to all port sites before insertion of ports (10mls 0.5% bupivacaine*). Use of three 5mm ports and one 10mm port. Low pressure CO2 insufflation (10mmHg). Meticulous washout at end of procedure. Instillation of 30mls 0.25% bupivacaine* around liver and gallbladder. No drains Method All cases of Elective Cholecystectomy done within July 1st, 2023, to October 31st 2023 at Frimley Park Hospital was included in the study. Electronic case notes and Operative notes was used to get required data. A total of 107 Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy was recruited Results Day case Rate was 45% (58 of 107 stayed overnight), Although 85% eventually went home the morning after the Surgery. Interestingly , 34% of those that stayed overnight had no Clinical indication to stay and was mostly Patient personal preference and delay in Recovery time. No surgeon documented the Pneumoperitoneum pressure used Conclusions Use of GIRFT recommended surgical technique. Proper documentation of the reason patient stayed overnight. All patients should be counselled Preoperatively to have someone to pick them once medically fit to go home even if recovery gets delayed to 20.00hrs.

paper.title: 986 Is the NELA Section on the CEPOD Form Completed for General Surgical Patients Upon Emergency Theatre Booking? - a Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) mandates the assessment of all emergencies surgical patients for inclusion in its database based on specific criteria. Fulfilment of these criteria prompts the addition of patient details and pertinent clinical information to the NELA database. Method In an initial audit, 50 CEPOD forms were retrospectively reviewed to assess the completion of the NELA section. A re-audit involving 40 CEPOD forms was conducted prospectively over a span of 10 days, following interventions aimed at improving NELA completion rates. Results The initial audit revealed that only 42.7% of the CEPOD forms completed by the general surgery team included the NELA section, indicating substantial room for improvement. Discussions with junior doctors and nurses highlighted various reasons for non-completion, notably a lack of understanding among newly rotated doctors regarding the significance of NELA. Consequently, interventions were introduced:Formal emails were sent to all surgical junior doctors.Informal discussions were held with surgical junior doctors and nurses.Posters were placed in proximity to where CEPOD forms were collected. Upon re-audit, the completion rate significantly increased to 87.5%, marking a substantial overall improvement of 44.8%. Conclusions Enhancing awareness among doctors and nurses resulted in more than a twofold increase in completion rates. Therefore, it is recommended to discuss about NELA with each new batch of junior doctors at the commencement of their rotations to increase awareness and emphasise the importance of NELA. Moreover, conducting a larger-scale study over an extended period is advised for a more comprehensive evaluation.

paper.title: EP584 - The standard of evening handover in the acute surgical department of a single regional centre: a closed-loop audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Handover is an important period that represents a potential risk to patient safety. The Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCSEng) have published guidelines on safe handover practice. The aim of this closed-loop two-cycle audit was to ensure general surgery patients at a single regional centre were handed over according to RCSEng guidelines. Method Evening handovers were prospectively audited between May 2023 to July 2023 using a proforma adapted from the RCSEng guidelines. A questionnaire relating to junior doctors’ views on the night handover was electronically disseminated prior to the first cycle. The intervention was an educational guide for foundation doctors on how to effectively hand over surgical patients, based on the RCSEng guidelines. P-values were calculated using a Mann-Whitney U test. Results 15 handovers were audited in the first cycle; of 84 patients handed over, 31% (26/84) met the RCSEng handover ‘minimum’ standard. 13 handovers were audited in the second cycle; 84 patients were handed over, the ‘minimum’ standard rate increased to 67% (56/84) (p=0.003). There were 25 responses to the questionnaire, 92% (23/25) were by foundation doctors, 48% (12/25) volunteered wanting more teaching on handovers. Conclusions Introduction of an educational handover guide is a useful method to improve the quality of surgical handovers, particularly in regional centres that may have a more complex case mix. This guide was later introduced as part of the ‘induction pack’ for foundation doctors rotating into surgery.

paper.title: 1056 Audit of Compliance with Local Guidelines on Opioid and Laxative Co-Prescribing in General Surgery Patients at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Constipation is a well-known side-effect of opioids, which are often prescribed in post-operative patients already at risk of ileus. Opioid associated constipation can further affect postoperative recovery and delay discharge. University Hospitals Birmingham guidelines suggest patients prescribed regular or as-required opioids for >1 day should be co-prescribed both stimulant and softener laxatives. This audit aims to assess compliance with these guidelines in the General Surgery department at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham. Method Inpatients under the upper gastrointestinal, sarcoma, and colorectal teams on a single date were identified and included. Retrospective review of drug charts was undertaken to identify patients prescribed opioids for >1 day and those co-prescribed laxatives. Stool charts were reviewed to assess bowel opening and Bristol stool charting. Results 87% (n=35) out of 40 patients were prescribed opioids. 34% (n=12) of these patients were co-prescribed laxatives; only 17% (n=6) were co-prescribed laxatives with both stimulant and softener action. Bowel motions were charted for 74% (n=26) of patients prescribed opioids. Conclusions Compliance with local guidelines on co-prescribing of laxatives with opioids is below expected. Accurate documentation of bowel motions and Bristol stool charting is important in guiding on laxative indication and prescription to prevent opioid associated constipation. Results of this audit will be shared with the department and education provided. Nursing staff will be encouraged to complete bowel charting in patients prescribed opioids. A re-audit will be undertaken after these measures are implemented.

audits.title: 1065 Beyond the Incision: Optimising Secondary Prevention Prescriptions for Vascular Surgery Admissions Through a Closed Loop Audit
audits.standard: Guidance-based secondary prevention with antiplatelets and statins
audits.finding: Antiplatelets started by discharge in 36% of those admitted without antiplatelet or anticoagulant; statins started in 20% of those without lipid-lowering therapy; 15% discharged on no secondary prevention.
audits.change: Education on guidance-based secondary prevention and modification of the daily handover proforma to monitor prescribing

paper.title: 1065 Beyond the Incision: Optimising Secondary Prevention Prescriptions for Vascular Surgery Admissions Through a Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Vascular surgery patients carry some of the highest chronic disease and mortality burden, often driven by atherosclerotic, pro-thrombotic pathophysiology. Cardiovascular mortality risk reduction through secondary prevention by anti-platelets and statins is essential, but studies repeatedly demonstrate deficiencies in initiating such therapies. We aim to improve the identification and initiation of secondary prevention agents for vascular surgery inpatients at a tertiary centre through education and structured handover practice. Method A retrospective audit was performed on pre-admission and on-discharge anti-platelet and statin prescribing in vascular surgery admissions from August-October 2023. Education on guidance-based secondary prevention therapies was delivered, and modifications to the daily handover pro-forma were implemented to monitor prescribing. A prospective post-intervention re-audit was subsequently performed on admissions from October-November 2023. Results On admission, 70% of the 89 pre-intervention and 49% of the 47 post-intervention cohorts presented with concurrent anti-platelet or anti-coagulant and statin therapy. Pre-intervention, anti-platelets were initiated by discharge in 36% of patients admitted without anti-platelets or anti-coagulants, and statins were initiated in 20% of patients admitted without lipid-lowering therapy. This increased to 55% and 41% of such patients respectively post-intervention. However, 15% and 13% of the pre- and post-intervention cohorts respectively remain discharged on no secondary prevention therapies. Conclusions Education and modifications to handover documentation improved the identification and prescribing of secondary prevention therapy for vascular surgery patients in relative terms. Patients without secondary prevention therapies accounted for a significant proportion of admissions irrespective of time-period and there remains further scope to improve secondary prevention prescribing in this high-risk patient group.

audits.standard: NICE antimicrobial prescribing guidance: stop/review date recorded for antibiotics
audits.finding: 56% had a recorded stop/review date.
audits.change: Informal discussions and an email to junior doctors on findings and NICE guidance, plus posters in doctors' stations.

paper.title: 1083 Assessment of Antibiotic Prescribing Compliance: Are We Adhering to NICE Guidelines for Recording Stop/Review Dates in Surgical Wards- A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim We've noticed instances where general surgical patients received antibiotics without a recorded stop/ review date in electronic prescribing system, potentially exceeding the recommended duration resulting in neutropenic sepsis in one instance . We aim to ensure compliance with NICE antibiotic prescribing guidelines by reviewing our practices and making necessary improvements for better patient care. Method Initial retrospective data analysis involved 50 inpatients receiving antibiotics in the surgical ward. For the subsequent re-audit, we implemented interventions and performed a prospective analysis on data from 40 patients over a two-week period in the same ward. Results Initial Audit Findings: Only 56% of patients had a recorded stop/review date for antibiotics. Discussions with junior doctors highlighted several reasons: Lack of Awareness of the NICE guideline of antibiotics stewardship. Patient Transfers: Patients moving between teams resulted in existing prescriptions without updated reviews. Paper Documentation: Decisions about antibiotics were documented in paper notes, not reflected on electronic prescribing system. Based on these findings, we implemented the following interventions: informal discussions and an email to junior doctors highlighting the findings and relevant NICE guidelines, along with placing physical posters in doctors' stations for easy reference. In the re-audit, 61.1% of patients had recorded stop/review dates, indicating more than 10% improvement. Conclusions Following discussions with prescribers post re-audit, our plan involves engaging with the electronic prescribing system. We propose adding an option to input review dates and making it mandatory to include stop/ review date when prescribing antibiotics to ensure sustained adherence to NICE guideline.

audits.standard: SIGN guidelines (16 criteria) plus 3 locally agreed criteria for immediate discharge letters

paper.title: 1099 Audit of Immediate Discharge Letters in General Surgery in Royal Alexandra Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To determine what percentage of immediate discharge letters for general surgical patients meet pre-defined standards. Method All immediate discharge letters (IDLs) for patients discharged over a week-long period from two general surgical wards in a single hospital were analysed. Results were compared to the 16 criteria outlined in current Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) guidelines, plus 3 further criteria agreed locally. A template for IDLs was then created and distributed amongst junior doctors writing IDLs after presentation at a local research meeting. Data was subsequently recollected recording the same criteria. Categorical data was analysed using a chi squared test. Results n=129 patients were included (n=67 in round 1; n=62 in round 2). Those without an IDL were excluded. On re-auditing, 15/16 (94%) of the SIGN criteria were documented more frequently, however only 5 of these were statistically significant (31.3%, p < 0.05). Results had also improved in all three of the locally agreed criteria, however only 1 of these was statistically significant. Overall, 0% of IDLs prior to the implementation of the template had all SIGN criteria present, rising to 6% after implementation of the template, however this was not statistically significant. Conclusions Implementation of an IDL template has improved the quality of IDLs for general surgery patients in the RAH, however further work is required to improve this further and create substantive change in the long-term.

audits.title: 1110 Thoracic Theatres: Audit of Theatre Efficiency
audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: Mean turnover time 94±14 minutes; handover to recovery 23±8 minutes and sign-in/transfer to anaesthetic room 36±6 minutes.

paper.title: 1110 Thoracic Theatres: Audit of Theatre Efficiency
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Turnover time is the cumulative time of processes between procedure finish (final dressing applied) and next procedure start (knife to skin). This audit aims to establish current turnover times and identify individual process times within patient turnover to improve theatre efficiency. Method This audit spanned between 22/5/2023-22/6/2023. Patient turnovers (N=41) from all elective thoracic procedures (N=61), across 19 operating days were examined. Operating days (N=2) with single cases were excluded from analysis. A process map was used to visualise the processes involved in patient turnover. Individual process times were extracted from Bluspier and data analysis performed using Microsoft Excel. All descriptive statistics are reported as mean±standard deviation with 95% confidence intervals. Results Mean procedure and turnover time were 93±16 and 94±14 minutes respectively. The audit revealed 2 main processes contributing to current turnover times, handover from theatre to recovery bay (23±8 minutes) and subsequent patient sign-in and transfer to anaesthetic room (36±6 minutes). Both processes make up 54±13 minutes of current turnover times. Recovery bay availability was influenced by ward/ ITU availability, with patients ready for discharge spent an extra 48±13 minutes in recovery pending ward transfer. This causes time blocks for the anaesthetic team who are unable to complete handover to recovery resulting in delays for subsequent patient sign-in. Conclusions Ideal solutions to improve turnover times would involve parallel processing with concurrent handover and patient sign-in and workforce expansion to improve ward availability. However, with limited resources, a cost-neutral solution would be difficult to achieve.

audits.standard: International standards for imaging in suspected acute appendicitis (not specified)
audits.finding: Ultrasound performed in 10%: sensitivity 44%, specificity 88%, PPV 57%, NPV 84%. CT performed in 22%: sensitivity 99%, specificity 100%, PPV 100%, NPV 88%.

paper.title: 1115 The Role of Ultrasound and Computer Tomography Imaging in the Management of Suspected Acute Appendicitis at a District General Hospital: A Clinical Audit Evaluating Our Practice Against International Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Definitive diagnosis of acute appendicitis (AA) continues to pose a clinical challenge. Computer tomography (CT) is the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosis, but ultrasound (USS) remains first-line and recommended for paediatric and young patients given the absence of ionising radiation. We conducted an audit evaluating the use of imaging as a diagnostic adjunct in diagnosing AA and whether it reduced the negative appendicectomy rate in a large UK district general hospital. A high NAR has both a significant patient impact (complications, increased hospital length of stay) and healthcare resource burden. Method We performed a retrospective analysis of electronic health records for a pre-Covid cohort of 344 patients who underwent a coded diagnostic laparoscopy/laparoscopic appendicectomy between 1st January 2019 and 1st January 2020. Histological confirmation of appendicitis was utilised as the gold-standard. Results USS was performed in only 10% of patients, particularly young females (16-35), and had 44% sensitivity, 88% specificity, 57% positive predictive value (PPV) and 84% negative predictive value (NPV). CT was performed in 22% of patients with 99% sensitivity, 100% specificity, 100% PPV and 88% NVP. Use of imaging (versus DLA) was associated with greater length of stay and readmission rates. Conclusions Despite its widespread use, ultrasound’s low sensitivity and PPV render its clinical utility debatable, particularly in females. Additionally, by counting occasions whereby ultrasound fails to visualise the appendix as negative results, its specificity is inaccurately increased. Therefore, CT remains gold standard given its highest sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing AA and its association with a reduction in NAR.

audits.standard: not reported

paper.title: 1134 Audit on Timeliness of Imaging in Bicep Tendon Ruptures
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess the time interval between the date of injury and the acquisition of imaging for patients suspected of bicep tendon ruptures. The primary objective was to identify areas for improvement in reducing delays and optimizing the diagnostic timeline. Method A retrospective analysis was conducted on a cohort of 28 patients presenting with suspected bicep tendon ruptures between January 2022 and September 2023 at Basingstoke North Hampshire Hospital. Electronic medical records were systematically reviewed to extract data on the time elapsed from the reported date of injury to the date of imaging, encompassing modalities such as ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Results The audit revealed considerable variability in the time taken to obtain imaging from date of presentation, with an average duration of 7.8 days. The average time from date of presentation to surgery performed was 23.2 days. Notably, delays were mainly due to patient unattendance and scheduling appointments for scans. Conclusions The findings underscore the importance of streamlining the diagnostic pathway for bicep tendon ruptures to reduce the time between injury and imaging/surgical procedure.

audits.standard: NICE guidance clinical audit tool for endovascular repair of popliteal aneurysms
audits.finding: All 11 patients had vascular MDT discussion before the procedure; all had appropriate antiplatelet therapy; 6 stents failed, 3 within one year, 1 amputation.

paper.title: 1142 National Audit of NICE Guidance for Endovascular Repair of Popliteal Aneurysms: The Kings Experience
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate care for patients undergoing covered stenting for popliteal aneurysms against NICE guidance, and to assess peri-procedural and post-procedural outcomes of patients. Method Retrospective collection of data in patients who had undergone endovascular repair of popliteal aneurysms from 30/5/2010 to 30/5/2023. 11 patients met inclusion criteria. Data collection was based on the NICE guidance clinical audit tool for endovascular repair of popliteal aneurysms. This included presenting symptoms, demographics, pre-procedure imaging findings, procedure details, duration of patency of the stent, peri-procedural complications, post procedure medical management and whether limb salvage was achieved. Results All 11 patients had vascular MDT discussion prior to procedure. Mean age was 71, 9 patients were male and 2 females. 5 stents remained patent to time of data collection or at the time of their death from other causes. There were no significant immediate complications. Of 6 failed stents, only one patient required amputation. Three patients had stents which remained patent for over a year with mean patency of 37 months, and 3 remained patent for less than a year. Stents that failed <1 year had reduced run-off vessels (mean 2). The smallest stent diameter (6mm) failed within 7 months. All patients had appropriate antiplatelet therapy. Conclusions Local experience of 11 endovascular stent for popliteal aneurysms. 6 failed and 3 failed within one year of insertion, with 1 patient requiring amputation. MDT input and full patient consent are mandatory prior to endovascular management of popliteal aneurysms. Technically, reduced run-off and narrower stents may be associated with poorer outcomes.

paper.title: 1168 Documentation During Upper Gastrointestinal Surgery Admission Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Admissions in surgery is one of the most important part of the patient care pathway and sets the trajectory for the rest of their stay. Without good documentation, the decisions made can be missed out and this will eventually lead to deficiency in the patient’s management. In this audit we aim to analyse documentation during admissions and look at ways to improve them. Method A retrospective review of documentation done during the admission for 50 random admissions in upper gastrointestinal surgery was assessed using the principles from Take Ten and the Shine Toolkit. Change implemented before second audit cycle: lecture at induction on how surgical assessment unit works, how admission and post-take ward round work, how to document & clarifications of job roles. The percentage of documentation was determined and going to be presented in a local audit meeting. Results 1st Audit Cycle vs 2nd Audit Cycle as percentage for documentation of History of Presenting Complaint (100%, 100%), NEWS (46%, 54%), Examination findings (96%, 94%), Diagnosis / Impression (94%, 94%), Advise to Patients (0%, 16%), Medication (42%, 54%) and Name of Clinician (60%, 72%). Conclusions The documentation during Surgical Admission improved in most areas and thus help lead to more safe and efficient patient care. However, there is still significant work that needs to be done. Further recommendations include implementing the Surgical Assessment for Emergencies (SAFE) Ward Round Tool, using electronic notes and availability of more computer on wheels.

paper.title: 1187 An Audit Assessing the Diagnostic Yield of Ultrasound Imaging for Suspected Acute Appendicitis in Paediatric Patients Against Royal College of Radiologists Benchmarks
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Prompt and accurate diagnosis of appendicitis in children is crucial to avert the risks of delayed treatment and reduce unnecessary appendectomies resulting from false-positive diagnoses. This audit aimed to evaluate the diagnostic sensitivity of ultrasound imaging in paediatric patients presenting with suspected acute appendicitis at a District General Hospital, seeking to meet or exceed the Royal College of Radiologists' (RCR) recommended target sensitivity of over 85% (1). Method In this retrospective study, we analysed the medical records of 102 children aged 2-16 who underwent appendectomies (open, laparoscopic, or diagnostic) over a two-year period. Ultrasound scans and corresponding medical records were reviewed to assess the concordance between pre-operative ultrasound findings and post-operative histopathology results. Results Among the 102 patients evaluated, histopathology confirmed appendicitis in 77 cases. Ultrasound correctly identified 52 of these cases, resulting in a diagnostic sensitivity of 67.5%, below the RCR's advised benchmark of 85%. For the 25 patients without histopathological evidence of appendicitis, ultrasound accurately diagnosed 17. Conclusions The diagnostic sensitivity of ultrasound for suspected appendicitis in our paediatric cohort was below the RCR guideline, highlighting a need for improvement. To enhance diagnostic accuracy, we recommend additional training for sonographers in paediatric appendicitis imaging and consideration of second-opinion protocols for equivocal cases. Further investigation into a dedicated paediatric ultrasound service may also be another way of to improve quality of scans.

paper.title: 1263 Audit on the Response to Raised National Early Warning Score (NEWS) in a Small District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Primary objective: percentage of patients seen by a clinician within the Trust's NEWS guidelines. Secondary objectives time interval for response, escalation to registrar/critical care outreach team (CCOT) and appropriate changes to NEWS monitoring. Method Retrospective study with a sample of 60 patients who scored 3+ in a single parameter or 5+ in total score. Events were categories to 3+ (in a single parameter), 5-6 and 7+. Timeline of the patient's raised NEWS were identified and documentation surrounding the relevant events were used to identify various information include: time of raised NEWS, time of escalation from nurse to clinician, time for clinician to review, escalation to senior clinician/CCOT, changes to NEWS monitoring. Results A total of 172 events occurred (NEWS 3+; 48, NEWS 5-6; 90, NEWS 7+; 34). Patients reviewed were 43.75%, 62.22% and 91.18% respectively. The median time for review for patients scoring 5-6 and 7+ were 1.03h and 1.00h respectively. Only 38.46% of patients scoring 5-6 and 20% of patients scoring 7+ were escalated to the registrar on call or CCOT. Changes to monitoring NEWS interval were 85.56% and 91.18% for NEWS 5-6 and NEWS 7+ respectively. Conclusions The data was presented at the local meeting to raise awareness. Downfalls of the audit included small sample size and the risk of implementing escalation changes during August handover.

audits.title: 1286 A Closed Loop Audit of the Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Elective Laparoscopic Cholecystectomies at a DGH
audits.standard: Local departmental antimicrobial guidelines for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
audits.finding: Adherence to guidelines 36%; correct antibiotics in penicillin-allergic patients 75%; co-amoxiclav overuse 60%.

paper.title: 1286 A Closed Loop Audit of the Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Elective Laparoscopic Cholecystectomies at a DGH
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To re-audit the compliance of departmental practice to the antimicrobial guidelines for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies. A Cochrane review found no evidence to support the use of antibiotic prophylaxis in elective cases. Method A retrospective study looking at all the elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies for the period between 1st June 2023 to 30th September 2023 using local Bluespier theatre software. Electronic operation notes were reviewed to identify cases where antibiotics were given. The main indications were bile spillage, conversion to open and cholecystitis amongst others. Total number of cholecystectomies carried out over the period was 92. At present gentamicin and metronidazole as a single dose was the choice. Results Antibiotic use during laparoscopic cholecystectomy is between 39% and 63% due to many cases not documenting the use of antibiotics. Adherence to guidelines reduced from 36% (2019) to 3% in 2023. Patients who received correct antibiotics allergic to penicillin was 75% (2019) and 100% in 2023. Continued lack of antibiotic documentation, use and indication in operation notes. Continued overuse of co-amoxiclav 60% (2019) and 87% in 2023. Conclusions Antibiotic prophylaxis in elective cholecystectomies was only performed correctly in 3% of cases. This can have a major impact on patient safety and also the financial aspect to the trust. Understanding why surgeons have failed to adopt the local guidelines may benefit in changing practice. We suggested an education session from the microbiology team to help better understand the importance of antibiotic stewardship and using laminated guidelines in theatre to ensure this is followed closely.

paper.title: 1293 Audit of Initial Management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding as per the British Society of Gastroenterology Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Lower gastrointestinal (LGI) bleeding is a frequent presentation to acute surgical teams. It can range in severity from mild to life-threatening, and most commonly presents with haematochezia. This data explores the implementation of the British Society of Gastroenterology’s guidelines at a District General Hospital lacking a management pathway for LGI bleeding. Method Data was collected on all patients presenting to the Emergency Department with per rectal (PR) bleeding. This was retrospectively collected from July to August 2023. Data collected included shock index at presentation, details for Oakland Scoring, hospital admission, complications, and follow up. Results All minor LGI bleeds (Oakland score of ≤8) were discharged with no readmission within 28 days. In July, four of 45 major bleeds were unstable, with one undergoing CT angiogram, compared to two of 27 in October with one undergoing CT angiogram. Of the 45 major bleeds in July, 32 were admitted (71.1%) and 13 were discharged (28.9 %), 5 without endoscopy. In October, 15 of 27 major bleeds were admitted (55.6%) and 12 discharged (44.4%), all with endoscopy. In July, three patients (23.1%) were re-admitted within 28 days, compared to one patient (8.3%) in October. Conclusions Despite integration efforts, there was minimal improvement in Oakland Scoring compliance, with many major LGI patients discharged. Nonetheless, all major bleed patients in cycle 2 had follow-up endoscopy organised and fewer patients were readmitted. This study could be improved upon with improved integration efforts for Oakland Scoring and Shock Index, such as providing the algorithm in a portable online format.

paper.title: 1296 A Closed Loop Audit to Evaluate the Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) Protocol in a Tertiary Oncoplastic Breast Reconstruction Unit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim A closed loop audit to assess the enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) protocol before and after implementation of an ERAS proforma, in patients who have undergone breast free flap reconstruction. To analyse the impact on patients after implementation. Method Retrospective data collection from March to June 2022 and September to November 2023, in a tertiary oncoplastic breast unit. Inclusion criteria: all patients who had undergone breast free flap reconstruction for breast cancer. Thirty-one patients in total. An ERAS proforma was designed in line with Trust standards and based on input from the oncoplastic breast MDT. The proforma included the following categories: pre-operation, operation day, day one, two and three post operation. The data was collected, analysed, and compared to data collected before implementation. Results The first audit showed poor adherence to the ERAS protocol, this improved after implementation of an ERAS proforma in the following areas: location of the proforma in notes, 0% found in notes before, 92% after. Anti-emetics prescribed 32% before and 100% after. Anti-inflammatory medication plus proton pump inhibitor prescribed 32% before and 100% after. Analgesia, laxatives, and enoxaparin prescribed in 100% of patients before and after implementation. Day 1 TWOC occurred 0% before and 50% after implementation. Day 2 drain documentation/management 26% before and 100% after. The average length of hospital stay was 5.5 days before, 3.75 days after. Therefore, inpatient hospitalisation was reduced by 1.75 days. Conclusions Adherence to an ERAS protocol is beneficial in managing patients during the perioperative period and leads to reduced inpatient hospitalisation.

paper.title: 1169 Local Trust Audit Reviewing the Use of NABCOP’s Fitness Assessment Guidance in Patients ≥70 Presenting to New Patient Breast Clinic in Royal Bolton Hospital Foundation Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Audit of Breast Cancer in Older Patients (NABCOP) has developed a fitness assessment form which should be completed for all patients who are ≥70 years when initially attending the breast clinic for suspected cancer. This form aims to standardise frailty assessment within this population and assist with treatment decisions. The form comprises of three sections: Clinical Frailty Scale, Abbreviated Mental Test Score and three further questions regarding co-morbidities. The Royal Bolton NHS Foundation Trust Breast Unit was audited against this national standard. Method This was a prospective audit assessing the compliance and completion of the fitness assessment form in patients ≥70 years attending new patient breast clinics over a two-week period. The results were then presented, and teaching provided to staff on the importance of this national standard. The fitness assessment forms were re-printed on yellow paper and the nursing staff were instructed to highlight patients ≥70 years on each clinic list. Data was then re-collected over another two-week period to close the audit cycle loop. Results During the first cycle, 14 patients who met the inclusion criteria were identified with a 0% compliance rate. After the interventions, as outlined above, the second cycle identified thirty-four patients with an 88.2% (30) compliance rate. Conclusions The compliance rate in using NABCOP’s fitness assessment score at the Royal Bolton NHS Foundation Trust Breast Unit significantly increased following education and the introduction of yellow paper visual prompts in clinics.

audits.standard: 100% of patients to have ACEi/A2RBs stopped at least 24 hours preoperatively, with clinical exceptions documented
audits.finding: 96% stopped; reasoning not documented for continuations (n=1).
audits.change: Team meetings to remind staff of the protocol (particularly ward and in-house unit staff), alongside the trust's new online prescribing platform.

paper.title: 404 A Reflection on a 3-Cycle Audit in the Use of Perioperative ACE-Inhibitors and A2RBs in Cardiac Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin-2-receptor blockers are stopped 24 hours preoperatively as continued use can cause hemodynamic instability and complications including kidney dysfunction, atrial fibrillation and increased mortality. To reflect on the results across 3 cycles to see if our recommendations have led to any improvements towards meeting the standard of 100% patients having ACEi and A2RBs being stopped at least 24 hours preoperatively with any clinical exceptions documented. Method There were 3 rounds of data collection (corresponding with each cycle) where patient inpatient notes and drug charts were reviewed. Emergencies and those not on ACE/A2RB were excluded. The first round of data was collected from 50 sequential patients admitted from October 2019 to January 2020, second round from 51 patients reviewed in December 2021 and the third round had been collected from 50 sequential patients admitted from January to June 2023. Results In cycle 1, 96% ACEi/A2RBs stopped with reasoning not documented for continuations (n=1). Recommendation was a team meeting to remind of protocol. In cycle 2, 76% ACEi/A2RBs stopped with reasoning not documented for 50% of continuations (n=12). Recommendation was a team meeting to remind of protocol, particularly ward and in-house-unit (IHU) staff. In cycle 3, 92% ACEi/A2RBs stopped with reasoning not documented for continuations (n=2). Conclusions The results suggest our recommendations have been effective along with the trust’s recent implementation of an online prescribing platform which has made it easier to track medications patients are given, reinforcing the positive impact of technology in reducing medical errors and ultimately improving patient outcomes.

audits.title: 407 Peri-Operative Usage of Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) in Cardiac Surgery: A 3-Cycle Audit Reflection
audits.standard: PPI the day before and day of surgery, continued until eating and drinking (until discharge if on DAPT); discharge letter to state indication and duration
audits.finding: Preoperative PPI 96%; discontinued once eating 25%; continuation documented 38%; discharge letter indication and duration 87%.

paper.title: 407 Peri-Operative Usage of Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) in Cardiac Surgery: A 3-Cycle Audit Reflection
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim PPIs reduce gastric ulceration after cardiac surgery; thus patients should receive it the day prior and of surgery. GI protection should continue until patient is eating and drinking, unless on DAPT and continued until discharge. Discharge letter should clearly state the indication and duration for prescribed PPI where patient is on DAPT. The aim of this 3-cycle audit study was to results to see if our recommendations improved compliance. Method Three cycles of data were collected from sequential patients where patient in-patient notes, drug charts and discharge letters were reviewed – first round (n=50, Oct 2019 - Jan 2020), second round (n=51, Dec 2021), third round (n=50, Jan to Jun 2023). Results Across 3 cycles, patients prescribed PPI preoperatively were 96%, 100% and 86% respectively. The data across 3 cycles showed that once drinking and eating, patients discontinued from PPI were 25%, 6% and 19% with continuations documented in 38%, 12% and 38% cases. 100% patients on DAPT were continued on PPI and after discharge with 87%, 68% and 62% having indication and duration for the PPI prescription documented in the discharge letters over 3 cycles. Conclusions Data over 3 cycles showed non-adherence to the standards persisted across most domains despite recommendations of team reminders of PPI protocols. This can be contributed to action-based errors in recording n drug charts as universal/standard documentation practices were not used. These could be mitigated by including guidelines on tick-box-checklists preoperatively, at ward rounds and discharge letters. This would be more time-effective, ultimately leading to better compliance.

audits.title: 590 VTE Prophylaxis Post-Thoracic Cancer Surgery: An Audit
audits.standard: NICE and MFT policy: 28 days of extended VTE prophylaxis after major (including thoracic) cancer surgery
audits.finding: Compliance 82%.
audits.change: Poster describing the MFT protocol on the thoracic ward and electronic version sent to junior team members.

paper.title: 590 VTE Prophylaxis Post-Thoracic Cancer Surgery: An Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The administration of extended VTE prophylaxis for 28 days has been recommended by NICE for patients following major cancer surgery in the abdomen or pelvis. Manchester Foundation Trust (MFT) has expanded upon this guideline to include patients having thoracic cancer surgery. However, the policy is occasionally not adhered to, owing to prescription errors and more. Our aim was to investigate policy compliance and identify areas for improvement to help optimise patient safety. Method For the first cycle, electronic records were scrutinised for patients who had thoracic surgery between 1st August 2023 to 14th August 2023 to ascertain if the above policy was followed. This included calculating the number of days for which Dalteparin was administered whilst the patient was in hospital, or, if the patient was discharged, (as in most cases), how many doses they were discharged with. Following this, a poster was created describing the MFT protocol and distributed across the thoracic ward, with an electronic version being sent on a secure messaging application to junior members of the team. For the second cycle the same method was adopted over a two-week period starting on 23rd October 2023. Results The first cycle demonstrated compliance as 82%. Following the intervention, compliance had increased to 90%. Conclusions The distribution of the poster highlighting the protocol had increased the number of patients receiving the correct VTE prophylaxis. However, with VTE being a serious post-operative complication, it is essential to aim for 100% compliance. Perhaps this can be achieved through further intervention such as departmental teaching.
