paper.title: 598 Chest Drain Monitoring Post-Thoracic Surgery: An Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Most patients have a chest drain inserted during thoracic surgery to remove fluid (such as blood, pus, or chyle) and air from the thoracic cavity. They are also inserted to create negative pressure within the pleural space to aid re-expansion of the lungs. The monitoring of chest drains is therefore vital to enable monitoring and thus management of surgical complications. Manchester Foundation Trust has a protocol concerning chest drain monitoring through documentation of certain parameters:Tube patencyDrain swingingDrain bubblingDrainage volume and typeDrain clampingDrain site conditionSuction levelBottle change date and time. Our aim was to investigate protocol compliance to ensure optimal patient management. Method For the first cycle, electronic records were scrutinised for patients who had thoracic surgery between 1st August 2023 to 14th August 2023 to ascertain if the aforementioned parameters were recorded. Following this, a poster was created highlighting the protocol and distributed across the department. For the second cycle the same method was adopted over a two-week period starting on 23rd October 2023. Results The first cycle demonstrated compliance for documentation of drain bubbling, fluid volume/type and suction as 90%, 84% and 87% respectively, and 0% for remaining parameters. The second cycle demonstrated compliance for documentation of drain bubbling, fluid volume/type, suction and drain site condition as 100%. Compliance for tubing patency was 14%, drain swinging 36%, drain clamping 21% and bottle change 21%. Conclusions The poster demonstrated improvement in documentation of all parameters, thereby aiding in the management of these patients.

audits.standard: Operation note as the standard for operation name in later documents
audits.finding: 30% of OR notes and 9% of ICU notes accurately named the operation; urgency incorrect or missing in 2% of OR and 87% of ICU notes.
audits.change: Standardised operation names and staff education.

paper.title: 615 Audit of Documentation of Operation Name During Hospital Stay
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Errors in the handover of patients from the cardiothoracic operating room (OR) to the intensive care unit (ICU) can compromise patient safety. We have previously shown that standardising the operation names and educating junior medical staff enhanced the accuracy of operation note titles. Aim This study aimed to assess operation name accuracy and consistency in OR and ICU notes, evaluating the impact of operation name standardisation and staff education. Method A prospective study of cardiac surgery patients at St. Bartholomew's Hospital was undertaken from November 29 to December 10, 2021. Operation notes were the standard and documents collected from the patients’ records were classed as fully accurate, containing acceptable/unacceptable variation, or inaccurate. Operation names were then standardised, and staff education followed. A subsequent data collection occurred from November 13 to November 19, 2023, under the same criteria. Results Pre-intervention, 30% of OR notes and 9% of ICU notes accurately named the operation. Post-intervention, this increased to 84% and 23%, respectively. Pre-intervention, the urgency was either incorrect or not documented in 2% of OR notes and 87% of ICU notes, which decreased to 0% and 29% post-intervention, respectively. Conclusions Improvements in documentation were observed post-intervention in both OR and ICU notes. However, significant discrepancies persisted in ICU notes. This is likely due to frequent staff turnover (every 2 years for surgical training, 3 months for ICU) and inadequate understanding of surgical details. In conclusion, continuous education is essential for sustained improvements in documentation accuracy.

audits.title: 1226 Audit of Chest Drain Stitch Removal in Thoracic Surgery Inpatients
audits.standard: Departmental guideline: remove chest drain stitches 5–7 days after drain removal
audits.finding: Compliance 20.8% (24 drains/stitches); stitches in place 6–44 days (median 10.5 days).
audits.change: Date of drain removal documented on the electronic medical record with a recommended stitch removal range.

paper.title: 1226 Audit of Chest Drain Stitch Removal in Thoracic Surgery Inpatients
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Most Thoracic Surgery inpatients undergo chest drain insertion during their hospitalisation. Some patients, however, experience extended stays or readmission after drain removal. Our departmental guidelines recommend removing stitches 5-7 days post-drain removal. This audit aims to evaluate and enhance our practice in this regard. Method This retrospective study included patients who remained as inpatients or were readmitted on day-7 following the removal of a chest drain that required stitches. The study was conducted in two cycles, the first cycle involved patients discharged from Thoracic Surgery between August 23rd and September 23rd. The second cycle took place six weeks after implementing an intervention that involved documenting the date of drain removal on the electronic medical records (EMR) with a recommended range for stitch removal. Results In the first cycle, there were 17 patients with 24 drains/stitches, with stitches remaining in place for a range of 6-44 days (median 10.5 days). In the second cycle, involving 14 patients with 22 drains/stitches, the range decreased to 4-18 days (median 7 days) post-intervention. Compliance improved from 20.8% to 54.5%. Importantly, we observed a reduction in incidents of bleeding, difficulty, or abandonment of stitch removal in the second cycle, as opposed to two cases in the first. Conclusions Timely removal of stitches following chest drain removal is essential for postoperative care, reducing the risk of complications associated with delayed removal. Our intervention significantly improved our practice. We recommend the continued implementation of EMR documentation as an effective means of enhancing patient care.

audits.standard: Assessment and documentation of septal haematoma, infraorbital nerve status and airflow symptoms
audits.finding: Septal haematoma documented 79%; airflow symptoms 32%.
audits.change: Presentation at ED teaching and board rounds, then a new trust guideline uploaded to the ED guidance app.

paper.title: 144 Title: A Repeat Cycle Closed Loop Audit Reviewing Emergency Department Referrals for Nasal Trauma to a Major ENT Centre; Practice Standards for Safe Care
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Facial trauma is a very common presenting complaint In Emergency care, referrals to ENT Emergency clinics (EC) without proper assessment risks complications and unnecessary clinic appointments. Complications that can follow nasal trauma include, septal haematoma, infraorbital nerve trauma and nasal blockage. Aim To assess clinical practice when reviewing nasal trauma and provide education and guidance to assist these reviews. Method A closed loop 3 cycle audit reviewed the documentation of clinical reviews for patients referred to ENT EC with nasal trauma. Cases were reviewed for assessment of septal haematoma, Infraorbital nerve trauma and airflow symptoms. Data was collected, analysed, and presented at the ED departmental teaching and morning board rounds. Data was then re-audited. A new trust guideline was uploaded to the ED guidance application and data was Re-audited. Each period of data collection covered 31 days. Results A total of 137 patients were included. Prior to the first intervention referrals were 26% higher than in both repeat cycles. Documentation of septal haematomas and airflow symptoms improved fractionally, increasing from 79% to 85% and 32% to 33% respectively. Infra-orbital nerve status was reviewed in 5% more patients after implementation of new trust guidelines. Conclusions Complications of nasal fractures are poorly assessed. Small improvements can be made with departmental teaching, but these changes will likely be temporary given the high staff turnover in ED. Implementation of clear guidelines can promote lasting change. This study demonstrates the benefit of continued education and pathway development on precision care while reducing burden on outpatient clinics.

audits.title: 653 An Audit of the Cancer Diagnosis Timeline Utilising a Telephone Triage System in the Two Week Wait (2WW) Head & Neck (H&N) ENT Clinic
audits.standard: Cancer diagnosis within 28 days and treatment within 62 days
audits.finding: Mean times to initial consultation, diagnosis and first treatment reported for 12 cancer patients (no figures given).
audits.change: Telephone triage by a head and neck clinical nurse specialist as an adjunct to clinic.

paper.title: 653 An Audit of the Cancer Diagnosis Timeline Utilising a Telephone Triage System in the Two Week Wait (2WW) Head & Neck (H&N) ENT Clinic
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim There is increasing focus on re-designing 2WW clinic pathways to improve their efficiency – aiming to diagnose cancer within 28 days and deliver treatment within 62 days. Our audit assessed if implementing a telephone triage system via a H&N Clinical Nurse Specialist could achieve this in the H&N 2WW Clinics. Method Following local audit approval, H&N 2WW referrals to the ENT department were reviewed – 2 months data prior to telephone triaging, and 2 months data utilising telephone triage as an adjunct to clinic. Patient demographics, primary referral symptom, diagnosis, timeline of consultations, and treatment were recorded using clinic letters, electronic records, and MDT outcomes. Results 273 patients were analysed; identification of 12 cancer patients from before telephone triage dataset and 14 cancer patients from the after dataset (non-H&N cancers, patients from other hospitals and those under maxillofacial were excluded). Tere was no significant difference in mean time to initial consultation (p=0.1875), mean time to diagnosis (p=0.0620), or mean time till first definitive treatment (p=0.7747). Analysing telephone triage consults alone (n=7), the mean time to initial consultation was reduced (p=0.0198), but the mean time to diagnosis (p=0.3130) and first treatment (p=0.7542) were similar. Conclusions This audit demonstrates objective evidence that telephone triaging does not delay cancer clinics or treatment from the current standard. If patients referred to 2WW clinic are initially telephone triaged, there is potential to significantly reduce the time to initial contact and there may be greater patient acceptability in terms of patient transport, time taken off work, etc.

audits.title: 815 A Retrospective Audit of the Management of Calcium Following Total or Completion Thyroidectomy, a Two Cycle Audit
audits.standard: Local guidelines for post-operative calcium management after total or completion thyroidectomy
audits.finding: 100% had calcium checked the following morning; 58% had Calcichew-D3 recommended before surgery; 3 readmitted with hypocalcaemia.
audits.change: Updated local guidelines, staff education session and a pre-operative pack (consent form, hypocalcaemia symptoms, Calcichew-D3 prescription if eligible).

paper.title: 815 A Retrospective Audit of the Management of Calcium Following Total or Completion Thyroidectomy, a Two Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Hypocalcaemia is a major complication following total and completion thyroidectomy, causing severe symptoms such as paraesthesia, seizures and increasing hospitalisation time. We aimed to minimise the incidence of complications and readmission due to hypocalcaemia following thyroid surgery by reviewing adherence to local guidelines and considering how current practice could be improved. Method Retrospective analysis of 26 case files was performed, notes were reviewed for documentation of prescription of Calcichew-D3 before surgery, timing of calcium and parathyroid blood tests and whether the local guidelines for post-operative care after total or completion thyroidectomy were correctly followed. A re-audit was performed after local guidelines were updated, an education session was delivered to staff and a pre-operative pack was produced. The pack included the patient’s consent form, symptoms of hypocalcaemia and, if eligible, a prescription of Calcichew-D3. Results 100% of patients had their calcium level correctly checked the following morning. Despite this, 3 patients were readmitted with hypocalcaemia following surgery. There was only evidence that 58% of patients had Calcichew-D3 recommended before surgery. Following the interventions, local guidelines were followed correctly in 100% of patients and no patients were readmitted due to hypocalcaemia over the audit period. Conclusions An update of local guidelines and education of staff led to an increased understanding of the management of hypocalcaemia following thyroid surgery and there was a reduced incidence of readmissions over the audit period. Furthermore, correct use of guidelines would lead to potential cost saving through avoidance of unnecessary blood tests.

paper.title: 1084 Clinical Audit of Surgical Site Infection in Emergency General Surgery Unit at London North West University Healthcare NHS Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To reduce the rate of wound infection in surgical patients in Emergency General Surgery Unit of Northwick Park Hospital. To access adherence to national guidelines by Emergency General surgery unit. To access the rate of Surgical site infection in Emergency General surgery unit at Northwick Park Hospital. To check if the rate of Surgical site infection in Emergency General surgery unit is in line with the national standard. Method This was an audit of NICE guideline((NG125)) undertaken in a retrospective manner. Data was collected through questionnaires and patient hospital records. Questionnaires where populated by contacting patients for feedback. Results Nice prescribed a target of 100% in the categories audited. The only exception is perioperative showering that NICE recommended should be carried out whenever possible. Pre-op Nose Swab 61% Perioperative showering 44% Theatre Wear 100% Informed to remove all jewelleries 97% Informed about pre-op antibiotics 66.67% Informed about intra-op antibiotics 14.29% Informed about closure method 77.14% Post op wound dressing services 44% Wound dressing education 49.29% Post op surgical site infection 6.76% Conclusions Overall, Northwick Park hospital maintain a commendable adherence to NICE guideline. This is evident from the very low rate of surgical site infection observed. Strict adherence could be seen in areas that are routinely recommended by NICE. Shortcomings recorded are due to failure in certain levels of communication than non-adherence to guidelines. To ameliorate this, it was concluded that checklist with all the shortcomings should be discussed with every patient and given leaflets to cover these before discharge.

audits.standard: Local CEPOD guidelines for time from booking to surgery
audits.finding: Overall 28% breached CEPOD time to surgery: abscesses 27% (of 30), appendicectomies 30% (of 33), colorectal operations 33% (of 21). By category: 18% of category 2, 31% of category 3, 26% of category 4, 37% of category 5 breached.

paper.title: 1178 A Study to Audit the Breach of CEPOD Guidelines in Emergency General and Colorectal Surgeries
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Is to audit any breach of local CEPOD guidelines by comparing the time of booking to the time of surgery, for emergency general and colorectal operations. Method The audit was done by gathering data about theatre booking time, comparing it to when the surgery took place, and calculating whether time to surgery breached the CEPOD guidelines or not. Study was conducted in the general and colorectal surgery department in Leicester Royal Infirmary, over a span of 2 weeks. All general surgical abscesses, appendicectomies, and emergency bowel operations were included in the study. Results A total of 90 emergency cases were selected for this study. These included 30 abscesses (perianal, perineal, gluteal, etc) of which 27% breached the CEPOD time to surgery. 33 appendicectomies (laparoscopic and open combined) were recorded, and 30% breached CEPOD time to surgery. There were 27 emergency bowel operations divided into 21 colorectal and 6 upper GI surgeries. Out of the colorectal operations, 67% required bowel resection, and 43% needed a stoma. 33% of all colorectal surgeries breached the CEPOD time to surgery guidelines. As per CEPOD categories, 18% of category 2, 31% of category 3, 26% of category 4, and 37% of category 5 breached the CEPOD guidelines. Overall, 28% of cases breached the CEPOD category. Conclusions This audit reveals there is scope of improvement in adhering to CEPOD guidelines while booking emergency general surgical cases.

audits.title: 1138 A Closed Loop Audit of Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Documentation with the Introduction of an Operation Note Template to Improve Adherence to the 2022 GIRFT Guidelines
audits.standard: GIRFT/RCS/ASGBI Best practice for Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Documentation (September 2022), 44 recommendations
audits.finding: Average adherence to the guideline 35%.
audits.change: Electronic operation note template designed in Microsoft Word with stakeholder feedback, rolled out November 2022.

paper.title: 1138 A Closed Loop Audit of Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Documentation with the Introduction of an Operation Note Template to Improve Adherence to the 2022 GIRFT Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess documentation of laparoscopic appendicectomies and measure the effect of introducing an electronic operation note template. Operation documentation is of great importance to patient care, clinical communication, facilitating research and providing a legal record. In 2022, GIRFT, RCS and ASGBI produced the ‘Best practice for Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Documentation guideline (September 2022) which contained forty-four recommendations. Method Between 1st June 2022 and 30th September 2022, 99 laparoscopic appendicectomies were performed at Broomfield Hospital, Essex whose operation notes were appropriate to be audited against the GIRFT guideline. Subsequently, an operation note template was designed on Microsoft Word using the guideline and refined with feedback from stakeholders including the surgeons who would be using it. The template was rolled out across the general surgery department in November 2022. Laparoscopic appendicectomies carried out between 1st December 2022 and 31st March 2023 were then reaudited. Results Between June and September 2022, prior to the introduction of the template, the average adherence to the guideline was 35%. Between December 2022 and March 2023, the average adherence was 55%, but was 89% in operation notes which used the template. Positive feedback on the template included ease of use and reduced time to complete compared to typing on a blank document. Conclusions This audit has demonstrated the important role templates play in significantly improving documentation and adherence to guidelines which positively affects patient care. The improvement in adherence even when the template was not used is likely due to the heightened awareness of the guideline.

paper.title: 1143 Audit of Conversion Rate from Laparoscopic to Open for Patients Undergoing Elective Colorectal Resection 2021-2022
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aims to compare the conversion rates from laparoscopic to open procedures for elective colorectal surgeries done in our hospital during 2021 and 2022 and to compare the results with the standard conversion rate of 14.3% as mentioned by the journal of society of laparoscopic and robotic surgeons in 2014. Method Data was collected from hospital computerised system. Inclusion criteriaPatients undergoing elective resection for colorectal cancer from January 2021 to December 2022.Patients undergoing elective colorectal surgeries for benign conditions including ulcerative colitis, sigmoid colon resections for recurrent diverticulitis, colectomies for endoscopically unresectable polyps with high grade dysplasia. Total of 41 patients underwent surgery in 2021, and 45 in 2022. Results Over the 24-month period, 86 patients underwent colorectal surgeries. Laparoscopic approach was attempted in 83 (96.5%) patients, and primary open surgery was performed in 03 (3.4%) patients. Of the 83 Laparoscopic procedures, 78 (93.9%) were successfully completed laparoscopically and 05 (6.1%) were converted to the open procedure. The annual conversion rate for colon cancer resections was 10.3% (3 of 29 converted to open surgeries in 2021) and 9.5% (2 of 21 converted to open procedures in 2022). The annual conversion rate for rectal cancer was 0% for both years; all 8 procedures completed laparoscopically in 2021 and all 11 procedures completed successfully laparoscopically in 2022. Conclusions Our audit showed that the conversion rate in our hospital for colorectal surgeries is only 6 % which is better than the international standards.

audits.title: 966 Managing Infection Risk in Flexible Cystoscopy: An Audit and Service evaluation
audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: Urinalysis performed and recorded in 227 appointments; 18 asymptomatic patients nitrite positive, 9 of whom were cancelled; no symptomatic patient had cystoscopy; 72 appointments had no infection safety netting documented.

paper.title: 966 Managing Infection Risk in Flexible Cystoscopy: An Audit and Service evaluation
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit and service evaluation was to investigate the way in which the infection risk associated with diagnostic and therapeutic flexible cystoscopy was managed in one NHS trust, and to consider the impact that positive urinalysis rates prior to flexible cystoscopy had on service delivery. Method All appointments for both diagnostic and therapeutic flexible cystoscopy across the trust were audited prospectively for a two-month period. Results 276 appointments were booked across this time period, of which 237 were attended and documented. Of these appointments, flexible cystoscopies went ahead in 219 patients and were completed in 215 patients, terminated early in 4 patients. Urinalysis was performed and recorded in 227 appointments. 18 asymptomatic patients tested positive for nitrites, indicating bacteriuria. 3 patients were symptomatic for urinary tract infection, including 1 patient who also underwent urinalysis and tested positive for nitrites. None of the patients who were symptomatic for urinary tract infection underwent flexible cystoscopy. Of the 18 asymptomatic patients who tested positive for nitrites, 9 were cancelled due to infection risk. Infection was the most common reason that a flexible cystoscopy did not go ahead. 72 appointments had no safety netting for infection risk documented. Conclusions There was an excellent rate of performing and recording urinalysis in this trust. There is room for improvement for the documentation of infection related safety netting. The decision to cancel appointments on the basis of infection risk in asymptomatic patients was taken on a case-by-case basis, though no symptomatic patients underwent flexible cystoscopy.

paper.title: 174 The Histopathological Assessment of Gastro-Oesophageal Carcinoma Resection Specimens: A Quality Improvement project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim HERO consensus and Royal College of Pathologists provide guidance for the minimum dataset pathological evaluation of gastro-oesophageal cancer resection specimens. The project aimed to assess and improve adherence. Method A retrospective study of the pathological evaluation of gastro-oesophageal cancer specimens resected surgically at a tertiary cancer unit (October 2021-March 2022), and re-audit (July-December 2022) following presentation of first cycle results. Results 26 and 23 specimens in rounds 1 and 2 respectively met inclusion criteria. Adherence was good in both rounds for reporting lymphovascular invasion status (92.3% vs 100%), correct reporting as R1 if tumour cells are found within 1mm of the margin (100% vs 100%), lesser curvature fat-blocking (100% vs 100%), and reporting of lymph node response following neoadjuvant chemotherapy (100% vs 100%). Improvement was seen in testing a minimum of 15 lymph nodes (88.5% vs 91.3%) and recording of resection margins in millimetres (CRM 77.8% vs 100%; LRM 80.8% vs 82.6%). One of the three specimens with <15 node yield was retested in round 1, compared with both specimens in round 2. Reporting of peri-oesophageal fat blocking showed no improvement (88.9% vs 77.8%). Conclusions Adherence was good during cycle 1, and there was improvement in most domains following presentation of results. Of note, both specimens in the second cycle with lymph node yield <15 were re-examined. Lymph node yield is determined by both surgical technique and avid pathology node search. The project proved to be an incentive for the MDT group as a whole to seek and adhere to good reporting practice.

paper.title: 840 Audit Cycle of Surgical Management of Traumatic Open Hand Wounds at BRI – Compliance with BSSH Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess whether the Plastic Surgery Department at Bradford Royal Infirmary are compliant with BSSH guidelines regarding timing of surgery for open soft tissue hand traumas (target rate 100%). Method Two retrospective data collection sets between 11th October 7th November 2021 and 7th March to 3rd April 2022 using Bradford’s Electronic Patient Records (EPR) and Xero PACS to review Plastic Trauma Clinic (PTC) clerking notes; Operation notes and Clinic letters. Patients included were all adult patients attending PTC with open soft tissue injuries needing definitive surgical treatment in an operating theatre/PTC. Results The initial study found a compliance rate of 74%, with a 62.5% compliance when it was the patient’s dominant hand. The number of individual soft tissues for repair was 14 for Flexor Tendon (FT), 17 for Extensor Tendon (ET) and Digital Nerve (DN) with compliance rates of 83.3% for FT and 76.4% for both ET and DN. The repeat cycle found an overall compliance of 72% with 62.5% for FT and DN and 81.5% for ET. Conclusions The main reason for non-compliance was due to hospital bed capacity and a lack of list space. Recommendations to improve theatre efficiency was made but despite this the same issues presented in the 2nd cycle. There was a total of 69 days of delay from the initial operation date, resulting in 17 overnight stays. Further recommendations to accurately plan allocated theatre time and not rely on the acute list to reduce cancellations have been made with a view to re-assess.

paper.title: 1032 Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy for Malignant Melanoma: An Audit Assessing Departmental Compliance with National Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To investigate and improve local departmental compliance with the current NICE Guidelines (2022) on sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) for malignant melanoma (MM). Method Two consecutive audit cycles of all patients undergoing SLNB for MM: Cycle A (1st June-22nd August 2023) and Cycle B (1st September–31st November 2023). Data collected from electronic records (Pathpoint/Cerner), including demographics; T-stage; Breslow Thickness; lymphovascular invasion (LVI); mitotic index; ulceration; intraoperative SNLB assessment and sentinel lymph node positivity. Results of Cycle A were delivered to the department prior to Cycle B. Exclusion criteria: SLNB not for MM (e.g., breast cancer), nodal clearance. Results Cycle A: 35 patients included: 20 Females + 15 Males, aged 33–80 years (Mean 62.26 years). Cycle B: 42 patients included: 15 Females + 27 Males, aged 25–88 years (Mean 60.0 years). Cycle B summary: 3/42 (7.1%) – no clear indication for SLNB (8.6% Cycle A) 0/42 (0%) - no T stage documented (0% Cycle A) 0/42 (0%) - no Breslow Thickness documented (2.9% Cycle A) 4/42 (9.5%) - no LVI documented (14.3% Cycle A) 4/42 (9.5%) - no mitotic index documented (14.3% Cycle A). Conclusions Our department demonstrated successful compliance with NICE guidelines on SLNB for melanoma at 92.6% in Cycle B (91.4% in Cycle A). Documentation of preoperative staging, Breslow Thickness and intraoperative narrative was also satisfactory at 100% for both cycles. Further work is required to ensure histology findings (Ulceration, Mitotic Index & LVI) and node appearance is accurately documented.

paper.title: 83 Quality Improvement Project on the Adherence to Hot Gallbladder Pathway Clinical Guidelines: An Improvement of the Hot Gallbladder Referral Pathway
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The quality improvement project’s main aim is to improve utilization of the Hot-Gallbladder(HGB) list. Although the guidelines are clear, a large number of referrals did not meet the criteria and were deemed inappropriate. We designed a self-explanatory proforma and added educational posters/aids that helped increase orientation and clarified the process and criteria. Method A set period of referrals was examined and audited and compared to the data collected post introduction of the proforma. The first audit cycle looked at patients referred for emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy during April-May 2023 which determined the need for interventions to improve utilization of the HGB list and adherence to guidelines. A well designed self-explanatory pro-forma was introduced along with informative posters. A second audit cycle was done during the months of June-July 2023 showing significant improvement. Results April-May 2023: 38 referrals, 4/34 accepted (10.5% successful). June-July 2023: 24 referrals, 7/24 accepted (29.2% successful). Average stay in hospital: April-May 2023: 6.45 days, June-July 2023: 3.88 days. Conclusions The introduction of the well-designed self-explanatory proforma has improved the quality of referrals and raised the awareness of the presence of the pathway. This has in turn improved utilization of HGB lists, decreased the load on elective lists and improved outcomes.

paper.title: 113 R-E-S-P-E-C-T: A Closed-Loop Audit Increasing the Quality of ReSPECT Documentation in a Tertiary Surgical Centre in the United Kingdom
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Resuscitation Council UK guidelines suggest Recommended Summary Plans for Emergency Care and Treatment (ReSPECT) must be considered for all patients at risk of deterioration or cardiac arrest or who want to have their wishes documented. This quality improvement project aims to evaluate the use of ReSPECT forms in acute general surgical admissions and improve compliance with the ReSPECT process. Method The audit was registered with the local audit department (REF: GENSUR/CA/2023-24/03). Data was collected in the form of random spot-checks, quantitatively and qualitatively evaluating the completion of ReSPECT forms for all patients admitted via the general surgical ‘take’ at a large inner-city hospital. The first intervention was the addition of ReSPECT forms to the surgical admissions proforma. Second-cycle intervention involved educating clinical teams about the importance of ReSPECT completion by delivering a teaching session and producing a novel poster to be displayed in the unit. Results The initial completion rate of accurate ReSPECT forms was 8%, with 30% counter-signed by the responsible consultant. Re-audit following the first intervention showed ReSPECT form completion rate of 27%, with 50% of forms counter-signed by a consultant. Conclusions The addition of ReSPECT forms to the surgical admission proformas is a simple and effective way of increasing compliance. Overall quality of ReSPECT documentation improved with our interventions, however, there remains scope for further improvement and ongoing education of clinical teams is paramount to improving compliance with the ReSPECT process long-term.

paper.title: 464 ENT Handover Audit Using ‘RAAAIDSSS’ Method: Initial Step in Excellent Patient Care
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Patient handover is vital in ensuring patient safety and quality of patient care, in line with Royal College of Surgeons Guidance of Safe Handover (2007). ‘RAAAIDDSSS’ method stands for resection (surgery), airway, anticoagulant, antibiotics, intake, drain, serology, scans, structure (plans). It shows comprehensive clinical updates for planning best management, ensuring smooth flow of activity and reducing morbidity. This method is ideal as otolaryngology patients often have altered airway anatomy and airway plans and consequently variable feeding routes. Aim To audit the compliance of RAAAIDSSS method. Method This is a prospective audit in ENT Department Imperial College Hospital NHS Trust, done in August and October 2023, with sample (n=100) for each cycle. The format was implemented in handover sheet and case presentation was run according to this method. Results First cycle showed good compliance to RAAAIDSSS handover method. The least compliant component is ‘structure’ which showed only 62%. Results were presented in local teaching. Second cycle showed significant improvement. Almost all components showed 100% compliance, except for the ‘intake’, which was 90%. Overall shows positive compliance to this handover method. Conclusions The department has showed improved compliance with the RAAIDSSS method. This audit brings significant positive impacts and changes to clinical practice in terms of patient safety, service efficiency and quality of patient care. This audit also holds valuable clinical value and opens doors for further audits as well as project expansion regionally and nationally.

paper.title: 805 An Audit on Managing Acute Pancreatitis in the Adult Critical Care Unit in a DGH
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of the audit is to describe current practice in the management of patients with severe acute pancreatitis admitted to ACCU and to improve quality and consistency of care for this group of patients by developing local clinical guidance on the use of antibiotics and nutritional support. Method A retrospective case note study of the 2-year period between 01/09/2020 to 31/09/2022 at a district general hospital. All adult patient admitted to critical care with acute pancreatitis was included in this study. Results A total of 11 patients were included in our study. 10 patients had antibiotics prescribed during their stay in critical care while one did not as advise by microbiologists. Antibiotic was initiated in 7 cases prior to admission to critical care, with 5 completed the courses of antibiotics which 3 of whom did not have a positive culture or any other sources of infection. With regards to nutrition support, 7 patients were fed via nasogastric tube and 1 with nasojejunal tube. 4 patients were not reviewed by a dietitian during their stay under critical care due to short length of stay over weekend. Conclusions This audit suggests the need for a separate management guideline on managing acute pancreatitis patients in critical care settings. Routine prophylactic antibiotics should be avoided. Regular microbiology rounds would be beneficial in improving quality of care. Early initiation of nutrition on patients in hypercatabolic state is a priority in improving care. Daily dietitian review would enhance the quality and consistency of care.

paper.title: 824 Assessing the Quality of Surgical Operation Notes in the General Surgery Department at a District General Hospital (QI Project)
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim assessing the current adherence to Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) guidance on the standards of documenting operation notes. There are 18 elements that must be present on operation notes including date and time of operation, name of surgeon and anaesthetist, type of anaesthesia, findings of operation, potential complications, closure technique, information on implants and signature of the surgeon. Method The present audit was a retrospective study of patients' notes to review their operation notes. 93 operation notes that were recorded August-September 2022 were reviewed in the first cycle. The second cycle reviewed 46 operation notes in May 2023. Results The outcome of the audit showed satisfactory adherence to majority of the RCS recommendations. Time of the operation was only recorded in 9% of operation notes in the first cycle which improved to 76% in the second cycle. Only 46% of operation notes in the first cycle were signed by a surgeon which improved to 67% in the second cycle. Conclusions Areas that mainly required improvement were identified to be recording time of the operation and signature of the surgeon in the first cycle. The result of the first cycle of audit was communicated to surgeons. The electronic operation note templates were also updated. The second cycle showed a significant improvement in the quality of operation note documentation in May 2023. A continuous cycle of audit should be implemented to ensure the documentation standards are maintained.

paper.title: 972 Improving Surgical Ward Round Documentation: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background The surgical ward round (WR) is a critical multidisciplinary process. Adequate documentation of WRs have medicolegal and patient safety implications. Checklists have been known to improve outcomes, but there is no set template recommended for WR documentation. Aim This quality improvement project aimed to firstly, identify areas of poor documentation in WR notes and secondly, to improve these areas with the use of a template. Method Over three months, 20 dates were randomly chosen with an online random data generator. Variables were identified from literature recommendations. WR notes from 54 patients were analysed (cycle 1). Results were discussed in an expert-led meeting, and templates were constructed. To assess any improvement, 20 prospective WR notes were similarly analysed (cycle 2). Results Templates significantly improved documentation of lab findings (p=0.02), investigations (p=0.02) and plan (p=<0.01). For all other variables, no significant change was found. Fluid balance and drug chart reviews were significantly worse after the template introduction. Fluid balance, Estimate Discharge Date (EDD) and nursing presence on the round scored particularly poorly in both cycles. Conclusions The use of a WR template improves some aspects of documentation. Further work and perhaps a more robust intervention is required to improve overall WR documentation.

paper.title: 1102 Maximising Safety on Surgical Ward Rounds with a Concise Ward-Round Template: A Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Concerns raised at clinical governance meetings highlighted incomplete ward round documentation and near miss events in prescribing. Checklists have demonstrated improved patient safety and ensure standards of care are maintained. We evaluated documentation and prescribing accuracy in a baseline audit and sought to improve these with the implementation of a concise ward-round template. Method We identified essential patient safety orientated criteria for ward round documentation from trust and departmental guidelines. Compliance with criteria was assessed by audit before and after the introduction of a standardised ward-round template. A root cause analysis was performed to identify reasons for errors between cycles and to optimise the design of the ward-round template. A poster promoting the template was circulated to junior doctors and the results presented in clinical governance. Each cycle included fifty consecutive patients. Results The baseline audit identified no ward-round documentation in 8% of inpatient days. Prescribing errors with near misses were identified in two cases. Poor documentation and communication were the most significant contributing factors in root cause analysis. After implementation of a ward-round template all inpatient days had a ward round entry, 96% using the template. Documentation of essential criteria improved from 32% to 93% (p<0.05) and there were no prescribing errors. Compliance with VTE guidelines improved from 70% to 98% (p<0.05). Conclusions This quality improvement project implementing a ward-round template improved documentation of essential patient safety orientated criteria and compliance with trust guidelines. Adherence to the ward round template was high several months after implementation, suggesting that ongoing use is viable.

paper.abstract: Abstract Aim In this Quality Improvement project, we aimed to enhance patient understanding of urological procedures. Our approach involved designing a BAUS QR code poster and integrating paperless leaflets into consultations, with the future goal of sustainability. Method Initial data collection from 30 patients, through a questionnaire during urology consultations, guided the project. The introduction of QR code posters linked to BAUS leaflets was assessed through a re-audit involving 25 patients. Results Results showed that all 55 participants used smartphones, with 71% utilizing them for medical searches. While 56% were initially familiar with QR codes, patient satisfaction remained consistently high before and after the QR code poster implementation. Among pre-operative patients, 85% received patient information leaflets initially, increasing to 100% patients receiving patient information leaflet post QR code poster implementation. Post-operative patients receiving patient information leaflets was only 40% but incremented to 72% after the QR code poster implementation. Conclusions The project demonstrated that QR codes, complementing verbal consultations and paper leaflets, effectively provided information on urological procedures and lifestyle advice. Importantly, this innovation supports the transition to a paperless approach, contributing to long-term sustainability.

audits.standard: RCS Good Surgical Practice consent guidance
audits.finding: Benefits and risks 100%, clinicians involved 100%, indication 87%, alternative treatment 62%, patient information leaflet with follow-up information 37%.

paper.title: 480 RCS Good Surgical Practice Consent Guidelines: An Audit of Compliance After the Introduction of Digital Consent
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Informed consent is an ethical and legal obligation of modern-day clinicians. It protects patients from harm and doctors from litigation. Digital consent may enhance patients’ satisfaction and understanding, whilst also facilitating shared decision making. At our institution, digital consent (Concentric®) was introduced to the General Surgery department in May 2022. Aim To evaluate whether electronic consent forms on Concentric® followed RCS Good Surgical Practice Guidelines. Method A retrospective review was conducted on all patients consented using Concentric® by the General Surgery team for the calendar month of August 2023. Endoscopic procedures, blood transfusions and duplicate consent forms were excluded. Data was collected based on current RCS Good Surgical Practice Guidelines. Additional information was extracted from the theatre management software (ORMIS), correlating the time of consent with the date of the procedure. Results Over the month, 398 consent episodes were evaluated. Compliance with RCS standards was as follows: benefits and risks of procedures (100%), clinicians involved (100%), indication for procedure (87%), alternative treatment (62%), and patient information leaflet with follow-up information (37%). Among elective procedures (186 episodes), only 32% of patients were consented prior to the day of surgery. Where there was a significant interval (>24 hours) between the original consent signing and the operation, only 52% had consent reconfirmed. Conclusions This audit identified areas of good practice and areas for improvement in relation to digital consent in general surgery. Making fields on the form mandatory would likely improve compliance with current RCS standards.

audits.finding: 17% of DCD and 0% of DBD pancreases, and 17% of DCD and 4% of DBD kidneys, exceeded national CIT recommendations. Median CIT DBD kidney 12:08, DBD pancreas 10:13, DCD kidney 10:30, DCD pancreas 07:44.

paper.title: 1089 Factors That Influence Cold Ischaemia Time in Deceased Donor Simultaneous Pancreas and Kidney Transplants: Results of a National Transplant Access to Theatre (NTACT) Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Various factors prolong cold ischaemia time (CIT) during simultaneous deceased donor pancreas and kidney (SPK) utilisation across the UK, impacting graft survival. However, there is a lack of data on these obstacles; therefore, this multicentre national audit aims to identify the factors that occur between the organs’ arrival at the implanting centre and transplantation. Method A prospective audit examining adult deceased donor SPK transplants across five UK transplant centres from February to September 2022. Precise time intervals between pre-transplantation checkpoints and perceived reasons for delays post-arrival at the implanting centre were recorded on RedCap platform. Descriptive statistics were used for analysis. Results Data from 29 SPK transplants were collected, with five exclusions for incomplete/incorrect data. Among these, 12 involved donations after brainstem death (DBD) organs and 12 donations after circulatory death organs (DCD). Median CIT for DBD kidneys and pancreas were 12:08 (IQR: 10:45-12:59) and 10:13 (IQR: 8:28-10:33), respectively. For DCD organs, corresponding figures were 10:30 (IQR: 09:13-12:17) and 07:44 (IQR:07:12-09:37). 17% of DCD and 0% of DBD pancreas and 17% of DCD and 4% DBD kidneys exceeded national CIT recommendations. Median times from organ arrival to knife to skin, warm ischemia (WIT) for pancreases, and patient arrival at the theatre were 03:17 (IQR: 03:00-03:48), 00:38 (IQR 00:31-00:43), and 01:41 (IQR: 00:52-01:57), respectively. Delays were reported in 96% of transplants. Conclusions This audit highlights significant proportions of organs exceeding national CIT cut-offs and identifies delays in organ utilisation requiring improvement.

paper.title: 1092 Perioperative Practices and Early Post-Transplant Outcomes in Deceased Donor Simultaneous Kidney Pancreas Transplants (SPK): Results of a National Transplant Access to Theatre (NTACT) Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Deceased donor simultaneous kidney-pancreas transplants (SPK) outcomes hinge on donor and recipient factors. Limited UK data on perioperative practices and outcomes prompted the National Transplant Access to Theatre (NTACT) study, aiming to unveil the current landscape. Method A prospective audit covered adult deceased donor kidney-only transplants in five UK centres from February to September 2022. RedCap recorded data and analysed descriptively. Results Among 29 SPK transplants, 24 were analysed. Preoperative antibiotics were universal, and consultant surgeons led all operations, though only 62.5% were directed by consultant anaesthetists. Central and arterial lines were standard, with 42% using advanced hemodynamic monitoring. Goal-directed fluid therapy, done using static parameters in 62.5% of cases, was common. Post-operatively, 75% were routed to the Intensive Care Unit. Encouragingly, 30-day mortality was 0%, and primary graft function rates were 83% for kidneys, 92% for pancreas. The median hospital stay was 12 days (IQR: 11-18), with a 29% readmission rate and 33% re-operation rate. Notably, readmission rates differed between Donation after Circulatory Death (DCD) and Donation after Brain Death (DBD) organs (17% vs. 41%). Conclusions Diverse perioperative practices and notable early complications were observed. While limited sample size precludes statistical associations, this underscores the need for future, more extensive studies.

paper.title: 367 Flexible Cystoscopy Audit in Patients with Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections (rUTI) / Lower Urinary Tract Symptoms (LUTS): A Path to Clinical Excellence and Cost Savings
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To minimize unnecessary flexible cystoscopy in patients with rUTI and LUTS, thereby enhancing patient care and optimizing the utilization of resources. Method Comprehensive data collection from the outpatient cystoscopy clinic, including demographics, indications (rUTI/LUTS), red flag symptoms and outcome. Results In October 2023, our DGH outpatient clinic performed 240 flexible cystoscopy procedures, with 24.1% (58 cases) for rUTI (32) and LUTS (26). Only 37.9% of patients exhibited one or more risk factors, necessitating flexible cystoscopy according to European Urological Association (EUA) guidelines. Additionally, over 13% of patients were under 40 years old with symptoms of rUTI/LUTS. Through collaborative efforts with the consultant body, we derived local consensus criteria for flexible cystoscopy, leading to the introduction of a new referral pathway. Departmental education may further contribute to a significant reduction in unnecessary procedures. Cost analysis, based on private clinic pricing, revealed a substantial predicted monthly saving. Conclusions The complex landscape surrounding the investigations and management of rUTI/LUTS, coupled with the decision on cystoscopy, often introduces uncertainty. By establishing a local consensus and implementing new criteria within our referral pathway, we have successfully brought clarity to the utilization of this procedure, which may result in enhanced and efficient patient care. Our adherence to EUA guidelines demonstrates our commitment to best practices. The predicted substantial cost savings emphasize the financial advantages of our interventions. Our collaborative and locally driven initiatives underscore our dedication to excellence in patient care and healthcare efficiency.

audits.standard: Guideline-recommended single instillation intravesical chemotherapy (SI-IVC) after TURBT for NMIBC
audits.finding: SI-IVC given in 3075 (39%) cases (low grade 48%, high grade 32%). In low grade cases, reasons for non-administration: surgeon did not request it (68%), requested but not given (7%), never given at the hospital (25%).

paper.title: 368 Single Shot Instillation Intra-Vesical Chemotherapy Administration: A Global Audit of Guideline Compliance – Results From the BURST-RESECT Study
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Auditing administration of Single instillation intra-vesical chemotherapy (SI-IVC) which has level 1 evidence in reducing cancer recurrence rate after Trans-Urethral Resection (TURBT) for non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). Method Using RESECT study (NCT05154084) data, a retrospective observational study was performed. Patients included underwent primary curative TURBT for bladder cancer. Cases were excluded if SI-IVC administration data was missing. The primary outcome was the rate of administration of SI-IVC. Results Data from 232 hospitals globally were included. After exclusions, there were 7933 (87.5%) cases analysed (44% low grade, 56% high grade NMIBC). SI-IVC was administered in 3075 (39%) of cases (Low grade + SI-IVC: 48%, high grade + SI-IVC: 32%). Considering low grade cases (3390), where SI-IVC is most beneficial, reasons listed for non-administration were “Surgeon did not request it” (68%), “Surgeon requested it, but it was not given” (7%) and “SI-IVC is never given at our hospital” (25%). Of 3566 cases where the surgeon did not request SI-IVC, 1497 (42%) the surgeon thought it was not indicated, 512 (14.4%) were because of potential contra-indications, no reason documented in 1210 (34%). Of these 2707 cases with no documented contraindication, 837 (31%) had low grade disease and likely would have benefitted. Conclusions The most common reason for non-administration of guideline recommended SI-IVC was that the surgeon did not request it, in almost one third of these cases the patient is likely to have benefitted. The RESECT study will test whether providing feedback and education to surgeons about their guideline compliance can improve compliance and outcomes.

paper.title: 1051 Audit of Statin Optimisation in Peripheral Arterial Disease and Abdominal Aortic Aneurysmal Disease
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim High-intensity statins are clinically an effective option for secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease and shown to improve patient outcomes, particularly in patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) or abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). NICE guidelines state Atorvastatin 80mg as the most cost-effective choice. This guideline provides a clear standard for all patients, which is auditable. Method A prospective study of 314 inpatients under vascular surgery of which 124 were part of the initial data collection. Following an educational intervention, 190 were collected in the second round. Exclusion criteria were applied to both cycles and a total of 52 and 67 patients remained respectively. Those that were switched to Atorvastatin 80mg on discharge were deemed to have been successfully optimised. Results Patients who were suitable for optimisation were compared to those who were discharged on Atorvastatin 80mg showing that 15 out of 52 patients were optimised in the first round and 43 out of 67 patients in the second round. Overall, the percentage optimised increased from 29% to 64% between the two cycles of data collection demonstrating a 2.2-fold increase in the percentage optimised. Conclusions Educational awareness between MDT members has successfully increased statin optimisation amongst PAD and AAA patients. This audit is applicable to most vascular comorbid patients and vital in preventative efforts to reduce the risk of future adverse limb or cardiovascular events, improving overall survival benefit.

paper.title: SP2.2 - A Retrospective Audit: Evaluating Changes in Negative Appendicectomy Rates from 2019 Before the Establishment of the Emergency General Surgery Service at a Tertiary Centre to 2022
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction and Aim Negative surgical exploration for suspected acute appendicitis remains prevalent, with a reported 20% rate in the UK Right Iliac Fossa Pain Treatment (RIFT) study. WSES guidelines endorse structured diagnostic pathways to decrease negative appendicectomy rates. To enhance acute surgery care, a dedicated Emergency General Surgery (EGS) service was established at a tertiary centre in 2020. This retrospective audit compares the negative appendicectomy rates between 2019 and 2022, therefore the main aim is to assess whether the introduction of a consultant-led EGS service influenced overall negative appendectomy rates. Methodology Appendicectomy numbers and histology results from 2019 and 2022 were analyzed. Histologically normal appendix cases were deemed negative appendicectomies, excluding unclear, other conditions, or missing reports. A retrospective review was conducted pre- and post-EGS service implementation. Results In 2019, 479 appendicectomies were audited, with a mean age of 34; 51% were female, and 20% were negative. Negative cases averaged 28 years, with 67% females. In 2022, 420 cases had a mean age of 40; 45% were female, 55% male, and negative rates reduced to 13%. Negative cases averaged 29 years, with 62% females. Conclusions Between 2019 and 2022, age groups were comparable. Negative cases in both years were more likely to be younger females compared to positive and total groups. The EGS service introduction demonstrated a notable decrease in negative appendectomy rates from 20% to 13% within two years, suggesting that consultant-led EGS services effectively reduce negative appendicectomy rates.

paper.title: SP5.2 - Reducing Elective Colorectal Surgical Site Infections with Change of Gloves and Instruments Prior to Abdominal Closure; A Multicycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Surgical site infections (SSI) carry a significant impact on patient morbidity, length of stay and antibiotic resistance. Our local colorectal unit has made several interventions over many years with no significant nor sustained improvement in the rate of SSI. The ChEETAh trial (Lancet, 2022) demonstrated a reduction in the rate of 30-day SSI by 13% with routine change of gloves and instruments (COGI) prior to abdominal closure. We aim to reduce our rate of SSI through implementation of COGI prior to abdominal closure; involving whole scrub team change of gloves and use of sterile instruments. Methods Adults undergoing elective colorectal surgery with an abdominal wound greater than 5cm were eligible for this study. Diagnosis of SSI was made based on at least one clinical indicator of infection or at least one symptom of SSI with data collection over 3 cycles spanning 11 months using clinical notes, imaging and microbiology results. The primary outcome was the diagnosis of a SSI involving the skin, subcutaneous, muscle or fascial layer up to 30 days post-operatively. Results The baseline SSI rate prior to intervention was audited at 29%. After implementation of COGI the rate fell to 23%. Further reinforcement of COGI and team education has demonstrated a further decrease in SSI to 15%. This has been sustained across a 6-month period post intervention. Conclusions Change of gloves and instruments is an effective, reliable and sustainable method to reduce the rate of surgical site infection in elective colorectal abdominal surgery.

audits.standard: European Hernia guidelines: smoking cessation and BMI <35 before elective umbilical/epigastric repair
audits.finding: 12% (N=7) known smokers; 13% (N=8) BMI over 35; smoking status clearly documented in only 15 cases; 10% (N=6) poor diabetic control (HbA1c > 48) not addressed.

paper.title: WP1.8 - No, we can’t repair your hernia: An audit to assess pre-operative optimisation for umbilical hernia repair
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims The European Hernia Association recently published guidelines which clearly outline the importance of pre-operative optimisation for those undergoing elective umbilical/epigastric hernias. The main factors of importance are: smoking cessation and BMI <35. This audit aimed to identify if we are adequately optimising our patients. Methods We retrospectively evaluated all elective umbilical hernia repairs from 1st January 2022- 31st December 2022 within a district general hospital setting. Clinic letters and pre-operative records were used to ascertain smoking status, BMI and diabetic control (HbA1c). Results 60 umbilical hernias were performed in our district general hospital setting from 1st January 2022- 31st December 2022. Of these patients, 12% (N=7) were known smokers and 13% (N=8) had a BMI of over 35 documented. Additionally, only in 15 cases, was there clear documentation of the patient smoking status. Out of these patients, 9 were subsequently found to be non-smokers and 6 remained smokers despite being given smoking cessation advice. Furthermore, in 10% (N=6) of these cases, there was poor diabetic control (HbA1c > 48), which was not addressed in clinic pre-operatively. Conclusion Patient factors such as smoking, obesity and diabetic control have been shown to significantly increase the rate of post-operative wound infections and complications. Patients are not being adequately optimised for elective procedures which puts them at increased risk of complications and increases the burden on limited NHS resources.

audits.title: WP1.9 - An audit of prophylactic antibiotic use in elective inguinal hernia repair
audits.standard: National guidance: no antibiotic prophylaxis for low-risk patients; single dose for high-risk patients
audits.finding: 53.33% of patients received antibiotics in line with national guidelines; 50.00% had prophylactic antibiotics overall

paper.title: WP1.9 - An audit of prophylactic antibiotic use in elective inguinal hernia repair
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims National guidance states that antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated in low-risk patients undergoing inguinal hernia repairs and that high-risk patients require a single dose. This audit aimed to compare the use of prophylactic antibiotics by general surgeons in a district general hospital performing elective inguinal hernia repair, to the current national guidance. The rate of post-operative wound infection was also recorded. Method All patients who underwent an elective inguinal hernia repair in the six months between January and June 2023, were identified retrospectively via the hospital database. Data was collected via the electronic patient record system on whether patients were prescribed antibiotics prophylactically at the time of surgery. Data was also collected on patient demographics including sex, age, BMI and rate of post-operative wound infection. Results The patient cohort was 94% male with an average age of 64. 94.79% of repairs were open. 53.33% of patients received antibiotics in line with national guidelines. Overall, 50.00% of patients in this audit had prophylactic antibiotics. The rate of post-operative wound infection was 1.04%, with 0% in patients who received prophylactic antibiotics and 2.08% in those who did not, which is not a statistically significant difference (P = 0.175). Conclusions Current evidence for antibiotic use is weak and therefore auditing local practice is essential in antibiotic stewardship. This audit is limited by the reliance on accurate record keeping, with regards to antibiotic prescribing and documentation of post-operative wound infections. Furthermore, patients may have had post-operative wound infections managed in the community setting.

paper.title: WP2.11 - Improving prescription of discharge medications for day case surgery patients using electronic patient records system (EPIC); a closed loop audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim It is important to provide patients who have undergone day surgery with appropriate analgesia, antiemetics, and laxatives. Failure to do this can result in a poor patient experience, patient requests for advice, readmission and morbidity. This study audited our adherence to the GIRFT guidelines for day case discharge prescribing. Methods Data was collected retrospectively on the discharge medications for all patients undergoing elective, day case laparoscopic cholecystectomy and inguinal hernia repair at two district general hospitals in our trust over a five-week period. A pre-populated discharge medication order set was then created on the Trust's electronic health records system (EPIC) to improve adherence to the GIRFT guidelines. Discharge medications were observed over a subsequent four-week period. Results Prior to our intervention, adherence to GIRFT guidelines was poor with 25% of patients only received the correct discharge medications. Following introduction of the pre-populated order set, 83% of patients received the correct discharge medications. Conclusions This audit demonstrates that utilizing electronic systems effectively can improve efficiency, ensure patient safety and enhance patient care.

audits.title: WP4.6 - Reducing Unnecessary Transfusion of Blood Products – A Quality Improvement Project in a General Surgical Department in a District General Hospital
audits.standard: NICE blood transfusion guideline thresholds
audits.finding: 112 units in 42 patients; 45 units (40.2%) prescribed per NICE guidelines; 23 units (20.5%) transfused back-to-back inappropriately.
audits.change: Departmental teaching sessions and posters of NICE transfusion thresholds on surgical wards.

paper.title: WP4.6 - Reducing Unnecessary Transfusion of Blood Products – A Quality Improvement Project in a General Surgical Department in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To audit adherence of transfusion of blood products against NICE guideline thresholds. To reduce unnecessary blood transfusions following departmental teaching sessions and installation of posters on surgical wards. Methods We retrospectively audited all patients receiving packed red cells transfusions consecutively across two consecutive four-month periods in a general surgery department. Departmental teaching sessions were held after the first audit cycle, supplemented by installation of posters including NICE guideline thresholds on surgical wards. The medical notes for each patient were assessed for pre-transfusion haemoglobin, indication for transfusion, and whether each transfusion was prescribed according to NICE guidelines. Results A total of 112 units of packed red blood cells in 42 patients and 133 units in 43 patients were transfused, respectively, before and after intervention. 45 units (40.2%) were prescribed according to NICE guidelines on first audit, improving to 67 units (50.4%) following intervention. 23 units of blood (20.5% of total) were transfused back-to-back inappropriately on first audit, reducing to 6 units (4.51% of total) after intervention. There were 2 self-limiting transfusion-related reactions (1.79%) on first audit, both in patients transfused above guidance thresholds, and no reactions following intervention. At a raw cost of approximately £135 per unit of donated blood, savings of £1830 were made over a four-month period (£5493pa), not including nursing and administration costs Conclusions Through simple local interventions and stricter adherence to transfusion thresholds, we reduced inappropriate above-threshold blood product transfusions in our hospital. This corresponded to a reduction in unnecessary blood-transfusion reactions and significant hospital savings.

paper.title: WP4.9 - Audit on writing outpatient clinic letters in the general surgery department at a tertiary care hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Clinic letters are crucial medical notes for a patient’s medical history and medico-legal purposes. We assessed the quality of clinic letters with the guidelines from the Academy of Medical Royal College suggested for writing a clinic letter. Method A retrospective collection of data was done from January – May 2023 and a total of 166 clinic letters were collected by independent authors and then analysed to avoid any bias in the collection. Results Multiple parameters were poorly documented and are mentioned in increasing order of missing data – Plan for patient/carer (37.5%), Care planning arrangements (44.6%), Complications (67.5%), Anaesthesia issues (89.4%), Allergies (94%), Diagnosis (94%), Time (99.4%), Preferred name (100%) and Personal identifiers (100%). These findings were presented in the clinical governance meeting and to improve the quality of the clinic letters, we created a generic clinic letter including mandatory parameters suggested by the guidelines. Conclusion There were a few parameters missing from the analysed clinic letters. An adequate intervention after being discussed in the clinical governance meeting, in the form of a generic clinic letter has been introduced. A repeat cycle is planned in 3-5 months to assess the improvement in the quality. There was a lack of documentation, which improved after the intervention advised by QIP. A teaching session for new junior doctors is planned at the induction session, to strengthen the importance of frailty documentation.

paper.title: WP7.4 - A closed loop audit assessing adherence to NELA frailty guidelines in over 75’s undergoing Emergency Laparotomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Background and Aims The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) 2023 recommend patients over 65 should have clinical frailty score (CFS) recorded, and, if frail or aged 80 or over, should have Care of the Elderly (COE) input. Due to the multi-morbid nature of frailty this population carry additional surgical and post-operative risk. This audit reviewed use of these recommendations at a large District General Hospital (DGH). Methods We performed a closed loop audit on all patients aged 75 and older who had an emergency laparotomy between September 2020 to December 2023. We collected data from their admissions, including CFS and if COE reviews had occurred. The data was analysed. Interventions included presentation at clinical governance, discussion with the COE consultant and a poster was developed for the surgical assessment unit. The data was again retrospectively collected to complete the audit cycle. Results A total of 94 patients were included. The initial audit found 0 patients had CFS recorded and 16% had COE review. The reaudit found significant improvement, with 92% of patients having CFS recorded and 46% having had COE review. Conclusion The second cycle audit has shown significant improvement at the DGH in recording CFS and organising COE reviews for patients over 75 having an emergency laparotomy. However, there remains scope for improvement. Suggested improvements include: a referral pathway to prompt COE reviews and the creation of the “general surgery geriatrician” similar to the ortho-geriatrician role. Organising COE reviews could improve patient outcomes and provide more holistic care.

paper.title: WP7.11 - An Audit of Geriatric Input and Analysis of The Barriers For Elderly Patients Undergoing Emergency Laparotomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Older people over the age of 65 years are recognized as higher risk surgical candidates and it is therefore recommended that their care should be coordinated through a multidisciplinary team (MDT) approach involving senior geriatricians, anaesthetists and surgeons. We audited 150 geriatric patients for medical input. Further in addition to the liaison services we analysed the characteristics of this group that would have benefitted from a liaison service. Methods An audit of 150 geriatric patients undergoing emergency laparotomy was carried. Our primary outcome was to look at input from geriatricians following laparotomy. Further we assessed the clinical characteristics of these patients and analysed the complexity of medical needs to benefit from a physician input. Results Only around 10% patients received a medical/geriatric input following an emergency laparotomy. Our audit highlighted the gap that exists in the clinical care for geriatric population against the NELA recommendations. Further we were able to work out a model of implementation for a geriatric liaison service. Conclusions Management of older patients with complexity requires surgical, critical care and geriatricians to collaborate. Implementing a local service with regular MDT’s will only serve to improve care and outcomes.

paper.title: WP8.3 - "Effectiveness of Malnutrition Screen and Interventions for Surgical Inpatients - A MUST Score Based Audit"
paper.abstract: Abstract Malnutrition significantly impacts surgical inpatients, affecting outcomes like infection rates, hospital stays, and wound healing. This audit evaluates the effectiveness of the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST) in identifying at-risk surgical inpatients and examines the subsequent interventions and nutrition assessments. Our prospective audit encompassed surgical inpatients admitted for elective procedures or via the emergency department. Data were collected through patient records and medical charts, focusing on MUST score completion, accuracy, and updates. The audit assessed staff training, consistency in scoring, and the quality of nutrition interventions documented by dietitians. Key findings revealed a high completion rate (83.3%) of MUST scores but identified significant inaccuracies due to insufficient consideration of BMI, weight loss, and acute disease effect. Only a minor percentage (15.6%) of patients had their MUST scores updated. Staff training inadequacies and inconsistent scoring practices were noted. Despite these limitations, clinical teams effectively identified at-risk patients using their judgment and promptly initiated interventions. A malnutrition awareness week was organised with the dieticians, and teaching sessions were conducted for the healthcare staff to enhance understanding and application of the MUST tool. This initiative aimed to raise awareness and improve the quality of malnutrition screening and management. The audit highlights the need for improved accuracy in MUST scoring, enhanced staff training, and ongoing professional development. Recommendations include comprehensive staff training, standardized documentation processes, interdisciplinary collaboration, and patient and family education. This audit underscores the importance of accurate malnutrition screening and effective interventions to improve patient care quality for surgical inpatients. It calls for action plans to address the identified gaps, thereby enhancing malnutrition management within healthcare settings.

paper.title: WP8.4 - A closed-loop audit on the use of abbreviations in consent forms in the digestive disease department at a tertiary care centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Consent forms can be misinterpreted due to the use of abbreviations and also in a court of law as a medico-legal document We performed this closed-loop audit to identify and improve the quality of medical consenting in this department. Method A prospective collection of data was done from July – Aug 2023 for the first cycle and Oct- November 2023 for the second cycle. 180 (100 surgical and 80 endoscopy) consent forms were analysed in the first cycle and 100 (50 surgical and 50 endoscopy) consent forms in the second cycle. Interventions in the form of posters, teaching sessions and discussions in the clinical governance meeting were used to improve the practice. Results In the first cycle, 99% of the surgery and 76 % of the endoscopy had abbreviations. The majority of abbreviations used were in the “risk” subsection (85% in surgical and 86 % in endoscopy) and in the title section (75% in surgical and 86 % in endoscopy). In the second cycle, 56% of the surgery and 4 % of the endoscopy had abbreviations. The majority of abbreviations used were in the “risk” subsection (42% in surgical and 78 % in endoscopy) and in the title section (38% in surgical and 66 % in endoscopy). Conclusion There was a significant drop in the use of abbreviations after the intervention. There were a few biases during the audit including unequal distribution of the consenting doctor. We are planning to improve this figure further by emphasising the importance of consent forms in the induction program of new juniors in the department.

paper.title: WP8.5 - Operative Documentation of Laparoscopic Appendicectomies at FVRH based on GIRFT - An Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Laparoscopic appendicectomy (LA) is the most performed abdominal surgery in the UK. Clear documentation is required to ensure safe and effective patient care. Aims To assess compliance with LA operative documentation at Forth Valley Royal Hospital using Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) guidelines. Methods 27 data points selected from GIRFT Guidelines were examined retrospectively for 172 LA procedures between 01/08/2022 and 29/09/2023. Completed numbers and percentages for each data point were calculated. Results Most consistently documented data points were intra-operative findings 168 (98%), details of closure 168 (98%) and method to secure appendix stump 161 (94%). Least consistently documented were drain insertion 7 (4%), estimated blood loss 5 (3%) and instructions for suture removal 6 (3%). 6 (37%) operative notes explicitly confirmed whether the appendix was removed in those with a macroscopically normal appendix. Conclusion Many data points had a high completion rate, whilst others had a low completion rate. We have highlighted discrepancies in documentation between surgeons which the department is hoping to streamline to avoid any gaps that could have patient care, legal or cost implications in the future.

audits.finding: Completion ANC 56 (44.1%), axillary radiotherapy 37 (29.1%), no further treatment 34 (26.8%); all with >3 macrometastases (n=10) had cANC; 58% of post-menopausal BCS patients with ER+HER2- T1 tumours (n=12) had further axillary treatment contrary to guideline.

paper.title: ThP1.2 - Management of breast cancer sentinel lymph node macrometastasis in the axilla; audit of current unit practice and evaluation of factors that influence patient management
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Detection of sentinel lymph node (SLN) macrometastasis for breast cancer no longer mandates further axillary surgery. Association of Breast Surgery (ABS) guideline provides recommendation to optimise patient management. It also acknowledges management uncertainties in specific patient groups. We aimed to examine our unit practice against national guideline and evaluate potential factors that influence axillary management. Methods Retrospective analysis of prospectively maintained electronic database determined clinico-pathological characteristics on patients diagnosed with SLN macrometastasis (n=127) at the Leeds Breast Unit (2020-2022). Axillary management was compared against ABS guideline. Results 56 (44.1%) received completion axillary node clearance (cANC), 37 (29.1%) axillary radiotherapy (aRT), and 34 (26.8%) no further axillary treatment. 80.3% had one macrometastasis. As per guideline, all patients who had >3 macrometastasis (n=10) underwent cANC. Type of breast surgery (mastectomy vs. breast conserving surgery; BCS) did not affect further axillary treatment rate (76.7% vs. 70.1%). Type of further axillary treatment varied with cANC commonest for mastectomy patients (78.3%) and aRT commonest for BCS patients (57.4%). In contrast to the guideline, 58% of post-menopausal BCS patients with ER+HER2- T1 tumours (n=12) received further axillary treatment. Where guideline stated management uncertainty, further axillary treatment was frequent; pre-menopausal patients (82%), T2 tumours (73%), lymphovascular invasion (74%), and extranodal spread (77%). Conclusion Our unit’s SLN macrometastasis management is mostly in line with national guideline but further work is required to avoid overtreatment. Where management uncertainty exists, patients commonly received further axillary treatment. Further research is required in these patient groups to optimise axillary management.
