audits.title: OGC SO36 - Complications of palliative oesophageal cancer stent insertion: Audit for a five year period
audits.standard: Published international standards (not specified)
audits.finding: 45% had stent-related complications; 14% stent migration into the stomach; 25% tumour overgrowth. Median survival after stenting 94 days.

paper.title: OGC SO36 - Complications of palliative oesophageal cancer stent insertion: Audit for a five year period
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Oesophageal stents are commonly used for the palliative treatment of inoperable oesophageal malignancy[1]. Stenting of the oesophagus may provide safe and quickly effective management for late-stage disease symptoms. However, there are common complications associated with the oesophageal stents. This audit looks at the types of early and delayed complications from oesophageal stenting, specifically for malignancy. We aim to stratify the types of complication, association between complications and the type of stent used, and the frequency of repeat stenting or repositioning. This will provide patients with better expectations of the complications and compare our practice against published international standards Method All fluoroscopy guided stent insertions between 1/1/2019 and 31/12/2023 for oesophageal malignancy were requested from the hospital radiology department. 101 patients were included for analysis. Their basic demographics were obtained, as well as a disease profile including tumour histology, staging and whether they underwent radiotherapy or chemotherapy. Complications of the stent insertion were then logged. The number of times stents were replaced or repositioned were noted. The type of stent, size parameters, features such as covering, antimigration device and anti-reflux valve were also assessed. In addition, any hospital admissions related to stent complications were also recorded. Results Of 101 patients, the median age was 75, with a higher proportion of male patients ( 71%). After stent fitting there was a median survival length of 94 days. 45% of patients had complications related to the stent. Stent migration was the most frequent complication, 14% of patients experienced stent migration into the stomach, which required repositioning or restenting. Both middle and lower oesophagus stents had equal complication rate. 25% of patients were reported to have overgrowth of tumour affecting the stent, and there was no significant difference in those fitted with a covered stent, meant to reduce overgrowth complications. Conclusion The complications directly resulting from oesophageal stents may adversely affect the palliation of oesophageal cancer patients. In this cohort, the most commonly occurring complications were migration of the stent, immediate symptoms after insertion, and overgrowth of the tumour. Although overgrowth of tumour is part of the disease progression, in many cases it made retrieval of the existing stent or reinsertion more difficult. Our results found no significant difference for complication rates between the different stents, nor the inclusion of antimigration devices. There were no deaths directly due to the stent and no oesophageal perforations reported.

paper.title: BN SO02 - Cholecystectomy HRG Coding Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Incorrect coding practices for elective surgical procedures carry significant financial implications at Trust level. In this project, we aimed to audit the current coding practices pertaining to laparoscopic cholecystectomies performed within the NHS WWL Foundation Trust during November 2021-October 2022 and calculate the financial burden resulting from this. Method A list of 194 patients undergoing a cholecystectomy and their allocated HRG coding at time of discharge was compiled by the coding department. A comorbidity and complication index (CCI) for each of these patients was calculated using the operation note together with hospital and GP records. With this information, the correct HRG coding for each patient was calculated and compared to their allocated coding at discharge to calculate the difference in tariffs generated. Results 69.23% of 194 procedures carried out during the reported time period were coded incorrectly. This amounted to a financial burden of £72,232 lost in potential tariffs, equating to £372.33 per cholecystectomy performed. Commonest CCI of 3 in 29% of patients with corresponding HRG code GA10J Commonest incorrectly allocated coding GA10K denotes a presumed CCI of 0 Conclusion High percentage of incorrectly coded procedures with significant financial implications at Trust level Currenty coding practice often incorrectly presumes a CCI index of 0 with subsequent incorrect GA10K coding. However, the appropriate coding for the vast majority of patients undergoing a laparoscopic cholecystectomy was GA10J. Education and awareness is underway to make improvements at a Trust level before re-auditing of data can commence.

paper.title: BN SO11 - Optimising Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A GIRFT-Based Audit and Efficiency Analysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) is the gold standard for managing symptomatic gallstone disease and is commonly performed as a day surgery procedure due to its safety and efficiency. Despite its established benefits, recent analyses at our local hospital revealed a decline in the day case rate for elective LC, falling below the national median as highlighted by the Get It Right First Time (GIRFT) data. Method We analysed patient data for elective LC performed between 1st October 2023 and 29th February 2024. The data included patient demographics, length of stay, and reasons for unplanned admissions. Procedures from the hot and emergency lists were excluded from the analysis. To enhance the day case rate, a business case was developed to extend recovery staffing levels and coverage hours in the DSU from 6pm to 9pm. Additionally, we requested the coding team to distinguish elective cases from hot list cases for more accurate future analyses. The impact of these changes will be evaluated in a subsequent audit cycle. Results During the observed period, 86 elective LC cases were performed, with a day case rate of 64% (55/86), exceeding the national median of 60%. The discrepancy with the GIRFT analysis was due to the inclusion of hot list cases in their data. The primary reasons for unplanned admissions included monitoring observations (46%), late afternoon extubations (29%), and intra-operative concerns (18%). The median length of stay for unsuccessful day cases was 1 day. Cost analysis estimated the unplanned admission costs at over £12,000 for LC alone during the observed period, based on the NHS National Tariff 2024/25. Conclusion This audit demonstrated that our day case rate for elective LC surpasses the national median. By identifying key factors leading to unplanned admissions, we implemented targeted interventions, such as extending recovery area hours. These measures aim to further improve the day case rate, enhance patient care, and achieve significant cost savings.

audits.standard: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy within two weeks of admission for biliary acute pancreatitis
audits.finding: 32.6% compliance.

paper.title: BN SO13 - Re-Audit of Biliary Pancreatitis Management: Enhancing Compliance with Timely Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Biliary acute pancreatitis requires timely management to prevent complications. Guidelines recommend laparoscopic cholecystectomy within two weeks of admission. A previous audit in our surgery department showed only 32.6% compliance with this guideline. This re-audit aimed to evaluate improvements in compliance, identify barriers, and provide insights for enhancing patient care. By retrospectively analyzing patient data from January to November 2023, we assessed progress and highlighted areas needing further improvement to align with established guidelines and ensure better patient outcomes. Method A retrospective analysis was conducted on a cohort of 32 patients admitted to the general surgery department with a diagnosis of biliary acute pancreatitis between January 2023 and November 2023. Patient records were reviewed to gather data on the timing of laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed within two weeks of the index admission. The compliance rate from this period was compared to a previous audit to assess improvements. Key barriers to timely intervention, such as the availability of ultrasound slots, hot gallbladder lists, and pre-assessment clinics, were also identified and analyzed. Statistical methods were used to confirm the significance of observed changes. Results he re-audit revealed a significant improvement in compliance with guidelines for the management of biliary acute pancreatitis. The percentage of patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy within two weeks of admission increased from 32.6% in the initial audit to 64.5% in the re-audit. However, the analysis identified persistent barriers to timely intervention, including limited availability of ultrasound slots, insufficient "hot gallbladder" surgical lists, and fear of difficulty of acute laparoscopic cholecystectomy. These findings highlight both the progress made and the areas needing further attention to enhance compliance and patient care. Conclusion The re-audit demonstrated a notable improvement in adherence to guidelines for the management of biliary acute pancreatitis, with a significant increase in timely laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Despite this progress, persistent barriers such as limited ultrasound availability, insufficient "hot gallbladder" lists, and pre-assessment clinics need to be addressed. Continuous evaluation and targeted interventions are essential to further enhance compliance, reduce complications, and improve patient outcomes. Ongoing efforts to refine clinical practices will help achieve the highest standards of care for patients with biliary pancreatitis.

audits.standard: 2021 ESGAR guidance on management of gallbladder polyps
audits.finding: 35 (36%) had laparoscopic cholecystectomy, including all with polyp >10mm; histology cholecystitis 69%, true gallbladder polyp 6%; 47% of symptomatic patients had two ultrasounds and two clinic appointments. Adherence to ESGAR was inconsistent.

paper.title: BN SO29 - Overinvestigation and unnecessary surgery for Gallbladder Polyps: An audit of compliance with ESGAR guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Incidental gallbladder polyps are increasingly reported on abdominal ultrasound and have a theoretical association with increased risk of gallbladder cancer. Most gallbladder polyps are actually gallstones and there is little evidence for any survival benefit or reduced rates of gallbladder cancer in patients under ultrasound surveillance. ESGAR guidelines attempt to standardize and rationalize surveillance protocols, balancing the risks of missed early cancers versus the costs of surveillance investigations. This audit aims to assess the investigation and management of gallbladder polyps as per ESGAR guidelines at a single NHS trust. Method An audit was conducted at a single NHS Trust in England. Searches were conducted on the electronic patient record for patients coded for K82.8 (Gallbladder pathology: other) from 01/01/2022 to 31/12/2023. Patient records were examined for radiological imaging confirming diagnosis of gallbladder polyp. Data was analysed using Microsoft excel and compared with the 2021 ESGAR guidance on management of gallbladder polyps. Results 97 patients were included. All polyps were diagnosed with abdominal ultrasound. Patients had, on average, two ultrasounds. 51% were seen in outpatients clinic. 35 patients (36%) underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy (including all patients with a polyp >10mm). Histology confirmed diagnosis of cholecystitis (69%), pseudopolyp (9%), gallbladder polyp (6%) and IPMN (3%). 74% (26/35) of patients that underwent cholecystectomy had biliary symptoms and 77% (20/26) had cholecystitis confirmed by histology. Despite having biliary symptoms at first assessment, 47% of polyp patients went on to have two ultrasounds and two clinic appointments. Conclusion The study confirms that the majority of ultrasound detected polyps are not neoplastic, and patients undergo multiple hospital visits, incurring significant non-therapeutic costs. Adherence to ESGAR guidelines is inconsistent. In the symptomatic cohort, however, a low threshold for laparoscopic cholecystectomy should be considered given the high likelihood of underlying stones.

paper.title: HPB SO25 - The impact of chest physiotherapy on post-operative recovery from open liver surgery: A quality improvement project
paper.abstract: Abstract Background The incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) after open liver surgery is high. Risk factors include age, body mass index, ex- or current smoker, and chronic lung disease. Early postoperative chest physiotherapy (CP), an essential part of any enhanced recovery protocol (ERP), can reduce PPCs, length of stay and healthcare costs. This study evaluated the uptake of CP after open liver surgery and resultant outcomes, following a quality improvement (QI) intervention. Method The project design involved two audit cycles: cycle 1 (C1) and cycle 2 (C2), each of five months duration, of consecutive patients undergoing open liver surgery, before and after a QI intervention (intensive preoperative patient education, poster campaign, increased engagement with physiotherapists regarding the importance of timely CP. Patients undergoing laparoscopic resections were excluded. Outcome measures included whether patients received postoperative CP at all, if so on which post-operative day (POD), for what duration, patient location, incidence of PPCs, and the length of postoperative stay. Statistical analysis was performed using (r 4-4.1) software, using the Chi-squared or Fisher’s Exact test. Results Despite more smokers/ex-smokers in C1(24%) versus C2(8%,p=0.04), only 18/50(36%) C1 patients received CP on POD1, versus 20/36(57%) in C2(p=0.07). Sixteen(32%) C1 patients received no postoperative CP, versus 7(19%) in C2(p=0.19). There were non-significant decreases in PPCs in C2(8%), versus C1(20%)(p=0.13). Three of four patients developing pneumonia in C1, and both those in C2, had no POD1 CP. Wards with higher physiotherapist:patient ratios had more POD1 CP: in C1 12/19(63%)[6/31(20%), p=0.001], and C2 14/15(93%)[6/20(30%) p=0.0001]. Median hospital stay was unchanged (4 days). Conclusion This QI project shows that even with an established enhanced recovery programme, the provision of postoperative chest physiotherapy is not universal. However, it can be improved with an education programme for both healthcare workers and patients.

audits.standard: PACT-UK synoptic reporting template for pancreatic cancer CT; compliance defined as more than 90% of information available
audits.finding: Compliance 0% for initial presentation scans and 4.2% (n=1) of 24 staging scans; the only compliant scan used the PACT-UK template

paper.title: HPB SO38 - Assessing current pancreatic cancer reporting practice against the PACT-UK Synoptic Reporting Template: An initial clinical audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background In the last decade, the incidence of pancreatic cancer has increased by 9% in the UK. The gold standard for initial assessment of pancreatic cancer (or even peri-ampullary cancer) resectability is pancreatic-protocol CT scan. The PACT-UK project introduced a synoptic template for pancreatic cancer to standardise CT reporting practice across UK and enable consistent reporting of pertinent aspects of resectability status such as vascular involvement of the tumour. The aim of this audit is to assess the quality of current CT reports received by a tertiary hepato-pancreato-biliary (HPB) unit against the standards set out by PACT-UK. Method A retrospective analysis of 66 patients who underwent pancreatic resection between September 2023 and May 2024 at a tertiary HPB centre was undertaken. Patients were excluded from the analysis if they underwent resection for benign pancreatic pathology, were diagnosed with pathology other than peri-ampullary cancer or did not have a formal report of their CT scan. Initial CT scans performed at presentation and if available, subsequent up-to-date staging scan prior to surgery were assessed against the PACT-UK reporting template, in accordance with their guidance. The audit was registered with our clinical audit team (no. 11643). Results In total, 42 patients with peri-ampullary cancers were included in this audit. All patients had a reported CT scan on presentation. Additionally, 24 patients had a reported staging CT scan. The compliance (i.e. more than 90% information available) with PACT-UK reporting standards was 0% for initial presentation scans and 4.2% (n=1) for staging scans. The only staging scan with >90% compliance was reported using the PACT-UK template. Majority (more than 80%) of CT scan reports lacked information on aspects such as pancreatic duct size, predicted tumour type and radiological stage, variant vascular anomalies, and arterial/venous involvement. Conclusion This audit highlights the substandard quality of current CT reporting for peri-ampullary cancer. There is an urgent need to adopt a structured and dedicated reporting template to address the issue. Utilising a template such as the one developed by PACT-UK will help ensure that relevant information is formally reported to facilitate optimal decision-making at MDT meetings, and assist surgeons in operative planning and oncologists in assessing treatment response.

paper.title: HPB SO60 - A Re-Audit: Radiological Investigations In Patients Diagnosed With Gallstone Disease
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Gallstones disease is very commonly encountered in general surgery and often detected by different modes of imaging. NICE guidance advises offering liver function tests and ultrasound where gallstones are suspected. MRCP and EUS are then considered if gallstones have not been detected. However, ultrasound is not always offered first line in patient cases, for varying reasons. This retrospective audit aims to assess the different radiological investigations used in gallstones against NICE guidance and the reasons behind this. Method Data was collected from a cohort of 108 patients over a 2 month period, all diagnosed with gallstones. The data collected included information regarding their demographics and imaging used to diagnose gallstones, as well as the reasoning when the first line investigation was not used. These results were then presented at the local general surgery CGM, findings were also communicated to doctors within the hospital. The audit was then repeated a year later with a similar cohort of patients, to compare findings. Results Mean age of patients decreased from initial audit to reaudit periodFemale preponderance in both audit and re-audit cyclePatients more likely to have imaging when abdominal pain present AND deranged LFTs as opposed to just one of the twoComparing total number of scans: less patients are undergoing CT scans (44 in audit period vs 31 in re-audit period)- 30% decreaseDecrease in number of patients having CTAP as first mode of scan (38 in audit period vs 21 in re-audit period). Total of 45 % drop. Conclusion While ultrasound scan is the first line radiological investigation where gallstones are suspected, it is not always the first to be used. This is for a plethora of reasons, including:Differing clinical judgment/ diagnostic uncertaintyDifferent clinicians/ specialities booking investigationsUnawareness of NICE guidanceLogistical delay in ultrasounds However, it does appear there has been improvement in adherence to NICE guidance between first and second cycle. Other modes of awareness will be implemented to further improve this, including publishing further guidance about NICE protocol within the trust so this is more easily accessible to doctors.

paper.title: HPB SO63 - A Closed-Loop Audit on Surgical Ward Round Documentation in a Tertiary Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Surgical ward rounds play a pivotal role in overall patient outcome during surgical and perioperative care. Clear and comprehensive documentations are crucial in providing an accurate account of ward round activities. We aimed to assess the quality of hepatopancreatobiliary (HPB) ward round documentation and the impact of a HPB surgical ward round proforma on the quality of documentation. Method 50 medical notes were reviewed in a tertiary centre to determine if key components of ward round documentation such as the date, time, diagnosis, procedure, consultant, person documenting, information communicated to patient, observations, investigations and management plan were documented. A proforma for ward round documentation was introduced. A re-audit was performed to review the impact of a proforma on ward-round documentation. Results The time of ward round, relevant history, NEWS and management plan were recorded in more than 50% of medical notes. However, the diagnosis, consultant, person documenting, information communicated to patient, wound review, medication review, fluid balance, investigations, follow up and discharge plans were documented in less than 50% of medical notes. After the introduction of a proforma, the date and time of the surgical ward round were documented in 94% of medical notes. 84% had initials of the consultants leading ward-rounds and the person documenting. More than 80% notes included relevant examination, information communicated to patient, wound and medications review. Conclusion Surgical ward round proformas have a role in improving ward round documentation. Good record keeping is essential for continuity of care, optimising quality of care and ensuring patient safety.

paper.title: HPB SO65 - An audit of the day-case rate of laparoscopic cholecystectomies at a busy district general hospital and factors affecting this
paper.abstract: Abstract Background The target day case rate of laparoscopic cholecystectomies at a busy district general hospital is 75%, as per Model Hospital Guidelines. The current rate at which day cases are achieved is 55%. This audit aims to identify factors relating to the DGH not reaching their day case target and explore potential solutions for these, with the intention to reduce patient’s hospital stay and, therefore, overall costs. Method 119 patients had undergone a laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the first five months of 2024. Exclusion criteria included hot cholecystectomies, common bile duct explorations and planned admissions. The remaining 85 patients were included in this audit. The data proforma included age, ASA, BMI, co-morbidities, Nassar grade, scheduled and actual time of operation and any reasons for delay. Results Of the 85 patients included in this audit, 34% (29) were not daycases. 11 remained an inpatient due to post-operative nausea or pain, 3 due to requiring an MRCP, 9 were kept in for monitoring, 2 had intraoperative bleeding, 3 had social issues and 1 required IV antibiotics. 58% of the 29 had afternoon operations. 48% of the 29 had a Nassar grade of greater than 1. 38% of the 29 had a BMI greater than 30. Conclusion Various reasons for a case to not achieve daycase status were found, with the most common being post-operative pain or nausea. It would prove beneficial to educate patients on common post-operative symptoms and focus on managing these symptoms effectively. Pre-operative appointments should aim to explore a patients home setting at the time of the operation and ensure to book inpatient stays for those who require it, in advance. Theatre lists should be optimised by giving high-risk patients morning slots.

paper.title: HPB SO67 - An audit to improve the perioperative administration of tranexamic acid (TXA) to reduce the need for peri- and post-operative blood transfusion in major HPB resections
paper.abstract: Abstract Background NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) triggered an ‘amber alert’ on 12 October 2022, meaning hospitals have been asked to put in place management plans to protect blood stocks. In line with these measures requested by NHSBT, The Royal College of Surgeons of England recommended using tranexamic acid in all adult surgical patients if more than 500ml of blood loss is likely. Results from the recent POISE-3 clinical trial confirm the quality, safety and cost-effectiveness of tranexamic acid in surgery, where more than 500ml of blood loss is anticipated. Method Patients were identified by searching the Sheffield Teaching Hospital (STH) operation note database using the key words: hepatectomy, pancreatectomy, liver resection, PPPD and pancreaticoduodenectomy. Retrospective case note review identified TXA administration, pre and postoperative haemoglobin level and blood transfusion prescription. Results 49 patients undergoing major HPB resection at Sheffield Teaching Hospitals (STH) from October 2022 to March 2023 were identified. Following the addition of a prompt in the WHO timeout pre-op checklist, a further 24 patients were reviewed. The audit compared the number of patients who received TXA, pre- and post-operative haemoglobin levels and incidence of intra- or postoperative blood transfusion (within 30 days) between the two groups. Including a prompt did not increase the likelihood of a pre-operative dose of TXA being administered. Mean change in haemoglobin and the proportion of patients requiring transfusion remained similar between the two groups. Conclusion Incorporating a preoperative prompt in the WHO timeout checklist did not improve adherence to guidelines for TXA administration in major HPB surgery. Future audits should continue monitoring these trends and investigating further strategies to optimise perioperative blood management. However, there are randomised controlled trials comparing TXA with placebo in liver resection and the recent TAC-PD trial showed that perioperative TXA did not reduce blood loss in pancreaticoduodenectomy.

paper.title: O2 Are elderly patients undergoing emergency laparotomy receiving appropriate geriatrician input: a closed loop audit as looking at NELA standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Patients over the age of 65 years undergoing emergency laparotomy (EmLap) have a higher 30-day mortality rate. NELA recommends that all surgical patients undergoing EmLap over the age of 65 have their clinical frailty score (CFS) documented on admission. Those aged 80 or above, as well as those aged 65 and above with a CFS of 5 or more, should have a prompt geriatrician review as an inpatient. Methods We completed an initial audit cycle over 6 months looking at the proportion of patients who had their CFS documents, and the proportion of patients who were referred for an inpatient geriatric review. We then implemented change by sharing clear ways of referring such patients via email, displayed posters in our offices and invited a senior Geriatric Medicine registrar to give a talk at our governance meeting. We then repeated the audit over another 6 months. Results In the first cycle, there were a total of 70 EmLaps, of which 42 were aged 65 years or more. Only 40% of these patients had a CFS documents and there were zero referrals to Geriatric Medicine. In the second cycle, there were 59 EmLaps, of which 40 were aged 65 years or more. 58% of patients had a CFS documented. 15 patients had an inpatient Geriatrician review. Conclusions We improved on our documentation of CFS and also increased our rate of Geriatrician referral for elderly patients undergoing EmLaps.

paper.title: eP12 Identifying and Managing Surgical Site Infections in Emergency and Elective General Surgery: A Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Surgical Site Infection (SSI) pose a significant health and economic burden to healthcare services within the United Kingdom. GIRFT and PHE have strongly recommended local auditing, protocols, and systems to identify, reduce and manage SSI across surgical specialities. Method A newly designed electronic SSI database was used to retrospectively screen and capture adult patients who underwent an emergency or elective general surgical procedure between January 2022 and March 2024. Records were automatically screened for biochemical changes suggestive of infection or keywords documented during ward round entries. Patients who met the criteria were highlighted as ‘probable infections’. Subsequently, a manual retrospective review of patient records was carried out to assess cases of actual infection. SSI was identified as described by the Centre for Disease Control (CDC). Results According to the database, 699 patients were identified, of which 21.8% were probable infections (153/699). Of those with a probable infection, 13% had a true infection documented (20/153). The median length of stay of those with a true infection was 15 days (6 – 170). 60% of infected cases were emergency surgeries (12/20) and 40% were open (8/20). 7.1% had documented cases of wound dehiscence (11/153), and 56% had clear documentation of a wound assessment post-operatively (86/153). Our intervention relied on creating an electronic SSI bundle to standardise documentation and capture true rate of infected cases in general surgical patients. Conclusion Heterogeneity and inaccuracy in wound assessment and documentation calls for robust, standardised methods to accurately capture SSI rates.

paper.title: eP24 Streamlining Diverticulitis Care: An Audit of Hospital Admission Practices
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Colonic diverticulosis affects about 25% of the population in developed countries, with 25% of these individuals developing symptoms, creating a significant burden on healthcare resources. This audit aimed to enhance clinicians' confidence in discharging patients with uncomplicated Hinchey 1 diverticulitis, reduce antibiotic use, ensure dietary advice is provided to all patients, and improve adherence to national guidelines for outpatient colonoscopy requests. Methods A prospective analysis was conducted, collating data on patients reviewed by surgical teams in A&E across two centres. Data collected included the date of admission, initial investigations (observations, bloods, imaging) and management (antibiotics, fluids, complications and follow-up colonoscopies). After the first cycle, we reported findings at our M&M session, teaching session and created posters throughout the department to reiterate the learning points. Results Prospective observations captured 20 patients in the first cycle and 15 patients in the second cycle, admitted between March-April 2024 and July-August 2024. Post-intervention, there was a positive correlation between admissions and the presence of significant co-morbidities, consistent with NICE guidelines. Although no reduction in IV antibiotic use was observed for uncomplicated diverticulitis, dietary advice significantly improved, with a 57.8% increase in specific guidance. Additionally, outpatient colonoscopy requests after diverticulitis flares rose by 30.7%, with notable improvements in the timing of these requests. Conclusions The interventions led to better adherence to guidelines, reducing unnecessary hospital admissions, and improving dietary advice and colonoscopy follow-ups. Targeted teaching and department-wide posters effectively enhanced guideline adherence, thereby improving patient outcomes.

paper.title: eP27 Treatment Escalation Plan (TEP) Completion Rates in Emergency Surgical Admissions: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims We aimed to audit treatment escalation plan (TEP) completion rates, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) decisions, in patients admitted under emergency surgery. Methods Data was retrospectively collected on all emergency surgical admissions in a district general hospital in March 2024. Exclusion criteria included patients under the age of 16 and patients discharged on the same day without an operation. Results were presented in a departmental meeting and a target of TEP completion on the first consultant ward round was set. The second cycle was completed in July 2024. Results 126 patients were admitted in March 2024 and 151 in July 2024. 19 patients (15%) admitted in March had TEP forms completed during their admission compared to 26 patients (17%) in July. In the first cycle 5 TEP discussions were completed by the parent surgical team (26%) compared to 11 in the second cycle (42%). The median time to TEP form completion from admission was 2 days in March and 1 day in July. 47 patients of the those admitted in March were operated on, of whom 39 did not have a TEP form (83%) compared to 69 patients operated on in July, 56 of whom had no TEP (81%). Conclusion TEP form completion rates remained low across both cycles, with an increase in the proportion of TEP discussions completed by the parent surgical team from 26% to 42%. Qualitative approaches may aid in understanding barriers to CPR discussions in emergency surgical patients and identifying strategies to improve TEP completion rates.

paper.title: eP48 Multi-cycle audit on antibiotic duration and stepdown following laparotomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To audit adherence to local guidelines on antibiotic stewardship in patients who underwent laparotomy, particularly, duration of antibiotics following definitive surgery/source control To increase antibiotic stewardship by reducing duration of antibiotic course and promoting consideration of early stepdown of antibiotics where clinically appropriate in patients following laparotomy Methods Data were reviewed for all adult general surgery patients who underwent laparotomy over a 4-month period in late 2023. Patients were excluded if there were incomplete or unavailable documentation relating to their operation or post-operative care. Data were extracted relating to patient demographics, type of operation and duration of antibiotic treatment post-operatively. Results were presented locally to the surgical team, highlighting trust-specific guidance on prescribing in intra-abdominal infection, and input from the microbiology team. A second 4-month cycle was completed in early 2024. Results Cycle 1: Data were extracted from 30 post-laparotomy patients. The most common indication for laparotomy was bowel obstruction (n=25), with confirmed perforation (n=8). The average duration of antibiotic treatment post-operatively was 11.2 days (± 7.7). Cycle 2: Data were reviewed from 49 post-laparotomy patients. 34 patients had bowel obstruction with 8 confirmed perforations intra-operatively. The average duration of post-operative antibiotic treatment was 8.6 days (± 5.8). Conclusions Duration of antibiotic therapy is significantly beyond what is recommended by microbiologists and local guidelines following source-control surgery. Possible contributing factors include surgical apprehension to stepdown or stop antibiotics in the peri-operative period, and system barriers caused by electronic prescribing.

paper.title: eP52 Enhancing Acute Pancreatitis Management through a Multidisciplinary Upper Gastrointestinal Team Approach: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Pancreatitis is a severe, acute inflammatory condition of the pancreas, potentially leading to life-threatening complications. This closed-loop audit assessed the impact of a newly established multidisciplinary Upper GI (UGI) team on the management of acute pancreatitis patients at Chelsea and Westminster Trust. Methods This closed-loop audit analysed 131 patients admitted with acute pancreatitis over two 6-month periods in 2023 and 2024. Data were prospectively collected on diagnostic timing, Glasgow score calculations, imaging, and referral practices, comparing these metrics to the first audit cycle. The first cycle occurred concurrently with the introduction of the in-hospital UGI team. Interventions following the initial audit included establishing weekly benign UGI multidisciplinary team (MDT) meetings with gastroenterology and radiology specialists, streamlining the ERCP pathway, creating a "hot" cholecystectomy pathway, and implementing targeted education within the surgical department. Results The second audit cycle demonstrated substantial improvements. Glasgow score calculation within 48 hours increased to 50%. Escalation of severe pancreatitis cases to higher care rose from 0% to 60%. Imaging within 24 hours achieved 100% compliance. The median time from admission to ERCP decreased to 5 days. Cholecystectomy rates within 2 weeks improved from 75% to 100%, and the transfer of non-gallstone pancreatitis cases to gastroenterology increased from 33% to 50%. Conclusion The audit highlighted significant advancements in acute pancreatitis management, including earlier diagnosis, timely surgical interventions, and enhanced multidisciplinary care, underscoring the positive impact of the implemented measures.

paper.title: eP55 Nela Compliance in A District General Hospital: A Clinical Re-Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background and Aim The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) is a national clinical audit, commissioned by the Health Quality Improvement Partnership (HQIP), under the National Clinical Audit and Patient Outcomes Programme (NCAPOP). NELA aims to enhance the quality of care for patients undergoing emergency laparotomies by providing high-quality comparative data from care providers. The aim of this re-audit is to assess compliance with NELA data entry by the trust, compare the results with the first audit cycle post-intervention and to ensure continuous trust compliance. Methods A re-audit was conducted using electronic data from emergency laparotomies performed between June and September 2024. All emergency laparotomies performed within this period were included, while non-emergency laparotomies and those outside the timeframe were excluded. The re-audit compared data from an initial audit cycle (which assessed data collection over a year), identifying compliance rates for data entry into the NELA database. Results In the initial audit, 111 laparotomies were performed, with 66% (n = 73) entered into the NELA database, while 34% (n = 38) were not. This re-audit revealed an increase in compliance, with 71% (n = 10) of 14 laparotomies entered, and 28% (n = 4) not entered. Conclusion The re-audit showed an improvement in compliance. Key interventions such as incorporating surgical registrars into the NELA team, redesigning the theatre booking form, and ensuring continuity of team roles during doctors' inductions were effective in boosting data entry rates. Continuous audits and improvements will help ensure sustained compliance and improved patient outcomes.

paper.title: eP66 Do emergency general surgery patients know their consultant? An audit based on the Francis Report
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction The Francis Report recommended introducing a responsible consultant, with a headboard showing this by the patient. It is frequently reported that patients are unaware of their responsible consultant. We set out to audit awareness of a responsible consultant at a tertiary referral centre. Methods Inpatients from March–August ’24 across 3 general surgical subspecialties (UGI, HPB and colorectal surgery) were included, with eligibility generated from ward round lists. Being unable to answer questions was an exclusion criterion. This audit was registered locally. After cycle 1, data presentation occurred, a change was initiated, then cycle 2 was conducted. Standard: 100% patients are aware of their responsible consultant. Results Overall, 107 patients were included. 68.6% (n=72) of patients with data were emergency admissions. There were insignificant demographic differences between cycles. Between cycles 1 and 2, patient awareness of responsible consultant significantly improved for UGI patients (p<0.001), and for all patients improved from 56.5% to 71.1%, though this difference was insignificant (p=0.089). Headboards showing named consultant improved from 43.5% to 53.3%, though this difference was insignificant (p=0.234). Conclusion During cycle 1, poor adherence existed. Results were presented to FY1 doctors and surgical departments, with juniors given whiteboard pens, aiding writing headboards. Cycle 2 results improved from cycle 1. It should be noted, electronic noting was introduced between cycles. Further cycles should aim to further improve headboards and improve awareness.

audits.finding: 31 (50%) entered; 4 (13%) met submission deadline; 18 (67%) registered more than 6 months after discharge; average delay 206 days.

paper.title: eP71 Audit of Emergency Laparotomy Workload in a District General Hospital: Are We Compliant with NELA Data Entry?
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) requires all emergency laparotomies to be registered on its database after completion of care. This audit aimed to evaluate our compliance with NELA data entry by comparing the hospital's workload with national NELA data. Method This retrospective audit was conducted over two cycles, covering a total of 30 months. The first cycle focused on NELA Year 8, a 12-month period, which included 61 patients. The second cycle assessed NELA Years 9 and 10, covering an 18-month period, with 75 and 38 patients, respectively. All emergency laparotomies were included, while elective surgeries and procedures not captured by NELA were excluded. Data were extracted from patient records and compared with the NELA database. Analysis was performed using Microsoft Excel. Results In the first cycle (Year 8), 61 procedures were eligible for NELA registration, but only 31 (50%) were entered, with just 4 (13%) meeting the submission deadline. Additionally, 18 (67%) cases were registered more than 6 months after discharge, with an average delay of 206 days. Following the intervention, the second cycle showed marked improvement. In Year 9, 84% of cases were registered, and in Year 10, 95%. The average time to data entry decreased to 100 days, and all cases were submitted before the deadline. Conclusion Timely NELA data entry is essential for accurate representation of departmental activity. Significant improvements in compliance were achieved through targeted interventions, demonstrating the effectiveness of focused efforts in meeting national audit requirements.

audits.standard: NCEPOD and GIRFT recommendations for suspected testicular torsion
audits.finding: 53.1% (n=17) reviewed by surgical team within 1 hour; 37.5% (n=12) explored within 1 hour of review; torsion in 21.8% (n=7), 3 (42.8%) needed orchidectomy.
audits.change: Data presented at local governance meeting and a new clinical pathway created.

paper.title: 1008 Management of Suspected Testicular Torsion – Audit of Current Practice
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Recent publications from NCEPOD and GIRFT have prompted a review of the care provided to patients with suspected testicular torsion. A local audit was performed comparing our practice to these new guidelines. Method All patients who underwent emergency surgery for suspected testicular torsion between 1stJanuary and 31stDecember 2023 were included in the audit. Primary outcomes were time from arrival to review by a surgical decision maker, and time from decision to operate to surgery. Secondary outcomes included post-operative diagnosis, procedures performed, and post-operative complications. Results 32 patients were included in the audit. 53.1% of patients (n=17) were reviewed by the surgical team within 1 hour of presentation and 37.5% (n=12) of patients underwent surgical exploration within 1 hour of surgical review. 21.8% (n=7) of patients were diagnosed with testicular torsion, 3 of which (42.8%) required an orchidectomy. A further 3 patients (9.3%) were suspected to have had testicular torsion which had de-torted by the time of surgery. Other post-operative diagnoses included hydrocoele (15.6%), epididymo-orchitis (21.9%) and torted hydatid of Morgagni (12.5%). 7 patients (21.8%) re-presented post-operatively: 3 were discharged with reassurance, 3 required antibiotics, and 1 required contralateral scrotal exploration following trauma. Conclusions Improvement is required to meet the standards recommended by GIRFT and NCEPOD. The data has been presented at a local governance meeting and a new clinical pathway has been created to facilitate prompt assessment and treatment of these patients. Data following its distribution has been collected and analysed.

audits.title: eP80 Transitioning from trauma: Audit on discharge quality for major trauma patients
audits.standard: RCP discharge summary toolkit; target 100% completion
audits.finding: Average completion 44.1%.
audits.change: Standardised discharge proforma for multiply injured patients, local training and education, then further reinforcement.

paper.title: eP80 Transitioning from trauma: Audit on discharge quality for major trauma patients
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Major trauma patients require complex multidisciplinary management with significant physical, medical, psychological, and social community rehabilitation needs. Clear effective communication on discharge is vital to ensure safe transition of care from hospital to community services. This audit aims to assess discharge quality, identify issues, and improve transition of care for major trauma patients. Methods Data was collected on major trauma patient discharge summaries before and after the implementation of a standardised discharge proforma, local training and education. Results were audited against the RCP discharge summary toolkit. The standard was that records would be 100% complete. Results The initial audit (n=20) revealed that discharges were often incomplete, unclear, and of insufficient quality with an average completion rate of 44.1%. Following proforma introduction, staff education and training this improved to 66.57%. Root cause analysis of issues comparing discharge between patients admitted on specialist major trauma ward (n=20,73.14%) vs outlier wards (n=20,60.00%) revealed significant disparity (t(50)=5.42, p=0.000). Following further reinforcement, a third cycle revealed improvement at 78.92% (trauma ward 81.08% vs outliers 76.76%; t(50)=2.12, p=0.037). Conclusion Major trauma patients are a unique cohort requiring comprehensive yet clear discharge to facilitate transition of care into the community. This can involve a multitude of different surgical specialties. Long-term quality improvement and education of rotational trainees on induction is essential for sustained quality. Patients on outlier wards are at higher risk of discharge issues. We present our proforma for multiply injured patients to improve discharge communication and patient care.

paper.title: eP85 Documentation of Consent in Appendicectomy: A Closed Loop Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this quality improvement project was to enhance documentation of informed consent for patients undergoing diagnostic laparoscopy and/or appendicectomy, ensuring compliance with legal standards and the Montgomery ruling. Methods Retrospective data were collected in an initial audit followed by two Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycles from handwritten consent forms of adult patients listed for emergency diagnostic laparoscopy and/or appendicectomy. Data included: grade of consenting clinician, pre-operative imaging, and documentation of recognised risks, for example, conversion to open and drain insertion. Interventions implemented between cycles included providing EIDO leaflets on the surgical unit and teaching consent practices during induction. Results Data from 54 patients were analysed (Initial=18, Cycle1=15, Cycle2=21). Consent was performed by SHO’s in 38%-47%. Significant improvements were observed in documenting risks such as blood transfusion (0% to 71.4%), drain insertion (16.7% to 85.7%) and adhesions (38.9% to 76.2%). Documentation of risks such as damage to structures, bleeding and infection remained above 90% throughout. EIDO leaflet use increased from 11.1% to 80.0% within the first cycle but decreased (66.7%) in the second. Overall documentation of COVID risk decreased from 66.7% to 28.6%. Conclusion The initial cycle revealed poor documentation of risks, correlating with lack of informed consent. Subsequent PDSA cycles demonstrated significant improvement, particularly in recording recognised risks such as blood transfusion, drain insertion and adhesions. These improvements align with the Montgomery ruling, which requires detailed disclosure of risks to patients. Continued focus and further implementation of information leaflets/ digital resources is required to ensure consistent practice.

audits.standard: Consensus guidelines: intra-operative packing for haemostasis; insufficient evidence for regular post-operative packing
audits.finding: Intra-operative packing 100%; regular packing after discharge recommended in 89%.

paper.title: eP87 To pack or not to pack (abscesses) - that is the question. An audit evaluating local practice and its estimated environmental impact
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Consensus guidelines in general surgery recommend intra-operative packing for haemostasis following incision and drainage (I&D) of perianal abscesses, but suggest there is insufficient evidence for regular post-operative packing. This audit evaluated current practice in a general surgery department regarding packing of perianal and cutaneous abscesses after I&D, and estimated associated carbon emissions. Methods Operation notes of I&D of abscesses were reviewed in two cycles over a 6 month period. After the first cycle, results were disseminated and discussed with the department, with a recommendation for regular packing after discharge only when considered necessary. Estimated carbon savings were calculated using published emissions factors. Results In cycle one, 100% of the 56 patients had intra-operative packing, and 89% were recommended regular packing changes after discharge. In the second cycle of 50 patients, there was a 10% reduction in intra-operative packing and 43% decrease in post-operative packing. Carbon emissions were estimated to be 16% lower for patients without regular post-operative packing (57 kgCO2e vs 68 kgCO2e), when calculating emissions for the entire patient pathway (including travel to healthcare facility, A&E attendance, surgery, and wound care consumables). Conclusion This ongoing QI project has demonstrated that there is a carbon saving associated with reducing regular post-operative packing after abscess I&D. There are likely to be other benefits, such as financial savings and improved patient experience, which could be assessed through future study. We continue to work on optimising the abscess pathway and disseminating best practice guidelines locally.

paper.title: eP93 The Effect of an eReferral Pathway on the Emergency General Surgical Take – A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To assess whether introducing electronic referrals for emergency general surgery in a single-centre District General Hospital would improve time efficiency in terms of quantity of bleeps and influence the number of general surgical admissions. Methods Data was collected retrospectively for patients admitted under general surgery between 9th to 13th and 16th to 20th September 2024. The primary outcome was the number of bleeps received by the surgical senior house officer (SHO) and registrar from 08:00 to 20:00. The secondary outcomes were number of patients clerked and admitted over a 24-hour period. The primary intervention was introduced on 16th September by emergency department (ED) stakeholders and consisted of all general surgical referrals being placed onto an online platform, with bleeps only reserved for patients of clinical concern. All ED and surgical staff members were given 1-weeks’ notice of this intervention with online access to guidance and training. Results During the first cycle, 188 bleeps were received, with an average of 37 bleeps per day (SHO: 11 and registrar: 26). A mean average of 34 patients per-day were clerked by the general surgical team with 17 admissions. Following the eReferral intervention, the total number of bleeps increased to 189 and averaged 38 per-day (SHO: 13 and registrar: 25). The average number of patients clerked increased to 39 per-day, with 22 admissions per-day. Conclusions An eReferral pathway has not been shown to mitigate the significant quantity of bleeps received by the general surgical on-call team and possibly increases the number of referrals.

audits.standard: National guidance: routine peri-operative paracetamol and post-operative NSAIDs
audits.finding: 89% received paracetamol peri-operatively (83% regular); less than half at maximum frequency; 34 avoidable IV paracetamol administrations; only 28% without contraindications prescribed post-operative NSAIDs (15% regular).

paper.title: eP95 Peri-operative Analgesia Use in Emergency Surgery: A Single-Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Pain management is widely recognised as a key part of peri-operative care. National guidance recommends routine use of paracetamol peri-operatively and NSAIDs post-operatively. Intravenous (IV) and oral paracetamol have equivalent analgesic efficacy. IV paracetamol has a higher carbon footprint, increased financial and time cost yet remains commonly used. NSAIDs are safe and effective for post-operative pain and have been shown to reduce opioid consumption in this setting. This audit investigated peri-operative analgesia practices for patients undergoing emergency surgery at our centre. Methods Retrospective data was collected for 47 patients undergoing emergency surgery over a one-month period. Prescriptions were reviewed using Electronic Prescribing and Medicines Administration software. Electronic records were used to identify patients with contraindications for NSAIDs, including structural kidney disease, stage 4 or 5 CKD, concomitant anticoagulation, asthma, and allergies. Results 89% of patients received paracetamol peri-operatively, 83% of which were regular prescriptions. Less than half received paracetamol at the maximum frequency. 83% of paracetamol prescriptions were for IV/oral route without preference for the oral. There were 44 (0.94 per patient) and 47 (1 per patient) pre- and post-operative IV administrations of paracetamol respectively. This included 34 avoidable IV administrations where patients were given oral medications concurrently. Only 28% of patients without contraindications were prescribed NSAIDs post-operatively, of which 15% were regular. Conclusions Prescribing and administration practices are crucial in ensuring optimal analgesic use. Further education regarding this topic and investigation into the barriers preventing maximal administration frequency, oral paracetamol & NSAID use is required.

paper.title: eP104 Use of Hospital NELA Data informs Quality Improvement Project leading to Reduced 30 day Peri-operative Mortality
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Regional surgical service provision reorganisation proposed moving Emergency General Surgery to “hub” centres to reduce operative mortality, nationally 11% on 1st NELA report 2015. We aimed to use unit NELA Data to inform emergency surgery pathway design & identify all high-risk (>5% risk of death) laparotomy patients requiring transfer. Previous Ambulance service audit had confirmed inability to identify at pre-hospital stage the need for laparotomy. Previous hospital audit had shown failure to identify need for laparotomy (1in 5 on National NELA) was associated with a 300% increase of risk of death. Methods All unit NELA cases in 1 year were reviewed & CT reports on unit database were reviewed to confirm indication for laparotomy identified (161 cases). The National NELA reports were reviewed to identify “high risk” characteristics; these were incorporated into an “Abdominal Pain Pathway” leading to abdominal CT in ED (ASA >2, previous surgery, sepsis, raised lactate, >45yrs). 2 cycles of the pathway over 2 fortnights of all patients presenting to ED were audited before pathway implementation. Results All patients requiring laparotomy identified on CT (164 cases NELA Yr6). Implementation of “Abdominal Pain Pathway” resulted in mortality reduction from 11.1% (Yr3) to 2.4% (Yr6) after implementation. Time to CT dropped from 2d19hrs to <4Hr. Conclusions Use of individual hospital NELA Data can inform emergency surgery pathways leading to reduced mortality - 11.1% to 2.4% (approximately 14 patients extra surviving on ∼160 pts/year). We recommend all units utilise NELA data to inform local policy via quality improvement process.

paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To identify General Surgery patients on elective and CEPOD theatre case lists and measure how often patients are offered a copy of their consent forms. In accordance with the Royal College of Surgeons guideline on consent- “Consent: Supported Decision-Making ”The patient should be offered a copy of their consent form after signing so they can review and retain. We aim to establish the number and percentage of patients receiving a copy of their consent forms in the General Surgery Departments at a Major Trauma Centre and a DGH. Methods Retrospective study. Patients were identified on Elective Surgical lists using Bluespier theatres Patients were identified on the CEPOD list during morning handover, confirmed surgical list from theatre coordinator on the day off and using Bluespier theatres Results 70 adult consent forms were reviewed during the patients admission over a period of 4 weeks. Data collected included number of patients provided a copy of the consent forms (0%). Interventions in an attempt to improve adherence to guidelines were introduced. A repeat audit of a further set of set of 35 patients was completed to assess the effectiveness of our interventions and there was an increased rate of 28% in the patients consent forms copies being offered as part of the consent process. Conclusion The results of this study suggests important areas of improvement. Our intervention has improved the quality of consenting within our hospitals. With these enhancements set to continue to further develop.

paper.title: eP119 Improving the Management of Frailty in Emergency General Surgery at a Tertiary Centre: An Audit of Current Practice and Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Frailty is present in many older patients that present as a surgical emergency. The physiological decline from frailty is associated with poorer outcomes, thus it is crucial that these patients are identified early in the surgical pathway. The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) stipulate that patients over age 65 should have a clinical frailty score (CFS) assessment and documentation at the first encounter with the clinical team. This allows Older Person's Assessment and Liaison (OPAL) teams to be consulted early to help guide a holistic overview of care needs. This audit assesses the implementation of the NELA recommendations at a tertiary surgical centre. Methods Two audit cycles were performed (May and September 2024) assessing all emergency general surgical admissions at Manchester Royal Infirmary for patients over age 65. Electronic patient records (EPR) were used to determine whether CFS was recorded and if OPAL were consulted. Quality improvement interventions included implementation of standardised rapid-use EPR documentation templates and staff education. Results Eighty-five patients were included in the audit. Prior to interventions, no patients admitted (0/47) had a CFS recorded and 13% (6/47) were reviewed by the OPAL team during their inpatient stay. Following intervention, a second audit cycle showed an improvement of CFS documentation to 50% (19/38) and OPAL review to 34% (13/38). Conclusion This audit demonstrates the effectiveness of EPR templates and staff training to improve early frailty identification and documentation in emergency surgical patients as well as better early OPAL involvement to improve clinical outcomes.

paper.title: eP121 Compliance of Emergency General Surgery Operation Notes at a Major Tertiary Acute Hospital in the United Kingdom to GIRFT Guidelines: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Medicolegal claims and litigation costs is estimated at £8 billion per year within the NHS in England, with 10% of cases involving General Surgery. Clear documentation is therefore critical to allow transparency and fair resolution of any medicolegal dispute. Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) works with many organisations including NHS Resolution to support the improvement of patient experiences and outcomes. This closed-loop audit assesses and improves compliance with GIRFT operation note guidelines within emergency general surgery where cases are more variable due to acute pathology. Method Operation notes for emergency procedures (appendicectomy, inguinal hernia repair, cholecystectomy and laparotomy involving bowel resection) Details were audited point by point against GIRFT Best Practise operation note guidelines. Results A total of 170 emergency surgeries were identified and analysed between February and May 2024 within our department. There were significant omissions of key surgical steps such as the identification of anatomic landmarks and intraoperative findings. We implemented a comprehensive Electronic Patient Record (EPR) operation note template based on GIRFT guidelines as a quality improvement measure. Notable improvements in documentation at a reaudit includes: appendicectomy (appendiceal base visible 0% to 68%, dissection of artery 46% to 96%), cholecystectomy (intraoperative findings 73% to 100%), inguinal hernia (testis in scrotum 0% to 100%) and laparotomy/bowel resection (staple-line check 5% to 66%). Conclusion This audit demonstrates the effectiveness of EPR templates as a tool to improve operative note documentation, and provides standardisation to promote clarity and transparency for both clinical and medicolegal purposes.

paper.title: eP122 A Tertiary Center Audit on SDEC Acute Appendicitis Pathway
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To improve the management of surgical SDEC pathway in patients presenting with clinical suspicion of appendicitis to Surgical Triage Unit STU in Nottingham University Hospital by following SDEC acute appendicitis pathway recommended by GIRFT. Methods This retrospective study enrolled 50 patients aged 16 years or older presenting with RIF to STU in June 2024. Data about patient demographics, clinical presentation and findings, investigation results, operative details, and post-operative/ post-discharge management plans were obtained from Electronic medical records of NUH. Acute appendicitis score AAS was calculated. Second cycle was carried out by collecting data from 26 patients in September 2024 after implementing interventions and developing local guidelines. Results On the first cycle, 85% of patients presenting with low AAS had imaging scans (CT/US) among which 2 presented with complicated appendicitis. 17 out of 50 (34%) underwent laparoscopic appendicectomy (12 within 24 hours) among which 14 had uncomplicated appendicitis. Antibiotics were only stopped in 53% of uncomplicated appendicitis patients after surgery. Only 34 out of 50 (68%) had recommended open access and safety netting instructions. Second cycle showed 93% of low AAS patients had imaging scans, 8 out of 9 patients underwent urgent surgery within 24 hours, antibiotics were stopped in 42% of uncomplicated appendicitis patients after surgery, and 92% of patients gained open access to STU. Conclusion This audit cycle improved post-discharge plans of SDEC pathway and highlighted the importance of imaging in clinically suspected cases in low AAS patients, and the continued need of improvement for antibiotic prescribing.

paper.title: eP127 Assessing quality and completeness of emergency general surgical operative notes: audit from a single institution
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To improve the quality and completeness of emergency (CEPOD) operative notes written by surgical trainees in a single institution Methods CEPOD operation notes from August 1st 2024 - August 31st 2024 were retrospectively reviewed and assessed against Royal College of Surgeons Good Surgical Practice recommendations of what to include in an operative note. Results Operation notes for 78 patients were assessed. 20% (N=16) were written by Core Trainees, 60% by Specialist Trainees (N=47) and 20% by Consultants (N=15). The areas that were most complete included: type of incision (N=71; 91%), operative diagnosis (N=74; 95%), operative findings (N=77; 99%) and the post-operative care plan (N=75; 96%). The areas that were least complete included: blood loss (N=5; 6%), DVT prophylaxis (N=20; 25%), details of implanted material where appropriate (N=2; 50%) and antibiotic prophylaxis (N=41; 52%). Conclusions Areas of improvement have been identified and have been addressed in the form of introducing a standard Emergency Surgery operation note template, introduced and accessible to all surgical trainees. A prospective re-audit is being undertaken in October 2024.

audits.standard: BOAST-15 blunt chest wall trauma guidance: surgical stabilisation within 48 hours (72-hour benchmark used)
audits.finding: Median time to SSRF 3 days (range 1–12); 74 (62.2%) within 72 hours and 45 (37.8%) delayed.

paper.title: 450 Timeliness of Surgical Stabilisation of Rib Fractures: An Audit Against BOAST-15 Guidelines in a Major Trauma Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess adherence to BOAST-15 blunt chest wall trauma guidelines on time from injury to surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF) at a major trauma centre and identifying factors influencing delays. A 72-hour benchmark post-injury was used, allowing an additional 24 hours beyond the 48-hour recommendation to account for assessment, conservative management trial, and surgical planning. Method Retrospective electronic note analysis (November 2020 - July 2024) was conducted to determine the date of injury and of SSRF. Patient characteristics such as Injury Severity Score (ISS), mechanisms of injury, ventilation requirements, ITU vs PTU stay, and pain relief methods were recorded. Results Of the 119 patients included, the median time to SSRF was 3 days(range 1-12), with 74 (62.2%) undergoing surgery within 72 hours and 45(37.8%) experiencing delays. Standard deviation of 2.41 days also highlights variability in timing. Longer ITU stays correlated moderately with increased time to surgery (Spearman’s coefficient 0.479, p<0.001), and assisted ventilation patients had a significantly higher mean time to SSRF (4.3 vs. 3.0 days, p=0.028). These findings suggest ITU and ventilation requirements could influence time to SSRF. Conclusions Streamlined pre-operative pathways and expedited multidisciplinary decision-making are needed to address delays in surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF). Given pre-existing evidence linking earlier surgical intervention for rib fractures to better outcomes, balancing timely intervention with patient safety is crucial. As this audit found limited correlation between most clinical variables and surgical timing, further exploration of other clinical, systemic, and logistical factors is needed to reduce delays and improve patient outcomes.

paper.title: 979 Optimising Surgical Documentation: A Vascular Department Audit Against RCSEng Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Clear and detailed documentation of surgical interventions is vital for ensuring continuity of care and patient safety. The Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCSEng) provides specific guidelines for operation notes, aligned with the GMC’s Good Medical Practice. Poor operative note documentation practices were identified in the Vascular Department at University Hospitals North Midlands. This project aimed to compare the department’s documentation practices against national guidelines, address identified shortcomings and evaluate improvements after implementing changes. Method A retrospective review of 34 consecutive vascular operation notes was conducted in January 2024. The notes were evaluated against national standards, and the results were presented in a teaching session for clinicians. A second cycle, analysing 30 operation notes from September 2024, followed to assess improvement. Data were processed using Microsoft Excel. Results The initial audit revealed significant deficiencies. Only 3% of the notes recorded the operation time, 32% noted the urgency of the procedure (elective or emergency), 12% mentioned intraoperative complications, and 9% reported extra procedures carried out. None documented blood loss or included a surgeon's signature. After intervention, the second cycle showed improvement: 6.67% of notes recorded the time, 13.3% commented on complications, 23.3% on extra procedures, 6.67% on blood loss, and 13.3% included a signature. However, documentation of the procedure urgency decreased to 10%. Conclusions This audit identified deficiencies in operative note documentation practices in the Vascular Department. While improvements were noted following intervention, further steps, including clinician education and revisions to the standard operation note proforma, are necessary to meet national standards.

paper.title: 54 An Audit of the NELA Standards in a Busy District General Hospital: 4 Years of Post-Operative Management and Outcomes in Emergency Laparotomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim An audit of the compliance of a busy district general hospital surgical department to the NELA Standards (2019 and 2023). Method Single-centre, retrospective audit of emergency laparotomies between April 2019 and December 2023. Patients were included if the NELA risk score was ≥5% (‘high-risk’) or if they were deemed ‘high-risk’ based on clinical judgement. Demographic, management, and outcome data were collected from the local NELA database and EPR and were analysed using Microsoft Excel. The primary outcome was the proportion of ‘high-risk’ patients directly admitted to critical care. The secondary outcome was the difference in length of stay (LOS) and 30-day observed/expected (O/E) mortality ratio between high-risk patients admitted to critical care and those admitted to the ward. This audit was approved locally. Results 709 laparotomies were performed and 161 (22.7%) were deemed ‘high-risk’ during the audit period. Of ‘high-risk’ patients, the median age was 74 (18-95), 52% were female, and the median mortality risk was 11.1% (3.1%-77.1%). 136 (84%) ‘high-risk’ patients were directly admitted to critical care with a median LOS of 22 days (4 days – 131 days) and a 30-day O/E mortality ratio of 0.98 (26 patients died). One of the twenty-five patients directly admitted to the wards was escalated to ICU care and one died. The median LOS of ward-admitted patients was 10 days (3 days – 49 days). Conclusions The parsimonious mortality risk score is a tool for post-operative management in emergency laparotomy, but appropriate clinical judgement can prevent excessive care and preserve critical care beds.

paper.title: 74 Surgical Precision: A Comprehensive Audit of Operation Notes at Shendi Teaching Hospital and El-Mek Nimer University Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Clinical audits are essential for enhancing the quality of clinical practice and patient safety by measuring outcomes and implementing changes based on best practices. Maintaining proper operative notes in surgical practice is crucial for patient safety, continuity of care, and legal compliance. This study explored the critical components of operation notes, the impact of suboptimal documentation on patient care, and the role of clinical audits in driving quality improvement initiatives. Method A retrospective clinical audit was conducted to assess the accuracy, completeness, and overall quality of operation notes for surgical procedures performed at El-mek Nimer University Hospital and Shendi Teaching Hospital. The audit standard criteria were from the Royal College of Surgeons. Results The implementation of the comprehensive audit at Shendi Teaching Hospital led to a notable improvement in the documentation of operative notes, with improvements ranging from 1% to 37%, except for a few items, such as the name of the operative procedure carried out, any extra procedure and the reason it was performed, anticipated blood loss, and antibiotic prophylaxis, which decreased. There was a general increase in compliance with the documentation guidelines for operation notes at both hospitals. Adherence to documentation guidelines could have been more suboptimal for most criteria measured. Conclusions The audits demonstrated a significant improvement in the documentation of postimplementation operation notes. These results underscore the importance of adhering to the guidelines set by the Royal College of Surgeons to ensure comprehensive and accurate medical records.

paper.title: 81 Prescribing of Appropriate Dual Antiplatelet Therapy Following Emergency Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting Procedure Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Dual antiplatelet therapy is an integral component of post-operative management following an emergency coronary artery bypass grafting procedure. Our aim was to assess whether patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting at Essex Cardiothoracic Centre were discharged with appropriate 1-year dual antiplatelet therapy according to EACTS guidelines. Method Discharge records were retrospectively reviewed between May-August 2023 to identify patients who underwent emergency coronary artery bypass grafting. Subsequently, eligible patients discharge summaries were reviewed to establish post-operative antiplatelet therapy status. The intervention implemented involved providing departmental education on dual antiplatelet guidelines to resident doctors and placing posters in the doctor’s office to serve as a point of reference. In addition, a registrar would counter-check antiplatelet medication on the day of patient discharge. A re-audit of patients discharged between September-November 2023 was conducted to assess the effects of the aforementioned intervention. Results Our results demonstrated, prior to intervention, 56 patients underwent emergency coronary artery bypass grafting between May–August 2023. Of which, 82.14% of patients had appropriate post-operative dual antiplatelet therapy on discharge, however 100% of patients had one antiplatelet drug prescribed on discharge. Following intervention, 55 patients underwent emergency coronary artery bypass grafting with 100% of patients being discharged with appropriate post-operative dual antiplatelet therapy. Conclusions Dual antiplatelet therapy following coronary artery bypass grafting is vital to prevent short term post-operative complications and improve long term outcomes. This audit demonstrates how departmental education and introduction of a check prior to discharge can help to improve achieving optimal dual antiplatelet prescribing.

paper.title: 123 How Useful Is Murphy’s Sign in Evaluating Acute Cholecystitis? a Clinical Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate if Murphy’s sign is being performed in line with NICE guidance for suspected cholecystitis. To evaluate the utility of Murphy’s sign for acute cholecystitis. Method 100 patients with appointments for suspected gallbladder pathology at the Surgical Same-Day Emergency Care unit were included. Data was collected on pre-ultrasound abdominal examination documentation and ultrasound findings. Results Murphy’s sign was examined for in 54% of patients: the emergency department (ED) examined for the sign in 54% of those assessed, and general surgery in 56%. When both teams examined for Murphy’s sign, the result differed in 24% of cases. For general surgery, Murphy’s sign had a sensitivity of 67%, specificity of 42%, positive predictive value (PPV) of 7% and negative predictive value (NPV) of 95%. For the ED, the sensitivity was 67%, specificity was 15%, PPV was 7% and NPV was 83%. Conclusions The completion rate was below the 100% NICE standard. An examination proforma has been developed to increase compliance, with a re-audit planned. There was high inter-rater variability between teams for the outcome of Murphy’s sign. There was a higher false positive rate in ED (85%) than general surgery (58%). Using the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve, Murphy’s sign when assessed by general surgery is marginally better than using chance alone to diagnose cholecystitis, whereas an ED assessment is marginally worse. The negative predictive value is high for both teams; a negative Murphy’s sign could be useful in assessing for the absence of cholecystitis but a positive result holds little value.

paper.title: 195 Close Loop Retrospective Audit of Acute Ureteric Stone Management: A Comparison with NICE Guidelines and GIRFT
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit evaluates adherence to the NICE guidelines and GIRFT recommendations for acute ureteric stone management, focusing on reducing stent insertions and promoting URS/ESWL for non-septic patients without clear indications for stenting. Method A retrospective audit was conducted in two cycles. The first cycle reviewed 89 patients admitted to ESH between August to November 2023, and the second cycle included 65 patients from July to September 2024. Data were collected from Powerchart notes and ward lists, analyzing the management referred from A&E to on-call team. Results Improvements were observed between cycles, including better adherence to serum calcium checks (47% to 66%) and dietary advice provision (17% to 72%). Stent insertions without clear indications or sepsis decreased from 83% to 57%. Conservative management rates declined from 65% to 46%, with reduced failure rates and more urgent treatments offered within 48 hours (35% to 53%). Efforts to improve follow-up led to a significant reduction in lost hot stone clinic follow-ups. Despite opening a hot primary URS theatre, reduced manpower and lack of CEPOD support limited its success, resulting in stent insertions for patients unlikely to pass stones due to pain, stone size, or location. Conclusion The audit demonstrates improvements in metabolic workup, patient counseling, and follow-up adherence, while highlighting gaps in theatre and manpower support for primary URS. Recommendations include developing a standardized care pathway, enhancing follow-up processes, and implementing datix or iPhase reporting for delays in primary URS and urgent stent decisions. Re-audit is planned in 6–12 months to assess progress.
