paper.title: 211 Improving Compliance with GIRFT Guidelines: A Cross-Site Re-Audit of Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Across Frimley Health NHS Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This re-audit evaluated the proportion of patients requiring overnight stays following laparoscopic cholecystectomy, investigated causes of delayed discharge, and assessed compliance with the Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) guidelines. It was conducted in Frimley Health NHS Trust as a cross-site comparison between Frimley Park and Wexham Park Hospitals to identify best practices. Updated GIRFT recommendations from September 2022 were adapted into Frimley Health’s local guidelines and evaluated during this audit. The guidelines suggest a 90%-day case rate with standardised surgical techniques, including patient positioning with a slight head-up angle, table rotation towards the surgeon, and intermittent pneumatic compression. Three 5mm ports, one 10mm port, and low-pressure CO₂ insufflation (10mmHg) are recommended. Local anaesthetic (30mls - 0.25% bupivacaine) should be instilled around the liver and gallbladder while avoiding surgical drains. Method This closed-loop audit compared data from the initial cycle (July–October 2023, Frimley Park, n=107) with a second cycle (April–June 2024) across Frimley Park (n=121) and Wexham Park (n=72). Data were retrospectively collected from case notes and operative records. Metrics included day-case rates, guideline compliance, reasons for delayed discharge, and 14-day readmissions. Results Day case rates improved from 45% to 70% at Frimley Park, with pain (30%) and drain monitoring (28%) as common causes of delays. Wexham Park achieved 77.8%, aligning with GIRFT targets. Both sites reported low 14-day readmission rates (9%) and consistent patient safety outcomes. Conclusions This cross-site audit facilitated shared learning and progress. Continued efforts are needed to enhance pain management, patient counselling, and adherence to surgical protocols.

paper.title: 212 An Audit on Single-Centre Compliance with BOAST Standards and Local Infection Control Policy for Safe Intraoperative Tourniquet Use in Plastic Surgery Theatres
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate tourniquet infection control and tourniquet safety compliance at Mid Yorkshire Teaching NHS Trust (MYTT) Plastic Surgery Theatres against trust's six-use-day tourniquet infection control policy and BOAST standards. Method A one-month retrospective audit reviewing electronic and paper records of plastic surgery cases where arm and digital tourniquets were used. The scrub team was surveyed regarding awareness of the six-use-day infection control policy, and if tourniquet cuffs were marked after each use. Data on tourniquet type, skin integrity, isolation, exsanguination, pressure, duration, and six-use-markings were analysed using Excel. Results Of 62 cases, 43 used arm tourniquets and 19 digitals. Tourniquet duration was documented in 90.3%, type in 67.7% and pressure in only 39.5% of operation notes. Electronic peri-operative pathway achieved 100% compliance, while paper care pathways had compliance rates of 90.3%, 97.7%, and 88.7% for type, pressure, and duration, respectively. Skin integrity, isolation, and exsanguination methods were not recorded in any notes. Fixed pressure of 250 mmHg was used in 95.3% of cases, exceeding BOAST standards in 53.5%. All cases met the 120-minute duration limit. Tourniquets were not marked but were disposed after each list. Conclusions Overall, tourniquets were used safely but written documentation was poor, indicating a clear need for improvement. Documentation by the scrub team was significantly better than by the operating team, with digital records providing more comprehensive documentation. 250mmhg was used irrespective of patients' SBP. Tourniquets were not marked as per trust policy. To improve practices, a teaching session and poster reminders have been introduced, with plan to re-audit.

paper.title: 213 Quality of Primary Care Referrals to the Breast Clinic for Patients with Gynaecomastia
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Gynaecomastia, the benign proliferation of male breast tissue, is a common condition with a variety of etiologies. Appropriate primary care referrals are critical for timely and effective management. This audit evaluates the quality of referrals to the breast clinic for gynaecomastia, focusing on adherence to referral guidelines and the inclusion of clinical details. Method A two-cycle retrospective audit was conducted at West Middlesex University Hospital (WMUH) in 2024. In the first cycle, primary care referral letters for patients with gynaecomastia were reviewed over a 6-month period. Data were analyzed to assess the completeness of referral information, including clinical history, physical examination, potential contributing factors. Interventions included GP education on referral guidelines, the introduction of a structured referral template, and distribution of educational materials. A second audit cycle was conducted after 3 months to evaluate the impact of these interventions. Results A total of 120 referral letters were reviewed. Only 58% (n=69) included a thorough clinical history, while 43% (n=52) documented findings from a physical examination. Evaluation of potential contributing factors, such as medication history or hormonal disorders, was included in 36% (n=43) of referrals. Imaging or blood test results were provided in 28% (n=34) of cases. Overall adherence to referral guidelines was 45% (n=54). Following interventions, referral letters were reviewed and analysed in the second cycle. Conclusions This two-cycle audit highlights substantial improvements in the quality of primary care referrals for gynaecomastia following targeted interventions. Structured referral templates and GP education proved effective in enhancing adherence to guidelines and ensuring comprehensive clinical information.

paper.title: 221 Follow-Up for Patients with Radiologically Diagnosed Gallbladder Polyps in Primary Care: A 2-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim In 2019, local care commissioning group released primary care guidance for interval ultrasound imaging of patients with gallbladder polyps based on size and risk factors. Primary outcome of this audit: number of polyp patients lost to follow-up (LTFU) in one GP practice. Method Search of electronic medical records for diagnoses inclusive of biliary polyp pathology, completed 22/05/2024. Data collected by 2 investigators: demographics, imaging indication, ultrasound findings, comorbidities, identification of LTFU, those indicated for referral for surgical assessment. Intervention: invitation for repeat imaging, or consultation with doctor. Results Search yielded 76 records, 4 removed as diagnoses were not polypoid pathology. Of 72 patients, 58% female. Median age 55.5(IQR:22.25) years. Self-reporting per GovUK ethnicities: 48.6% white, 15.3% other(Arab/other), 13.9% other Asian, 8.3% mixed, 5.6% Indian, 5.6% Black Afro-Caribbean, 2.8% undeclared. 30/72(41.6%) patients were LTFU, 31/72(43.1%) complied with guidance, 11/72(15.3%) were due appointments within guidelines. Indications for abdominal imaging: 30(41.7%) for abdominal pain, 23(31.9%) for incidental deranged liver function tests, 4(5.6%) for change in bowel habit, and 15(20.8%) other abdominal complaints. 4 had no documented polyp size; of 68 patients, mean size at diagnosis was 5.2±2.7mm. 16/68(23.5%) had >1 polyp at diagnosis. Median months overdue: 36(IQR 45.5). Of high-risk factors identified, Indian ethnicity was associated with 46.6% greater average polyp size. Conclusions 41.6% of individuals were LTFU, key factors ensuring adequate follow-up were patient education, and empowered health accountability to self-report for imaging. 100% of individuals were returned to surveillance following intervention.

paper.title: 235 A Retrospective Audit on the Use of Staging Scans in Patients with Gleason 3+4/4+3 Prostate Cancer in a Single Specialist UK Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Patients with suspected prostate cancer undergo diagnostic staging and grading with mpMRI and biopsy +/- metastatic staging. Guidelines advocate against the routine use of bone scans in patients with low-risk disease but recommend staging CT and bone scans in patients with unfavourable intermediate risk disease (Gleason 4+3) and/or patients with locally advanced disease (T3). We aimed to audit the use of staging scans in patients with Gleason 3+4/4+3 prostate cancer. Method Patients diagnosed with Gleason 3+4/4+3 prostate cancer in 2022 were identified. Data was retrospectively collected using electronic patient records including the presence/absence of cribriform pattern on biopsy histology, local tumour stage (T stage), and PSA (>20/<20). Results 196 patients with Gleason 3+4/4+3 prostate cancer were included in the analysis, 49/196 (25%) of whom had evidence of cribriform histology. All patients with a PSA>20 (N=22) underwent staging with at least a bone scan. 50/93 (54%) patients with Gleason 4+3 had staging scans performed. 3/79 (4%) of Cambridge Prognostic Group 1 patients (Gleason 3+4, PSA <20, T2) had staging scans. Patients with cribriform were more likely to undergo staging scans (X2 p<0.001). Conclusions The use of staging scans in patients with PSA >20 was excellent. However, there was variation in the use of staging scans in patients with T3 disease and/or Gleason 4+3. In patients with favourable intermediate risk disease, staging scans are occasionally being performed unnecessarily. We recommend the use of a proforma to help prompt decision making as to which patients require staging scans as recommended by international guidelines.

paper.title: 289 Evaluating Documentation Accuracy for K-Wire Removal Timing in Hand Surgery: An Audit Study
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Accurate documentation is crucial for patient safety and continuity of care. The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) guidelines, published in 2014, emphasize the need for detailed postoperative care instructions, such as recording K-wire removal timing. Concerns about inconsistent documentation of K-wire removal prompted this audit. Proper documentation minimises risks such as infection, wire migration, ensures optimal healing, and prevents unnecessary delays or interventions. Inadequate records can lead to inappropriate appointment bookings, resulting in unnecessary healthcare costs and resource use. Aim To assess the baseline accuracy of K-wire removal documentation and implement interventions for improvement. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on 100 operative notes from 02/08/2023 to 12/09/2024 for hand surgery patients who underwent K-wire fixation. Key variables assessed included K-wire removal date, K-wire size, date and time, name of surgeon, operative procedure, operative findings, and closure details. Data were analysed using R 4.4.0, including Chi-Square test and Cramér’s V to evaluate associations between variables. Results 27% of patients lacked documentation for K-wire removal date, and 22% lacked documentation for K-wire size. Other variables achieved 98-100% accuracy. A significant and moderate association (p = 0.00002075, Cramér’s V = 0.464) was found between documenting K-wire removal date and size. Conclusions Gaps in documenting K-wire removal date and size highlight areas for improvement. The significant association between these variables suggests that enhancing the accuracy of one will positively influence the other. Laminated posters and educational interventions have been implemented, and a second audit cycle is planned.

paper.title: 313 An Audit of Lynch Syndrome Testing Practices at Kettering General Hospital Against NICE Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Lynch syndrome (LS), a hereditary colorectal cancer predisposition, necessitates timely and accurate testing to facilitate early intervention and risk reduction. NICE guideline DG27 recommends comprehensive LS testing for all newly diagnosed colorectal cancer patients. This audit assesses the adherence of Kettering General Hospital (KGH) to these guidelines. Method Data were analyzed from 34 patients (aged ≥18 years) diagnosed with colorectal cancer between 1 January 2022 and 31 March 2022. The primary outcome measures were the time to IHC results and referral rates for genetic testing. Results All patients received immunohistochemistry (IHC) testing. However, only 15% received IHC results within the recommended 7–10 days. Only 50% of patients with MMR-deficient IHC results were referred for genetic testing. While 100% of patients with available tumor tissue underwent testing, the delays in IHC results and low referral rates for genetic testing highlight significant areas for improvement. Conclusions This audit reveals substantial discrepancies between KGH's LS testing practices and NICE guideline DG27 recommendations. To improve efficiency and timely diagnosis, we recommend appointing a clinical lead to optimize the LS testing pathway, enhance inter-specialty collaboration (including obstetrics and gynecology), and align local protocols with national guidelines. Targeted educational initiatives should improve awareness among healthcare professionals and patients. Further research with a larger sample size is warranted to validate these findings and inform the development of more effective LS testing pathways.

paper.title: 328 Assessing Patient Satisfaction and Confidence in Post-Operative Wound Care: A Clinical Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess patient satisfaction with post-operative wound care and education, focusing on confidence in managing wounds at home and identifying areas for improvement. Method A survey was conducted over one month in a skin dressings clinic, involving 25 patients. Questions addressed satisfaction with post-operative wound care, confidence in home wound management, and the provision of educational materials. Results Of the patients surveyed, 96% were either satisfied or very satisfied with their post-operative wound care. However, only 12% reported feeling somewhat confident in managing their wounds at home, and 12% indicated they would have felt more confident with additional information. Notably, 22% of patients reported not receiving a pre-operative educational leaflet. Conclusions While overall satisfaction with care is high, gaps in patient confidence and education remain. To address these issues, a target of 100% leaflet distribution is proposed, alongside the development of a more detailed leaflet covering wound expectations and post-operative care instructions. Implementing these measures and re-auditing will help evaluate their impact and ensure continuous improvement in patient education and confidence.

audits.standard: Royal College of Surgeons advice to provide patient information leaflets; BAUS TURBT leaflet
audits.finding: 30% (6 of 20) provided with the TURBT PIL.
audits.change: Email to all consultants and registrars encouraging use of PILs (departmental reminder).

paper.title: 335 Ensuring Informed Decisions: A Single Institution Closed-Loop Audit on Patient Information Leaflet Use for Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Obtaining informed consent is crucial in-patient care, ensuring patients are aware of the risks, benefits, and procedures before surgical treatment. The Royal College of Surgeons advises providing patients with patient information leaflets (PILs) to support their understanding. The British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) provides QR codes linking to its leaflets, which can be easily added to electronic clinic letters. This audit aimed to assess clinicians’ use of the BAUS “Transurethral Telescopic Resection of a Bladder Tumour” leaflet when listing patients for Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour (TURBT) at an NHS hospital in North- West England. Method Retrospective data was initially collected for 20 patients who underwent TURBT between October and November 2024. The clinic letters corresponding to the appointment listing the patients for TURBT were reviewed to identify whether the aforementioned BAUS leaflet was provided, either in physical form or via a QR code. Following this, an email was sent to all Consultants and Registrars, encouraging the use of PILs. A re-audit was then conducted. Results Initially, just 30% of patients (6 of 20) were provided with the TURBT PIL. However, after a departmental reminder, the provision rate increased to 80%, with 16 of 20 patients receiving the leaflet in the re-audited data. Conclusions While there was notable improvement in providing the PIL, further efforts are needed to ensure all patients receive written materials to support informed decision-making. Standardising the provision of PILs and conducting regular re-audits are essential to ensure full compliance and optimise patient understanding.

audits.title: 427 Histological Findings in Emergency Appendicectomy and Impact on Patient Management: A Retrospective Audit
audits.standard: Follow-up protocols: colorectal MDT referral for neoplastic appendix histology
audits.finding: Acute appendicitis confirmed in 279 (91.5%); 7 (2.3%) neoplastic findings; all NET and adenocarcinoma cases referred to colorectal MDT.

paper.title: 427 Histological Findings in Emergency Appendicectomy and Impact on Patient Management: A Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is a leading cause of acute abdominal pain, with faecaliths and lymphoid hyperplasia being common etiologies. However, unusual pathological findings, such as parasitic infections, benign, or malignant neoplasms, although rare, significantly alter patient management. This audit aimed to evaluate the histological findings from appendicectomies in our unit and assess whether appropriate follow-up was undertaken, specifically through colorectal multidisciplinary team (MDT) referrals. Methods We retrospectively reviewed appendicectomy cases from March 2022 to March 2024. Patient records were identified through CEPOD theatre lists, including both laparoscopic and open appendectomies. The audit focused on identifying histological outcomes, patient demographics, and adherence to follow-up protocols, particularly for neoplastic findings. Exclusion criteria included patients without histology or those treated conservatively. Results A total of 305 patients underwent appendicectomy. Histological analysis confirmed acute appendicitis in 279 cases (91.5%). Fifteen cases (4.9%) were negative for acute appendicitis, while seven cases (2.3%) involved neoplastic findings: three neuroendocrine tumors (NET), one florid follicular hyperplasia, and three appendix adenocarcinomas. Other rare findings included pinworm infestation, fatty metaplasia, and mucocele. All cases of NET and adenocarcinomas were referred to the colorectal MDT for further management. The average age of patients with NET was 32 years, with all managed in accordance with current guidelines. Conclusions Routine histopathological examination (HPE) of appendectomy specimens plays a crucial role in identifying uncommon pathologies that alter patient management. Our findings support the continued practice of routine HPE for all appendicectomy specimens, given the significant implications of neoplastic findings.

audits.standard: National guidance that medical documentation is clear, accurate and legible

paper.title: 430 A Closed Loop Audit on Legibility of Post-Operative Instruction Documentation in Otolaryngology Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim National guidelines recommend that medical documentations should be recorded clearly, accurately, and legibly. Illegible post-operative instructions pose risk to patient safety due to misinterpretation. We aimed to assess the compliance to these guidelines within an ENT unit. Method Retrospective analyses of a total of 40 operation notes, each being the last case from each otolaryngology theatre list to prevent selection bias, in Castle Hill Hospital, Hull, were included. The first loop included 20 cases between August 2023 and September 2023 whereas the second loop included 20 cases between March 2024 and April 2024. The responses from three staff members were averaged to decide on the legibility of each note. The data from the first loop was analysed and the results presented to the department to raise awareness, followed by the second loop. Results The first loop showed that only 35% (n=7) of the operation notes were legible and 25% (n=5) were electronic notes. Legibility of electronic notes and handwritten notes were 100% (n=5) and 13% (n=2) respectively. After raising awareness on these findings to the department, the second loop showed improvement of legibility to 65% (n=13) and increased in use of electronic notes to 50% (n=10). Electronic notes remain 100% (n=10) legible whereas handwritten notes legibility improved to 30% (n=3). Conclusions This closed loop audit showed that there is less than 100% compliance with national standards and further improvements required. This audit proved that electronic notes were 100% legible hence should be encouraged.

audits.standard: Major Trauma Network Northwest London guidelines
audits.finding: 58.4% adherence to guidelines; primary and secondary survey documentation 92.1% and 81.2%; imaging times 3 h 10 min (general) and 6 h 29 min (silver trauma).
audits.change: Educational sessions, presentation of findings to stakeholders, an ED trauma lead assigned each shift and a silver trauma toolkit.

paper.title: 441 Improving Trauma Call Effectiveness and Adherence to Guidelines: A Two-Cycle Audit in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The high volume of trauma calls, leading to resource allocation issues, staff dissatisfaction, and patient safety concerns, prompted this project. The aim was to evaluate trauma call effectiveness, adherence to Major Trauma Network Northwest London Guidelines, patient outcomes, and the impact of interventions on imaging timelines and documentation. Method Trauma calls were reviewed over two audit cycles (1/4/24-10/6/24 and 14/10/24-14/11/24). Interventions between the two periods included educational sessions, the presentation of findings to key stakeholders and relevant departments, and the assigning of an emergency department trauma lead at the start of each shift. In addition, a silver trauma toolkit was introduced for staff to follow. Key metrics included call appropriateness, protocol adherence, documentation rates and patient outcomes. Results In the first cycle, 216 trauma calls (101 adults, 98 silver, 17 paediatric) were recorded, with 58.4% adherence to guidelines. Primary and secondary survey documentation rates were 92.1% and 81.2%, respectively. Average imaging times were 3 hours 10 minutes (general trauma) and 6 hours 29 minutes (silver trauma). Post-intervention, 70 calls (30 adult, 38 silver, 2 paediatric) were logged, with adherence increasing to 71.8% for general trauma and 100% for silver trauma. Primary and secondary survey documentation improved to 96.9% and 90.6%, and imaging times reduced to 2 hours 29 minutes (general) and 3 hours 21 minutes (silver). Conclusions Education, divisional discussion, and assigning a trauma lead reduced inappropriate calls and improved adherence to guidelines and documentation. However, education in a department with high staff turnover or temporary staffing remains a challenge.

audits.standard: Trust Rib Fracture Pathway
audits.finding: Battle score documented 5%; correct analgesia 10%; lidocaine patches 12.5%; rib block within 24 hours when indicated 25%.
audits.change: Presentation of first-cycle results and circulation of the trust Rib Fracture Pathway.

paper.title: 499 Rib Fracture Pathway Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Blunt chest wall trauma accounts for 15% of emergency department presentations worldwide. Multi-disciplinary care pathways and risk stratifying scores are used to identify and treat high risk patients and prevent complications. This closed loop audit aimed to assess and improve compliance to our Trust’s Rib Fracture Pathway. Method The audit was conducted at a single NHS trust. All patients admitted with rib fractures between 01/02/2024 and 31/03/2024 were included in the first cycle. The intervention included presentation of the first cycle results and circulation of the trust Rib Fracture Pathway. The second cycle included all patients with rib fractures admitted between 01/07/2024 to 31/08/2024. Patient electronic notes were analysed and data recorded in Microsoft Excel. Results There were 40 and 41 patients included in the first and second audit cycles respectively. Documentation of Battle score increased from 5% to 15% and prescription of correct analgesia increased from 10% to 35%. The percentage of patients who received lidocaine patches increased from 12.5% to 56%. The percentage of patients, in whom it was indicated, that received a rib block within 24 hours of admission increased from 25% to 38%. There was no improvement in consultations with Major Trauma Centers for patients that fulfilled discussion criteria. Conclusions In summary, our audit has shown improvement in compliance with the current Rib Fracture Pathway, however overall compliance remains low. Development of a rib fracture prescribing ‘careplan’ and update of our trust Rib Fracture Pathway are currently in progress to enhance patient care.

audits.title: 535 A Clinical Audit of Out-of-Hours Red Cell Transfusions in a Regional Hospital
audits.standard: NICE blood transfusion guidelines, with five local criteria for appropriate out-of-hours transfusion
audits.finding: 70.6% of 51 out-of-hours RCC units were appropriate; 29.4% not indicated
audits.change: Planned: verbal proforma before re-audit and guidelines on appropriate requests

paper.title: 535 A Clinical Audit of Out-of-Hours Red Cell Transfusions in a Regional Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim It is recognised that transfusing outside of ‘routine’ hours is less safe and should be avoided unless clinically essential. This audit evaluates out-of-hours red cell concentrate (RCC) transfusions by indication. Method We identified prospectively RCC transfusions occurring out of hours in our institution over a one-month period. Indications were examined against NICE blood transfusion guidelines. Based on these guidelines and advice from our local haemovigilance officer we defined five criteria for an appropriate out of hours transfusion. Transfusions fulfilling any one of these criteria were defined as appropriate. Results Following withdrawals, data on 51 units of RCC transfused out of hours were included in the analysis of which 70.6% were defined as appropriate as per our criteria. Transfusion recipients were male in 54.9% of cases. The mean pre-transfusion haemoglobin (Hb) level was 7.6 m/dL. The mean post-transfusion Hb was 8.4 m/dL. Incidence of active haemorrhage was 31.4%. Incidence of symptomatic anaemia was 51%. The haemoglobin level was appropriately low in 29.4% of cases. 3.9% of the transfusions were given in the context of perioperative haemorrhage. A further 3.9% were given for low haemoglobin pre-operatively. There were no recorded transfusion complications. Conclusions Although the majority of transfusions were clinically indicated, 29.4% of out-of-hours RCC transfusions were not indicated under our criteria. We recommend the implementation of a verbal proforma prior to a re-audit, with a view to improving patient safety and compliance. Guidelines outlining appropriate requests should be developed and reasons for delays in the transfusion process be explored.

audits.standard: Accurate ICD, OPCS-4 and HRG coding based on clinical documentation
audits.finding: ICD and OPCS-4 codes changed in all 4 cases after clinician validation.
audits.change: Clinician-validation of codes with the clinical coding team and amendment of HRG codes.

paper.title: 643 Audit of Accuracy of Clinical Coding for Complex Abdominal Wall Surgeries
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate coding is crucial to ensure appropriate remuneration for clinical procedures. The coding process is prone to error as coders, who are non-clinical, rely on clinical documentation to determine what they believe are the appropriate ICD and OPCS-4 codes. This is particularly complex in plastic surgery where operations often have subtle differences. This study audited the accuracy of coding of complex abdominal wall reconstructive operations in the Royal Free Hospital and reviewed its financial implications. Method Patients were included who underwent complex abdominal wall reconstructive surgeries, which we defined as requiring both general surgery and plastic surgery input, between August and November 2024. Their overall HRG codes, and corresponding ICD and OPCS-4 codes, were reviewed for accuracy based on documentation available for each patient. Results were discussed with senior clinicians and the clinical coding team and HRG codes were amended as appropriate. Results Overall, four cases were included. Changes were made to ICD and OPCS-4 codes in all 4 cases. The addition of the clinician-validation process led to more accurate coding for these cases, resulting in significant financial savings of, on average, £6,000 per case. Conclusion This audit emphasised the importance of collaboration between clinicians and coders to ensure accurate clinical coding and minimise potential financial loses for NHS trusts. Increased awareness of clinical coding by the clinical team and clear documentation are essential.

audits.standard: NICE 2022 melanoma guideline: SLNB for Breslow >1mm, consider for 0.8-1mm with ulceration, lymphovascular invasion or mitotic rate ≥2/mm2
audits.finding: Compliance 97.4%.
audits.change: Ongoing departmental audit (no specific intervention described).

paper.title: 672 An Audit of Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsies for Malignant Melanoma
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy (SLNB) has been used as staging tool for Malignant Melanoma for over 20 years. This audit sought to ensure that standards are being met in melanoma patients undergoing SLNB at the Royal Free Hospital. Method A retrospective audit examined electronic notes for patients undergoing SLNBs for melanoma from September-November 2024. NICE guidelines 2022 set our standard to determine eligibility for SLNB. It recommends SLNB in melanoma patients with a Breslow thickness >1mm or to consider SLNB in patients with Breslow thickness 0.8-1mm with at least one of ulceration, lymphovascular invasion or a mitotic rate ≥2/mm2. Results After screening, 61 patients were included. 15/61 (24.6%) of these patients had a Breslow thickness between 0.8 and 1mm. 7/15 (46.7%) patients were appropriately offered SLNB due to having a mitotic index ≥2/mm2. 7/15 (46.7%) did not meet criteria for SLNB. 1/15 (6.7%) did not have documented lymphovascular invasion, ulceration or mitotic index and therefore potentially did not meet criteria. The lymph nodes from all 15 of these patients were negative for melanoma deposits on histopathology. Overall departmental compliance was 53/61 (87%), which was reduced compared to 97.4% at the previous audit cycle. Conclusions SLNB carries risks of increased morbidity and mortality and therefore it is very important that it is carried out on eligible patients only. Despite ongoing audit within the department, sustained change has not yet been achieved. This audit highlights the importance of further intervention to ensure long-lasting compliance with the NICE 2022 standard for SLNB in patients with melanoma.

paper.title: 698 Rate of Testicular Torsion and Variations in Operative Techniques for Scrotal Exploration - a Single Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Establish the rate of testicular torsion and variations in practise of scrotal exploration from a single-centre, general surgical unit. Method Following local approval, data was collected from 1st June to 1st November 2024 and stored securely on an NHS database. The primary outcome was rate of testicular torsion at scrotal exploration. Secondary outcomes were types of incision, rate of orchidopexy and suture material used. Outcomes were compared to recent guidelines submitted by BAUS/BURST consensus (FIX-IT study). Results During this period, 41 scrotal explorations were performed with an average population age of 14-years (range 4 to 28) of whom 4 (9.8%) were confirmed to have testicular torsion. An orchidectomy was performed on one patient with an unviable testicle, while the other 3 had bilateral orchidopexies. Of those with no signs of testicular torsion, 10 (27.0%) had torted cyst of Morgagni and 9 (24.3%) had suspected epidydmo-orchitis. Thirty-three of these patients underwent orchidopexy (89.2%) of whom 3 were bilateral and only a single patient had documented evidence of bell-clapper deformity. A transverse and longitudinal para-median incision were the most common approach (43.9% and 41.5%, respectively) and the majority of orchidopexies were 3-point fixations with polydioxanone (PDS) suture (66.7%). Conclusions The rate of torsion at exploration was comparatively low to other national observational studies. There is variation amongst general surgeons in the decision making and operative technique for scrotal exploration. Following local intervention aiming for consensus, a second cycle will be performed.

audits.standard: HSE National Clinical Guideline no. 26 on sepsis protocol initiation (sepsis 6 bundle)

paper.title: 711 A Clinical Audit of Adherence to Sepsis Protocol Initiation at Ward Level in a Level 3 (General Hospital)
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction A 7-week retrospective audit on management of hospital inpatients who meet the criteria for sepsis protocol initiation as per HSE National Clinical Guideline no. 26 Aim To evaluate and identify areas of quality improvement in clinician compliance with HSE national clinical guideline no 26 on initiation of sepsis protocol for inpatients in a level 3 General Hospital. Method A retrospective audit was completed covering 7 weeks. Cases which met the triggers for sepsis protocol initiation were identified from clinical notes of patients transferred and discharged from two inpatient wards in a level 3 hospital. Cases with ED initiation of protocol were excluded. Compliance with sepsis protocols was assessed through completion of the HSE proforma or clinical documentation. Patient demographics, admission diagnosis, adherence to the sepsis 6 bundle, and aspects completed were recorded. Results 295 cases were audited. 36 (12.2%) Positive sepsis triggers were identified. Use of existing HSE proforma was low (13.89% of cases). This form was completed in only 1 case. Average completion of the six aspects of the sepsis bundle documented was 55.5%. Antibiotic administration had the highest compliance rate (31/36). Conclusions Use of the existing HSE proforma was minimal. As a result, compliance with Sepsis protocols varied significantly between clinicians. Revision of the sepsis proforma is required with further education for clinicians on identification and compliance required.

audits.title: 743 Adherence to Prophylactic Antibiotic Guidelines in Elective Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of Current Practice
audits.standard: SIS, NICE and local trust guidelines: no prophylactic antibiotics for low-risk elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy
audits.finding: Guideline adherence 5.3%; 94.7% received prophylactic antibiotics contrary to recommendations.

paper.title: 743 Adherence to Prophylactic Antibiotic Guidelines in Elective Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of Current Practice
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) is commonly performed for conditions such as symptomatic cholelithiasis, gallstone pancreatitis, and acute or chronic cholecystitis. This audit assessed prophylactic antibiotic use in elective LC at a district general hospital and evaluated adherence to established guidelines. According to the Surgical Infection Society (SIS), the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), and local NHS trust guidelines, prophylactic pre-operative antibiotics are not recommended for low-risk patients undergoing elective LC, as they do not significantly reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs). Method A retrospective audit was conducted on elective LC cases performed from January 2024 to July 2024. Data from medical records and operation notes were reviewed to assess antibiotic use, guideline adherence, SSI rates, and the cost impact of unnecessary antibiotics. Patients with biliary infections, intraoperative bile spillage, on-table cholangiogram or common bile duct exploration, and gallbladder malignancies/polyps were excluded. Results Seventy-six patients were included in the audit. Guideline adherence was observed in only 5.3% of cases, while 94.7% received prophylactic antibiotics contrary to recommendations. The postoperative complication rate was 3.9%, with three patients affected: one with an SSI, one with an intra-abdominal collection, and one with a surgical site hematoma. The SSI occurred in a patient who did not receive antibiotics, though this finding lacks statistical significance due to the small size of the no-antibiotic subgroup. Conclusions The audit highlights poor adherence to guidelines for prophylactic antibiotic use in elective LC, emphasizing the need for educational interventions to improve guideline compliance and reduce unnecessary antibiotic costs.

paper.title: 750 ‘BARI-MED’ AUDIT a Multi-Disciplinary Team Audit Streamlining Medication Prescription on Discharge for Bariatric Patients
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Patients undergoing bariatric surgical procedures must go home post operatively with 6 weeks of liquid/crushed medications as well as a liquid diet as per British Obesity & Metabolic Surgery Society (BOMSS) guidelines. There were inconsistencies in the medications, formulations and durations prescribed on discharge for patients undergoing bariatric procedures. This closed loop audit aimed to improve prescription accuracy of discharge medications dispensed for patients having bariatric procedures at a tertiary centre. Method A retrospective first cycle was performed from July 2023- December 2023. A digital prescription tab/checklist was then created by working with the MDT (Specialist pharmacist, bariatric CNS) based on patient feedback and financial factors. A prospective second cycle was performed from April 2024 – May 2024 after educating junior doctors, ACPs, trainee pharmacists about bariatric surgery guidelines and about the digital new prescription tab. Results Accuracy increased in all medications prescribed on discharge from cycle one (n=35 patients) to cycle two (n=12 patients) after . Paracetamol liquid prescription improved from 49% (cycle 1) to 58% (cycle 2), codeine phosphate tablet from 11% (cycle 1) to 42% (cycle 2), senna liquid from 11% (cycle 1) to 58% (cycle 2) and ondansetron liquid from 20% (cycle 1) to 58% (cycle 2) and lansoprazole dispersible tablet from 97% (cycle 1) to 100% (cycle 2). Enoxaparin prescription was consistently 100% across both cycles. Conclusions Successful implementation of the digital prescription checklist with the collaboration of MDT members lead to improved prescription accuracy and better patient outcomes for bariatric surgical procedures on discharge.

audits.standard: NICE NG2 1.2.7: single dose of intravesical mitomycin C at first TURBT for new bladder cancer
audits.finding: 5-10% compliance.
audits.change: Initial audit presented at departmental meeting in 2023.

paper.title: 836 Single Installation of Mitomycin C in New Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: A Clinical Re-Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To measure the adherence of our tertiary urology service to providing a single dose of intravesical Mitomycin C (MMC) during the first transurethral resection of a bladder tumour (TURBT) in patients with newly diagnosed bladder cancer (NICE guidelines NG2 1.2.7). Method A single centre ambidirectional re-audit was performed and included patients with newly diagnosed bladder cancer who underwent their first TURBT. Data was collected from 2022 to 2023 and during 2024. Demographic and clinical details were collected from electronic systems, where available. Local audit and ethical approval were granted. Results An initial audit carried out in 2022 and presented at a departmental meeting in 2023 showed 5-10% compliance. A re-audit collected data from March 2024 to August 2024. One hundred and thirty patients were screened, and 77 patients were included (62 male, 15 female). MMC was given in 28 patients (36% compliance). 86% of these patients were administered MMC post-operatively rather than during the operation (n=24). In 63.6% of the total cases, MMC was not given (n=49). In 76%, there was no documented reason for not giving MMC (n=37). In 7 of 49 cases (14%) MMC was not given due to bleeding-related risks. Conclusions Improvements in the adherence of providing MMC to newly diagnosed bladder cancer patients during TURBT are needed. In a planned third cycle of the audit, the impact of introducing a novel electronic prescribing system and encouraging the use of new TURBT proforma will be measured.

audits.standard: SAGES guideline on drain use after laparoscopic cholecystectomy
audits.finding: Drain used in all patients (100%), though indicated in only 16.6%.
audits.change: Education of the surgical team on the SAGES guideline.

paper.title: 839 An Evaluation of Drain Usage After Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A Dual-Cycle Audit at a Tertiary Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To audit our practice of drain tube insertion after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, in accordance with the SAGES guideline. Method This prospective audit was conducted in three phases:Pre-intervention (August – October 2023): Data was collected on all consecutive adult patients undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy.Educational intervention: The surgical team was provided the importance of the audit and educated about the SAGES guideline on drain use.Post-intervention (November - December): Data was again prospectively collected to complete the audit cycle. Results In the first cycle, there were 30 patients (mean age 45.77 years), 26 were female (86.7%). Drainage was used in all patients, despite it being clinically indicated in only 16.6% of the cases. In the second cycle, involving another 30 patients (mean age 47.03 years). The findings showed that a drain was used in 53.3% of patients, despite only 23.3% of the patients requiring it. Significantly, following the educational intervention, the rate of drain usage in inappropriate cases was reduced by a significant 60.87% (from 100% to 39.13%). Conclusions This audit, the first of its kind in a tertiary centre in a low-income country like Syria, highlights the value of evidence-based practices in enhancing patient care. It confirms that routine drain placement after uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy is unnecessary, leading to reduced hospital stays, complications, and costs, while fostering surgical team awareness of quality improvement initiatives in resource-limited settings.

paper.title: 864 A Clinical Audit Assessing the Accuracy of Documenting Complications When Consenting Patients for Laparoscopic +/- Open Appendicectomy in Morriston Hospital (South Wales, UK)
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Laparoscopic Appendicectomy: Consent compared to EIDO standards. The primary aim(s) of our project were to assess the documentation of risks associated with laparoscopic +/- open appendicectomies compared to EIDO standards, to improve consenting techniques and documentation of risks associated and to compare the data between The University Hospital of Wales (UHW) and Morriston Hospital. Method Prospective data collection was carried out for 6 weeks at different times across both sites. Patients booked for appendicectomy were located on TOMS (Citrix) or TheatreMan. Once idenfitied, patient consent forms were reviewed in clinical notes. Data were extracted from consent forms regarding the documented risks of procedure for 16 patients. No patient identifiable data was recorded. A period of intervention was applied in the form of information posters and clinical audit meeting presentations to educate clinicians on the risks. Re-audit was performed through another 6-week period on 16 different patients at both sites. Results Out of 16 complications (EIDO standards), 13 complications were more likely to be included on consent forms post-intervention. The average number of risks documented on consent forms was 13 post-intervention, compared to 9 pre-intervention. At UHW, there was a 20% increase in documented complications, compared to a 40% increase in Morriston. Pre-intervention, consent conversations were rarely documented in patient notes. Post-intervention, 31% of informed consent conversations were recorded in clinical notes in Morriston, and 40% in UHW. Conclusions Departmental education demonstrated improved consent for appendicectomies. Future work should focus on understanding patient retention of consent conversations and a trial of pre-populated electronic consent forms.

paper.title: 895 Enhancing Frailty Assessment and Geriatric Liaison in Acute Surgical Admissions at Bedford Hospital: A Quality Improvement Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Frailty is a key factor influencing surgical outcomes in older adults, linked to higher risks of complications, prolonged hospital stays, and increased mortality. National guidelines, including those from National Emergency Laparotomy Audit(NELA), recommend early frailty screening. This audit assessed frailty documentation in surgical admissions across general surgery, urology, and vascular specialties and evaluated the impact of introducing a frailty liaison service. Method A retrospective audit was conducted over two months (June–July 2024), reviewing emergency surgical admissions to the Surgical Assessment Unit (SAU). Data collected included demographics, operative interventions, Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) scores, and evidence of geriatrician input. Following the audit, a frailty liaison service was introduced, consisting of biweekly ward rounds. A second audit cycle (September–November 2024) was performed to assess changes in frailty documentation and geriatrician referrals. Results In Cycle 1, none of the patients aged ≥65 years had frailty scores documented, and no patients received geriatric input. After introducing the frailty liaison service, Cycle 2 showed a significant improvement, with 88% (103/117) of patients having a documented CFS. Of these, 43% (44/103) were identified as frail (CFS ≥5). However, only 18% (8/44) of frail patients received geriatric input, with delays in referral contributing to under-referral. Conclusions Introducing a frailty liaison service improved the documentation of frailty but highlighted gaps in timely geriatric input. Key recommendations include implementing a mandatory electronic referral system, improving referral workflows, and increasing ward round frequency. A re-audit within six months will measure the effectiveness of these interventions.

audits.change: Teaching session at departmental teaching and a template operation note.

paper.title: 900 A Single-Centre 2-Cycle Audit of Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour Post-Operative Documentation
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim TURBT procedures are carried out aiming to resect bladder tumours, and the events and findings documented in the operation note heavily influence the decision and action taken by the urology multi-disciplinary team (MDT) going forwards. However not all operation notes are completed with the information required, e.g. tumour size, number or location. We have carried out a 2-cycle audit to assess the documentation of essential information in TURBT post-operation notes, to identify and optimise any scope for improvement in recording and allow for better decision making in the MDT. Therefore, our aim is to assess operation note documentation for TURBT cases to assess whether all required information is being recorded. Method 25 patients were identified in a single centre across a 3-month period undergoing a TURBT. As an intervention, there was a teaching session at our local urology departmental teaching, as well as implementing a template operation note for staff use to ensure all information is documented. We compared our results to a standard checklist by Kikuchi et al. Results Initial results showed that 24% of the 25 cases audited record whether there was a pre-op rectal examination, whilst 40% comment on tumour number and 32% record whether there was felt to be complete tumour resection. Whilst 96% do record tumour location, even this figure was not 100%. Conclusions All staff documenting TURBT operation notes should use the template op note checklist provided to ensure there is thorough information recorded.

paper.title: 937 Adherence to MMR Reporting Standards in Newly Diagnosed Colorectal Cancer as Part of the Lynch Syndrome Workup Pathway: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Lynch syndrome is an inherited condition caused by mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, which significantly increases the risk of colorectal, ovarian, endometrial, and small bowel cancers. According to NICE guidelines, individuals diagnosed with colorectal cancer (CRC) should undergo screening for Lynch syndrome through immunohistochemistry (IHC) testing for MMR proteins or microsatellite instability (MSI). Early identification of Lynch syndrome can guide personalised management strategies. This re-audit evaluates the Trust's adherence to the recommended Lynch screening pathway. Method Patients diagnosed with CRC between March and April 2024 were identified from multidisciplinary team (MDT) meeting records. Data collected from electronic patient records included patient demographics, diagnosis dates, TNM staging, IHC MMR results, and additional tests for BRAF and MLH1 hypermethylation. Reporting dates for these tests were also reviewed. Results 32 cases were reviewed, with 100% undergoing MMR testing, compared to 97% in the initial audit. The average time from biopsy to histology results was 8 days (range 2-22), an improvement from 8.6 days (range 4-32) previously. MMR results were reported within an average of 4.3 days, with 97% reported within 10 days, up from 90% in the first audit. Four patients showed MMR deficiencies, with three undergoing additional BRAF and MLH1 methylation testing. The time between MMR and MLH1 results significantly improved, averaging 91 days, compared to 251 days in the previous audit. Conclusions The Trust’s adherence to Lynch syndrome screening has improved, now meeting NICE targets. Continued audits are necessary to ensure sustained compliance with national guidelines.

paper.title: 1007 Improving Discharge Letter Timeliness in Vascular Services: A Two-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Discharge letters are crucial for ensuring continuity of care between secondary and primary care providers. Delays can lead to disrupted follow-up care, medication errors and patient safety risks. According to Trust guidelines, discharge letters should be available to GPs within 24 hours of discharge. This audit aimed to assess delays in discharge letters within the Vascular service at University Hospitals North Midlands, identify contributing factors, and propose recommendations to improve timeliness. Method This retrospective audit consisted of two cycles. The first cycle, conducted from May to June 2022, identified delays and informed interventions presented to the clinical team. The second cycle, conducted from December 2023 to February 2024, re-evaluated progress. Data included time from discharge to letter authorisation, admission reason, procedures undertaken and patient location. Results In the first cycle, 52 delayed discharge letters were identified, with an average delay of 14.6 days. In the second cycle, delays were reduced to 35, but the average delay time increased to 19.4 days. Significant improvements were seen in Central Treatment Suite Day cases, which demonstrated no delay in 2024. However, 44% of delays in both cycles were angioplasty cases performed in interventional radiology, where no juniors are based. Conclusions Overall, a reduction in the number of delayed discharge letters was shown, paired with an increase in the average delay. Presenting the second cycle findings led to agreed changes, including assigning responsibility for interventional radiology letters and keeping patients on vascular lists until letters are completed. A new audit cycle is underway to assess further improvements.

paper.title: 1030 A Completed Audit Cycle on Listed Complications on Consent Forms for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy at a Single Centre, Heartlands Treatment Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction GMC Guidelines state that consent forms should make patients aware of all the probable complications of procedures and surgeries. This audit aimed to assess whether all 8 NHS-listed and other relevant complications were mentioned in consent forms. Two complete audit cycles were carried out, with an intervention implemented after the first cycle to improve compliance with the guidelines on documenting potential procedure complications followed by a second cycle. Method A single-center prospective study was conducted on patients undergoing Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy between August 2023 to December 2024. Data was collected on complications recorded, additional procedure requirements, and the consenting person’s grade. After the first cycle, the data were analyzed, and departmental awareness was raised, followed by a second cycle. Results Thirty first cycle records showed compliance for bile-duct injury and bleeding was 100%, infection at 90%, and visceral injury at 83%. Anaesthetic risks, 56.7%, and post-cholecystectomy syndrome, 45%, had the lowest compliance. Audit presentation alongside awareness posters via team messaging platforms, resulted second audit cycle of 13 records where a compliance of 100% was noted for all NHS-listed complications except for visceral injury (84.6%) and venous thromboembolism (61.5%). Compliance improved for all other complications except for pain where compliance was reduced by 48%. Conclusions Listing relevant complications in consent forms is crucial. Awareness through different platforms aside from audit meetings can help raise compliance. On-going audit cycles will help maintain compliance as new residents rotate to the department. Procedure-specific consent forms complementing specific patient information sheets will be the ideal next step.

paper.title: 1044 Improving Surgical Handover Quality: A Two-Cycle Audit Using RCS Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Effective handovers are essential for patient safety and continuity of care in surgery. The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) has developed comprehensive guidelines in which a minimum dataset is recommended for inclusion when handing over patients to incoming surgical teams. This audit aims to evaluate and enhance the quality of surgical handovers in a tertiary hospital by measuring current practices against the RCS guidelines. Method A two-stage Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA) cycle was conducted. Data on surgical handover sessions in a tertiary hospital over a week was collected and handover sheets were retrospectively reviewed. Following the first cycle, a standardized handover sheet was developed. In the second cycle, posters were placed to reinforce these guidelines. Compliance was re-audited at 1-month intervals after each intervention to assess improvements and monitor progress. Results In the first cycle, 50 handovers were reviewed, revealing deficiencies in key areas such as patient identification (75%), date of admission (30%), location (80%), responsible consultant (40%), diagnosis (60%) and results of significant/ pending investigations (50%). Re-audit data demonstrated significant improvements after implementing interventions, including standardized handover sheets and posters. Patient identification rose to 95%, diagnosis 75%, date of admission 50%, location 88%, responsible consultant 60%, diagnosis 75% and results of significant/ pending investigations 67%. Overall compliance with the RCS minimum dataset improved from 45% to 75%. Conclusions The audit demonstrated that targeted interventions improved compliance with RCS guidelines for surgical handovers. This highlights the effectiveness of structured interventions in enhancing the safety and reliability of surgical handovers.

audits.standard: British Society of Gastroenterology LGIB guidelines
audits.finding: 11 (25%) had no imaging, treatment or procedure; 6 (14%) unnecessary admissions per BSG criteria; 7 (16%) transfused, 3 (7%) not meeting BSG criteria; 2 (5%) CT angiogram with Shock Index <1; 4 (9%) with Shock Index >1 had no CT angiogram.

paper.title: 1048 Evaluating Inpatient Management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding - A Retrospective Single Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aims to evaluate inpatient management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding (LGIB) at a single District General Hospital over a 2-month period using British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines as gold standard management. Method Data of patients admitted with LGIB in August and September 2024 was retrospectively collected. Results Patients with LGIB were admitted 44 times across 2 months. 11 patients (25%) had no imaging, treatment or procedure with a combined total of 29 bed days between them. 6 of them (14%) were unnecessary admissions as per met BSG criteria. 9 patients (20%) had no imaging or procedure and were treated with intravenous fluids alone. They also accounted for 29 bed days. 3 of them (7%) were unnecessary admissions as per BSG criteria. 4 patients (9%) were treated with tranexamic acid. 7 patients (16%) had blood transfusions including 3 (7%) who did not meet BSG criteria for transfusion. 2 patients (5%) had a CT angiogram against guidelines as both had a Shock Index <1 although one was anaemic and hypotensive. Meanwhile, 4 patients (9%) had a Shock Index >1 and did not have a CT angiogram as guidelines suggest. 3 patients (7%) had inpatient flexible sigmoidoscopies despite being haemodynamically stable with the reason for inpatient intervention given as ‘ongoing bleeding’. Conclusions A significant proportion of LGIB admissions have minimal or no intervention. Inpatient management does not appear to follow BSG guidelines. Work needs to be done to prevent unnecessary admissions including research into the use of Virtual Wards for this patient group.

audits.standard: Local gentamicin dosing and serum level monitoring guidelines

paper.title: 1059 Audit of Adherence to Gentamicin Guidelines in a Tertiary Hospital Surgical Unit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Gentamicin is frequently administered to surgical patients for both prophylaxis and treatment of infections. Proper dosing and administration are crucial to maximize its therapeutic efficacy and minimize adverse effects. Local guidelines have been established to standardize dosing and monitoring practices. This audit aims to assess the appropriateness of gentamicin prescriptions in a surgical unit. Method This audit was conducted in a tertiary care hospital surgical unit over two months. Data were collected from gentamicin charts of surgical patients. The parameters assessed include the accuracy of initial dosages and the adherence to monitoring serum levels in accordance with these guidelines. Initial dosage accuracy was determined by comparing prescribed dosages to guideline-recommended values. Results In the first cycle, a total of 48 patients were reviewed throughout a one-week period. Initial dosage accuracy was high, with 70% of prescriptions aligning with recommended weight-based dosing protocols. However, adherence to serum level monitoring guidelines was suboptimal with only 55% of patients having serum levels measured within the appropriate timeframe. After implementing targeted interventions, including poster displays and departmental teaching, a reaudit at one and two months demonstrated substantial improvements. 92% of initial gentamicin dosages were accurately prescribed while adherence to monitoring serum levels has increased, with 78% of patients receiving timely measurements. Conclusions The audit demonstrated that targeted interventions such as appropriate visual reminders and departmental teaching, significantly improved adherence to guidelines for gentamicin prescribing.

paper.title: 1091 An Audit to Evaluate the Effectiveness of the Implementation of an Enhanced Recovery Programme (ERP) Discharge Checklist for Elective Colorectal Cancer Resection Patients Is on Length of Stay in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Enhanced Recovery Programs (ERPs) in colorectal surgery, popularized in the early 2000s, are associated with reduced morbidity and shorter hospital stays. However, their success depends on effective implementation by surgical teams. An audit at a District General Hospital revealed delayed discharges in over 50% of elective colorectal surgery patients. As a result, an ERP discharge checklist was introduced to improve discharge efficiency. This study evaluates its impact. Method A single-center, retrospective audit was conducted using patient data from January 5 to June 27, 2024. Compliance with the ERP discharge checklist was assessed, including outcomes such as length of stay, catheter removal, and first flatus. Results The audit included 45 patients (22 males, 23 females) who underwent elective colorectal cancer surgery without stoma formation. The median length of stay was reduced (4 vs 5 days), more patients were discharged on the day the checklist was completed (61% vs 46%), and a higher percentage had catheters removed on day 1 (80% vs 63%). The most common reasons for discharge delays were weekends (6 cases) and co-morbidities (6 cases). Conclusions This audit demonstrates that the ERP discharge checklist contributes to a reduced length of stay following elective colorectal cancer surgery. Improving weekend discharges is a focus for future work, with plans to implement junior doctor education and a weekend discharge strategy for elective colorectal patients.

paper.title: 1097 Improving Infant Male Circumcision Practices: A Two-Cycle Clinical Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate practices and outcomes of male baby circumcisions using Plastibell technique at the Musamedics clinic, assess compliance with WHO guidelines for early infant male circumcision, and enhance patient care through an iterative audit process. Method This two-cycle audit reviewed 209 cases in the first cycle and 120 cases in the second cycle. Data, including demographics, procedural details, and outcomes, were collected and analysed. Findings from the first cycle were presented to staff, with recommendations discussed and implemented before the second cycle. Key metrics included documentation quality, local anaesthesia administration, discharge efficiency, and complication rates. Results Documentation completeness improved markedly, with missing data on gestation reduced from 4% to 0.8%, and on Plastibell size from 10% to 5.8%. Compliance with post-operative checks increased dramatically from 0% to 98.3%. The local anaesthetic dose was optimised, with a mean reduction from 2.36 ml to 2.18 ml, and variability decreased (SD 0.72 to 0.48). Time for anaesthesia to take effect improved from a mean of 4.63 minutes (range: 3–10) to 4.36 minutes (range: 3–8). Intraoperative complications dropped from 2.5% to 0.8%, with only minor bleeding recorded. Discharge efficiency increased significantly, with 91.6% discharged within 15–30 minutes, compared to 55% in the first cycle. Conclusions The audit demonstrated significant improvements in compliance with best practices, documentation, local anaesthesia practices, and patient flow, while maintaining a low complication rate. Structured audits and collaborative staff discussions were instrumental in achieving these enhancements. Future efforts will focus on incorporating long-term patient follow-up to assess outcomes and satisfaction.

paper.title: 1099 Enhancing Patient Safety in the General Surgery Department Through Timely Treatment Escalation Plans: A Standard Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Treatment escalation plans (TEPs) are critical for ensuring patient safety upon admission and during clinical deterioration. It is essential that TEPs are completed promptly after admission to meet established standards. This study aimed to evaluate whether TEP completion times in the general surgery (GS) department of a hospital in central London align with the trust’s standard, which specifies that TEPs should be completed within 36 hours of admission. A standard audit was conducted, comparing the average time to complete TEPs before and after an educational intervention. Two audit cycles were undertaken, including all emergency admissions under GS. The time from admission to TEP completion was measured. After the first cycle, an educational intervention was implemented, consisting of posters distributed to junior doctors encouraging prompt TEP completion. The second cycle assessed the intervention’s impact. In the first cycle, the average time to complete TEPs was 39.6 hours, which decreased to 34.6 hours in the second cycle. Although this reduction did not achieve statistical significance (p > 0.05), the average completion time met the trust’s standard after the intervention. The average age of patients was 61.6 years in the first cycle and 56 years in the second. Additionally, the percentage of patients discharged before TEP completion decreased from 15% to 5%. This study highlights the positive impact of educational interventions on junior doctors, improving adherence to guidelines and enhancing patient safety.

paper.title: 1108 An Audit of the Completeness of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Documentation and the Development of a Consistent Electronic Documentation Template
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The complete documentation of operative procedures is important for its medico-legal implications as well as enabling better post-operative care for patients. The Royal College of Surgeons England (RCSE) has set out guidelines for what should be recorded within all operative documentation. We undertook an audit to determine compliance rates with these guidelines and developed an electronic template document for use within our trust EPR system. Method We examined the operative notes for all Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy cases, both elective and emergency, within a 2-month period at Chelsea and Westminster hospital (N=30) and recorded which of the criteria set out in the RCSE guidance was included. We devised an EPR template document which included all the guidance criteria as well as utilising drop down menu’s with commonly used options to improve ease of use and free text space to allow for more description. This template was advertised through a poster presentation to the specialist registrar’s responsible for writing operative notes. Results Our audit showed poor initial compliance for the following criterion: Operative Indications (33%), Positioning and Skin Preparations (27%, 10%), Number of Clips Applied to Cystic Duct/Artery (53%), Post-Operative Antibiotic requirement (57%), Post-Operative Bloods (20%), VTE Prophylaxis (40%) and post-admission follow up (57%). Conclusions Initial audit shows poor compliance in several areas of key documentation. Our EPR template helps to improve compliance with the national guidance on operative documentation for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy, with our work able to be expanded to include other common General Surgical Procedures such as Appendicectomy.

audits.standard: NCEPOD 2010 recommendation of routine geriatrician input; target 95% of eligible emergency laparotomy patients (aged 80+ or 65+ and frail) receiving geriatric review

paper.title: 1121 Comprehensive Care for Geriatric and Frail Surgical Patients: A Multi-Cycle Audit and Review of Outcomes
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim A National Confidential Enquiry of Patient Outcome and Death 2010 report highlighted deficiencies in care for elderly surgical patients, recommending routine geriatrician input. This audit, conducted in a district general hospital’s general surgery department, aims for 95% of eligible emergency laparotomy patients to receive geriatric review and compares 30-day mortality and average length of stay (LOS) to national averages. Method A multi-cycle audit with three periods of data collection, analysed patients aged ≥80 or ≥65 and frail undergoing emergency abdominal surgery. Data sources included patient notes, electronic referrals, and the NELA database. Results 2017/18: 13 patients, 15.4% 30-day average mortality, 23% geriatric review. A liaison consultant was employed as a result. 2020/21: 14 patients, 15.8% mortality, 17.7-day average LOS, 64.3% geriatric review. Following this, an eReferral system was introduced, but the liaison role became vacant. 2023/24: 26 patients, 3.8% mortality, 23.2-day average LOS, 4.2% geriatric review. Conclusions Despite initial improvements, the department remains noncompliant with national standards. The department is underperforming compared to national averages for LOS (11 days) and geriatric review (33.2%) but a better 30-day mortality (9.0%). The department remains noncompliant with national standards. Dedicated time in geriatricians’ job plans is needed for consistent reviews, but reliance on a single individual creates vulnerabilities. A multidisciplinary team approach is essential for reliability. Following this audit cycle, the liaison role was re-established. Recommendations include mandatory clinical frailty scoring on admission, appointing a 'geriatric lead' surgeon and integrating geriatric care into resident inductions, with summary posters present in the doctors’ office.

paper.title: 1126 Reporting of Thyroid Cytology Specimens and Their Correlation with Thyroid Histology: The 1st Cycle of an Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate compliance with RCPath standards for thyroid cytology, including the inclusion of Thy categories in all reports, distribution of cases across categories, correlation of cytology results with histology after thyroidectomy, and adherence to MDTM discussion standards for high-risk categories (Thy4/Thy5). Method A retrospective review of 253 thyroid cytology and histology samples from July 2023 to October 2024 was conducted across two tertiary centres within the same NHS trust. Reports were assessed for Thy category inclusion and prose explanations. Histological correlation from thyroidectomy specimens was analysed where available. Prevalence rates for malignancy and neoplasia were calculated for each Thy category. Compliance was measured against benchmarks: 100% inclusion of Thy categories, a Thy5 PPV of 97–99%, and 100% MDTM discussion for Thy4 and Thy5 cases. Results All reports (100%) included Thy categories and prose explanations, meeting RCPath standards. Case distribution showed Thy3f (32%) and Thy5 (19.2%) as the most prevalent categories. Malignancy prevalence rates were Thy5 (92.3%), Thy4 (85.7%), Thy3f (35%), and Thy3a (25%). MDTM discussion rates were 100% for Thy4 and Thy5, while Thy3f (76.4%) and Thy3a (63.6%) had lower rates. Conclusions While Thy5 PPV remains strong (92.3%), it falls short of the benchmark (97-99%), necessitating improvements in diagnostic accuracy. MDTM discussions met standards for high-risk categories but were lower for indeterminate categories (Thy3a/Thy3f), highlighting opportunities for improvement. Enhanced multidisciplinary collaboration, targeted interventions and a planned re-audit aim to address these gaps and ensure alignment with national standards.

audits.standard: Association of Breast Surgery guidelines for axillary management; axillary recurrence below 5% at 5 years
audits.finding: All patients with U3 or higher ultrasound underwent biopsy; 25/26 B4 biopsies had ANC; axillary recurrence 3 (1.27%) at 5 years.

paper.title: WTP6.01 Audit of Preoperative Axillary Staging and Axillary Recurrence in Early Invasive Breast Cancer at a Single Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims This study aimed to assess our hospital's compliance with the Association of Breast Surgery guidelines for axillary management in early breast cancer. The guidelines recommend preoperative axillary ultrasound for invasive breast cancer, with ultrasound-guided biopsy for suspicious findings. Sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) is the preferred staging procedure, and axillary node clearance (ANC) is advised for confirmed axillary node metastasis. Effective staging should ensure axillary recurrence rates remain below 5% at 5 years. Methods Data was collected for patients undergoing axillary procedures between October 2017 and October 2018. Inclusion criteria were invasive breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) with mastectomy. Exclusions included prior breast cancer or axillary procedures for non-breast cancer reasons. Key data included preoperative imaging, biopsy findings, surgical interventions, and 5-year outcomes. Results Among 235 patients (mean age 61), 61.7% had invasive cancer, 37% had DCIS, and 1.3% had both invasive cancer and DCIS. SLNB was performed in 203 patients, ANC in 26, and axillary sampling in 2. All patients with ultrasound findings of U3 or higher underwent ultrasound-guided biopsy. Of 26 patients with suspicious (B4) biopsies, 25 underwent ANC, while 1 underwent SLNB with no recurrence at 5 years. Axillary recurrence occurred in 3 patients (1.27%), two of whom experienced local recurrence first. Conclusion Our data show high compliance with staging guidelines and a low axillary recurrence rate of 1.27%, well below the 5% benchmark at 5 years, supporting the effectiveness of current practice.

audits.standard: NICE: SLNB for mastectomy for DCIS; considered in high-risk breast-conserving surgery

paper.title: WTP6.04 Identifying Patients Undergoing Surgery for DCIS Suitable for Sentinel Node Biopsy – a Single Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a non-invasive breast cancer precursor, confined to the ducts, with a very low risk of lymph node metastasis (<1%). The NICE guidelines recommend sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) for patients undergoing mastectomy for DCIS to detect occult invasive disease. For breast-conserving surgery (BCS), SLNB is considered in high-risk patients, such as those with extensive microcalcifications, a palpable mass, or mass-like lesions, due to the added morbidity and resource use of SLNB. Method Data were prospectively collected from patients undergoing BCS or mastectomy for DCIS at a single unit between 2017 and 2022. Parameters included pre-operative tumor size, histological grade, type of surgery, and postoperative tumor size and histology, with SLNB data recorded where applicable. Results Eighty-five patients underwent WLE and 17 mastectomy. Mean age was 62 years in both groups. Four high-risk BCS patients underwent upfront SLNB; one had microinvasion. Of the 81 BCS patients without upfront SLNB, three developed invasive disease and underwent SLNB as a second procedure. The odds ratio for upfront SLNB in high-risk patients was 8.66 (95% CI: 0.68–109.9, p=0.0956), indicating higher likelihood of invasive disease postoperatively, though not statistically significant, due to small sample size. Conclusions This audit supports selective SLNB for high-risk patients undergoing BCS. While the high-risk group was more likely to have invasive disease, the result was not statistically significant due to the small sample size. Further studies are needed to refine SLNB indications in DCIS.

audits.title: 862 Blood Product Utilisation in Breast Surgery: An Audit of Clinical and Financial Outcomes
audits.standard: Local guideline: group and screen for mastectomy and reconstruction
audits.finding: Group and screen done in 90% of mastectomy/reconstruction and 21% of WLE/SLNB cases; no transfusions.

paper.title: 862 Blood Product Utilisation in Breast Surgery: An Audit of Clinical and Financial Outcomes
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Preoperative blood grouping and saving is routine for elective breast surgery, though transfusion requirements are low (3.8%, higher in reconstruction). Current guidelines at St. Vincent’s Hospital recommend group and screen for mastectomy and reconstruction but lack protocols for wide local excision (WLE) or sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB). This audit assessed adherence to these guidelines and evaluated the cost-effectiveness of preoperative group and screen in breast surgery. Method This retrospective audit reviewed 129 patients who underwent elective breast surgery between 9 September and 28 November 2024. Data collected included demographics, surgical details, haemoglobin levels, and transfusion requirements. Analysis was performed using R 4.1, and findings were presented to relevant stakeholders. Results Of the 129 patients (median age 63.5), 40 (31%) underwent mastectomy/reconstruction, and 85 (66%) underwent WLE/SLNB. Preoperative group and screen were performed in 90% of mastectomy/reconstruction cases and 21% of WLE/SLNB cases. No patients required transfusion. At least 24 unnecessary type and screen orders were identified, incurring additional costs. Conclusions Routine group and screen for elective mastectomy and reconstruction is widely adhered to but resulted in no transfusions, questioning its necessity. For minor procedures, testing is infrequent and variable. These findings highlight the economic inefficiency of unnecessary preoperative blood sampling, suggesting that clinical judgment based on patient-specific risk factors could improve cost-efficiency while maintaining safe care standards.
