paper.title: 946 Post-Operative Venous Thromboprophylaxis: An Audit on Departmental Compliance with Association of Breast Surgery (ABS UK) Recommendations
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) can cause significant post-operative morbidity and mortality. In breast cancer patients, this represents the second most common cause of death and has a combined incidence of <0.4% after all procedures¹,². The Association of Breast Surgery have recommendations on chemoprophylaxis in identified high risk groups². Aim This audit aimed to assess departmental VTE outcomes and guideline compliance. Method Retrospective audit of patients undergoing breast surgery under one consultant between December 2023-November 2024. Data was collected from electronic/paper patient records and included: demographics, operation type, anaesthetic type/duration, hospital stay and VTE on imaging. Results 169 patients underwent surgery, 119 (73.5%) for malignant pathology: 35 mastectomy and 84 conservative surgeries. Three patients had immediate reconstruction. Eleven patients had general anaesthetic duration >3 hours, and 22 patients had predisposing conditions for VTE. Two patients, undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy and mammoplasty, had chemoprophylaxis prescribed. Although 1 patient underwent imaging for suspected pulmonary embolism, all patients were negative for VTE. Conclusions Departmental VTE outcomes were compliant with the national risk (<0.4%), in-line with current guidance. VTE chemoprophylaxis was not commonly prescribed in higher risk groups, however this did not impact outcomes. VTE prophylaxis in breast surgery should be considered differently to other general surgery procedures: further work is required to create a breast-specific, standardised local protocol.

audits.title: 838 Cutting Through the Chaos: An Audit on Operating Theatre Delays
audits.standard: Zero preventable delays and 100% required hair removal (trust guidelines)
audits.finding: Delay in arrival in the anaesthetic room 81%; delay from theatre arrival to operation start 52%; hair removal before theatre 41%.
audits.change: Education of clinicians and posters promoting the 'Ready4Theatre' initiative (showered, hair removed, changed).

paper.title: 838 Cutting Through the Chaos: An Audit on Operating Theatre Delays
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To identify where theatre delays occur in cardiothoracic theatre and develop simple, low-cost, easily applicable methods for improvement. Method Prospective data was collected over one week. Standards were zero preventable delays, and 100% occurrence of required hair removal as stated in trust guidelines. After the first cycle, education to relevant clinicians alongside educational posters promoting the "Ready4Theatre" initiative, which includes being showered, hair removal and changed, were distributed to improve adherence and reduce theatre delays. Repeat prospective data was collected again. Results The greatest reduction in delays was in arrival in the anaesthetic room from 81% to 51%, and time from arrival in the theatre to the operation starting from 52% to 36%. This suggests that the simple measures to enable patients to be ready were effective. This is supported by the fact that 90% of patients underwent hair removal before arrival in the theatre, compared to 41% before. However, 86% of patients still had delays in some areas of their theatre journey, and hair removal in 50% of patients was inadequate. Conclusions Simple measures such as increased awareness and educational posters can reduce delays over a short period. However, improvements were still required, which could be achieved by developing trust guidelines. Guidance regarding hair removal improved adherence to this standard; however, it was still inappropriate, and therefore, future work will provide easy-to-refer posters that depict detailed hair removal guides. Although focused on cardiac surgery, the basic principles of "Ready4Theatre" could be deployed by other specialities to reduce preventable delays.

audits.standard: ENT UK guidelines for paediatric tonsillectomy discharge information

paper.title: 265 An Improvement in Paediatric Post-Tonsillectomy Discharge Information
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Tonsillectomy is a common paediatric surgical procedure. Post-tonsillectomy bleeding is a significant risk (2-5%.) In extremes, bleeding can be fatal. Prompt presentation to emergency department is crucial. ENT UK have constructed guidelines for paediatric tonsillectomy discharge information- highlighting where to present with certain complications and how to prevent them. This project aimed to audit local compliance with guidelines and subsequently improve discharge information. Method A retrospective audit was performed analysing paediatric post-tonsillectomy discharge summaries over two 4 -week cycles 9/9/24-7/10/24 (baseline) 21/10/24-18/11/24 (post-intervention). Patients were identified through hospital admission records and data recorded in a standardized excel spreadsheet. A survey was distributed to the local department to formulate the intervention (one-click inserts of pre-defined discharge summary information- “snippets”). Results There were 28 patients identified in the first cycle. Only 21% of discharge summaries stated to go to ED if they had a significant bleed (6). 7% stated to see the GP if they had a persistent fever (2). 78% stated to take regular analgesia (22) and 46% stated the importance of a regular diet (13). 15 patients were identified in the second cycle. 93% of discharge summaries stated to go to ED if they had a significant bleed (14). 73% stated to see the GP if they had a persistent fever (11). 100% stated to take regular analgesia (15) and 73% stated the importance of a regular diet (11). Conclusions There was an improvement with all discharge information post snippet. Further cycles are warranted looking at parent understanding and satisfaction of the information.

audits.standard: not reported

paper.title: 1128 ENT Treatment Room Swabs Audit and Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of this audit and quality improvement project was to: assess the frequency of ear swabs in the ent treatment room; determine if patients being swabbed had follow-up arranged and if swab results changed management. Method All treatment room visits for acute ear presentations during october and november 2023 were reviewed. Information was collected from clinical portal and collated on excel. Following review of results, quality improvement measures were implemented, including the display of a poster in the ent treatment room with indications for swabbing. Data was collected again in october and november 2024. Results In the first audit cycle, swabs were taken in 77% of acute ear presentations. There was no follow-up in 20% of patients who were swabbed and swab results changed management in 9% of cases. The recommendation following review of these results was that there should be specific indications for ear swabs which might ultimately lead to a change in management. Patients should also have follow-up arranged to ensure that swab results are actioned. In the second audit cycle, swabs were taken in 47% of cases and there were fewer patients who did not have follow-up arranged (12%). Swab results changed management in 11% of cases. Conclusions This audit has shown that swab results change management in very few acute ear presentations therefore swabbing should not be a routine part of patient assessment. Our quality improvement measures have helped to reduce the frequency of unnecessary investigations and ensure that patients are followed up appropriately.

paper.title: 160 Awareness of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding Guidelines Among Surgical Doctors and Efforts to Improve Them. a Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess education levels of lower GI bleeding guidelines among surgical doctors and measures to improve them. Method The BSG guidelines for lower GI bleeding were taken as the gold standard format. A questionnaire(10 questions in a google survey document) was made to assess the knowledge of the finer points of the guideline. The survey was taken up predominantly by registrars and all participant responses were documented electronically and anonymized. An informal teaching session was held subsequently along with uploading of the guidelines onto the trust software, which allowed for easy referral by all staff members. The same survey was conducted again to note the improvement in knowledge levels. Results In both cycles of the audit 18 members took part including 14 registrars and 4 SHOs. Following the measures undertaken the awareness levels of the BSG guideline increased from 7 to 12(38% to 66%). The awareness of using the shock index to determine the need for a CT angiogram increased from 5 to 14(27% to 78%).The knowledge of the Oakland score for safe discharge of patients increased from 9 to 13(50% to 72.2%). Improvement of patients being scored for safe discharge from 7 to 11(38% to 61%). Conclusions Our initiatives have resulted in better knowledge levels among surgical doctors regarding lower GI bleeding guidelines used in the emergency setting resulting in better compliance and a safer patient environment.

audits.finding: Combined 86 patients: non-operative management successful in 60%, 40% surgery; 78% of adhesional SBO with water-soluble contrast managed non-operatively.

paper.title: 487 Optimising Non-Operative Management of Adhesive Small Bowel Obstruction: A Closed-Loop Audit Driving the Creation of Trust-Wide Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Small bowel obstruction (SBO) is a common surgical emergency with diverse management practices, as highlighted by the National Audit on Small Bowel Obstruction (NASBO). This study explores variations in patient characteristics, treatment strategies, and outcomes to identify practice differences that may impact patient outcomes, aiming to streamline management guidelines for SBO. Method This prospective study was conducted at a district general hospital in the UK, focusing on patients presenting with SBO to the emergency general surgery service. The first cycle, from December 2023 to March 2024, included 40 patients, while the second cycle, from May 2024 to July 2024, included 46 patients. Data on the timeline from diagnosis to resolution, with emphasis on non-operative management, were extracted from the hospital database and analysed using descriptive statistics in Excel. No patient identifiers were used, and approval was granted by the information governance team. Results A total of 86 patients were included, with a median age of 75 years. Mechanical causes were identified in 97% of cases, with adhesions affecting 47%. Non-operative management was successful in 60%, while 40% required surgery. Among patients with adhesional SBO, 78% of those who underwent a water-soluble oral contrast challenge were successfully managed non-operatively. Nutritional support was documented for 76% of patients, and 37% experienced recurrent SBO, with 80% requiring emergency surgery. Conclusions The use of water-soluble oral contrast showed a high success rate, emphasizing its potential in non-operative management. Close monitoring of recurrent SBO cases may reduce the need for surgical intervention.

paper.title: eP60 Management of splenic trauma at Aintree University Hospital: an audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Damage of the spleen can result in haemorrhage and life-threatening haemodynamic instability. This study aimed to evaluate the management of traumatic splenic injury at a major trauma centre against current international guidelines, and identify areas of good practice and areas for improvement. Methods Data was obtained from an existing data set of trauma patients presenting between 2018-2022. Patients with splenic injury confirmed on CT scan were included. Electronic and scanned notes were reviewed for data collection, and results were analysed. Standards included:80% of patients received CT/FAST scan100% of patients receiving correct grading of their splenic injury according to American Association for Surgery of Trauma (AAST) guidelines.100% of patients received correct treatment based upon the World Society of Emergency Surgery guidelines. Results All patients underwent CT scan (n=115). 73% received AAST grading, of whom 93% were graded correctly. 64% had non operative management in the form of conservative management and/or interventional radiological embolization. 37% underwent operative management. 5% failed conservative management and required surgery. 37% were managed according to WSES guidelines. Management was undetermined in 27% due to lack of AAST grading. Patients with WSES III and IV had a lower adherence to management (40% and 43% respectively) versus WSES I and II. Conclusion This audit highlights the variability in current guideline adherence and applicability for the management of splenic trauma. Intervention, education, and re-audit are required to improve patient outcomes.

audits.title: 405 A Single-Centre Retrospective Audit to Determine Utilisation of Parenteral Nutrition in Paediatric Surgery
audits.standard: ESPGHAN 2005 paediatric parenteral nutrition guidelines: optimal benefit with ≥5 days PN
audits.finding: 28 PN episodes; sub-optimal PN in 15 (54%), with median 3 days of full-dose feed.

paper.title: 405 A Single-Centre Retrospective Audit to Determine Utilisation of Parenteral Nutrition in Paediatric Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Parenteral Nutrition (PN) is utilised in surgery to support post-operative recovery and meet metabolic demands. However, the use of PN in the paediatric surgical population is not well-characterised, with risks associated with overprescription. We aimed to investigate if current PN use in paediatric surgical patients reflects general paediatric artificial nutrition guidelines. Method A single-centre retrospective audit was conducted to assess PN usage over one year (2023) in paediatric surgery, excluding neonates. Data collected included: patient demographics, duration of PN and complications encountered. Optimal benefit was standardised at receiving ≥5 days PN based on guidelines by European Society for Paediatric Gastroenterology Hepatology and Nutrition (ESPGHAN) in 2005. Results A total of 27 patients (19 M: 8F) were identified (median age: 8 years, range: 2 months–16 years) with a total of 28 PN episodes recorded. Sub-optimal PN was common (n = 15, 54%) with the population receiving 3 days of median full-dose feed. PN was utilised most commonly following: appendicectomy and bowel obstruction (n = 7 per group, 25% respectively). There were nine complications (32%) with central lines, namely: loss of access resulting in abrupt cessation of PN (n = 4) and infection (n = 2). No significant difference in PN duration optimisation was observed with pre-nutritional dietician review. Conclusions This study shows the potential risk of overprescription and adverse events of sub-optimal PN use in paediatric surgical patients. There is a need for targeted national guidelines specific for paediatric surgical populations; with future prospective national studies informing healthcare professionals of optimised feeding regimes.

paper.title: 1027 Improving the Management of Gallbladder Disease: A Quality Improvement Audit on Imaging Delays, Surgical Timing, and Length of Stay
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To identify inefficiencies in managing gallstone-related conditions at Barnet Hospital—focusing on imaging delays, surgical timing, and length of stay (LOS)—and propose an innovative Hot Gallbladder Pathway (HGB) to improve outcomes and resource utilisation. Method A retrospective audit of 125 consecutive patients admitted with gallstone-related complications was conducted between 26 June and 26 September 2024. Data on demographics, imaging, surgery, and LOS were collected from electronic records and analysed against NICE and AUGIS guidelines. Results Of 125 patients (median age 61 years [IQR 45–76]; 39.2% male), 54.5% presented with acute cholecystitis. Median delays were 5 days [IQR 2–15] for MRCP and 8 days [IQR 6–13] for ERCP. Only 18.4% underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC), with a median time to surgery of 95 days [IQR 43.5–324.5], far exceeding the recommended 7 days. LOS was prolonged (8 days [IQR 5–14]), with imaging delays and readmissions (49.6% of patients were readmitted) compounding inefficiencies. Conclusions This audit highlights substantial deviations from national standards, demonstrating the need for systemic change. The proposed HGB pathway integrates expedited imaging, dedicated theatre lists, and multidisciplinary collaboration to optimise care delivery. Scalable across NHS trusts, this model aligns with national priorities to enhance outcomes, reduce costs, and address regional disparities in gallstone disease management.

audits.title: 481 Improving Practices in Extravasation Injury Management: A Retrospective Audit
audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: Time of recognition documented in 53%; infusion stopped and limb elevated in 67%; injury photographed in 56%; plastic surgery advice sought in 81%.
audits.change: Hospital-specific extravasation guideline proposed; staff education and re-audit planned.

paper.title: 481 Improving Practices in Extravasation Injury Management: A Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Extravasation, the leakage of drugs/fluids into surrounding tissues during intravenous administration, can cause severe complications such as necrosis, gangrene, and contractures if not promptly managed. This audit aimed to evaluate current management practices for extravasation injuries at our hospital and develop a standardised protocol to reduce morbidity and improve patient outcomes. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on all cases coded as extravasation injuries in our electronic patient records (EPIC) from 2018 to 2023. Data collected included time of injury recognition, type of extravasated agent, site of injury, initial management strategies, referral to plastic surgery, complications and outcomes. Results A total of 36 cases were identified, with 53% involving irritant agents and 47% vesicants. Initial management was inconsistent: time of recognition was documented in 53%, infusion stopped, and limb elevated in 67%, and injury photographed in 56%. Plastic surgery advice was sought in 81% of cases. Complications, including skin necrosis, blistering, and compartment syndrome, were observed in 22%, and 11% of cases required surgical intervention. Conclusions The incidence of documented extravasation injuries appears lower than in other trusts, highlighting gaps in recognition and coding. This audit revealed significant variability in management practices, highlighting the need for a hospital-specific guideline, emphasising detailed documentation and coding, early identification, prompt intervention, and standardised management protocol. Implementation of these guidelines has the potential to improve patient outcomes and reduce complications. Future steps include staff education and a re-audit to evaluate the impact of the new guideline.

paper.title: 193 Breaking Barriers in Achieving Excellence for National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) Documentation: A Successful Quality Improvement Framework
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This QIP conducted at the Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother Hospital (QEQMH) addresses the insufficient documentation of patient data entry on the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) website. The focus is centred on surgical patients who had emergency general abdominal surgery at QEQMH. Our aim is to reach the target of ≥85% formal mortality risk assessment documented on NELA to achieve the Emergency Laparotomy Best Practice Tariff 2023-2025 for our trust. Method We conducted two Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles over a one-year period across 60 surgical patients at QEQMH who meet the inclusion criteria for NELA, evaluating the completion of their data entries on NELA website. The proposed interventions include presenting at Clinical Governance meetings of Surgical and Anaesthetics departments, conducting surveys, enhancing induction process to provide Surgical trainees with NELA website log-in details and creating a QR code on CEPOD booking form to facilitate documentation. Results The audit highlighted deficiencies in recording surgical patients who had emergency general abdominal surgery on NELA, revealing only 11.7% (n=7) were documented. 3 months after our interventions, we re-audited to assess for improvement and recorded a 76.2% increase in documentation with 86.2% (n=50) using the NELA tool, achieving our compliance target of ≥85%. Conclusions Engaging with Surgical and Anaesthetics team is a key aspect; this involved identifying challenges, providing instructions, and creating feedback channels. We were successful in significantly improving the use of NELA Patient Data Entry tool after implementing interventions and have a multifaceted strategy to involve the Peri-operative (POPS) team and IT department in the future.

audits.title: 329 Audit of Compliance of Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) Risk Assessment and Prescription of Prophylaxis in the General Surgery Directorate at Darlington Memorial Hospital (DMH)
audits.standard: NICE VTE guidelines
audits.finding: Risk assessment completed 90.7% (16.3% delayed); prophylaxis prescribed 88.4%.

paper.title: 329 Audit of Compliance of Venous Thromboembolism (VTE) Risk Assessment and Prescription of Prophylaxis in the General Surgery Directorate at Darlington Memorial Hospital (DMH)
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess compliance of VTE risk assessment and prescription of prophylaxis in General Surgery directorate at DMH according to NICE guidelines and compare it with the compliance of the cohort following implementation of teaching, posters, and verbal reminder interventions. Method A single day for each cohort, 17th July 2024 and 18th October 2024, were randomly selected for analysis. Inpatients under the General Surgery directorate were isolated on the EPR system and data collated from these records. Those awaiting review, those who hadn’t yet had a decision for admission, and patients admitted under different specialties were excluded. VTE assessment and prescription were classified into No/Yes/Yes, Delayed. Results Overall improvement in the completion of VTE Risk assessments between audit cycles (96.4% vs 90.7%), though a higher proportion of the assessments delayed (35.7% vs 16.3%). Overall improvement in the number of patients with VTE Prophylaxis prescribed (96.4% vs 88.4%), with the majority being prescribed on admission. Conclusions VTE is one of the most preventable causes of mortality and morbidity in hospitalised patients. Surgical inpatients are at an increased risk, typically due to the nature of their condition and the effect on Virchow’s Triad, and appropriate risk assessment and prescription of prophylaxis paramount. Frequent teaching and reminders are effective intervention to keep up VTE compliance, therefore repeated reminders should be delivered to the working doctors. Going forward, a qualitative audit to assess reasoning for increased delayed assessments, and introduction of teaching at induction should be considered.

audits.finding: Essential information missing in several domains.

paper.title: 601 Are Surgical Ward Rounds EPIC? – Audit of Ward Round Documentation Following Introduction of an Electronic Health Care System
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the impact of an Electronic Healthcare system on the safety (documentation of essential information) and accuracy of history and decision making within the daily ward round notes in a surgical unit. Method A prospective audit of general surgical ward round notes was undertaken in September 2024. These were audited against the RCS Edinburgh’s SHINE Ward Round Tool and a consensus from the unit Consultants of the “ideal” ward round note (recording of essential and accurate information). Following the initial data collection cycle, a feedback session was held with the resident doctors in the unit responsible for ward round documentation. Notes were re-audited one week following this session. ANOVA was used to compare the two audit cycles. Results 434 and 533 notes were audited in cycle 1 and cycle 2, respectively. In both cycles, essential information in several domains was missing. However, following the educational session, there was improvement in recording of names of team members present, examination findings, patient understanding and management plan (p <0.05). There was no improvement in recording of diagnosis, new issues, observations, VTE and antimicrobials (p>0.05). Conclusions Accurate documentation of the patient journey is fundamental to safe and effective patient care. The introduction of a new electronic system provides an opportunity to facilitate improved documentation. The utilisation of templates as prompts provides an opportunity to enhance patient safety.

audits.standard: Local guideline: IV co-amoxiclav plus gentamicin first line; gentamicin, teicoplanin and metronidazole if penicillin allergic; stop 24 hours post-surgery or continue 5-7 days if no source control
audits.finding: Compliance with IV co-amoxiclav and gentamicin 4.0% (2/50); penicillin-allergic regimen adherence 4.0% (2/50); mean duration 4.59 days; 54.0% (27/50) received under 5 days.
audits.change: Two teaching sessions and guideline dissemination via posters.

paper.title: 618 Improving Adherence to Antibiotic Prescribing Guidelines in Patients with Intra-Abdominal Sepsis: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Intra-abdominal sepsis is a critical condition requiring timely and appropriate antibiotic therapy. Local guidelines recommend IV co-amoxiclav with gentamicin as first-line treatment and IV gentamicin, teicoplanin, and metronidazole for penicillin-allergic patients. Antibiotics should be discontinued 24 hours post-surgery or continued for 5-7 days if source control is not achieved. This audit assessed baseline adherence to guidelines and evaluated the impact of targeted interventions. Method A baseline audit of 50 patients admitted under the general surgical team between January and March 2023 was conducted. Data on demographics, diagnoses (20 cholecystitis, 12 appendicitis, 10 colitis, 8 cholangitis), antibiotic regimens, and duration were collected. A re-audit of 48 patients (18 cholecystitis, 10 appendicitis, 12 colitis, 8 cholangitis) was performed between August and November 2024 after two teaching sessions and guideline dissemination via posters. Results Baseline compliance with IV co-amoxiclav and gentamicin was 4.0% (2/50), improving to 33.3% (16/48) post-intervention. Penicillin-allergic regimen adherence increased from 4.0% (2/50) to 6.25% (3/48). Antibiotic duration improved from 4.59 days to 5.71 days, with fewer patients receiving under 5 days (54.0%, 27/50 vs. 39.6%, 19/48). Gentamicin was the most underprescribed antibiotic. Overuse (>7 days) occurred in 12.0% (6/48) of post-intervention cases. Conclusions Targeted education significantly improved adherence to prescribing guidelines for intra-abdominal sepsis. Further audits are necessary to sustain progress and address remaining gaps in practice.

paper.title: 736 Diagnostic and Documentation Quality in First-Time TURBT Performed in North Devon District Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Audit our TURBT operation note and documentation quality practice against NICE guidelines for diagnosing bladder cancer (1.2.6 and 1.2.7 i.e tumour size and number, and mitomycin instillation) Assess the requirements in the documentation related to NICE recommendations. Implement the action plan to meet the NICE recommendations Re-audit after 6months Assess the quality improvement after-action planning Method Retrospective data collection of consecutive patients who underwent transurethral resection of bladder tumour for a new bladder tumour diagnosis from August 1st, 2022, to February 28th, 2023, with the help of a spreadsheet. Re-audit; Data collection from August 1st, 2023, to February 28th, 2024 (6 months after the action plan) compared to results before the action plan with the help of a spreadsheet. Results 78.20% of operation notes didn't include the instillation of mitomycin and its justification for not giving. 98.71% of operation notes mentioned tumour number and 88.46% of operation notes mentioned tumour size. After the implementation of action plans, the quality of documentation of operation notes is improved doubly. Conclusions Bladder cancer is the seventh most common cancer in the UK. Most bladder cancers (75 to 80%) are non-muscular invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC). They are usually treated by telescopic removal of cancer (TURBT) followed by the instillation of chemotherapy into the bladder which is proven to decrease relative risks of occurrence by 39%. Our NDDH is one of the most remote acute hospitals in mainland England and will decrease the burden on NHS and the public with just exact documentation of operation notes.

audits.standard: Local Acute Abdomen pathway
audits.finding: Imaging within timeframe 60%; surgical review within timeframe 38.2%; antibiotics within 1 hour for septic patients 80%; NELA score documented 5.5%.

paper.title: 761 Closing the Loop: Evaluating and Enhancing Adherence to a Local Acute Abdomen Pathway
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute Abdomen pathways are a staple in Trust guidelines, allowing clinicians to identify deteriorating patients with surgical pathology, and manage them accordingly. We aimed to assess adherence and improve upon the local Acute Abdomen pathway. Method During the first cycle, patients who underwent emergency abdominal surgery over a 3-month period were identified using the hospital’s theatre logbook. Following this, an updated pathway was created. The cycle was closed 7 months later, where patients were identified via specific presenting complaints highlighted by post-take ward round documentation. Data was analysed using Fisher's Exact test, with a p-value of <0.05 being statistically significant. Results A total of 55 and 91 patients were audited in our first and second cycles respectively. 78% of patients had emergency imaging requested within the pathway’s timeframe, compared to 60% initially (p-value =0.03). 91% were surgically reviewed within the guideline’s time frame compared to 38.2% in the initial cycle (p-value <0.01). 50% of septic patients received antibiotics within 1 hour as opposed to 80% in the initial cycle (p-value = 0.33). 1% of patients had a NELA score documented as compared to 5.5% in the initial cycle (p-value = 0.15). Conclusions Having implemented changes, we have demonstrated statistically significant improvements in the adherence to the pathway. Positives such as surgical review and CT request time should be reinforced and continued. With limitations identified, we have suggested further changes which we hope to re-audit after incorporating them into hospital guidelines ensuring enhanced outcomes; ultimately hoping to contribute to advancing national standards.

paper.title: eP73 “Why Radiology Requests are not Being Accepted”, a quality improvement audit in a surgical department
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Radiology requests serve as the primary communication tool between clinical physicians and radiologists, enabling radiologists to provide accurate diagnostic support. This audit aimed to evaluate the radiology request acceptance rate, identify common reasons for request rejections, and implement measures to improve request quality. Method According to the Royal College of Radiologists, radiology requests should include comprehensive and relevant information, although specific content requirements are not defined. The audit was conducted in two cycles: the first in September-October 2023 and the second in August 2024. Patients were randomly selected from clinical handover records and SACU clinic logs. Radiology requests on the TrakCare system were reviewed to determine their acceptance status, assess the quality of information provided, and identify reasons for requests being placed on hold. Results During the first audit cycle, 73% (52/71) of radiology requests were accepted. The primary reasons for rejections included inappropriate imaging (21%, 4/19), duplicate requests (21%, 4/19), and insufficient clinical details (21%, 4/19). Following these findings, a structured request format was developed, and staff were educated on its use. In the second audit cycle, the acceptance rate improved significantly to 89% (89/101). Conclusions A high-quality radiology request should include a concise patient background, current symptoms, examination and investigation findings, relevant differential diagnoses, and the clinical situation. Radiology requests should be presented as well-informed proposals rather than directives. Implementing a structured request format can enhance communication, optimize resource utilization, and expedite patient care planning for improved outcomes.

paper.title: 1136 Turning Data into Action: A Regional Audit and Quality Improvement Project to Elevate Core Surgical Training Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate and improve access to theatre and clinic opportunities, and overall training standards for Core Surgical Trainees (CSTs) in the East of England (EoE). Method A combined quality improvement and audit approach reflecting JCST Quality Indicators was adopted across three data collection cycles (December 2023, April 2024, November 2024), involving 50 CSTs across 14 trusts in EoE. Structured surveys and direct communication were used to collect quantitative and qualitative data, analysed using Excel statistical tools and thematic analysis. Findings were synthesised into actionable recommendations and presented to the Surgical Trainee Committee and trust leadership, facilitating targeted interventions, including rota redesign, resource reallocation, and improved planning processes. Results Response rates were 47%, 69%, and 58%. Initially, 45% (9/21) of trainees reported consistent access to theatre, which increased to 68% (21/31) and 78% (20/26) following interventions. Clinic access remained lower, with 19% (4/21), 39% (12/31), and 50% (13/26) reporting scheduled clinic time. Consistently, >75% report inability to attend mandatory teaching. Barriers included service provision demands, short rotations, prioritisation of other staff (junior SpRs and PAs), workplace culture and insufficient protected time. Improvements were observed in six trusts; however, three showed no measurable progress, highlighting systemic challenges. Conclusions This project demonstrates the value of data-driven decision-making, stakeholder collaboration, and tailored interventions in driving meaningful improvements. While regional progress is encouraging, addressing persistent disparities requires national-level policy changes in addition to strong local leadership. These findings highlight the importance of evidence-based frameworks in transforming complex systems to achieve equitable and sustainable outcomes.

paper.title: 953 Improving Documentation of Operation Notes for Transurethral Resection of Bladder Tumour: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate documentation of transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) is vital for patient care and outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate and improve TURBT documentation at a general hospital in London by implementing a standardised operation note template. Method In cycle 1, TURBT operation notes from March–August 2023 was reviewed against an 8-point checklist to identify poorly documented domains. A 12-point standardised template was introduced in June 2024. Cycle 2 re-audited notes from July–October 2024 to assess for improvement. Results Cycle 2 (n=9) had higher documentation compared to cycle 1 (n=40) in the following domains: number of tumours (100% vs 86.21%), size of largest tumour (88.89% vs 65.52%), tumour characteristics (100% vs 89.66%), recurrent or primary tumour (66.67% vs 31.03%), carcinoma in situ assessment (55.56% vs 3.45%), clinical tumour stage (55.56% vs 10.34%) and separate base biopsy (66.67% vs 10.34%). Cycle 1 showed higher documentation rate for detrusor muscle visualisation (71.43% vs 55.56%). Additional useful domains which were included in the template showed good completion rate; tumour location (100%), ureteric orifice involvement (77.78%), visually complete resection (66.67%), and perforation assessment (77.78%). Conclusions The introduction of a standardised TURBT operation note greatly improved documentation. This will enhance post-operative follow up care by ensuring all essential information is included for accurate bladder cancer risk group stratification.

audits.standard: GIRFT day-case laparoscopic cholecystectomy rate (national median 60%)

paper.title: SP1.05 Optimizing Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A GIRFT-Based closed loop audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) is the gold standard management for symptomatic gallstone disease and is usually performed as a day case. A Getting it Right First Time (GIRFT) analysis at our institution highlighted a decline in the rate of day-case elective LC. This prompted an audit and subsequent quality improvement initiative. Methods We analysed patient data for elective LC between October 2023 and February 2024. Analysis identified areas for improvement, leading to the development of a business case and implementation of two interventions. First, the day surgery unit (DSU) recovery’s operational hours were extended to 9 PM. Second, the local anaesthetic (LA) protocol during LC was modified. In addition to port sites, LA was also infiltrated into the liver bed, thereby improving postoperative pain control and early mobilization. Following this, a re-audit was conducted between March and August 2024. Results Initial data from 86 elective LCs between October 2023 and February 2024 revealed a day-case rate of 64% (55/86), above the national median of 60%. The primary reasons for unplanned admissions were DSU closing at 6 PM, intraoperative concerns and post-operative pain. As per NHS national tariff 2024/25, the cost of unplanned admissions (median 1 day) was approximately £12,000. Our re-audit encompassing 101 elective LCs demonstrated an increase in our day-case rate to 73% (74/101). Conclusion This data suggests that extending DSU hours and optimizing LA techniques can positively impact day case rates. These findings have implications for resource utilization, reducing inpatient bed occupancy, associated costs and improved patient satisfaction through reduced hospital stays.

paper.title: SP3.02 Unnecessary Preoperative Blood Tests for Patients Undergoing Abscess Incision and Drainage: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background + Aims According to NICE, ASA grade 1 or 2 patients should not receive preoperative blood tests for abscess incision and drainage (I&D). This audit investigated the incidence of preoperative blood tests for low-risk abscess I&D at our centre and evaluated the financial implications. Methods Data was collected retrospectively over a 4-month period (December 2023 – April 2024). Information about type of abscess drainage, ASA grade, and preoperative blood tests was recorded. The findings were disseminated to the department, and posters were hung advising not to take bloods for routine abscess I&D. The same data was collected over another 4-month period (May 2024 – September 2024). Results In the initial study period, 71 cases of abscess I&D were recorded; 55 cases were ASA 1 or 2. Of the ASA 1 and 2 cases, 50 cases (91%) had routine bloods done. These tests amounted to £2,151 spent. In the re-audited period following intervention, 63 cases of abscess I&D were recorded; 55 cases were ASA 1 or 2. Of the ASA 1 and 2 cases, 15 cases (27%) had routine bloods done. These tests amounted to £406 spent during the follow-up period. Conclusions In our General Surgery department, educating staff that ASA 1 and 2 patients do not require pre-operative blood test for abscess I&D led to a reduction of patients receiving blood tests from 91% to 27%. This intervention saved the department £1745 during the 4-month period and will save the department more than £5,000 per year.

paper.title: SP3.05 Improving Fluid Resuscitation and Maintenance Prescription Practices in Surgical Admissions: Closed loops double audits
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Intravenous fluid plays a vital role in perioperative care. Despite this, adherence to the British Consensus Guidelines on Intravenous Fluid Therapy for Adult Surgical Patients remains suboptimal. This quality improvement initiative aimed to evaluate and enhance fluid prescription practices for surgical admissions, addressing gaps in compliance. Methods Data were collected retrospectively from CERNER for both audits' cycles. The first audit cycles covered the period from April to May 2024, with resuscitation data set including 59 patients and maintenance dataset listing 53 patients. The second cycle, a re-audit, was conducted from 26 September to 1 November 2024, with resuscitation dataset including 53 patients and maintenance dataset listing 24 patients. Results Initial findings revealed only 43% of patients received optimal fluid resuscitation, with 36% receiving no fluids and 34% prescribed non-optimal fluid types. For maintenance fluids, 74% of patients were prescribed fluids, with only 66% meeting daily sodium requirements and 47% meeting free fluid requirements. Following targeted interventions, significant improvements were observed in the re-audit. Optimal fluid resuscitation increased to 83%, with non-optimal prescriptions decreasing to 17%. Fluid prescription rates improved from 64% to 94%. For maintenance fluids, prescription rates increased to 91.7%, sodium requirements to 91.7%, and free fluid targets to 75%. Additionally, the use of appropriate fluid types improved from 36% to 45.5%. Conclusions Educational interventions proved effective in improving adherence to GIFTASUP guidelines for fluid resuscitation and maintenance in surgical admissions. Sustained improvements require ongoing training for junior doctors and routine monitoring to ensure high standards of perioperative care.

paper.title: SP3.09 Promoting Good Clinical Practice Certification Amongst Resident Doctors in a Major Surgical Emergency Unit: a Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims The Surgical Emergency Unit (SEU) promotes research literacy and involvement amongst Foundation doctors and higher trainees, including through weekly resident-led Research, Audit, and Presentations (RAP) meetings and mandatory completion of NIHR Good Clinical Practice (GCP) online training, which familiarises professionals with international standards for clinical research. This quality improvement project (QIP) aimed to promote GCP training amongst new SEU resident doctors from August-October 2024. Methods This two-cycle QIP aimed to increase the proportion of residents that had completed GCP training. Cycle 1 involved an instructional email alongside verbal instructions in a morning handover, morbidity and mortality meeting, and weekly RAP meeting. Cycle 2 involved a reminder email to individuals who had not completed training alongside a reminder in the departmental newsletter. Results 43 resident doctors worked on SEU over this period. Prior to cycle 1, 37.2% had completed training. Completion rose to 51.2% after cycle 1 and to 62.8% after cycle 2 (p=0.001). Including only full-time SEU staff (n=27), completion was 48.1% prior to cycle 1, 63.0% after cycle 1, and 77.8% after cycle 2 (p=0.008). Amongst Core Trainees, completion was 100% after cycle 1. Commonly reported reasons for training non-completion included insufficient time and clinical pressures. Full qualitative analysis of these reasons using thematic analysis is planned. Conclusions The SEU encourages a culture of involvement in clinical research amongst residents, including through regularly scheduled, resident-led research meetings. In this context, encouraging completion of GCP training through departmental meetings, newsletters, and direct emails was effective in significantly improving compliance.

paper.title: SP4.04 A Standards-Based Audit of Elective Procedures in a Tertiary Care Vascular Surgery Department in London
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims In accordance with the NHS Constitution, our centre mandates that if a procedure (open or endovascular) is cancelled for non-clinical reasons, it must be rescheduled within 28 days. In this paper we aim to:Evaluate the department’s compliance with NHS guidelines for rescheduling cancelled procedures within 28 days.Identify avenues for improvement in current outcomes. Methods Procedure outcomes from 1st March to 31st August 2024 were reviewed, including number of procedures listed (scheduled, completed and cancelled), reasons for cancellations, and if cancellations were rescheduled within 28 days. This was communicated to the Consultants, the Admissions and Waiting List Manager, and the Cardiovascular Service Manager. Data from 1st October–30th November 2024 was collected using the same metrics to evaluate changes in performance. Results Of 402 initially scheduled procedures, 165 were cancelled. Rescheduling rates at 28 days were 14.75% (17.5% for open and 12.0% for endovascular). Following implementation of targeted departmental collaboration, the second data cycle reported improved rates of rescheduling - 65.2% (15/23) for open and 87.7% (57/65) for endovascular procedures. However, bed unavailability remained the major reason for cancellations. Conclusion Surgical postponement and cancellations are currently a major challenge as highlighted in the nationwide project, PACE (Postpone and Cancellations in Elective care). Our study indicates that facilitating structured dialogue within a surgical department and increasing awareness of guidelines enhanced compliance with performance targets.

paper.title: SP4.08 Enhancing Pediatric Appendicitis Care in Alignment with GIRFT Guidelines: A Two-Cycle Audit at a District Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims The audit aimed to evaluate the management of pediatric appendicitis at a District Hospital against GIRFT (Getting It Right The First Time, June 2022) guidelines. It sought to identify areas for improvement in diagnostic pathways, surgical timing, and antibiotic protocols across two audit cycles. Methods A retrospective review was conducted over two cycles: the first from May to October 2022 (27 patients) and the second from January to December 2023 (48 patients). Data included demographics, time to surgery, pre- and post-operative antibiotic use, histological outcomes, and complications. Results In the first cycle, the negative appendicectomy rate was 22%, and the median time to surgery was 23 hours. Antibiotics were inconsistently prescribed pre-operatively (81%) and post-operatively, with limited adherence to best practice. The complication rate was 18%. By the second cycle, interventions had reduced the negative appendicectomy rate to 4%, aligning below the national average of 10%. The median time to surgery improved to 19.25 hours, with 85% of patients receiving pre-operative antibiotics. However, unnecessary post-operative antibiotics were given in 35% of simple cases, and only 86% of complex cases met the 48-hour guideline. Complication rates fell to 6%. Conclusions The second cycle demonstrated significant improvements in negative appendicectomy rates, time to surgery, and complication rates, reflecting enhanced adherence to GIRFT guidelines. However, variability in antibiotic prescribing persists, necessitating protocol standardization. Continued focus on diagnostic tools, such as clinical scoring and imaging, and consistent antibiotic stewardship are crucial for sustaining and furthering these improvements.

paper.title: SP4.09 A follow up audit of negative appendicectomy rates in a single site acute hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims The negative appendicectomy rate (NAR) in the UK is estimated to be 20%. Negative appendicectomies (NA) carry an unnecessary risk to patients and a financial burden on the healthcare system. This study evaluated clinical practices at a single site acute hospital to identify ways to reduce NAR and compared outcomes to a study performed in the same hospital (2019), in which preoperative imaging was 69% and the NAR was 10.3%. Methods Data from appendicectomy/diagnostic laparoscopy cases for appendicitis (June–December 2024) were analysed retrospectively. Variables assessed included inflammatory markers (WCC, CRP), NEWS scores, length of stay (LOS), imaging, intraoperative findings, and histopathology. Results 100 patients underwent appendicectomies/diagnostic laparoscopy, (56% male, mean age of 38±16 years). 86 were admitted after initial assessment, while 14 had planned returns. Same-day appendectomy occurred in 37 cases. Mean LOS was 2.8±2.38 days. On admission, 22% had normal WCC(<10x109/I), 22% normal CRP(<10mg/L), and 4% both normal. 47% of patients had an initial NEWS score of 0. Preoperative imaging was performed in 88%, mostly CT (n=83), with appendicitis reported in 96% (17 complicated vs 63 uncomplicated). Imaging and intraoperative findings regarding nature of appendicitis correlated in 76%. Of available histopathology (n=84) 98% confirmed appendicitis, with an institutional NAR of 3% (all male). Conclusions Increased cross-sectional imaging has reduced our NAR, highlighting the importance of surgeon-radiologist collaboration. Appendicitis should not be excluded based on normal inflammatory markers alone. The study recommends CT imaging as an effective strategy to reduce NAR.

paper.title: SP4.12 An Audit of the investigations of suspected ureteric/kidney calculus in adults in Great Western Hospital, Swindon
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Renal or ureteric colic secondary to urinary stones is common, with an annual incidence of 1–2 cases per 1000 people. It also has a high recurrence rate ranging from 50% to 80%. Most of these patients presenting to the A&E are initially managed by the general surgery on-call juniors and then subsequently referred to urology. NICE guidelines (NG118) recommend urgent low-dose non-contrast CT of the urinary tract for adults with suspected renal colic and ultrasound scans instead of CT if a woman is pregnant. It also recommends measuring serum calcium for adults as a part of the metabolic assessment. The audit aimed to evaluate the local practice compared to the NICE guidelines. Methods A retrospective review of 101 non-pregnant adult patients presenting to the A&E or surgical assessment unit with suspected renal or ureteric colic was conducted (58 patients for cycle 1, 43 patients for cycle 2). Patients were consecutively recruited from the general surgery on-call list (Cycle 1: March-May 2024) (Cycle 2: October - December 2024). Verbal demonstration, email reminders, and added notes to the handover sheet were completed before the completion of cycle 2. Results 100% of CT of urinary tract was performed within 24 hours of presentation in both cycles. Serum calcium was measured in 21% and 72% of patients in Cycle 1 and 2, respectively. Conclusion All patients had a CT of urinary tract performed within the timeframe recommended by NICE Guidelines. There has been a significant improvement in the measurements for calcium.

audits.standard: Correct waste segregation guidelines
audits.finding: Average total waste 5.9kg per case, mostly clinical; recyclable waste 17%; much non-infectious recyclable waste wrongly placed in clinical bins.

paper.title: SP9.10 Rethinking waste for a greener tomorrow in General Surgery: A two-cycle audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims In this study, we aim to assess the current implementation of waste management strategies at an NHS district general hospital (DGH) in general surgery. We have surveyed the volume of waste produced in a variety of cases. Methods We observed elective and emergency cases. For each case, we weighed the waste produced - both recyclable and clinical. After the first cycle, we have distributed surveys and posters to raise awareness of the correct waste segregation guidelines. Thereafter, we have re-surveyed the volume of waste produced after each case. Results The average total waste produced was 5.9kg in our first sample, with majority of the waste being clinical. A significant proportion of non-infectious recyclable waste was incorrectly placed into the clinical waste bin. In our second cycle, the average waste total waste after each operation was higher; however, this may have been because our second sample included longer operations. There has been a noticeable improvement in the appropriate usage of segregated waste into smaller cases; the proportion of recyclable waste usage increased from 17% to 28%. Conclusion On average, 5.9kg of waste is produced after an operation in general surgery, which is mostly clinical. However, we have shown it is possible to improve waste segregation by raising awareness. Key statement We have demonstrated that waste segregation in our trust is not optimised. Further education of staff and raising awareness at meeting and creating posters are the next steps currently being taken for improvement.

audits.title: MTP1.14 Optimising Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of Success Rates and Influencing Factors
audits.standard: National target of 75% day-case completion
audits.finding: 64 (90.1%) booked as day cases, with day-case success rate 74.4%.

paper.title: MTP1.14 Optimising Day Case Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of Success Rates and Influencing Factors
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is a common procedure for gallstone disease, with national targets recommending a 75% day-case completion rate to improve patient care and optimize healthcare resources. This audit evaluates factors influencing day-case success at Ealing Hospital to identify opportunities for improvement. Methodology A retrospective analysis was conducted on 71 elective laparoscopic cholecystectomies performed between January and July 2024. Data, including patient demographics, surgical duration, recovery times, intraoperative findings, and surgery start and end times, were analyzed to identify predictors of day-case success. Emergency cases and incomplete records were excluded. Results Of the 71 cases, 64 (90.1%) were booked as day cases, with a success rate of 74.4%. Age was a significant predictor, with patients under 60 achieving higher success rates (82.4%) compared to those aged 60–79 (55.6%) and over 80 (33.3%) (p=0.002). Surgical duration strongly influenced success, with operations lasting ≤120 minutes significantly more likely to succeed (OR 2.1, p=0.015). Although early morning surgeries achieved slightly better outcomes (76.9%), start and end times were not statistically significant predictors. Intraoperative findings such as normal anatomy correlated with higher success rates (72.4%), while adhesions (60%) and large gallbladders (33.3%, p=0.048) reduced success. Drain placement, comorbidities, and postoperative pain were common reasons for overnight stays, with only 37% of failures anticipated preoperatively. Conclusion Achieving a day-case success rate of 74.4% aligns closely with national targets. Younger age, shorter surgical duration, and straightforward anatomy were key predictors of success. Enhanced patient selection and surgical efficiency can further optimize outcomes.

audits.finding: not reported

paper.title: MTP3.06 Optimizing Blood Retesting Intervals: A Surgical Audit on FBC and U&E Tests in surgical in-patients
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Frequent Full Blood Count (FBC) and Urea & Electrolyte (U&E) testing in surgical patients can lead to unnecessary phlebotomy, increasing risks such as infections and prolonged hospital stays. This audit aims to assess compliance with recommended retesting intervals and implement improvements to enhance patient safety and optimize resource utilization. Financially, save hospital resources as per saving un-necessary blood tests we could save Millions of pounds every year, which can be used in other benefits. Methodology A retrospective analysis was conducted using hospital system data from 70 randomly selected surgical patients in two cycles first August,2024 cycle 2nd cycle is December 2024. A total of 731 blood test requests (FBCs +U&Es) were reviewed. Requests were categorized as compliant or non-compliant based on national guidelines (Royal College of Pathology, NHS England and NICE guideline), with non-compliant tests further classified as either unnecessary or missed but necessary. Ethical considerations ensured patient confidentiality. Results The second audit cycle demonstrated:A 49% improvement in appropriately requested necessary tests.A 5% reduction in unnecessary blood tests.An overall 22.8% increase in compliance with best practice guidelines. Conclusion Enhancing awareness among surgical teams and incorporating guideline-based recommendations led to improved compliance with appropriate retesting intervals. Future initiatives should involve allied healthcare professionals, expand monitoring to all blood tests, and integrate routine teaching into new doctor inductions. Regular audits remain crucial in sustaining and further optimizing blood testing practices in surgical care. This way we could save more than 100,000 £ monthly in every hospital.

paper.title: MTP4.04 Decarbonisation of Surgery - Making the laparoscopic cholecystectomy tray smaller, undertaken as prospective audit leading to quality improvement by reducing unjustified energy wastage and reducing cost
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To cut down the size of the upper GI general tray (UGIGT) used in laparoscopic cholecystectomy containing around 63 instruments to a much lesser by removing the ones that are never used in LC but sterilized and packed every time the tray is prepared. The intended effect of the project is to prevent wastage of water, carbon emissions, cost by avoiding sterilisation of instruments that are never used but packed and sterilised each time. Method Our sample size was 100 LC, in which we included 90 elective and 10 emergency cases. We recorded the type and the number of each instrument that were used from the UGIGT with the help of scrub nurses in each surgery. A survey was also done to make sure all the surgeons were happy with with the contents of the new tray. Results We found that out of 63 instruments on the tray we used maximum of 19 instruments and minimum of 7 in those 100 LC that we audited. Most of the instruments that were used were common, however, there were some rare occasions when few other instruments were used from the tray. Around 5000 liters of water and carbon emissions of 220kgs were unjustified waste in 100 surgeries in around the period of 5 months. Conclusion Created a new smaller tray called 'Lap general tray' (60% lesser instruments), to be used for LC and can also be used of appendicectomy and laparoscopic inguinal hernias as the principle remains the same.

paper.title: MTP7.04 The Extended Surgical Team – The role of the doctor’s assistant as part of the surgical team, a closed loop audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims As part of a larger scale project looking to improve surgical training for foundation doctors. We hope to quantify the impact of the introduction of a doctor’s assistant role as part of the extended surgical team. This project looks to quantify the quality of documentation for all surgical admissions against set national standards. Methods Assessed against the Academy of Medical and Royal Colleges – Guide to Record Keeping Standards, we reviewed documentation for all general surgical admission prior to and following the employment of a doctor’s assistant. Data collections each took place over a 1-week period. Results 40 and 35 patients were admitted respectively over the two cycles. Key areas of success Proportion of consultant reviews documented to be occurring within 14 hours of admission increased from 47% to 97%. Continued high standards in the use of a standardised proforma / MUST score completion and VTE prescriptions (>85%) Social history taking improved from 58% to 75% Key areas of concern Although some improvements in completion of dementia screening tool and oxygen prescriptions occurred, there is still room for improvement. Conclusions The valuable doctor’s assistant role provides a primarily administrative role within the team to enable foundation doctors to partake in tasks deemed to be of more educational value, as per the recent ASiT survey[1]. Increased variety of sessions are now available for foundation doctors. In further projects we hope to demonstrate any impact on individual wellbeing and satisfaction with the post for doctor's and doctor's assistants.

paper.title: MTP7.17 An audit project on the completion of treatment escalation plan (TEP) for surgical patients for decisions about the ceiling of care in a tertiary care major NHS trauma
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims The objective of this project is to evaluate the number of acute and elective surgical patients with variable frailty (Rockwood) score admitted on the surgical floor with or without documented ceiling of care in the form of a treatment escalation plan (TEP) form. Methods A closed loop audit was performed after getting approval from the local R & D department. Data was collected from the patient case notes. The results of the first loop of the audit project were discussed in the departmental clinical governance meeting in the presence of the frailty consultant. After getting recommendations, data for the second loop of the project was collected. Results The case notes of seventy-eight consecutive acute and elective surgical admissions were reviewed in the first loop of the audit. The first loop of the audit cycle yielded only 58 % (45/78) of surgical patients who had a documented ceiling of care in the form of a completed TEP form. After the implementation of the recommendations and regular reviews of patients with variable frailty scores by the frailty consultant, the documentation and decisions about the ceiling of care improved to 83 % (65 patients out of a total of 78 patients recruited in the second loop of the audit). Conclusion Decisions about the ceiling of care in the form of completed TEP proforma in surgical admissions provide greater autonomy to the patients, relatives, and help the surgical doctors to determine the ceiling of care, especially out of hours. Current audit project demonstrates improved compliance in the second cycle.

paper.title: MTP8.11 A Service Review and Retrospective Audit of Diagnostic Imaging and Clinical Outcomes in Acute Appendicitis: Evaluating Service and Adherence to the World Society of Emergency Surgery 2020 Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is one of the most common general surgical emergencies, requiring prompt, evidence-based care to minimise morbidity and improve outcomes. This audit aimed to evaluate diagnostic interventions and clinical outcomes in acute appendicitis at our trust, in accordance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) 2020 guidelines. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients diagnosed with acute appendicitis. Patients undergoing appendicectomy from August 2023 to July 2024 were included. Key metrics assessed were diagnostic imaging use, time to surgery, length of stay, and complication rates. Results Among 119 patients, pre-operative diagnostic imaging was performed in 92.5% of cases. Of 97 CT scans, the positive predictive value was 96.9% when confirmed by histology. A discrepancy rate of 45.2% was observed in distinguishing uncomplicated from complicated appendicitis on CT versus intra-operative findings. CT imaging was used in 96% of patients over 40. Complicated appendicitis was reported intra-operatively in 44.5% of patients with a drain usage rate (34.4%). The negative appendicectomy rate was 4.2%, with malignancy identified in 1.7% of patients. The mean length of stay was 8.5 days (SD 4.5) for complicated cases and 1.4 days (SD 0.98) for uncomplicated cases with 89.1% of patients undergoing appendicectomy within 24 hours. Postoperative complications occurred in 10.1% of cases. Conclusion This audit demonstrates strong compliance with guidelines for timely intervention and imaging, whilst demonstrating low complication and negative appendicectomy rates. Our results suggest areas for improvement in post-op length of stay, minimising use of intra-operative drains, and imaging reporting accuracy.

paper.title: TTP2.04 Unravelling the Genetic Enigma of Lynch Syndrome: An Audit of Practice in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Lynch syndrome, caused by germline mutations in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, is the most common hereditary cause of colorectal cancer (CRC) in the UK, contributing to approximately 1,100 new cases annually. This autosomal dominant condition necessitates timely genetic testing and surveillance. This study aimed to assess adherence to NICE guidelines in the Lynch syndrome testing pathway for CRC in our department. Methods A retrospective review of newly diagnosed CRC cases from January 2022 to December 2023 was conducted using the hospital’s electronic database. Focus was placed on identifying MMR deficiency in histology reports and documentation in MDT outcome proformas, followed by an analysis of genetic testing referrals for MMR-deficient cases per NICE guidelines. Results Out of 193 diagnosed CRC cases, 17 (8.8%) exhibited deficient MMR (dMMR). Genetic testing revealed 14 cases with MLH1 mutations and 3 with mutations in non-MLH1 genes. Genetic testing referrals were made for 5 dMMR cases, resulting in 2 somatic variations, 2 with no variants, and 1 missed referral. The missed referral was promptly addressed with follow-up testing. Conclusion Lynch syndrome requires lifelong surveillance and genetic counseling. This study underscores the importance of adhering to NICE guidelines to ensure timely genetic testing and appropriate referrals. An interprofessional approach, including Surgical and medical oncology, gastroenterology, genetic counselors, and specialist nurses, is essential for comprehensive patient care. Education and collaboration among healthcare professionals are key to improving Lynch syndrome management as guidelines evolve.

paper.title: TTP3.02 A three-cycle audit reviewing compliance with Enhanced Recovery after Surgery (ERAS) protocol following colorectal resections
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This 3-cycle audit looks at our local compliance with the ERAS protocol to improve patient outcomes. Methods Mixed method study. Per cycle, this prospective project of 10 consecutive patients undergoing elective colorectal resections identified quantitative data for assessment of compliance levels (30 total). Qualitative response to changes were sought from the wider MDT to assess the response to the booklet and suggestions for improvements. Data collection took place over a 2-year period. Interventions included staff education and a comprehensive post-operative ERAS booklet for completion during the inpatient stay. Results Key areas of success:Average length of stay between cycles 2 and 3 reduced from 9 to 6Compliance improvements in oral nutritional supplementation, promotion of deep breathing exercises, oral fluid intake and completion of stoma care plans; all now average >90% compliance.More clear documentation regarding time out of bed and mobilisation on/off the ward. Key areas of concern:Poor documentation of discharge planning – less than 50% had this documentedMany patients are declining nutritional supplementationQuantification of mobilisation remains low (<50%) Conclusions Overall, the introduction of an ERAS protocol booklet to inpatient care has shown significant improvements in compliance with numerous aspects of the ERAS protocol. This project demonstrated the importance of multi-disciplinary team working to ensure the best outcomes. paper.title: TTP4.03 MRCP use in gallstone pancreatitis audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction The use of magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) scanning to identify common bile duct (CBD) stones in those presenting with gallstone pancreatitis is controversial. The guidance is not agreed for those with mild/moderate risk of CBD stones. This leads to significant differences in the management of this phenomenon. The aim of this two-cycle audit is to quantify consultant attitude toward MRCP scans for patients admitted with gallstone pancreatitis. Method During the year of 2022, all patients admitted with clinical and biochemical gallstone pancreatitis to a surgical unit were included. Data pertaining to MRCP scan use was assessed. An assessment of change to acute management as a result of this scan was made. This data was shared with all surgical consultants at a local meeting and then the same data parameters were measured over the following 6 months. Results The first cycle highlights that 87% of patients received an MRCP scan. 86% of scans showed no radiological evidence of CBD stone. 24% of patients had an acute surgical procedure. The second cycle shows that 59% of patients were offered an MRCP scan, 82% showed no CBD stone and 25% of patients received an emergency procedure. Conclusion A similar proportion of patients receive an emergency procedure upon their index admission for gallstone pancreatitis, despite a 28% drop in MRCP scan use following departmental education. The use of MRCP does not acutely change management in the majority of cases.

paper.abstract: Abstract Background Gallbladder and biliary tree ultrasound is the gold-standard imaging modality for diagnosing gallbladder pathology. Adherence to the Royal College of Radiologists' (RCR) standards ensures an accurate and consistent reporting system. Aim To assess adherence to the Royal College of Radiologists' gallbladder and biliary tree ultrasound standards, including gallbladder neck, bile echogenicity, wall thickness, common bile duct (CBD) assessment, and CBD lumen measurement. Method The first cycle involved a retrospective review of the ultrasound scans of 70 patients at Princess of Wales Hospital (POWH) and Neath Port Talbot Hospital (NPTH). The results were presented in the joint audit meeting. We implemented several interventions, including introducing a new local reporting protocol, educational posters, and teaching sessions on gallbladder US reporting. In the second cycle, prospective data of 45 patients at POWH and NPTH was reviewed and presented. Results In the first cycle, adherence was as follows:Gallbladder neck assessed: (7.1%)Echogenicity of bile reported: (17.1%)Wall thickness commented on: (55.7%)CBD assessed: (84.3%)CBD lumen measured: (45.7%) In the second cycle (45 patients), adherence improved:Gallbladder neck assessed: (77.8%)Echogenicity of bile reported: (33.3%)Wall thickness commented on: (75.6%)CBD assessed: (97.8%)CBD lumen measured: (44.4%) Conclusion The audit showed a remarkable improvement in adherence to RCR reporting standards for Gallbladder and biliary tree US, particularly in gallbladder neck assessment and CBD evaluation. However, further improvement is needed in documenting bile echogenicity and CBD lumen measurement. Continued monitoring and staff education are essential for sustainable improvement.

paper.title: TTP7.10 Compliance with NCEPOD Guidelines in the Management of Acute Pancreatitis - A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The management of acute pancreatitis requires prompt identification and treatment of the underlying cause. Early antibiotics are not recommended initially, as organ dysfunction is not primarily due to bacterial infection. For gallstone pancreatitis, cholecystectomy should ideally occur during the initial hospitalization once symptoms improve. This audit aimed to assess management practices against NCEPOD recommendations to influence future practice. Methods We conducted a retrospective analysis of acute pancreatitis cases diagnosed biochemically or through imaging from June to October 2023, presenting results at a local meeting. We recommended increasing “hot chole” slots and establishing dedicated waiting lists for gallstone pancreatitis. We re-evaluated these changes from June to October 2024. Results 64 patients were audited in the first cycle, compared to 66 in the second. Gallstone pancreatitis was diagnosed in 33 (51%) and 32 (48%) patients, respectively. MRCP and/ or EUS usage for unclear aetiology rose from 37% to 48%, while inappropriate antibiotic prophylaxis decreased from 42% to 28%. Previous admissions for gallstones decreased from 12 (36%) to 5 (16%). Early cholecystectomy rates improved from 18% to 31%. Conclusions There was a reduction in antibiotic prophylaxis and an increase in MRCP and/ or EUS usage for unclear aetiology. Additional “hot chole” slots and dedicated waiting lists improved early cholecystectomy rates and reduced repeat admissions with gallstone flare-ups.

paper.title: TTP7.14 Audit of Management of Testicular Torsion in a Rural General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Patients who present with suspected testicular torsion to our hospital are managed by the on-all general surgeons because of long travel time to the nearest hospital where urology service is provided. Currently there is no established guidelines/protocol locally or in the Health Board regarding management of this condition. The aim of this audit is to review the management of all patients who presented to our hospital with suspected “Testicular Torsion” over the last 5 years and compare it against the available national & international guidelines aiming to develop a local protocol. Methods A retrospective study included all the patients who underwent scrotal exploration for suspected testicular torsion in our hospital between January 2019 and January 2024. Patient were identified from emergency theatre surgical register and Information Technology department. Data were collected from the patients’ notes, Welsh Clinical Portal and Welsh Patient Administration System. Results 34 patients had exploration of the scrotum for suspected torsion during this period. 13 patients were found to have torsion testicle, the testicle was found to be non-viable in 4 out of them. 3 patients with testicular torsion with non-viable testicle on exploration presented very late after onset of symptoms (1-3 days). Conclusions Management of these cases is done in a timely manner however a local protocol is being developed includes direct referral to the on-call surgical registrar to further decrease time to theatre. It includes TWIST score to guide diagnosis. Raising awareness of children and their carers/parents is of paramount importance.

paper.title: TTP8.03 Reaudit of Radiological Discrepancies in Emergency Laparotomies: A Comparison of Two Audit Cycles (Dec 2019–Dec 2020 vs. Jan 2021–Jan 2024)
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims/Objectives This reaudit aimed to assess changes in the frequency, classification, and factors contributing to discrepancies between radiological CT findings and operative findings in emergency laparotomies, comparing results from two audit cycles. Methods The initial audit (2019–2020) included 114 cases, while the reaudit (2021–2023) analyzed 328 cases. Both audits evaluated discrepancies (major, minor, nil), and examined factors such as age, gender, reporting type, and timeliness. Statistical analyses, including chi-square tests and p-values, were used to identify trends. Results The initial audit found a discrepancy rate of 27.2%, with 11.4% classified as major. Reporting delays were noted, with only 23% completed within 24 hours. Recommendations focused on improving pre-operative communication and radiologist expertise. The reaudit showed a reduced discrepancy rate of 5.8%, with 21.1% major and 73.7% minor discrepancies. Age, gender, and reporting type showed no significant associations (p > 0.05). Discrepancies were often linked to complex conditions, while common findings like adhesional small bowel obstruction (14.9%) and gastric perforation (5.2%) demonstrated strong radiological accuracy. Conclusion The reaudit demonstrated a significant reduction in discrepancies, reflecting improvements in radiological accuracy and processes. Efforts should focus on refining workflows, enhancing diagnostic accuracy for complex cases, and ensuring timely reporting to maintain high standards and improve outcomes.

paper.title: TTP8.11 Audit of Compliance, Documentation, and Score validity in Emergency Laparotomy Care: An overview of NELA scoring
paper.abstract: Abstract Background This audit evaluated compliance with (NELA) standards, analyzed mortality outcomes, and examined the predictive utility of NELA scores. Emphasis was placed on preoperative risk assessment, documentation practices, and identifying gaps in care for emergency laparotomy patients. Methods A total of 57 cases were reviewed, collecting data on patient demographics, NELA mortality scores, and documentation of preoperative and postoperative management. Multidisciplinary team input and mortality risk communication were analyzed. The sensitivity and specificity of NELA scores for predicting mortality were assessed using a 10% threshold. Results Significant gaps in documentation practices were observed. Although NELA scores were preoperatively calculated in 94.7% of cases, mortality risk discussions were documented in only 17.86% of consent forms, suggesting limited communication of risks to patients or their next of kins. Elderly care team involvement was documented for just 12.5% of older patients (≥60 years). Critical care input was noted in 66.07% of cases, leaving a third without evidence of multidisciplinary collaboration. The NELA score demonstrated limited sensitivity (33.33%) for predicting mortality. While specificity was higher (84.31%), two-thirds of deceased patients were classified as low risk, raising concerns about the score’s reliability in identifying patients at risk of mortality. The overall mortality rate was 5.26%, with deceased patients being older (mean age 72.7 years). Conclusion The audit highlights substantial gaps in documentation, particularly in communicating mortality risks and involving elderly care teams. The limited sensitivity of NELA scores suggests the need for supplementary tools to improve risk prediction and care planning for emergency laparotomy patients.
