paper.title: WTP2.10 Appendicitis Patient Pathway at an East Midlands Hospital - a closed loop audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background GIRFT data shows only 12.4% of patients in Leicester, Leicestershire, and Rutland (LLR) achieve the target 2-day length of stay (LOS) and place the region in the highest quartile for average LOS. An initial audit in 2023 found just 4.4% of patients met the target LOS. Since then, theatre and imaging capacities have increased. Aims This study aimed to evaluate overall LOS and time intervals between admission, imaging, operation, and discharge. Secondary aims included assessing digital consent adoption following its departmental implementation in 2022. Methods Data from 91 adult patients undergoing laparoscopic appendicectomy between 04/01/2023 and 04/03/2023 were analysed. Paediatric cases were excluded. Times for admission, imaging, operation, and discharge were retrieved from ICE, ORMIS, and Concentric Health. Data were analyzed using Excel, with weekday and weekend admissions compared via independent samples median tests. Results Mean times were: presentation to imaging (8.91 hours), imaging to operation (26.82 hours), operation to discharge (53.94 hours), and total LOS (3.74 days). LOS improved to 3.7 days (from 4.3), with 14.3% meeting the 2-day target. Imaging-to-operation time decreased significantly (29.15 vs. 26.82 hours, p=0.003). Weekend admissions had significantly shorter imaging-to-operation times (36.23 vs. 21.91 hours, p<0.01). Digital consent adoption increased to 98% from 78% last year. Conclusions LOS and time intervals have improved with enhanced imaging and weekend capacity, alongside increased digital consent uptake. However, LLR remains in the highest GIRFT quartile, necessitating further optimisation.

paper.title: WTP2.12 An Audit of anastomotic leak rate and mortality after abdominal surgery in a specialised Surgical Emergency Unit at John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Expected anastomotic leak rates in the context of general surgery vary depending on type of anastomosis, but generally range from 0.5-18% [1]. This audit aimed to assess anastomotic leak rate after abdominal surgery from an entirely emergency population in a specialised Surgical Unit at John Radcliffe Hospital, Oxford. Methods Anastomotic leak rates were audited based on M&M data and patient records between 25/03/2024-02/01/2025. Data including patient demographics, type of join, length of stay, rate of leak/ return to theatre, and mortality were collected. The rate of stoma formation vs anastomosis was not assessed in this audit. Results Overall 78 cases (M=33, F=45) were analysed. Median age of patients was 67.5 years, mean ASA was 2. Leak and return to theatre rates were both determined to be 4% (n=3). Of the three recorded anastomotic leak cases, two were small bowel anastomoses, and one was ileocolic anastomosis. Mortality rate was 4% (n=3); one patient passed away due to other co-morbidities unrelated to the operation. Median length of stay was 10 days. Conclusions It is possible to have an acceptable rate of anastomotic leak in an emergency setting. To further this, it may be beneficial to audit the rates of stoma formation vs anastomosis in managing surgical emergency cases. References 1. Ellis, C.T. and J.A. Maykel, Defining Anastomotic Leak and the Clinical Relevance of Leaks. Clin Colon Rectal Surg, 2021. 34(6): p. 359-365.

paper.title: WTP3.03 Enhancing Laparoscopic Appendicectomy documentation: A GIRFT & ASGBI based closed loop audit and quality improvement initiative
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate and comprehensive operative notes are essential for effective clinical communication and serve as valuable documentation for reviewing surgical procedures. This audit evaluates the quality of laparoscopic appendicectomy (LA) operation notes at our hospital against the best practice guidelines set by Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT), Royal College of Surgeons England (RCS), and the Association of Surgeons of Great Britain and Ireland (ASGBI). Methods A retrospective review of LA notes (n=29) between June and July 2024 was conducted. Following this, areas for improvement were identified, leading to the development of a standardised proforma and an educational poster to enhance documentation practices. This first cycle was presented at our departmental meeting. Copies of the educational poster and standardised proforma were displayed in the surgeons’ room. A second data collection cycle was undertaken between October and November 2024 (n=27) to determine the impact of these interventions. Results Out of the 31 measured variables recommended to be included in operation notes we found that 19 variables were included in less than 70% of notes in the first cycle. After our interventions, there were overall improvements in documentation across 26 out of 31 (89.7%) measurable variables. Moreover only 7 variables had an inclusion rate of less than 70%. While most domains showed progress, minor gaps remained in documenting appendix location and arterial division methods. Conclusion This audit highlights the effectiveness of the newly implemented proforma and poster in achieving better adherence to the guidelines. Accurate documentation is essential for good clinical practice and patient care.

paper.title: WTP8.06 Supportive Decision-Making: An audit on consent in General Surgery at Tertiary Centre and adherence to guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims This study audited the quality of consent forms for General Surgery patients listed for elective and CEPOD emergency theatre cases, focusing on how often patients were offered a copy of their consent forms. The Royal College of Surgeons recommends providing patients with a copy for review and retention. This is critical as inadequate consent resulted in 1,194 claims between 2014–2019, costing the NHS £202 million, primarily in surgical specialties and gynaecology. Methods A prospective study was conducted at a Major Trauma Centre and a District General Hospital. Patients were identified from elective surgical lists using the Bluespier Theatre software and from CEPOD lists during handovers. Adults with mental capacity and clinical stability were included. Post-operative feedback was also collected through a retrospective qualitative study. Results Over three months, 141 consent forms were reviewed. In the first cycle (40 patients), all forms were adequately completed, but none (0%) were offered a copy, and only 1 patient (2.5%) received one. After implementing educational interventions and poster reminders, the second audit (101 patients) showed marked improvement: 76 patients (74%) were offered a copy, and 68 patients (67%) received one (percentage differences: 74%, p<0.05; and 64.8%, p<0.05). The result of this study suggests guidelines on consent forms are not being strictly followed at a tertiary hospital site. With encouragement, poster reminders and education the rate of patients receiving a copy of their consent was improved. Our intervention has improved the quality of consenting within our hospitals and thus patient experience.

paper.title: WTP8.08 Snapshot audit of adherence to hospital infection prevention and control policy pertaining to the monitoring of IV cannulae. A quality improvement project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims A quality improvement project was undertaken in a small district general hospital to investigate whether Infection and prevention control policies pertaining to IV cannulation were being followed. This guidance stated that cannulae should be: correctly dressed and labelled, documented in the electronic record and assessed twice daily to ensure there are no signs of thrombophlebitis. Methods On 15th May 2024 every inpatient in the hospital with a cannula was examined to assess whether the aforementioned criteria had been met along with the duration of time the cannula had been in and examination findings. Results It was found that 38%(n=86) of inpatients had a peripheral cannula sited. Of these, over 30% were documented in the notes and only 10 cannulae had a date label attached. The time since insertion of the cannula ranged from 24 to 240 hours. There were 26 cannulae that had spoiled dressings in situ and evidence of thrombophlebitis in 18 cannulae, which, once identified were promptly removed by staff. Conclusions From this audit it was concluded that there should be more awareness of the basic standards set out by the trust on IV cannulation to help prevent pathogenic infiltration into the cannulae. These results have been presented at the hospital’s grand round and a poster detailing these recommendations has been created to highlight the areas of concern and hopefully improve clinical practice. The audit will undergo a second cycle to investigate whether these interventions have improved things.

audits.standard: Trust policy of two-stage consent process
audits.finding: 58% of electronic consent forms generated on the date of surgery rather than at first clinic consultation.

paper.title: WTP8.15 An audit of the consent obtaining process and shared decision making in elective surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Consent obtaining process in surgery is a legal requirement and an important element to uphold ethical and patient-centred care. This audit examines the adherence of consent obtaining process to trust policy of a two-stage consent process, focused on the dates of generating electronic consent form, patient signature and consent confirmation against the date of surgery. Methods A retrospective audit on all patients that underwent elective operation in the general surgery department in a selected month, within a trust comprising of 2 hospitals, totalling 270 patients. Date of electronic consent form generation, patient signature and consent confirmation is audited against date of operation. EIDO forms (patient leaflet information) is also audited as linked to the e-consent form, and if documented on clinical letter of first consultation. Result Analysis identified poor adherence to the two-stage process of consent seeking, although all initial consultations comprise of the shared-decision making process, 58% of collected data suggests electronic consent forms are generated on the date of surgery rather than first consultation in outpatient clinic. Delayed consent generation compromises the consent obtaining process, leading to avoidable pressures and human error. The main error identified is consent confirmation signed but not dated, notably seen in consent forms generated on date of surgery. Conclusion Action and improvements must be made in the consent obtaining process, especially in relation to electronic consent forms to avoid legal disputes and promote satisfactory clinical communication.

paper.title: eP267 Audit of Cholecystostomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Percutaneous gallbladder drainage (PGB) should be restricted to managing patients who are unfit or unable to undergo early cholecystectomy. We audited the indication for PGB in our Trust and the fate of patients who underwent PGB. Methods All patients who underwent PGB over a 13 month period were included. Data were collected on demographics, Charlson comorbidity index (CCI), CRP, NEWS and location in the hospital at the time of PGB request. Length of stay, hospital encounters, incidence of delayed cholecystectomy and any morbidity and mortality were recorded. Results 84 patients underwent PGB. The median age was 73. At the time of PGB request 55% of patients had a (CCI) of 0–4, a median NEWS of 2 and CRP of 272. 76% of patients were being managed on a regular surgical ward. Following drain insertion, 23% of patients experienced morbidities. Patients with PGB required a mean/ median of three extra visits. Delayed cholecystectomy was performed in 45% of patients. 66% of these were Nassar Grade IV difficult procedures. Mortality was observed in 9 patients. Conclusions A significant proportion of patients undergoing PGB satisfied the criteria for emergency cholecystectomy. Insertion of PGB has a considerable impact on patients and healthcare systems. Cholecystectomy following PGB is complex.

paper.title: eP294 A Retrospective Audit: Evaluating the Management of Acute Pancreatitis at the Surgical Emergency Unit of a Tertiary Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To evaluate severity scoring, underlying causes, and management pathways in patients presenting to the Surgical Emergency Unit at a tertiary centre with acute pancreatitis. Methods Retrospective analysis of patient records over two months (September–October 2024). Data collected included demographics, aetiology, severity scoring, management and outcomes. Key metrics were admission duration, rate of operative interventions, time to surgery [TTS], and complications. Results Eighty-one patients were analysed. Formal scoring using the Glasgow-Imrie system was completed in 9 patients, with a median of 2 [range: 0-3]. Gallstones [33 cases] and alcohol excess [18 cases] were the primary aetiologies. Seventy patients were admitted, with an average length of stay of 5.73 days. Three patients developed serious complications requiring ITU admission [admission NEWS Score: 3-10], with one patient suffering cardiac arrest and multi-system organ failure, resulting in death on the day of admission. Six patients were managed via an ambulatory pathway for further investigation [MRCP/US/EUS] which confirmed 4 cases of gallstone pancreatitis. Twenty-one patients with gallstone pancreatitis underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy; 14 during index admission [TTS: 6.5 days, range: 1–18 days], with average length of stay as 8.5 days. One case was following ambulatory investigation [TTS: 31 days]. Five cases were discharged for elective day-case surgery [TTS: 9-11 days]. Conclusion Severity scoring was underutilised, limiting risk stratification and care planning. Management pathways, including timely surgical intervention within 6 weeks and ambulatory care were effective, with most patients discharged without complications. Serious cases were escalated appropriately, reflecting robust acute care management.

paper.title: eP446 Optimising Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Operation Notes: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Operation notes serve as the standard documentation of intraoperative findings. The Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCS) and NHS England introduced the Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) program, outlining 32 essential components for operation notes. This study evaluates the quality of laparoscopic cholecystectomy operation notes before and after implementing GIRFT recommendations. Methods A retrospective analysis of laparoscopic cholecystectomy operation notes from two biliary surgeons over a two-year period was conducted. Following the first audit cycle, GIRFT recommendations were implemented. Operation notes were then reassessed and compared before and after adopting these recommendations. Results A total of 245 operation notes were included. There were 132 operation notes in the first cycle and 113 in second cycle. All operation notes included 19 out of 32 recommended points, such as operation indication, consent, date/time of operation, surgical checklist, skin preparation and drugs administered. Further details are specified in the table below. Additionally, incorporating instant digital upload of intraoperative photos could further improve documentation and prevent data loss.

audits.standard: Royal College of Physicians national falls guidance and local protocol

paper.title: eP514 General Surgical Inpatient Falls: An Audit of Current Practices
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims As the surgical population is becoming older and frailer, the risk of inpatient falls is increasing. This audit aimed to assess how well we were complying with preventing and managing falls on the general surgical patients over 64 years per Royal College of Physician national guidance. Method We conducted an audit from 25/11/23 - 25/12/23 of all inpatient falls. Demographic and admission data were captured, along with falls risk assessments when completed. Further data included circumstances of the fall, the extent of harm, use of falls proforma and further medical review. Data was collected and analysed from physical and electronic notes, using Microsoft Excel. Results 14 patients had an inpatient fall of whom two had multiple falls. Median age was 80 (range 59-91) with male:female ratio 10:4 All patients were assessed for risk of falls within 24 hours of admission. None of the falls were unwitnessed. All falls were reviewed, however in only 10 cases (71%) was local protocol fully followed. 57% (8/14) were further investigated (radiology/bloods). One patient came to moderate harm. One patient who was admitted with a fall and further fell, died. Conclusions All patients were adequately assessed for risk of falls, but these still occurred, resulting in use of additional resources. Use of the standard proforma for assessing these patients is not routinely used. Raising awareness of falls risk and management is desirable.

paper.title: eP587 Ceiling of Care and Escalation Pathway Decision Making in General Surgical Patients at JCUH – Loop Completion
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim South Tees Trust resuscitation guidelines (on intranet) suggest that escalation plan for all the patients must be completed within 24 hours of the admission. Primary aim of this audit is to assess compliance to local trust guidelines in the general surgery department and the reaudit is to complete the loop after the recommendations from first cycle have been implemented. Inclusion – all patients admitted under the department of general surgery at James Cook University Hospital from the emergency department from 1 Jan 2025 to 22 Jan 2025. Methods Registered as an audit with the Clinical Audit team at JCHU with an id of 1835. Retrospective data collection from the colorectal and upper GI patient lists. A total of 100 patients included in the study. Variables collected include patient number, age, sex, date of admission, date of discharge, LOS, ceiling of care discussion and date, date of DNACPR, DNACPR in community, DNACPR in hospital. Intervention – email was sent to all the junior doctors and Consultants in general surgical department, highlighting the findings of first cycle and importance of ceiling of care documentation. Results All the patients placed on ward based level of care died in the hospital. 10 patients with community DNAR did not have documentation of the same in the clerking documents. Conclusion The adherence in 1st cycle was 6.18% and it has come down to 5% in second cycle. We plan to organise teaching session for all the general surgical junior doctors to adhere to the trust guidelines.

audits.standard: NICE CG188: LC within 1 week of diagnosis; BBUGSS morbidity <10%
audits.finding: None (0/61) had LC within 1 week; 26 (43%) had grade II and IIIa complications.

paper.title: 243 Timeliness of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy in Acute Cholecystitis: An Audit of Compliance and Associated Morbidity
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This study aimed to assess local adherence to guidelines set out by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) and the British Benign Upper Gastrointestinal Surgical Society (BBUGSS): offering early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) within 1 week of an acute cholecystitis diagnosis to minimise complications (CG188), and morbidity post-LC of <10%. Method Medical records of 61 patients, who underwent LC for acute cholecystitis at a district general hospital between May 2023 and February 2025, were reviewed for admission dates, operation dates, and postoperative complications, which were graded using the Clavien-Dindo classification. Results Of the 61 LCs, none were performed within 1 week of diagnosis with acute cholecystitis, and were elective instead, many of which were day-cases. One patient underwent a percutaneous cholecystectomy, and later a LC. 26 patients experienced grade II and IIIa complications (43%) following LC. Conclusions No patients underwent a LC within 1 week of diagnosis with acute cholecystitis, failing to meet NICE CG188 guidance. Elective LC was performed instead. Delayed surgery may have been due to patients’ comorbidities, severity of inflammation, limited theatre capacity, or surgeon availability. Morbidity post-LC exceeded the <10% BBUGSS benchmark, potentially linked to delayed intervention or patients’ pre-existing comorbidities. Future work should focus on identifying and addressing such barriers to early surgery and evaluate interventions to improve compliance and patient outcomes.

paper.title: 270 An Audit Looking at the Peri-Operative Management of Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Surgical Patients Under the Upper Gastrointestinal Team at Royal Liverpool University Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains a major preventable cause of postoperative morbidity and mortality. Inadequate prophylaxis may raise thrombotic risk by up to 30%. This audit evaluates compliance with VTE prevention guidelines in the Upper Gastrointestinal (UGI) surgical team at the Royal Liverpool University Hospital, focusing on prescription accuracy, timing, and peri-operative assessment. Method A retrospective audit was conducted for patients undergoing invasive UGI procedures from 1/12/24 to 31/1/25. Data from electronic patient and prescribing records included surgical urgency, VTE risk assessments, pharmacological (enoxaparin) and mechanical (anti-embolism stockings) prophylaxis, dosing accuracy (weight/renal adjusted), administration timing, perioperative suspension, and inpatient VTE events. Results Among 96 patients, 99% had risk assessments completed. Combined prophylaxis was advised in 71%, with enoxaparin prescribed in 84%. Yet, 11% received prophylaxis when not indicated, while 6% missed it despite indications. Appropriate dosing occurred in 82%, with 40 mg once daily most common. Administration timing met guidance in 79%, and 76% began within 24 hours. Prophylaxis was suspended peri-operatively in 40%, typically with two missed doses. Anti-embolism stockings were prescribed in 87%, with 93% appropriate. In hospital VTE occurred in 6%. Conclusions Overall compliance with assessment and prescribing was high, but issues were found in peri-operative assessment accuracy, prescription errors, missed doses, and timing. Suspension decisions seemed subjective, and missing critical care data limited the analysis. Targeted education, standardised protocols, and re-auditing are recommended to enhance adherence and reduce preventable VTE complications in surgical patients.

paper.title: 304 Impact of ICU Bed Availability on Admission of High-Risk Emergency Laparotomy Patients: An Audit of NELA and P-POSSUM Correlation
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess whether ICU admission following emergency laparotomy aligns with preoperative mortality risk scores (NELA or P-POSSUM) Method A retrospective audit was conducted on emergency laparotomy cases performed between January 2019 and November 2024 at Huddersfield Royal Infirmary. Cases were identified using the hospital’s theatre electronic record system (Bluespier) by two independent reviewers. Electronic patient records were reviewed to obtain NELA or P-POSSUM scores. ICU bed data was recorded daily and obtained from ICU staff. Patients were stratified by risk category (low, medium, high) based on their predicted 30-day mortality, and analysed against ICU admission status. Statistical analysis included chi-square tests. Results Of 620 laparotomies, 241 had NELA scores and 86 had P-POSSUM scores documented. Upper GI laparotomies made up 4% of the total number of laparotomies. The mean NELA and P-POSSUM scores were 9.74% and 14.19% respectively. Among high-risk patients (NELA or P-POSSUM >10%), 31.94% and 28.12% respectively were not admitted to ICU despite the availability of ICU beds on most days. Chi-square analysis showed a significant association between risk category and ICU admission (p < 0.00001). Conclusions ICU admissions generally aligned with higher risk scores, particularly NELA. However, a notable proportion of high-risk patients were not admitted despite available beds, suggesting the need for improved documentation, risk-based triage, and escalation protocols to ensure equitable critical care access.

audits.finding: ITU lights 20%, radio 70%; HDU lights 56%, radio 56%; night-time noise 46 dB; RCSQ ITU 53.5, HDU 34.8

paper.title: 370 Evaluating Noise and Light in Critical Care and Their Impact on Patients’ Sleep: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Sleep quality is often impaired in hospitalised patients, particularly in critical care, and is associated with worse outcomes such as increased delirium. Environmental factors, including excessive noise and bright lighting at night, contribute significantly to sleep disruption. This audit evaluated compliance with local guidelines on noise and light control and their impact on patients’ sleep. Method Compliance with the trust guideline ‘lights out and radios off by 10 pm’ was assessed in the Intensive Therapy Unit (ITU) and High Dependency Unit (HDU). Night-time noise levels were recorded at 4-hourly intervals. Patient-reported sleep quality was assessed using the Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire (RCSQ). A second cycle was then conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions such as raising awareness of critical care staffs, offering eye masks and ear plugs to patients, and clustering nursing intervention and care overnight. Results Compliance improved in both ITU (lights: 20% to 30%; radio: 70% to 70%) and HDU (lights: 56% to 70%; radio: 56% to 80%). Average night-time noise levels fell from 46 dB to 40 dB. Reported sleep duration increased in ITU (5.1 to 5.3 hours) and HDU (4.0 to 5.5 hours). RCSQ scores improved in both units (ITU: 53.5 to 56.4; HDU: 34.8 to 60.2). Fewer patients reported being disturbed by noise and monitor alarms (ITU: 33% to 25%; HDU: 80% to 30%). Conclusions Targeted environmental changes improved both compliance with sleep-promoting guidelines and patient-reported sleep quality. Ongoing education and interventions are recommended to sustain improvement and optimise sleep conditions in critical care.

audits.standard: Chole-QuIC target: 80% of eligible patients to have cholecystectomy within 8 days
audits.finding: 31/53 (58.5%) eligible acute gallstone disease patients had cholecystectomy within 8 days; 25/40 fit acute cholecystitis patients had inpatient cholecystectomy.

paper.title: 48 Audit on the Management of Patients Admitted with Acute Gallstone Disease
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To quantify the proportion of eligible patients admitted with acute gallstone disease receiving a cholecystectomy within 8 days at our hospital, using Chole-QuIC’s methodology. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on all patients admitted with acute gallstone disease to our district general hospital between 01/08/24-31/10/24 (n=119). Hot cholecystectomy candidates were identified using Chole-QuIC’s methodology. Additional data was collected for: surgery waiting times, starvation time (nil by mouth, NBM), length of stay, investigations and interventions. Data was analysed using GraphPad Prism. Results Out of 119 patients, 71.4% and 57.1% underwent CT and ultrasound scans respectively. 77/119 (64.7%) were acute cholecystitis (AC) patients, 7 of whom had percutaneous cholecystostomies. 40 AC patients were fit surgical candidates. 25/40 had inpatient cholecystectomies whilst 15 were discharged with outpatient cholecystectomies. AC patients with inpatient cholecystectomies had lower median surgery waiting times (3 vs 31 days, p< 0.0001). 5/15 discharged AC patients were re-admitted within 30-days. Median NBM days in AC patients was slightly higher in the inpatient cholecystectomies cohort compared to those discharged with outpatient cholecystectomies (2 vs 1 day, p=0.0204). Median admission length was higher in AC patients who had inpatient cholecystectomies (5 vs 3 days, p< 0.0071). Overall, 31/53 (58.5%) eligible acute gallstone disease patients received a cholecystectomy within 8 days. Conclusions There are significant challenges to meet the 8-day surgery rate of 80% targeted by Chole-QuIC in our unit. Inpatient cholecystectomies in the AC patients reduced surgery waiting times and prevented re-admissions but had drawbacks including longer fasting and admission duration.

paper.title: 353 Re-Audit on the Utilization of CT Scans in Acute Pancreatitis Management Following Implementation of Local Policy in a Northwest NHS Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute pancreatitis is a frequent emergency surgical condition where CT scans play a key role in diagnosis and monitoring. However, overuse of CT imaging can lead to unnecessary radiation exposure and higher healthcare costs. A previous audit, presented at AUGIS 2023, revealed that 28% of CT scans performed for acute pancreatitis were unnecessary. Following this, hospital staff received targeted education and retraining on the local imaging policy. This audit aimed to assess adherence to the local hospital policy regarding CT scan use in acute pancreatitis after the intervention. Method A retrospective review was conducted on 32 patients admitted under the Emergency Surgical Team with acute pancreatitis between August and October 2023. The mean age was 53.2 years, with a slight female predominance (53.1%). CT scan utilization and indications were evaluated against local policy standards. Results CT scans were performed in 23 patients (71.8%). Among these, 15 (46.1%) were done in patients without diagnostic amylase levels, 3 (9.4%) after 72 hours to evaluate complications, 3 (13.0%) for co-existing abdominal pathology (such as pancreatic cancer or abdominal aortic aneurysm), and 1 (4.3%) due to suspicion of an alternative diagnosis. Only 1 CT scan (4.3%) was classified as unnecessary, reflecting a 95.6% compliance rate with the imaging policy. Conclusions This audit demonstrates a substantial improvement in adherence to imaging guidelines following targeted education and retraining. Continued staff education and periodic audits are recommended to sustain appropriate and cost-effective use of CT scans in acute pancreatitis management.

audits.standard: AUGIS/BSG: all acute pancreatitis patients to have a validated severity score documented within 48 hours of admission

paper.title: 379 Improving Documentation of Severity Scores in Acute Pancreatitis: A Two-Cycle Audit Against AUGIS Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Severity scoring in acute pancreatitis is vital for early risk stratification, guiding escalation decisions and improving patient outcomes. The Association of Upper Gastrointestinal Surgeons (AUGIS), alongside the British Society of Gastroenterology, recommends that all patients with acute pancreatitis have a severity score documented within 48 hours of admission using a validated tool. Aim To assess adherence to AUGIS-endorsed guidelines on severity score documentation in acute pancreatitis and evaluate the impact of local quality improvement interventions. Method A retrospective audit was carried out across two cycles:Cycle 1 (1 Jan – 28 Feb 2025): 24 patients were identified. Only 4 (17%) had severity scores documented.Intervention: Local initiatives included FY/SHO teaching, staff posters summarising guidelines, and an electronic documentation template.Cycle 2 (1 Jun – 12 Jul 2025): 23 patients were reviewed. Seven (30%) had documented severity scores — all completed within the first 24 hours. One additional case was incomplete due to pending labs.Scoring systems used included Glasgow-Imrie, Modified Glasgow, and BISAP, based on clinician preference and data availability. Conclusions Following low baseline compliance, structured educational and system-level interventions improved both the rate and timeliness of severity score documentation. Embedding these practices into routine care supports adherence to AUGIS guidelines and enhances early risk stratification in acute pancreatitis.

paper.title: 186 Improving Emergency General Surgery Theatre Efficiency Through a Structured Warm List Pathway: A Closed Loop Audit at a Tertiary Hospital in London
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To improve Emergency General Surgery (EGS) theatre efficiency through the implementation of a structured Warm List pathway, aligned with GIRFT principles. Method A closed loop audit was conducted over two cycles. The first cycle reviewed EGS lists from January to June 2023. The second cycle, from October 2024 to March 2025, followed the implementation of a Warm List pathway. Data were collected on list usage, procedures performed, cancellations, and discharge outcomes. Results In the first cycle, 57 out of 71 scheduled lists were completed. A total of 102 procedures were performed (average 1.8 per list), with eight lists cancelled due to no suitable emergency cases. Same day discharge was achieved in 37 percent of cases. The Warm List pathway introduced defined inclusion criteria: patients ASA I or II, low anaesthetic risk, suitable for hernia repair or lymph node biopsy, able to attend on short notice, commute within one hour, aware of possible cancellation, and accompanied by an escort. Patients were reviewed, consented, and added to the Warm List for rapid scheduling. Following implementation, 12 additional patients were safely operated on using previously unused time. Conclusions The Warm List pathway improved EGS theatre utilisation and patient flow, reducing cancellations and enhancing efficiency. This approach supports better use of emergency theatre resources and improved patient experience.

paper.title: 319 An Audit on Calls to Surgical ACU Consultants: Frequency, Outcomes Andpathway Appropriateness in Altnagelvin Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate the referral patterns, triage outcomes, and documentation practices of consultant-led calls to the Acute Surgical Ambulatory Care Unit (ASACU), and to identify areas for improvement in service delivery and governance. Method A prospective audit was conducted between 14/04/2025 and 09/05/2025. Consultants covering ASACU logged all incoming clinical calls in real-time over a 13-day period. Data collected included the source of contact, triage outcome, and whether the call was formally documented. A total of 45 calls were captured and analysed. Results General Practitioners initiated 78% of the calls, highlighting primary care as the predominant referral source. Only 2 calls originated from the Emergency Department. Of the 45 calls, 24 (53%) resulted in ASACU referrals, 9 were redirected to the ED, and the remainder were managed via outpatient pathways or consultant advice. Despite effective triage decisions, only 40% (18/45) of calls were documented formally, raising concerns about clinical governance. Good practices included real-time data collection, high primary care engagement, and categorisation of diverse call outcomes. Conclusions This audit demonstrates effective consultant triage and strong engagement with primary care but identifies a significant gap in call documentation. Recommendations include implementing mandatory documentation, standardising referral protocols, reducing informal contact routes, and disseminating clear ASACU referral criteria. A follow-up re-audit is planned to assess the impact of these changes and ensure sustained improvement.

paper.title: 183 Management of Patients with Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer (HDGC) at Leeds Teaching Hospitals Trust (LTHT): A Clinical Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Is mainstream genetic testing for HDGC (CDH1) effective within the setting of an UGI Cancer MDT? Method A retrospective analysis from 2009-2019 identified failures to refer eligible patients for CDH1 testing, and led to a collaboration between UGI, Oncology and Clinical Genetics services to mainstream genetic testing for HDGC within the UGI Cancer service. A Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) was introduced, and outcomes re-evaluated. Results In the 10 years prior to introduction of the CDH1 SOP, 17 patients with confirmed diffuse type gastric cancer fulfilled CDH1 testing criteria. A further 7 patients did not have histological subtype recorded. 12/17 patients (70%) were referred to Clinical Genetics and 10 (58%) underwent CDH1 testing. 3 patients were diagnosed with a pathogenic CDH1 mutation. In the 2.5 years following introduction of the SOP, 25 patients with diffuse type gastric cancer fulfilled CDH1 testing criteria and had this documented in the MDT minutes. 15 patients were seen at our institution and 13/15 (87%) underwent mainstream CDH1 testing. 3 patients were diagnosed with a pathogenic CDH1 mutation. The remaining 10 patients were seen at peripheral centres where mainstream testing is not currently available, only 2 (20%) patients were referred to Clinical Genetics for consideration of CDH1 testing. Conclusions Mainstream genetic testing for HDGC (CDH1) within an UGI Cancer service is feasible and can lead to improved uptake of CDH1 testing for eligible patients. There is scope to widen access to mainstream testing and improve referral pathways in centres where this is not available.

audits.standard: Quality indicator: complete photo-documentation of eight standard OGD landmarks
audits.finding: Complete eight-site documentation in 6.35%; upper oesophagus 15.9%, GOJ 73.0%, fundus 76.2%, body 34.9%, incisura 27.0%, antrum 49.2%, duodenal bulb 41.3%, D2 79.4%.
audits.change: Planned: structured reporting templates, operator education and feedback (not yet implemented).

paper.title: 217 An Audit on Image Documentation in Upper GI Endoscopy
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Complete photo-documentation of eight standard oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) landmarks is a key quality indicator yet remains inconsistently achieved in routine practice. We conducted a retrospective surgical audit to quantify completeness of eight-site OGD documentation Method We reviewed 59 OGDs performed from 1st to 15th of May 2025 Patient demographics, pathology outcomes and the rate of photograph capture at eight anatomical sites were recorded. Complete eight-site documentation and individual landmark photo-rates were analysed Results Patients’ median age was 57 years (range 18–89) with a female:male ratio of 33:26. Complete eight-site photo-documentation was achieved in only 6.35% of procedures. Individual photo-rates varied widely: upper oesophagus 15.9%, GOJ 73.0%, fundus (retroflexion) 76.2%, gastric body 34.9%, incisura/angulus 27.0%, antrum 49.2%, duodenal bulb 41.3%, and second part of duodenum 79.4%. Gastroenterologists performed the majority of OGDs (n=27; 45.8%) averaging 4.15 sites documented, Surgeons performed 17 OGDs (28.8%) with an average of 3.94 landmarks documented and gastroenterology trainees performing 15 OGDs (25.4%) with an average of 4.73 landmarks documented. Conclusions This baseline audit reveals marked heterogeneity and suboptimal completeness in OGD photo-documentation, with full eight-site capture achieved in fewer than one in fifteen examinations. The findings underscore the need for targeted interventions such as structured reporting templates, operator education and regular feedback to standardise practice and improve documentation quality. We will present these results at an upcoming surgical conference and initiate a second audit cycle following implementation of improvement measures.

paper.title: 199 Improving Timeliness and Availability of Bariatric MDT Outcomes on Electronic Patient Records: A Quality Improvement Initiative
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To improve the documentation and timeliness of bariatric multidisciplinary team (MDT) outcomes on electronic patient records (EPR), ensuring clinicians have prompt access to care plans and reducing delays in patient management. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of all patients discussed at bariatric MDT meetings between 2023 and 2024. Data were collected on the presence of an MDT outcome on the EPR and the time delay between the meeting date and EPR entry. In January 2025, a quality improvement intervention was introduced: live documentation of MDT outcomes during the meeting. The audit cycle was repeated for patients discussed between January and May 2025. Results In the initial audit cycle (n=1499), 227 patients (15.3%) had no MDT outcome documented on the EPR. Among the 1272 patients with a report, only 8.5% (n=108) had same-day entries, with an average delay of 36 days (range 0–550). post-intervention (n=294), only 11 patients (3.7%) lacked an EPR report. Of the remaining 279 patients, 43.4% (n=121) had same-day entries, and the average delay decreased to 3.8 days (range 0–121). Conclusions Live reporting of bariatric MDT outcomes significantly improved documentation rates and reduced reporting delays on EPR. This intervention enhances timely access to patient management plans, promoting more efficient and coordinated care.

paper.title: 29 Evaluating Adherence to NICE Guidelines for Urgent Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy in Acute Cholecystitis: A Clinical Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate adherence to NICE guidelines recommending laparoscopic cholecystectomy within seven days of acute cholecystitis diagnosis, benchmarking against the Cholecystectomy Quality Improvement Collaborative (Chole-QuIC) national standards. Method A retrospective audit reviewed 257 consecutive laparoscopic cholecystectomies from January to March 2025, with 66 indicated for acute cholecystitis. Time from symptom onset to surgery was assessed against NICE standards (Warttig et al., BMJ, 2014). Results Of 66 cases, 18.2% (12/66) underwent surgery within seven days, and 21.2%. Only five cases were documented to have utilized the dedicated hot gallbladder pathway, with 40% (2/5) meeting the seven-day target. Average time to surgery was 68 days, with delays due to waiting lists, booking issues, delayed presentation, and associated comorbidity (analysis ongoing). Conclusions Adherence to NICE guidelines (18.2%) is below Chole-QuIC benchmarks, where top sites achieve 20–60% for surgery within 8 days. We are currently further analyzing reasons for delayed surgical intervention. Recommendations include optimizing the hot gallbladder pathway and improving communication to align with NICE and Chole-QuIC standards.

paper.title: 43 Audit of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Operative Notes in a DGH
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Operation notes are essential documents in patient care. The use of standardized guidelines, such as those endorsed by recognized organizations, is crucial to ensure consistent and detailed record-keeping. Documenting parameters specific to laparoscopic cholecystectomy provides valuable information for management in the event of complications and it also provides direction for follow-up care. Aim This audit aims to assess the quality of laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative notes in our trust by comparing them against NHS England’s GIRFT (Getting It Right Rirst-Time) recommendations. It also aims to Identify areas for improvement and implement targeted interventions. Method A retrospective audit of 78 laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative notes conducted in 2024 were selected by systematic random sampling. Data were compared against GIRFT recommendations. After intervention, a re-audit of 78 laparoscopic cholecystectomy operative notes from 2025 was done using the same methodology and compared against initial audit. Results Significant improvement was observed in the re-audit compared to the initial audit, after intervention in the form of surgeon education and use of modified operation note proforma specific to laparoscopic cholecystectomy was implemented. Documenting significant steps involved in Laparoscopic cholecystectomy for example, details of calot’s triangle dissection, details of bile/gallstone spill and its management and mention of port used to extract gallbladder increased by 13%, 42%, and 48%, respectively. Conclusions This audit demonstrates a significant improvement in operative note quality by implementing interventions from an initial audit, emphasising the importance of use of recommendations issued by GIRFT. Audits should be conducted at regular intervals to sustain improvements.

paper.title: 197 A 13-Month Retrospective Audit of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy Across a Multi-Site NHS Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate practice and outcomes of laparoscopic cholecystectomy across a large NHS Trust, assessing indications, imaging pathways, surgical approach, and complications. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on all patients listed for cholecystectomy between January 2024 and January 2025 across three sites. Data included demographics, imaging, surgical modality, complications, and 90-day readmission. Results 675 patients underwent cholecystectomy (73% female, mean age 53.6 years). The most common indication was symptomatic biliary colic (46%), followed by gallstone cholecystitis (28%) and gallstone pancreatitis (14%). Most cases were elective (79%), with CholeQuIC (13%) and emergency (8%) pathways. Laparoscopic surgery was performed in 89.5%, with robotic and subtotal approaches in 3.0% and 4.1%, respectively. Pre-operative ultrasound was performed in 93%, and 36% underwent MRCP. Of those, 31% proceeded to ERCP for stone retrieval. A drain was inserted intra-operatively in 14% of cases. The overall complication rate was 2.2%, including retained stones (1.3%), wound infections (1.3%), and bile leaks (0.9%), with no significant variation based on pre-operative imaging modality. Complication rates were higher in emergency presentations (5.6%) compared to elective cases (2.0%). Readmission rate was 3.9%. Elective cases achieved an 87% day-case rate, exceeding NICE targets. Conclusions Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is delivered safely and consistently across the Trust with excellent outcomes. However, MRCP was used in over one-third of cases, often without influencing complication rates, and may contribute to delays and additional costs. A more selective, evidence-based imaging strategy incorporating intraoperative ultrasound may reduce unnecessary MRCP use, streamline patient care pathways, and improve cost-effectiveness while maintaining clinical safety and outcomes.

audits.standard: BSG and UEG: at least six biopsies from two or more oesophageal levels
audits.finding: Of 174 dysphagia patients, 121 (69.5%) received six biopsies; 11 (6.3%) had fewer than four; 66 (37.9%) multilevel with unspecified locations and only 40 (23.0%) clearly documented segmental biopsies.

paper.title: 240 Improving Adherence to Oesophageal Biopsy Protocols for Suspected Eosinophilic Oesophagitis: A Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Eosinophilic oesophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, immune-mediated condition that has become an increasingly recognised cause of oesophageal dysphagia, particularly in younger individuals. Accurate diagnosis requires histological confirmation, which depends on adequate mucosal sampling during oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD). Current guidelines from the British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) and United European Gastroenterology (UEG) recommend taking at least six biopsies from two or more oesophageal levels. This Quality Improvement Project (QIP) aimed to assess local adherence to these biopsy protocols and identify opportunities for improvement. Method A retrospective review of 250 patients referred via the two-week wait (2WW) pathway for dysphagia and upper gastrointestinal symptoms was conducted over a four-month period (December 2024 to March 2025). Following the exclusion of 42 patients with non-EoE indications, 208 patients were included. Data were collected on biopsy number, anatomical distribution, and quality of documentation. Results Of 174 patients presenting with dysphagia, 121 (69.5%) received six biopsies. Seventeen (9.8%) received four biopsies, three (1.7%) received five, and 11 (6.3%) had fewer than four biopsies. Seven to eight biopsies were taken in 4.0% of cases. Documentation was suboptimal: 66 (37.9%) had multilevel biopsies with unspecified locations, and only 40 (23.0%) had clearly documented segmental biopsies. In the food bolus group (n=7), 71.4% received multilevel biopsies. Conclusions: Adherence to biopsy protocols and documentation standards for suspected EoE remains inconsistent. Targeted interventions are being implemented, including clinician education, updated documentation templates, and procedural checklists. A re-audit will assess their impact.

paper.title: 326 Are GIRFT Standards Being Met? a Comparative Audit of Cholecystectomy Operation Notes by Biliary and Non-Biliary Surgeons
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim High-quality operation notes are vital for safe post-operative care, effective communication, and medico-legal protection. The RCSEng and GIRFT guidelines recommend clear, comprehensive, and preferably typed documentation for all procedures (total score 32). This audit assessed the quality of cholecystectomy operation notes against these standards, comparing biliary versus non-biliary surgeons. Method This multicentre retrospective cohort study included consecutive adult patients who underwent elective or emergency cholecystectomy across three hospitals between August 2023 and July 2024. Cases were grouped based on whether the operating surgeon was classified as biliary or non-biliary specialist. Operation notes were audited against GIRFT guideline criteria, and results were compared between the two groups. Results Of 564 patients, 405 (71.8%) were female, with a median age of 53 years. Biliary surgeons performed 125 (22.2%) procedures, while non-biliary surgeons performed 439 (77.8%). Emergency cholecystectomies were more frequently performed by biliary surgeons (44.8% vs 35.1%, p=0.047), who also had a higher rate of typed operation notes (94.4% vs 59.0%, p<0.001). The median GIRFT score was significantly higher among biliary surgeons (29 [IQR 27–31]) compared to non-biliary surgeons (19 [IQR 16–21]), p<0.001. Notably, none of the non-biliary surgeons achieved a perfect score (32/32). Conclusions This audit highlights a clear and concerning gap in compliance with GIRFT standards among non-biliary surgeons. The marked disparity in operative note quality carries important implications for patient safety, medico-legal accountability, and clinical continuity. To address this, the implementation of typed, standardised operation notes should be mandated, with targeted interventions to ensure adherence to national documentation standards.

paper.title: 28 Improving Monitoring and Severity Stratification in Acute Pancreatitis: A Quality Improvement Study Using BISAP Score Implementation
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate and improve compliance with national guidelines on the monitoring and severity assessment of acute pancreatitis patients, by introducing the BISAP (Bedside Index for Severity in Acute Pancreatitis) scoring system into routine clinical practice. Method A baseline review of case notes was conducted for 30 consecutive patients admitted with acute pancreatitis. Compliance was assessed against NICE and BSG guidelines, focusing on documentation of severity stratification, frequency of observations, and appropriate escalation. A structured intervention was implemented: the BISAP score was introduced via educational sessions and integrated into clerking proformas using the printed format. A re-audit was performed on a subsequent cohort of 30 patients. Results Initial data revealed poor compliance: only 10% of patients had documented severity scores, and regular monitoring was inconsistent, especially in moderate-to-severe cases. Following BISAP implementation, documentation of severity assessment increased to 80%, with improved early identification of high-risk patients. Escalation to higher care was more prompt in severe cases, and overall documentation of fluid balance, observations, and investigations improved significantly. Conclusions Integrating the BISAP score printed format into standard clerking led to a marked improvement in severity documentation and monitoring compliance in acute pancreatitis. This low-cost intervention can help standardise care, facilitate early escalation, and potentially improve patient outcomes.

paper.title: 237 Audit of Operative Note Quality in HPB Surgery: Adherence to RCS Good Surgical Practice Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess adherence to the RCS Good Surgical Practice (2025) standards in HPB operative note documentation and additionally evaluate documentation of intraoperative adjuncts—Pringle’s manoeuvre, ICG fluorescence, intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS), and frozen section—in liver procedures. Method A prospective audit of 75 HPB operations was conducted. Operative notes were reviewed for compliance with RCS 2025 documentation standards, including key parameters such as incision, findings, complications, closure, estimated blood loss (EBL), prophylaxis, and postoperative instructions. Intraoperative adjunct documentation was analysed for liver procedures specifically. Results High adherence was observed for core parameters including incision (93%), findings (100%), closure (100%), postoperative instructions (100%), and surgeon signature (100%). Lower compliance was noted in the documentation of EBL (20%), specimen details (71%), and extra procedures (13%). Among 9 laparoscopic liver resections, ICG usage was documented in 2 cases (22%). Pringle’s manoeuvre was recorded in all applicable liver resections. IOUS and frozen section documentation were present in 25% and 30% of relevant cases, respectively. Conclusions This preliminary audit demonstrates strong compliance with core RCS documentation standards in HPB surgery. However, documentation of intraoperative adjuncts in liver procedures remains inconsistent. Planned interventions include implementing a standardised electronic operative note template, delivering educational sessions, and placing visual reminders in theatres. A second-cycle audit will be conducted in August, with loop closure planned by September.

paper.title: SRS52 - When risk goes unspoken: an audit of consent documentation for laparoscopic appendicectomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Accurate and comprehensive documentation of risks during the consent process is essential to respect patient autonomy and meet national standards set by the General Medical Council (GMC) and Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) England. We conducted a retrospective audit of 68 consent forms for laparoscopic appendicectomy over a three-month period at our institution. Each form was reviewed for documentation of 17 key risks identified through national guidelines and consultant consensus, including common complications such as bleeding, infection, and conversion to open surgery, as well as specific organ injuries and intraoperative contingencies. Overall, only four risks were documented in more than 75% of cases: bleeding (98.5%), infection (95.6%), injury to nearby structures (83.8%), and conversion to open procedure (88.2%). Documentation of specific organ risks was variable, with bowel injury noted in 61.8% of forms, bladder injury in 36.8%, and ureter injury in only 22.1%. Among 46 female patients, documentation of gynecological risks was present in just 30.4%. Other important risks, including hernia formation (63.2%), death (13.2%), and need for reintervention (23.5%) were frequently omitted. These findings reveal poor compliance with GMC and RCS consent guidelines, highlighting a lack of procedure-specific and gender-specific risk documentation. In response, a procedure-specific consent template has been introduced, and a re-audit is planned to evaluate its impact on improving consent quality and compliance. This audit underscores the need for structured consent processes to ensure informed decision-making and medicolegal safety in laparoscopic appendicectomy.

paper.title: SRS55 - Improving consent form compliance in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a closed-loop audit using pre-printed risk templates
paper.abstract: Abstract Informed consent is a fundamental component of safe surgical practice, yet we identified inconsistent documentation of risks in laparoscopic cholecystectomy consent forms at our institution. Comprehensive disclosure of all material risks is essential for patient understanding and medicolegal protection, but variability exists, especially in emergency surgery. We conducted a retrospective audit of 46 emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy consent forms over seven months, assessing documentation compliance for 15 commonly accepted risks. Pre-intervention results showed wide variability: while bleeding, infection, and conversion to open surgery were documented in 100% of cases, less frequent risks such as keloid formation (17.4%), death (2.2%), and chest infection (6.5%) were often omitted. To improve consistency, we introduced a pre-printed consent form template listing all standard risks, implemented across the surgical team. A re-audit of 23 subsequent consent forms over two months demonstrated complete compliance, with all 15 risks documented in 100% of cases. This simple, low-cost intervention significantly improved risk documentation quality, enhancing patient safety and alignment with national guidelines. Although limited by a smaller post-intervention sample and short re-audit period, the approach is scalable and easily replicable in similar settings. Standardizing consent documentation through pre-printed templates represents an effective strategy to ensure thorough risk communication and support informed surgical decision-making in laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

paper.title: SRS101 - A closed loop audit assessing the rate of surgical site infections after wound closure with sutures in Major Lower Limb Amputations
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Major lower limb amputations (MLLA) are a last resort treatment for patients with peripheral arterial and diabetic foot disease. A significant number of patients subjected to MLLAs will develop a surgical site infection (SSI), which can have an impact on patient morbidity and mortality. This audit, based in a single Vascular centre, aimed to assess whether the materials that MLLA skin wounds were closed with are an associated risk factor for SSIs. Methods A closed-loop audit was carried out by retrospectively looking at the notes of all patients who had undergone MLLA between August 2022 to January 2023. The material used to close skin was identified for all patients, as was the presence of any SSI. The data was presented at a local audit meeting and a re-audit was carried out 6 months later. Results A total of 64 patients were included. In the first cycle, the SSI rate was 40% (10/25), with staples being statistically significant (Fischer exact test value: 0.0027, P < 0.05) at increasing the infection rate. Following the second cycle, the SSI was 10.2% (4/39), with sutures being statistically significant (Fischer exact test value: 0.0154, P < 0.05) at reducing the infection rate. Of the risk factors that were analysed, none were statistically significant between the two groups of patients. Discussion Closing MLLA wounds with sutures rather than staples appears to reduce the rate of SSI. Due to the low sample size, this audit cannot exclusively show that closing MLLA with staples increases the risk of infection.

paper.title: SRS169 - An audit of Global Vascular Guidelines implementation at two large teaching hospitals in differing healthcare settings
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction The Global Vascular Guidelines (GVG) provide a framework for assessment and management of patients with Chronic Limb Threatening Ischaemia (CLTI) as laid out by Conte et al. (2019). This audit describes compliance with GVG standards across two teaching hospitals in different healthcare settings: UK (Higher Income Country) and Sri Lanka (Lower-Middle Income Country). Aim Our aim was to identify key similarities, differences, and barriers to implementation of these guidelines. Methods All new CLTI patients admitted or seen in outpatient podiatry clinic at Guy’s and St Thomas’ Hospital (GSTT) and National Hospital of Sri Lanka (NHSL) between 1/5/2024–31/5/2024 were included. Data were collected according to recommendations set out in the GVG. Statistical significance was analysed with Fisher’s Exact Test. Results Sixty-five patients were included (GSTT: 38; NHSL: 27) and forty-nine outpatients (GSTT: 21; NHSL: 28). Among the Inpatients, GVG-compliant foot examination was poorly performed, (GSTT: 10 (26%); NHSL: 0 (0%), P = 0.004). Among the Outpatients, GVG-compliant foot examinations were performed in all 21 outpatients at GSTT but in none of the 28 outpatients at NHSL (0%, P < 0.001). Limb severity scoring systems were utilised for all outpatients seen at GSTT, whereas only 5 of 28 outpatients at NHSL (18%) had scoring systems documented (P < 0.001). Conclusions Implementation of the GVG is challenging, with even large teaching hospital centres failing to meet all the recommendations for assessment of patients with CLTI. Further work is needed to understand the barriers to implementation and address these.

audits.standard: Guidance recommending selective pus swabbing for recurrent, persistent or treatment-resistant abscesses

paper.title: SRS385 - Audit of routine pus swabbing in abscess drainage: are we following guidance?
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Routine pus swabbing during incision and drainage of uncomplicated cutaneous abscesses remains common despite guidance recommending selective use for recurrent, persistent, or treatment-resistant cases. This audit assessed whether routine swabbing influences clinical outcomes and evaluated adherence to current guidance in emergency general surgery practice. Methods A retrospective audit of 122 consecutive abscess I&D cases was conducted between January and April 2025. Data were extracted from electronic records and operation notes. Firth penalised logistic regression was used to analyse associations between patient and treatment factors and 30-day readmission and reoperation, adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, abscess site and discharge on antibiotics. Descriptive statistics summarised case-mix and swab utilisation patterns. Results Median age was 38 years; 57.4% were male. Pus swabs were taken in 76/122 (62.3%) cases, with results acted upon in only 5/76 (6.6%). Thirty-day recurrence was nearly similar for swabbed versus non-swabbed patients (3.9% versus 4.3%). Discharge on antibiotics was associated with higher odds of recurrence (aOR 13.76; 95% c.i. 2.11–151.91; P = 0.004). Notably, 80% of recurrences occurred in patients discharged on antibiotics. Age, sex, diabetes, and abscess site were not significant; Reoperation events were rare (3/122); adjusted estimates had very wide 95% CIs and should be interpreted cautiously. Conclusions Routine swabbing rarely altered management and showed no outcome benefit, with likely confounding by indication for antibiotics–recurrence signal. Current practice appears to over-utilise swabbing relative to guidance. A selective swab policy targeting complex, recurrent or systemically unwell patients, or where antibiotics are planned, could optimise resources.

audits.standard: not reported

paper.title: 387 Time Matters: A 2.5-Year Audit of Delays to Appendicectomy and Their Impact on Outcomes in Emergency General Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Appendicectomy is the gold-standard treatment for acute uncomplicated appendicitis, yet delays to surgery may increase perforation risk, operative difficulty, postoperative complications, and length of stay (LOS). This audit aimed to evaluate waiting times from ED, diagnostic confirmation to appendicectomy, and to assess their relationship with surgical outcomes, complications, and LOS. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of appendicectomy cases between September 2022 and May 2025. Electronic patient records were reviewed on the HIVE system across 23 predefined variables, including demographics, symptom duration, ED arrival time, imaging modality, operative approach, surgical duration, complications, and LOS. Of 496 cases identified, 22 were excluded, leaving 474 patients for analysis. Results Patients ranged from 5–86 years (median 31); 56% were male. Symptom duration varied from hours to 14 days. Appendicitis was confirmed via CT in 67% and USS in 10%, with 15% undergoing no imaging. Laparoscopic appendicectomy accounted for 91% of cases, with a 5.9% conversion rate. Perforation was reported on imaging in 16% and intra-operatively in 28%. Time-to-surgery ranged from 3 to 116 hours (mean/median 18 hours). Only 50.6% underwent surgery within 18 hours of ED arrival, although 75% were operated within 18 hours of diagnostic decision. Mean operative time was 92 minutes; 30% required postoperative drains. A further 9% required postoperative imaging and 12% re-presented or required follow-up for complications. Conclusions Substantial variation in time-to-surgery exists, with longer delays linked to higher perforation rates and increased postoperative intervention. Streamlined pathways are required to optimise outcomes and minimise preventable morbidity.

audits.standard: NICE: direct access pelvic ultrasound for women aged 55 or over with visible haematuria and/or abnormal cancer risk markers

paper.title: 1392 Adherence to NICE Guidance for Endometrial Cancer Detection in Women ≥55 Years Referred With Visible Haematuria: A Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim NICE guidelines recommend direct access pelvic ultrasound for women aged ≥55 years presenting with visible haematuria and/or abnormal cancer risk markers (unexplained anaemia, thrombocytosis, or hyperglycaemia) to exclude endometrial cancer. However, awareness and implementation of this guidance within urology remain variable. This audit aimed to assess local adherence to NICE guidance and its diagnostic yield for endometrial cancer in this population. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of all female patients aged ≥55 years referred to the haematuria clinic in 2023. Data collected included demographics, haematuria type, blood results, imaging, referral pathway, ultrasound utilisation, and cancer outcomes. Adherence was defined as performance of pelvic ultrasound in patients meeting NICE criteria. Results 216 patients were reviewed. Overall compliance with NICE guidance was 1/17 (5.8%). Three patients (1.3%) were diagnosed with endometrial cancer. Flexible cystoscopy was normal in all three cases. CT urography failed to identify gynaecological pathology in one patient. Trans-abdominal ultrasound detected endometrial thickening in one case, prompting urgent gynaecology referral and cancer diagnosis. The third patient had a pre-existing diagnosis as she was referred simultaneously to urology and gynaecology due to unclear bleeding source. None of the three patients met NICE haematological or biochemical trigger criteria. Conclusions This audit demonstrates poor adherence to NICE guidance due to limited awareness within the flexible cystoscopy team. Failure to perform pelvic ultrasound risks delayed cancer diagnosis, particularly as CT urography alone is insufficient to exclude endometrial pathology. Urologists should proactively apply NICE criteria and ensure early gynaecological referrals to improve diagnostic safety and pathway efficiency.

audits.standard: British Society of Gastroenterology: index or early (within 2 weeks) cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis; delayed surgery for moderate/severe

audits.change: Listing gallstone pancreatitis patients as P2 when booking, cancelling other elective activity when required, and encouraging inpatient cholecystectomy.

paper.title: 422 Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy in Gallstone Pancreatitis – Audit and Improvement of Trust Performance
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute pancreatitis (AP) is associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Gallstones account for up to 40% of cases, and up to 20% of patients who retain their gallbladder may experience recurrence. British Society of Gastroenterology guidance recommends index or early (within 2 weeks) cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis, with delayed surgery in moderate/severe cases. We assessed our guideline adherence and evaluated service improvements following interventions. Method A retrospective review was conducted of adults admitted with AP in two cycles: 01/06/2024–30/09/2024 and 01/02/2025–31/07/2025. Data collected included aetiology, length of stay (LOS) and timing of cholecystectomy. Severity graded using the Modified Atlanta criteria. Post-baseline intervention included listing gallstone pancreatitis patients as P2 when booking, cancelling other elective activity when required, and encouraging inpatient cholecystectomy. Patients were excluded if unfit, declining surgery, out of area, or with clearly documented justified delays. Mann-Whitney U and Chi-Squared tests for non-parametric and categorical data, respectively, in STATA. Results Gallstones were the most common cause of AP in both cycles. Adherence to BSG guidance improved to 86% from 71% following intervention (p=0.71). Patients undergoing index cholecystectomy displayed increased median LOS from 3 to 6 days (p<0.05). Non-compliance to guidelines due to inadequate documentation and slow outpatient processing. Conclusions Guideline adherence improved following intervention, driven by prioritisation of inpatient cholecystectomy. Increased LOS due to difficulty accessing CEPOD theatre. Lack of statistical significance likely reflects small sample sizes. Further gains may be achieved through improved documentation and clearer pathways for outpatient management of gallstone pancreatitis.

paper.title: 853 Optimizing Supported Consent for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: An Audit of a DGH
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To improve patients’ preoperative understanding of Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (LC) ensuring better-informed consent. To ensure the documentation of the supported consent process meets the standard of the GMC's Guidance on Informed Consent. Method A Pilot audit tested a survey tool designed on Microsoft Forms on 8 patients. The tool was refined with advice from industry experts and administered to 42 patients on the morning of their operation. Questions evaluated retention of complications of LC (eg, Bile leak) and the documentation of the consent process, including receipt of both an eConsent form via email to deliberate upon and the EIDO LC patient information leaflet (PIL). The patient was asked what a gallbladder was. Separate forms were used to capture “SHO” grades and consultant opinions. Results Despite 88% receiving the EIDO PIL, 19% of patients did not know what a Gallbladder was or described the wrong organ. 76% of patients had a day-of-surgery consent. 50% of consultants said they weren’t allocated enough time to initiate consent to this standard. SHO grades were unsure they understood the potential procedural complications, but they ‘took’ day-of-surgery consent, nevertheless. Conclusions Consent and its documentation have not kept pace with its modern expectations, for LCs done at our DGH. A department teaching session was conducted. SHOs are now being allocated to clinics with consultants. Two videos are being made: a training video for SHOs that covers initiating the consent process and an operative video of a representative LC for patients. The effect of these will be subsequently measured.

paper.title: 1080 Assessing Surgical Education and Exposure Amongst Foundation Trainees in the Yorkshire and the Humber Deanery: A Comparative Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction National concern persists regarding limited operative exposure and training opportunities for Foundation Doctors in surgical posts. This Yorkshire and the Humber deanery-wide audit evaluates the adequacy of surgical training opportunities and preparedness for Core Surgical Training (CST) relative to accepted standards. Method A questionnaire was distributed to Foundation Year 1 and 2 Doctors across the Yorkshire and the Humber deanery assessing hospital size, surgical specialty, theatre exposure, procedural experience and career guidance. Descriptive and comparative analyses (F1 vs F2; district general hospital (DGH) vs tertiary centres) were performed, with audit standards derived from RCS England, GMC NTS 2024, and GIRFT productivity guidance. Results 82 responses were analysed (F1 n=51, F2 n=31). 96% undertook at least one surgical post in the 2024-25 year; 54.9% expressed interest in a surgical career. Only 42% had consistent theatre access, 25.9% assisted in surgical procedures, 11% received regular feedback and 20.5% reported career guidance; further, 8% felt prepared for CST. Quality ratings clustered at 1–2 of 5 and DGH vs tertiary differences were small with both underperforming benchmarks. Identified barriers to training include: rota gaps, list cancellations, and lack of protected time. Conclusions Surgical exposure for Yorkshire and the Humber Foundation Doctors falls substantially below national expectations. Deficits in theatre access, procedural supervision, feedback, and mentorship threaten early surgical skill development and CST readiness amid rising competition ratios (2025 candidate ratio ≈8.6:1). Targeted interventions at hospital, trust, deanery, and national levels are required to restore training quality and equity.

paper.title: 810 Bariatric Procedures Cancellations and Utilisation of the Operating Theatre (Re-Evaluating Our Practice)
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Bariatric surgery cancellations have significant implications for patient safety, waiting lists, and theatre efficiency. An initial audit at our centre demonstrated a high cancellation rate and substantial same-day cancellations, prompting an improvement project. Method A retrospective review of all bariatric procedures between January–December 2024 was conducted (Loop 1). A total of 154 cases were identified, with 47 true cancellations (30.5%). Causes, timing of cancellations, and adequacy of pre-operative assessment (POA) were analysed. Interventions introduced included: early POA scheduling immediately after MDT; routine anaesthetic-led assessment for all bariatric patients; improved action on abnormal POA results; and a telephone follow-up clinic targeting long-waiters and high-risk patients. Re-audit was performed from May–October 2025, evaluating 75 eligible cases. Results Loop 1 demonstrated a 30.5% cancellation rate, with 34% due to patient choice, 46.8% due to medical non-fitness, 8.5% due to resource issues, and 10.6% undocumented. 40.5% occurred on the day of surgery and 46% within 10 days pre-op. Loop 2 showed marked improvement: cancellations reduced to 17.3% (13/75), with only 2 same-day cancellations (vs 16 initially). Patient-choice cancellations decreased from 16 to 4 cases, and resource-related and unclear cancellations were eliminated. Medical cancellations also significantly improved, with earlier identification of optimisation issues. Patients were seen in POA an average of 40 days after MDT. Conclusions Early POA, universal anaesthetic assessment, timely optimisation and structured follow-up markedly reduced bariatric surgical cancellations, particularly high-impact same-day cancellations. These interventions significantly improved theatre utilisation, patient flow, and peri-operative safety. Continuous POA pathway refinement is recommended.

audits.standard: GIRFT orbital fracture pathway: appropriate imaging and ophthalmic/orthoptic referral
audits.finding: All 27 had CT; 12 met criteria for plain radiographs but only 3 (25%) had them first; 15 had ophthalmic and 13 orthoptic assessment; 12 had neither.

paper.title: 535 A Retrospective Audit on Assessing Orbital Fracture in Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery in a Teaching Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Orbital fracture is a common presentation in oral and maxillofacial surgery. Management often involves inputs from multi-disciplinary teams. The aim of the audit is to evaluate the assessment pathways on the appropriateness of imaging modalities and referral to ophthalmic and/or orthoptic assessment against the Get It Right First Time (GIRFT) pathway. Method A retrospective audit study was conducted between January and December 2024. Patient lists were reviewed to identify patients presenting with orbital fracture. Patients aged 18 or above were included in this study. Electronic case note review was subsequently performed. Results 27 patients were included in this study. All 27 patients underwent CT scan for diagnosis with 3 patients who initially had a plain film X ray prior to CT. 15 patients attended ophthalmic assessment with 13 attended orthoptic assessment. Among the 12 patients who received neither ophthalmic nor orthoptic assessments, none of them demonstrated positive findings on physical examination aside from mild bruising or swelling. Conclusions 12 patients met the criteria for plain radiographs on initial assessment. However, only three (25%) had plain radiographs initially and all subsequently underwent CT imaging. The findings showed the inconsistency on the choices of imaging and indicated the need for a local protocol. Standardised guidelines on imaging choices with a checklist of physical signs should be adopted to reduce the use of CT. Referral pathways for ophthalmic and orthoptic assessment would enhance the consistency of patient care.
