audits.standard: European Hernia Society guidelines: perioperative antibiotics only for high-risk hernia repairs
audits.finding: Perioperative antibiotics given in 87.8% overall: 89% elective groin, 85% elective ventral/umbilical, 80% emergency repairs.
audits.change: Departmental standardised 'high-risk criteria' defining when antibiotics are indicated, with departmental education.

paper.title: 727 Implementing High-Risk Criteria to Optimise Perioperative Antibiotic Use in Hernia Surgery: A Two-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim European Hernia Society (EHS) guidelines recommend perioperative antibiotics only for high-risk hernia repairs, yet overuse remains common in clinical practice. We conducted two audit cycles to evaluate local compliance with these guidelines and implemented a targeted intervention to reduce unnecessary antibiotic administration. Method All adult patients undergoing elective or emergency groin, umbilical, epigastric, or ventral hernia repair were included. Incisional, parastomal, and complex abdominal wall repairs were excluded. Cycle 1 findings were presented locally and nationally, after which a departmental intervention was introduced: a standardised set of “high-risk criteria” (e.g. smoking status, large umbilical hernia, immunosuppression, or recurrent hernia cases) that defined when perioperative antibiotics were indicated. Data was extracted from operative and perioperative documentation. Antibiotic use was treated as a binary variable. Descriptive statistics were calculated, and differences between cycles were analysed using a two-proportion z-test. Results Cycle 1 included 227 hernia repairs (173 elective; 54 emergency), with perioperative antibiotics administered in 89% of elective groin, 85% of elective ventral/umbilical, and 80% of emergency repairs (combined usage 87.8%, SD 0.33). After introduction of the high-risk criteria, Cycle 2 (n=262) demonstrated a reduction in antibiotic use to 48.1% (SD 0.50), representing a 39.7% absolute decrease (p < 0.0001). Postoperative complication rates remained low and did not increase between cycles. Conclusions Implementation of clearly defined high-risk criteria, coupled with departmental education, led to a substantial and statistically significant reduction in perioperative antibiotic use without compromising patient safety. This demonstrates that simple, evidence-aligned interventions can effectively improve antimicrobial stewardship in hernia surgery.

audits.title: 1026 Non-Lump Presentations of Breast Cancer: An Audit at an NHS One-Stop Clinic
audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: Non-lump presentations 19.4% (n=19); symptom documentation 100%; palpation score recorded in 73.7% (n=14) of non-lump cases; clinical examination sensitivity 64.3% in this subgroup.

paper.title: 1026 Non-Lump Presentations of Breast Cancer: An Audit at an NHS One-Stop Clinic
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To quantify non-lump initial presentations among confirmed breast cancer cases, assess documentation quality, and determine clinical detectability on examination. Method A retrospective audit of all patients attending Whipps Cross Hospital's one-stop breast clinic over a six-month period was conducted. Cases with histologically confirmed breast cancer were included. Data collected: referral source, presenting symptom, and palpation score (P1–P5). Results Over six months, 2,611 patients attended the clinic, and 98 cancers were diagnosed. Of these, 17.3% (n=17) were screen-detected, 2.0% (n=2) were known cancer patients, and 80.6% (n=79) were primary presentations. Among primary cases, 61.2% (n=60) presented with a lump, while non-lump presentations accounted for 19.4% (n=19), including 18 incidental findings (18.4%) and one patient (1.0%) with symptoms other than a lump (breast pain). Symptom documentation was complete (100%) for all encounters; however, palpation score was recorded in only 73.7% (n=14) of non-lump cases; of these, 64.3% (n=9) were clinically abnormal (P>2) and suspicious for malignancy (P≥4). Clinical examination sensitivity for detecting malignancy in this subgroup was 64.3%. Conclusions Almost one in five breast cancers presented without a palpable lump, and clinical examination identified malignancy in fewer than two-thirds of these cases. This low sensitivity challenges proposals to assess non-lump presentations clinically without full triple assessment. Incomplete documentation further undermines assessment standards. A major limitation was the absence of routinely collected data on initial presentation, which restricted interpretation. Future audits require comprehensive datasets and should explore strategies to enhance documentation quality and improve recognition of atypical presentations.

audits.standard: ESVS 2023 guidelines and Global Vascular Guidelines: antiplatelet, high-intensity statin, lipid profile, BP <140/90, smoking cessation advice, HbA1c within 3 months

paper.title: 1058 Evaluating Comprehensive Best Medical Therapy and Lifestyle Optimisation in Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischaemia: An Integrated Audit of Adherence to ESVS 2023 Cardiovascular Standards and Global Vascular Guideline Recommendations
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Comprehensive best medical therapy (BMT) remains fundamental to the management of Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischaemia (CLTI). The 2023 European Society for Vascular Surgery (ESVS) guidelines advocate consistent provision of antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statins, lipid profiling, blood pressure optimisation, and structured smoking cessation counselling. The Global Vascular Guidelines complement these recommendations by emphasising lifestyle modification and robust glycaemic assessment, including HbA1c testing within three months for diabetic or high-risk patients. This audit examined how closely current inpatient practice aligns with these combined guideline standards. Method A retrospective audit was undertaken over a 2-month period, reviewing consecutive inpatients with confirmed CLTI. Key measures included antiplatelet and statin prescription, completion of a lipid profile during admission, discharge blood pressure <140/90 mmHg, documentation of smoking cessation advice for active smokers, and availability of HbA1c within the previous three months. Results Of 35 CLTI inpatients, 80% received statin therapy and 60% received antiplatelet treatment. A lipid profile was completed in only 1 of 34 patients (2.9%). Blood pressure targets were achieved at discharge in 29 of 35 patients (82.9%). Smoking cessation counselling was documented in 5 of 36 active smokers (13.9%). HbA1c within three months was available in 14 of 49 diabetic patients (28.6%). Conclusions Adherence to evidence-based BMT and lifestyle optimisation in CLTI remains inconsistent, with notable gaps in lipid assessment, smoking cessation support, and glycaemic monitoring. Implementing structured clinical pathways, automated prompts, and routine lifestyle documentation may enhance delivery of guideline-directed care.

paper.title: 65 Improvement of FY1 Fluid Review Quality in Urology Using a Novel Electronic Proforma: A 2-Cycle Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit aimed to assess the quality of FY1 fluid reviews within a high-volume tertiary Urology centre and to implement a novel electronic proforma to improve compliance with NICE guidelines on fluid assessment. A secondary aim was to evaluate FY1 confidence in performing fluid reviews and enhance this through targeted teaching. Method All documented FY1 fluid reviews over two weeks (02/09/24–15/09/24) were prospectively collected using our electronic clinical software TrakCare, recording compliance with NICE-defined clinical parameters. FY1 confidence in fluid prescription was assessed via an anonymous questionnaire (response rate 75%, n=15) using a 5-point Likert scale. An electronic proforma, incorporating NICE-recommended review parameters as headers, was subsequently introduced into TrakCare, accompanied by Urology-specific fluid management teaching to all FYs. The audit was then repeated over three weeks (11/11/24–01/12/24), with follow-up questionnaires distributed (response rate 50%, n=10). Data were analysed using Stata-BE v19.0 for Mac. Results There were 26 reviews in the first cycle and 23 in the second. Following proforma implementation, documentation improved significantly for recording fluid balance (78% vs 38%, p<0.01), heart rate (96% vs 35%, p<0.01), and blood pressure (96% vs 38%, p<0.01) amongst other clinical features. Initially, 27% of FY1s reported sufficient fluid management teaching prior to starting FY1 and 27% had confidence in performing reviews, increasing to 90% post-intervention. Conclusions The introduction of an electronic proforma significantly enhanced FY1 documentation and compliance with NICE fluid assessment standards. Focused teaching and the structured electronic prompt improved FY1 confidence in fluid management.

paper.title: 121 Assessment and Management of Suspected Testicular Torsion in Children and Adolescents: Impact of Local Quality Improvement and Compliance with Contemporary National Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Testicular torsion is a time-critical paediatric emergency. Recent national recommendations (NCEPOD and GIRFT, 2024) emphasise senior review and urgent operative intervention to optimise testicular salvage. This second-cycle audit assessed current performance against these standards and evaluated the effect of sustained local quality improvement (QI) measures. Method A retrospective audit was performed of patients <18 years undergoing scrotal exploration for suspected torsion between January 2023 and June 2024. Time to senior review, time to theatre, use of pre-operative ultrasound, and operative outcomes were collected and compared with a historical cohort (2011–2015) following earlier pathway and education interventions. Results Eighty patients were included. Torsion was confirmed in 14 cases (17.5%), with one orchidectomy (1.3%). Median time to senior review was 101 minutes (IQR 65–147), with 19% reviewed within one hour. Median time from decision to operate to theatre start was 77 minutes (55–96), with 13% meeting the target of surgery within one hour. Compared with the historical cohort, orchidectomy rates improved significantly (8.5% to 1.3%, p=0.045), while ultrasound use and torsion detection rates remained similar. Conclusions Local QI interventions have contributed to improved testicular salvage; however, timely senior review and theatre prioritisation remain ongoing challenges in achieving full compliance with national standards.

paper.title: 256 Straight to the Point: Improving Nasal Fracture Care Through a Face-to-Face-First Pathway - a Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess whether changing from a telemedicine-first to a face-to-face-first (F2F) pathway for suspected nasal fractures improved timeliness of care and reduced clinician consultation time, whilst maintaining compliance with ENT UK standards (≤ 21 days). A secondary aim was to evaluate whether patient age influenced the likelihood of manipulation under anaesthesia (MUA), informing potential age-based triage refinement. Method Data were collected retrospectively for two audit cycles. The pre-intervention cohort followed a telemedicine-first pathway; the post-intervention cohort was reviewed F2F initially. For each patient, age, date of injury, telemedicine and F2F appointments, and date of MUA were recorded. Time intervals from injury to each stage and total consultations were calculated. Comparisons were made using t-tests. Violin plots visualised age distribution for MUA and non-MUA patients. Results Mean time to F2F review decreased from 16.5 to 13.3 days (p=0.0068). Mean time to MUA reduced from 15.2 to 13.9 days (p=0.19), with 100% completed within 21 days. The proportion of MUAs ≤ 14 days increased from 38.9% to 57.1%. Consultations per patient fell from 1.23 to 1.04 (15% reduction), and discharge from ENT services occurred earlier (15.2 to 12.2 days, p=0.0019). MUA patients were younger (mean 31.3 vs 41.7 years, p=0.009). Conclusions The F2F-first pathway improved patient access to assessment, reduced consultation burden, and maintained compliance with national standards. The findings highlight opportunities for an age-based triage system to enhance efficiency. This audit demonstrates a sustainable service improvement model with clear implications for patient-centred care, reduced duplication of reviews, and more efficient clinic workflow.

paper.title: 288 Improving Operation Note Documentation Against Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) Standards: A Completed Audit Cycle in the Department of Surgery, Holy Family Hospital, Pakistan
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Incomplete operation notes compromise postoperative management, handover, and medicolegal accountability. We aimed to audit operation-note compliance in surgical unit 1, Holy Family Hospital, Pakistan, against the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) Good Surgical Documentation Checklist and evaluate the standardized performa with real-time theater reminders. Method A two-cycle retrospective clinical audit was performed. Cycle-1 reviewed 100 consecutive emergency and elective major general surgery notes against the 23 RCS documentation elements (2022). Interventions included the introduction of a revised RCS-based operation note template, real-time OT reminders, and staff awareness feedback in morning meetings. Cycl-2 was reaudited six weeks post-intervention. Patient data and identifiers were anonymized and confidential. Results Cycle-1 showed critical absence of 5 RCS elements in all notes (n=100): estimated blood loss, antibiotic prophylaxis, time-in, complications, and nature of surgery (0%). Other major deficiencies appeared in the operative diagnosis (30%), OT staff names (43%), anesthesiologist details (73%), incision details (70%), and DVT prophylaxis in 3/37 relevant cases (8.1%). Furthermore, a greater completion rate (>95%) was highlighted in the remaining elements, e.g., surgeon name, operative findings, postoperative care instructions, assistant name, procedure name, and time out. Following intervention, cycle-2 demonstrated significant improvement across 22/23 elements as highlighted in complications (98%), time-in (89%), estimated blood loss (96%), and antibiotic and DVT prophylaxis (83% and 80%, respectively). OT staff names were the least compliant across all elements (71%). Conclusions A standardized RCS-based template combined with low-resource OT reminders and staff feedback produced high improvement in operation-note compliance, supporting patients' postoperative care and improved medicolegal accountability.

audits.standard: EAU (2025) and BAUS: pre-operative AFP, beta-hCG and LDH, and repeat 5-7 days post-orchidectomy; target 90% or more
audits.finding: Pre-operative markers complete in 100%; repeat markers within 5-7 days in only 3/23 (13%) against a 90% target; post-operative marker plan documented in 26%.

paper.title: 290 Post-Orchidectomy Tumour-Marker Testing in Suspected Testicular Cancer: An Audit Against EAU and BAUS Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate compliance with guideline-recommended timing of post-orchidectomy tumour-marker testing (in 5-7 days) in patients undergoing radical inguinal orchidectomy for suspected testicular germ-cell tumours, and to identify key pathway failures contributing to delayed staging. Method A retrospective audit was performed at a single UK district general hospital, examining all adult patients who underwent radical inguinal orchidectomy for suspected testicular cancer over two years (15/11/2023–14/11/2025). Data were collected from electronic patient records, theatre systems, discharge documentation and MDT conclusions. Compliance with preoperative AFP, β-hCG, and LDH measurement and repeat testing within 5–7 days postoperatively was compared against EAU (2025) and BAUS guideline standards. Documentation of a clear post-operative marker plan was also assessed. Results 23 orchidectomy cases were identified (median age 43 years; 78% malignant germ-cell tumours). All patients had complete pre-operative tumour markers (100% standard achieved). Only 3/23 (13%) had AFP/β-hCG/LDH repeated within the guideline window of 5–7 days post-surgery, against a target of ≥90%. Although 48% eventually had markers checked, these were often delayed by weeks to months and mostly initiated at MDT review. A clear post-operative marker plan was documented in only 26%, indicating this as the key driver of non-compliance. All malignant cases were escalated to MDT review; however, the absence of timely markers risks missing Stage IS disease. Conclusions The current pathway delivers excellent pre-operative marker compliance but fails to provide guideline-compliant early post-orchidectomy tumour-marker testing. Introducing automatic post-operative blood test scheduling and pathway education is required to ensure timely staging and oncological safety.

audits.title: 311 Improving Surgical Site Infection Surveillance in Vascular Surgery: Findings from a Single-Centre Audit
audits.standard: UKHSA SSI definitions; national pooled vascular SSI figures and GIRFT
audits.finding: 7 SSIs (4.8%) in 145 procedures (125 patients); skin preparation absent in 36% of operative records and dressing type unspecified in 28.9%.

paper.title: 311 Improving Surgical Site Infection Surveillance in Vascular Surgery: Findings from a Single-Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Surgical site infections (SSIs) are a major source of postoperative morbidity, unplanned readmissions, and healthcare costs. Vascular surgery carries a higher risk due to patient comorbidities and complex surgeries. This audit aimed to evaluate SSI rates within a single vascular surgery department and establish sustainable prospective SSI data collection. Method A retrospective review was undertaken of 145 predominantly arterial procedures (125 patients) between March–April 2025. SSIs were defined using UKHSA criteria, as surgical wound infections within 30 days of surgery. Exclusion criteria included previously infected wounds in the context of osteomyelitis, DM and revision surgeries for non-healing wounds due to poor vascularisation. Results Case mix comprised 69.7% elective procedures. 13.6% of patients needed more than 1 procedure. Seven SSIs were identified (4.8%). Five cases required antibiotics, one surgical re-intervention, and one was managed conservatively. There were no unplanned ITU admissions and only one readmission within 30 days. Documentation was frequently incomplete, with skin preparation absent in 36% of operative records and dressing type unspecified in 28.9%. Conclusions The observed SSI rate appears higher than national pooled vascular figures, reflecting the arterial inpatient case mix studied. Prospective surveillance will be conducted via a departmental spreadsheet, with SSIs systematically coded from electronic records and reviewed weekly at the vascular MDT. A dedicated induction poster has been developed and incorporated into staff induction to ensure sustainability across rotations. These measures support compliance with national quality improvement initiatives, including GIRFT, and provide a framework for accurate prospective surveillance.

audits.standard: GIRFT and Royal College of Surgeons post-operative documentation standards

audits.change: Recommended: standardised post-operative proforma and trainee education.

paper.title: 380 Where We Stand Against the National Standards: A Multi-Centre Audit of Post-Operative Appendectomy Documentation in Adult and Paediatric Populations
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim High-quality post-operative documentation is essential for correct care and reducing complications. National recommendations from Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) and the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) emphasize the need for clear, standardized post-operative records that reliably communicate post-operative plans. This audit evaluates local post-operative appendectomy documentation against GIRFT and RCS standards to identify compliance and improvement opportunities. Method A retrospective review of appendectomy cases undertaken between March and April 2025 at Frimley Park Hospital (FPH) and Wexham Park Hospital (WPH) was performed. Patients were identified through the trusts’ electronic records, and post-operative notes were reviewed. Documentation was assessed for completeness in key domains: antibiotics, blood tests (if indicated), recovery location, observation frequency, drain removal (if applicable), VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis, diet instructions, discharge planning, suture removal, and follow-up arrangements, the presence of signatures and photo attachments. Compliance was calculated as the proportion of cases meeting each standard. Results Eighty-three patients were identified (45 FPH, 38 WPH). Compliance varied by domain and site. High-compliance areas included antibiotic documentation (87% FPH, 68% WPH), VTE documentation (80% FPH, 55% WPH), and diet instructions (94% FPH, 90% WPH). Poor compliance was noted for recovery location (7% FPH, 10% WPH), observation frequency (4% FPH, 7% WPH), and suture removal (22% FPH, 16% WPH), with details often vague or incomplete. Conclusions Post-operative appendectomy documentation only partially meets standards. Key shortfalls relate to post operative monitoring and removal of sutures. Introducing a standardized post-operative proforma and education for trainees may improve documentation consistency.

audits.title: 406 The Long Road Home: A Single-Centre Audit into Postoperative LOS After Aortic Surgery
audits.standard: National benchmark length of stay of 7 days or less
audits.finding: Only 26% achieved LOS of 7 days or less; 54% had ICU step-down delays despite clinical readiness.

paper.title: 406 The Long Road Home: A Single-Centre Audit into Postoperative LOS After Aortic Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Open aortic surgery is high-stakes and high-risk for long recovery. The aim of this audit was to assess LOS after open aortic surgery, compare characteristics between patients with standard versus prolonged LOS, and identify opportunities to improve perioperative flow. Method All patients undergoing open aortic surgery from January 2024 to September 2025 were included. Of the fifty-two, two remained inpatient and were excluded. Patients were divided into Group 1 (LOS ≤7 days; n=13) and Group 2 (LOS >7 days; n=37). Demographics, ASA grade, operative complexity, level of postoperative care, ICU LOS, and ICU step-down delays were analysed. Results Only 26% of patients achieved the national benchmark LOS of ≤7 days. Group 1 had lower perioperative risk (30% ASA 2; 70% ASA 3), whereas Group 2 had greater physiological burden (24.3% ASA 2; 62.1% ASA 3; 10.9% ASA 4; 2.7% ASA 5). Median ICU LOS was shorter in Group 1 (3 days) compared to Group 2 (7 days). All Group 1 procedures were infrarenal AAA repairs, while Group 2 included complex cases such as TAAA, JRAAA, aorto-iliac repair, and ruptures. Higher levels of postoperative support were more common in Group 2, with 32.4% requiring Level 3 care versus 15.3% in Group 1. Overall, 54% of patients experienced step-down delays despite clinical readiness. Conclusions Prolonged LOS was associated with greater patient complexity, higher ASA grade, and delays in ICU step-down. In response, our unit will implement a structured ICU de-escalation protocol and explore adoption of a vascular-specific ERAS pathway to streamline recovery and reduce delays.

audits.title: 432 Enhancing Surgical Documentation: A Clinical Audit on Operative Notes Compliance
audits.standard: Royal College of Surgeons of England operative note documentation guidelines
audits.finding: Compliance with RCS standards 69%; postoperative template use 18.2%; electronic documentation 60%.
audits.change: Facilitated online access to the theatre system, consultant induction, user guides and mass communication to surgical teams.

paper.title: 432 Enhancing Surgical Documentation: A Clinical Audit on Operative Notes Compliance
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit, conducted at a secondary care hospital (Dr Gray's Hospital), aimed to evaluate the quality of operative note documentation in reference to the Royal College of Surgeons of England (RCS) guidelines and assess the utilisation of the online theatre-based system. Method A retrospective review of operative notes was undertaken across two audit cycles, with an intervention introduced between cycles. The intervention included facilitated online access, consultant induction, dissemination of user guides and mass communication to surgical teams. Results In the first cycle, 70 operative notes were assessed, followed by 66 in the second. Compliance with RCS documentation standards improved significantly from 69% to 96.6% post-intervention. Use of the post-operative template increased from 18.2% to 44.1% and electronic documentation remained at 60%. The absence of timely online access at staff induction was identified as a major barrier to electronic note access. The audit demonstrated that structured interventions can markedly enhance the quality and completeness of operative notes. This, in turn, will facilitate improved documentation and continuity of care, post-operative management and medico-legal standards. Key recommendations include ensuring early electronic access for new staff along with a structured induction of user guide, documentation protocols and ongoing monitoring to maintain high standards. Conclusions This quality improvement initiative highlights the critical role of electronic surgical operation notes in maintaining patient safety and clinical efficiency.

audits.title: 433 From Scan to Scalpel: A Retrospective Audit of Imaging and Surgical Timeliness in Acute Abdomen Following Digitalisation of CT Vetting
audits.standard: Royal College of Surgeons guideline standards for imaging timeliness in acute abdomen
audits.finding: Median time from admission to imaging 6 hours 8 minutes; compliance with RCS imaging standards 28%.
audits.change: Digitalisation of the CT vetting workflow.

paper.title: 433 From Scan to Scalpel: A Retrospective Audit of Imaging and Surgical Timeliness in Acute Abdomen Following Digitalisation of CT Vetting
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate whether digitalising the CT vetting workflow improved imaging timeliness, adherence to Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) guideline standards and surgical pathway efficiency in adults presenting with acute abdominal pain. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of adults referred to general surgery with acute abdominal pain at Ealing Hospital. Outcomes were compared before and after implementation of digital CT vetting. Measures included radiology process intervals, compliance with RCS targets, surgical pathway intervals and clinical outcomes. Continuous variables were analysed using Mann–Whitney U tests and categorical variables using Fisher’s exact test. Results Time from admission to imaging improved significantly following implementation of the digital vetting process. Median time decreased from 6 hours 8 minutes pre-intervention to 4 hours 35 minutes post-intervention (p=0.0488). Radiology process mapping showed descriptive improvement in several intervals, although the interval from scan completion to first report increased significantly from 13 minutes to 27 minutes (p=0.0404). Compliance with RCS imaging standards increased from 28 percent to 38.5 percent, but the change was not statistically significant (p=0.68). No significant differences were found in time to first surgical review (p=0.904) or time to surgery (p=0.1138). Clinical outcomes also remained similar. Conclusions Digitalising CT vetting improved overall imaging timeliness but did not accelerate surgical review or operation. Broader workflow optimisation is required to translate imaging gains into improvements in surgical timelines and outcomes for high-risk patients.

audits.standard: BOAST/BSSH (2021) guidance on safe use and documentation of intraoperative upper limb tourniquets

paper.title: 499 Improving Patient Safety in Upper Limb Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit of Tourniquet Use Practices Against BSSH/BOAST Guidance in a Tertiary Plastic Surgery Trauma Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Upper limb tourniquet use carries recognised risks, making adherence to BOAST/BSSH safety standards vital in modern trauma surgery practice. Aim The aim of this closed-loop audit was to assess compliance with BOAST/BSSH (2021) guidelines on the safe use and documentation of intraoperative upper limb tourniquets within a single tertiary plastic surgery trauma centre, identify areas of poor compliance, implement targeted interventions, and evaluate subsequent improvement. Method A retrospective audit was undertaken reviewing operative and anaesthetic documentation from upper limb trauma cases. Data were collected using a standardised proforma. The first audit cycle analysed 50 cases performed between 5–30 March 2025, identifying documentation rates for key standards including skin condition assessment, method of exsanguination, skin isolation, tourniquet pressure, tourniquet time, and complications. Interventions introduced included departmental teaching, circulation of guideline material, placement of laminated reminders on tourniquet machines, and development of an electronic documentation template. A second cycle of 50 cases (5 September–31 October 2025) assessed compliance post-intervention. Results Significant improvements were observed across multiple parameters following intervention. Documentation of pre-operative skin condition improved from 33% to 50%, post-operative assessment from 0% to 50%, skin isolation method from 80% to 100%, and safe tourniquet pressure documentation from 94% to 100%. No tourniquet-related burns occurred in either cycle. Tourniquet time recording remained unchanged, with 4% lacking clear documentation. Conclusions Targeted interventions led to improvements in key documentation standards relating to tourniquet safety. Ongoing staff education and refinement of electronic mandatory fields are required to optimise compliance and sustain improvement.

paper.title: 538 Audit of Abdominal Pain Pathway for Paediatric Surgery Patients in Compliance with Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute abdominal pain is a high-risk paediatric presentation, with appendicitis being the most common surgical emergency. Variation in management can lead to delayed diagnosis or unnecessary surgery. This audit assessed Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital’s (NNUH) compliance with Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT) best-practice standards for acute appendicitis. Method A six-month retrospective audit was undertaken of children aged 0–16 years presenting with acute abdominal pain to the emergency department. Data were collected across 17 GIRFT-derived standards including analgesia, diagnostic assessment, MDT review, imaging access, surgery <24 hours of admission, antibiotic stewardship, intraoperative sampling, and post-operative outcomes including negative appendicectomy and readmission rates. Outcomes were compared with GIRFT recommendations and national benchmarks. Results Fifty-three appendicectomy cases were reviewed. Readmission rates were 0% at 6 months (0/53) and 2.9% at 3 years (8/275), both significantly lower than the national benchmark of 9.7% (p<0.05). The negative appendicectomy rate was 1.9% (1/53), lower than the national average of 6.1% (p>0.05). Full compliance was achieved across 15/17 audited standards. Identified areas of improvement related to peritoneal swab sampling and surgery being performed within 24 hours of admission. Conclusions NNUH demonstrates high compliance with GIRFT paediatric appendicectomy guidance; our audit suggesting this is associated with improved outcomes. Structured assessment and targeted investigations likely contribute to low negative appendicectomy rates, while low readmission rates reflect effective antibiotic stewardship, pain management and MDT involvement. Following departmental education, a re-audit to assess compliance with all 17 GIRFT standards should be undertaken.

audits.standard: Local group and save sample protocols

paper.title: 549 ‘Group and Save’ Practice in Emergency and Elective Surgery: An Audit of Adherence in a Surgical Unit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Surgical centres around the UK have their own protocols regarding routine collection of ‘group and save’ (G&S) samples prior to emergency and elective surgeries, due to lack of guidance provided by governing bodies. A single G&S sample costs £29. Our aim was to establish the indication for, and adherence to, G&S sampling in emergency and elective procedures in our unit. Method A retrospective audit was conducted within a surgical department at a tertiary centre over one month. Data was collected for all emergency and elective procedures; number of G&S samples collected, indication for the procedure and intra-operative transfusion received. Following intervention targeted to pre-operative clinics via posters and email communication, the audit cycle was repeated. Results 391 procedures were performed in cycle 1 (153 emergency, 238 elective) and 450 in cycle 2 (171 emergency, 279 elective). In cycle 1, 203 G&S samples were collected, 52 (26%) of which were not indicated - 25/82 (30%) emergency, 27/121 (22%) elective. In cycle 2, 73 of 260 samples taken were not indicated: 44/114 (28%) emergency, 29/146 (20%) elective. This represented an avoidable monthly cost of £1508 in cycle 1 and £2177 in cycle 2, corresponding, respectively, to £18,096 and £25,404 per annum. Conclusions This audit highlights gaps in adherence to local G&S sample protocols; despite a small decrease in unnecessary samples taken for elective procedures, emergency procedures remain a problem. Given the significant cost burden to the NHS, review of current guidelines and further reinforcement of compliance to guidance is important.

paper.title: 552 Appendix Out, Antibiotics Out: A Closed-Loop Audit of Post-Operative Use of Antibiotics After Appendicectomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is the most common abdominal surgical emergency worldwide, with around 50,000 appendicectomies performed annually in the UK. The World Journal of Emergency Surgery and British Medical Journal have issued peri-operative antibiotic guidelines, advising against postoperative antibiotics for uncomplicated appendicitis and against extending antibiotics beyond 3–5 days postoperatively in complicated cases. We audited antibiotic use in acute appendicitis at our district general hospital against these guidelines and aimed to improve stewardship by reducing unnecessary and prolonged antibiotic courses. Method Appendicectomies were identified using electronic theatre logs, retrospectively for the first cycle (October–December 2024) and prospectively for the second (April–June 2025). Our intervention consisted of and presenting our findings at our local surgical forum and clinical governance meeting and disseminating a poster displayed in emergency theatres. Results A total of 70 and 53 appendicectomies were identified in the first and second cycles respectively. Among uncomplicated cases, 90.2% in the first cycle wrongly received postoperative antibiotics compared with 84.4% in the second, a reduction of 5.8%. Antibiotic courses for complicated appendicitis averaged 7.8 days in the first cycle compared with 6.3 days in the second, a reduction of 1.5 days. Whereas, uncomplicated appendicitis averaged 2.9 days in the first cycle, versus 2.7 days in the second, a reduction of 0.2 days. Conclusions This audit demonstrated poor adherence to international recommendations, particularly the routine use of postoperative antibiotics in uncomplicated cases and prolonged regimens in complicated appendicitis, highlighting key areas for improvement that may be relevant across surgical services nationally.

paper.title: 560 Stop the Bleed: Audit of the Management of Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding at Cavan General Hospital, Republic of Ireland
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) is a common emergency with mortality rates of 5–10%. NICE (CG141, QS38) and BSG guidelines emphasise early resuscitation, risk stratification using the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS), timely endoscopy, and evidence-based pharmacological therapy. This audit assessed local practice against these standards. Method A retrospective review of 40 adult patients admitted with suspected UGIB from January–December 2024 was conducted. Data were extracted from clinical notes, laboratory results, transfusion records and endoscopy reports. Compliance was benchmarked against NICE/BSG standards and UK AUGIB audit results. Results Initial assessment was strong: 100% had complete vital signs documented, 100% received IV access, and 97% received fluid resuscitation. However, GBS was not documented in most cases, representing a major variance from recommended practice. Pre-endoscopy PPI use was high (∼98%). Among suspected variceal bleeds (13%), compliance with guideline therapy was suboptimal: 50% received terlipressin and 83% received prophylactic antibiotics. Endoscopy occurred in 85% of patients, but only 63% were scoped within 24 hours (mean delay 42.8 h). Only 1/5 variceal cases met the <12-hour target. Transfusion practice was appropriately restrictive (mean Hb 7.5 g/dL pre-transfusion; documentation 94%). No rebleeding or endoscopy-related complications were reported; 9% required repeat endoscopy. Conclusions Strengths included effective initial resuscitation, high PPI compliance, and appropriate transfusion thresholds. Key deficiencies were absence of GBS scoring, delayed endoscopy, and incomplete variceal bundle adherence. Implementation of a UGIB proforma, anticoagulation/variceal checklists, and improved endoscopy access is underway. Re-audit is planned within 12 months.

audits.title: 564 Audit of Pregnancy Testing in Girls Over 12 Years Presenting with Acute Abdominal Pain
audits.standard: Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital guidance: 100% of girls over 12 years with acute abdominal pain have a pregnancy test on admission
audits.finding: Only 13.3% had a documented pregnancy test; 86.7% had no evidence of testing.

paper.title: 564 Audit of Pregnancy Testing in Girls Over 12 Years Presenting with Acute Abdominal Pain
paper.abstract: Abstract This audit evaluates compliance with pregnancy testing guidelines for girls over 12 years presenting with acute abdominal pain. According to Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital guidance, all patients within this group should undergo pregnancy testing as part of the initial assessment. The objective of this audit was to determine whether pregnancy testing is consistently performed and appropriately documented, including confirmation of test completion and recorded results. A retrospective review was undertaken of the 150 admissions to CHED or CAU involving girls over 12 years presenting with acute abdominal pain. Data were collected from May 2024 to May 2025 using Symphony, ICE and ED clerking records. Variables extracted included age, admission date, and documentation of pregnancy testing with results. The audit standard was set at 100% compliance with pregnancy testing on admission. The audit found that only 13.3% of cases had a documented pregnancy test, while 86.7% had no evidence of testing within the records. Among documented tests, 20% recorded a negative result, 1% a positive result, and 30% indicated that a pregnancy test was performed without a documented result. In these cases, the result was presumed to be negative. Nursing staff reported that pregnancy test documentation is entered within nursing notes on Symphony and that dipstick testing is the method most frequently used. The audit demonstrates a need for improved documentation regarding whether pregnancy testing was offered, performed or declined, as well as consistent recording of results. Recommendations include ensuring completion of pregnancy testing and integrating results within the management plan and nursing documentation.

paper.title: 601 Compliance With Perioperative Antibiotic Guidelines in Patients Undergoing Emergency Appendicectomy: A Three-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is the leading acute surgical emergency worldwide, with variable use of perioperative antibiotics. This audit completed the third cycle reviewing compliance with the World Society of Emergency Surgery acute appendicitis 2020 and local guidelines. Method Our third audit cycle retrospectively identified 59 adult patients undergoing an emergency appendicectomy between 1st September 2025 - 1st November 2025 in one NHS trust. Two previous audit cycles in 2022 and 2023 led to interventions of local presentation with informative posters displayed in clinical areas, and an operative note proforma for appendicectomy. Data were collected on demographics, severity of appendicitis, perioperative antibiotic use and any post-operative complications. Compliance to audit standards was then reviewed. Results Reporting our three audit cycles, compliance with preoperative antibiotic usage was improved, from 85% initially to 87% and within this audit cycle 95% of patients received preoperative antibiotics in line with local and international guidelines. Omission of postoperative antibiotics for patients with simple appendicitis was compliant in 79%, 100% and 97% of patients respectively. Patients with complicated appendicitis had postoperative antibiotics appropriately for 3-5 days in 12.1%, 20% and 61% of patients. Conclusions Over three audit cycles, interventions including departmental educational resources, creation of local guidelines and an operative note proforma have shown significant improvement in compliance with guidelines for perioperative antibiotics use. However, the postoperative antibiotic use in patients with complicated appendicitis has ongoing disparity, requiring further clinician education and targeted initiatives to ensure safe patient care and antibiotic stewardship.

paper.title: 622 Compliance With ABS 2023 Phyllodes Guidelines in the Buckinghamshire Breast Unit: An Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Phyllodes are rare breast tumours. Surgical excision remans the mainstay but a recent international survey demonstrated wide variation in practice. Emerging data suggests that narrower excision margins can be safely accepted; reflected in new ABS guidelines. This audit aimed to assess unit practice against latest national guidance for excision margins. Method Hospital records were searched using operative codes to identify phyllodes excised during the last 5 years. A retrospective case-note review was conducted by trainee surgeons using a pre-determined proforma. Results 34 women underwent excision of phyllodes between May 2018- Oct 2023. 18 (53%) were benign, 8 (24%) borderline and 4 (12%) were malignant. One was upgraded to sarcoma and 3 (9%) downgraded to fibroadenoma. 29 women (85%) were treated with breast conservation, 5 (15%) underwent mastectomy. Most underwent one operation (59%, n= 20) but 29% (n=10) required two and 12% (n=4) three to obtain clear margins. 11 patients underwent repeat surgeries for either incomplete excision (benign) or tumour at margin i.e. 0mm margin (borderline). One mastectomy was indicated for malignant phyllodes when 11mm margin was not accepted after WLE. This case may have avoided mastectomy under new guidelines. Conclusions Our unit is not yet fully compliant with latest ABS Phyllodes guidance but the audit did not identify excess mastectomies to obtain wide-clear margins. However, 41% (n=14) required >1 operation to obtain clear margins and patients require counselling about this prior to surgery. Performance will be re-audited in due course after disseminating new guidance within departmental and regional networks.

audits.standard: ACPGBI emergency colorectal surgery guidelines on acute diverticulitis and follow-up endoscopy
audits.finding: 41/106 (39%) with an indication had no follow-up endoscopy; 42/55 without an indication had endoscopy; antibiotics given to all but 2 uncomplicated patients and 85% admitted.

paper.title: 711 A Retrospective Audit on the Management and Follow Up Practices of Acute Diverticulitis
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The ACPGBI guidelines in emergency colorectal surgery lays out a framework for the management of acute diverticulitis and for indications for endoscopic follow up after recovery from diverticulitis. The aim of this audit was to evaluate the management practices of acute diverticulitis at the University Hospital North Durham. Method A retrospective cross-sectional study covering a period of 1 year, which included all patients presenting with acute diverticulitis. Results Study population included 161 patients of which 67% had uncomplicated diverticulitis. In the uncomplicated group, antibiotics were prescribed in all but 2 patients and 85% of this group were managed as inpatients with an average hospital stay of 3.5 days. Although 106 patients had an indication for follow up endoscopy as per guidelines, 41 of them didn’t have an endoscopy. From the 55 patients for whom endoscopy was not indicated, 42 had an endoscopy (11 colonoscopies and 31 flexible sigmoidoscopies). The excess cost incurred by doing endoscopies for whom it was not indicated was £35,202. Four malignancy/high grade dysplasia lesions were detected in the group for whom endoscopy was indicated while none were found in the group who had endoscopies without an indication. Conclusions Most patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis were managed as inpatients and had antibiotics although the guidelines recommend otherwise. The lack of clear departmental protocol meant that many inappropriate endoscopy referrals were made resulting in significant cost to the hospital. Many patients for whom endoscopy was indicated did not have it done (39%) which may result in pathologies being possibly missed.

paper.title: 746 Optimising Delivery of Postoperative ERAS Pathways in Colorectal Surgery: A Multidisciplinary Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) guidelines are used internationally, aiming to minimise perioperative stress, maintain physiological function and support patient recovery through pre-, intra- and post-operative interventions. The audit aimed to assess adherence to the post-operative ERAS guidelines in the local colorectal department. Method A retrospective audit was undertaken of patients undergoing elective colorectal procedures via the ERAS pathway over a 9-month period. Local standards based on international ERAS guidelines were used to audit prescribing of regular medications and analgesia, nutrition, mobilisation and duration of catheter and patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) use. Multidisciplinary feedback was obtained on findings and an admissions protocol was developed. A flowchart depicting the protocol was placed at workstations. New ERAS patients were specifically highlighted on handover documents and templates developed for ward-round use. A re-audit was initiated following introduction of the protocol. Results The initial audit included 68 patients, 51 of whom were on regular medications, however only 37% had these prescribed on the day of surgery. Preliminary re-audit findings over 3 months demonstrate improvement in prescribing rates to 62%. Documentation of the reasoning for extended use of catheters and PCAs was initially missing in 45% and 74% of cases respectively making analysis difficult. Early post-intervention results indicate improvement in documentation, although a comprehensive analysis is ongoing and will be completed over the coming months. Conclusions A multidisciplinary protocol improved adherence to colorectal ERAS guidelines. Sustained improvement will require ongoing engagement from the MDT and education of doctors rotating into the department.

paper.title: TPTh 9.09 Audit of the Timing of Cholecystectomy in Gallstone-Induced Pancreatitis: Adherence to Guidelines and Impact on Patient Outcomes
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Gallstone-induced pancreatitis (GIP) is a major cause of surgical admissions in the UK. Early cholecystectomy, ideally during index admission or two weeks following discharge, is recommended by national guidelines to prevent recurrent biliary events. To assess adherence to these guidelines at University Hospital Monklands (UHM) and evaluate the clinical impact of delayed cholecystectomy. Method Retrospective data collection was conducted for patients admitted with gallstone-induced pancreatitis between September 2023 and September 2024. Data were retrieved under Caldicott approval. Exclusion criteria included severe pancreatitis, frailty, and refusal. Outcomes measured: timing of cholecystectomy, readmission rate, and time to intervention. A re-audit (Jan–Jun 2025) followed the pathway implementation. Results First Cycle: Of 69 total cases, 8 were excluded; 2 deaths; 59 eligible. Procedures performed: 30 (50.8%), timely procedures: 9 (15.2%), mean delay 11.2 weeks. Nineteen (32%) readmitted, 10 with recurrent GIP. Second Cycle: 41 admissions, 11 excluded; 30 eligible. 15 operated (50%), 13 (43%) timely—12 during index admission, 1 within 2 weeks post-discharge. Compliance improved following the expedited cholecystectomy pathway and live tracker introduction. The audit identified poor adherence to guidelines in the first cycle, with significant readmission and recurrence rates. Root causes included lack of structured follow-up, delays in anaesthetic clearance, and limited theatre availability. Implementation of expedited pathway and live tracker improved outcomes. Further gains depend on multidisciplinary cooperation and sustained monitoring. Conclusions Performing cholecystectomy during index admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis reduces readmission and complications. Structured pathways and real-time Tracking enhances adherence to standards. Continued re-audit recommended.

paper.title: 752 Use of Percutaneous Cholecystostomy in the Management of Acute Cholecystitis: A Retrospective Audit on Its Indications
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute cholecystitis (AC) represents a major contributor to emergency general surgery admissions, accounting for approximately 30% of cases. While laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC) remains the gold standard treatment, its safety is reduced in patients with significant comorbidities or physiological compromise. For individuals deemed unfit for general anaesthesia, percutaneous cholecystostomy (PC) is recommended by the Tokyo Guidelines (TG) as an alternative. This audit evaluates local adherence to TG indications for PC and examines associated patient outcomes. Method A retrospective audit was conducted at Dumfries and Galloway Royal Infirmary, reviewing all patients undergoing PC between October 2019 and January 2024. Data collected included demographics, Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), ASA grade, ECOG status, inflammatory markers, imaging modality, time to drain placement, drain duration, complications, and incidence of interval cholecystectomy. Adherence to TG indications—CCI ≥6 and/or ASA ≥3, or septic shock with organ dysfunction—was assessed. Results 60 patients underwent PC during the study period, with complete data available for 58. The adherence rate to TG indications was 76%. Interval cholecystectomy occurred in 32% of patients meeting TG criteria compared with 43% of those who did not. Outcomes were consistent with published evidence, including the CHOCOLATE trial, which demonstrates poorer outcomes in lower-risk patients managed with PC rather than LC. Conclusions PC use at our centre largely aligns with TG recommendations. The higher interval cholecystectomy rate and inferior outcomes among patients not meeting TG criteria underscore the importance of appropriate patient selection. Clinically fit patients with lower comorbidity should preferentially undergo early LC to optimise outcomes.

paper.title: 756 Junior Clinicians Can Deliver Safe ENT Emergency Care: Audit of Otitis Externa Management
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The Ear, Nose and Throat Emergency Clinic (E clinic) at a UK tertiary hospital is staffed by junior clinicians from F1 to ST2 level. It manages a defined set of urgent presentations including recurrent epistaxis, sudden sensorineural hearing loss, and otitis externa (OE). This first cycle of a three-part audit evaluated the ability of junior clinicians to manage OE safely and effectively, with specific focus on recognition of scope of practice and appropriate senior escalation. Method A retrospective review identified 243 true cases of OE. A random sample of 100 appointments were analysed. Data collected included documentation quality, escalation decisions, antimicrobial choice, swab use, and safety related prescribing behaviours. Errors were categorised using predefined criteria. Results 40 appointments involved suspected complication or atypical features including possible cholesteatoma, persistent otalgia, or hearing loss following infection resolution. Of these, 24 were escalated appropriately to the on-call registrar or consultant led clinic, while 16 showed no documented escalation. Antimicrobial prescribing was determined appropriate in 78% of cases, based on empirical need or prior swab results. Common errors included inadequate documentation, insufficient microbial coverage, and unnecessary steroid use. Five cases involved prescription of an ototoxic topical medication without documented visualisation of an intact tympanic membrane, and 1 case involved ototoxic prescribing despite a documented perforation. Conclusions OE can be effectively managed within a junior led clinic. However, safety and consistency could be improved ahead of the second audit cycle through supportive protocolisation and structured induction teaching.

paper.title: 770 Audit of Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) Negative Referrals to Urgent Suspected Cancer Pathway in Mid and South Essex NHS Foundation Trust (MSE)
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction National Guidance stipulates that Faecal Immunochemical Test (FIT) should be used in primary care to guide referrals to the Colorectal Urgent Suspected Cancer Pathway (USCP). With normal blood count and normal examination, there is 0.1% chance of finding a colorectal cancer if a patient is FIT-negative. These patients should be managed on a non-USCP. In MSE, the Rapid Diagnostic Centre (RDC) still receive up to 20% FIT-negative patients on the USCP. As no FIT-negative internal pathway exists in MSE, patients are still being offered endoscopy at index referral. Aim To review how many confirmed cancers were FIT-positive and how many were FIT-negative. Method MSE and shared GP records were searched between December 2023 and October 2025. 20752 patients were referred on the USCP, 1037 were confirmed cancer. Results 925 (89.2%) patients were FIT-positive, 9 (0.87%) were FIT-negative. Of these nine FIT-negative, five had iron deficiency anaemia (IDA), two had significant weight loss and two had anal mass. 103 had no FIT test, of these 37 were emergency admissions or incidental findings; 13 were from surveillance; 37 had other red-flag symptoms; 16 were IDA. Conclusions FIT-negative cancer is rare (0.87%), and these patients all had other symptoms/clinical indications which warranted investigations on the USC pathway. Local data supports the national guidance that FIT-negative patients with normal blood count and normal examination, can be safely reassured and/or managed on a non-USC pathway. This audit has supported the proposed change that FIT-negative referrals to the USCP should be discharged and managed on other pathways.

paper.title: 776 Quality of Long-Term Follow-Up After Bariatric Surgery in Primary Care: A Quality Improvement Audit Comparing UK and Overseas Surgery Patients
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To assess whether bariatric surgery patients registered at a UK general practice are receiving long-term follow-up in accordance with national recommendations, including NICE CG189/NG246 and BOMSS 2020 guidance, mandating specialist follow-up for at least a year post-surgery and lifelong annual monitoring in primary care. A secondary aim was to compare follow-up outcomes between patients who underwent surgery in the NHS, privately in the UK, and abroad. Method A retrospective review of electronic records identified 29 eligible bariatric patients (April 2009–September 2025). Data extracted included evidence of specialist follow-up, discharge communication, annual review(s), biochemistry monitoring, supplementation, and weight documentation. Outcomes were compared between UK versus abroad-operated patients using Chi-square testing. Results Continued involvement of a bariatric service was documented in 100% of NHS patients, 87.5% of private UK patients, and 0% abroad. Discharge letters into shared care were received in 81.8% (NHS), 100% (private), and 30% (abroad). Evidence of 1 annual review was 45.5% (NHS), 62.5% (private), and 40% (abroad), while ≥2 reviews occurred in 0%, 25%, and 10%. Annual biochemical monitoring occurred in 54.5% (NHS), 62.5% (private), and 50% (abroad). Evidence of lifelong multivitamin supplementation was lowest abroad (20% vs 81.8% NHS). Weight review was also poorest abroad (10% vs 45.5% NHS). Patients treated abroad demonstrated significantly reduced communication into primary care and lower adherence to supplementation. Conclusions Compliance with national standards is suboptimal, particularly among patients receiving surgery overseas. Service improvements include recall alerts, a structured bariatric review template, and strengthened communication pathways. Re-audit in 12 months is planned.

audits.change: Educational posters and email summarising BSG guidelines and audit recommendations.

paper.title: 790 Management of Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding in a District General Hospital- Clinical Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Lower Gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB) is a common indication for hospital admission, accounting for 20% of all GI bleeding cases and 3% of annual surgical referral in the UK. Reported inpatient mortality rate of 3.4% to 17.8%, highlighting the need for timely assessment and management. The aim was to assess adherence to British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) guidelines on LGIB and identify areas of improvement. Specific objectives include assessment of initial management, risk stratification, diagnostic and therapeutic intervention. Method Retrospective analysis of patients admitted with LGIB for >24 hours over two 3-month audit cycles. Data collected includes anticoagulant use, Digital rectal examination (DRE), shock index (SI), Tranexamic acid (TXA) and CT-angiography (CT-A). Action plan implemented after the first cycle involved distributing educational posters and email summarising BSG guidelines and key audit recommendations- DRE for all patients, risk stratification with SI and Oakland score, avoiding TXA (HALT-IT trial) and CT-A use in haemodynamically unstable patients (SI >1) or active bleeding. Result 32 patients (M:F 1:1.3) were reviewed in the second cycle, compared with 34 in the first. DRE compliance improved from 79% to 91%, Oakland score documentation was unchanged, TXA use decreased from 44% to 38% and CT-A reduced from 29% to 19%. Conclusions LGIB is a potentially life-threatening condition requiring prompt and effective management. This audit demonstrated improved compliance in current practice, highlighting that ongoing education and continuous improvement in clinical practice, reinforced by adherence to established guidelines are essential to further optimise patient outcomes.

paper.title: 804 Improving Antimicrobial Stewardship in Acute Urology: A Two-Cycle Targeted Intervention Audit Using a Composite Compliance Framework
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Antimicrobial resistance is a growing challenge in the UK. The 2025 ESPAUR reports rising E. coli resistance to frontline UTI antibiotics. Inappropriate antimicrobial prescribing contributes significantly to this trend. We applied a multi-domain compliance framework across two audit cycles to assess antimicrobial prescribing in a tertiary urology centre. Aim To assess local guideline adherence using a multi-domain composite framework and evaluate whether interventions improved antimicrobial stewardship. Method We prospectively analysed acute urology admissions at Liverpool University Hospitals. Data included diagnosis, culture results, antibiotics, and length of stay. Prescribing was assessed across four domains: initiation, subsequent changes, discharge, and duration. Domain-level compliance and a patient-level composite score (0–4), adjusted for non-applicable domains, were calculated. Length of stay was compared across composite-score groups using the Kruskal–Wallis test. Interventions included QR-code posters, teaching sessions, and a faculty meeting. Results 84 patients were analysed: 44 in cycle 1; 40 in cycle 2. Initial antibiotic choice improved from 59% to 82%. Duration compliance also improved from 61% to 68%. Subsequent antibiotic changes were similar between cycles (86% in cycle 1; 81% in cycle 2). Discharge antibiotic choices remained at 61%. Composite compliance increased from 43% to 53%; in cycle 2, 33% were compliant, 20% had justified deviations, and 48% had unjustified deviations. Length of stay differed (p=0.002), reflecting differences in illness severity rather than compliance. Conclusions Cycle-based interventions improved antimicrobial prescribing, although discharges remained suboptimal. The multi-domain composite framework used in this audit offers a reproducible approach to quantifying antimicrobial stewardship with potential for wider implementation.

audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: CT correctly identified 4 of 13 complicated and 16 of 18 uncomplicated appendicitis cases; for complicated appendicitis sensitivity 31%, specificity 100%, PPV 100%, NPV 69%, false-negative rate 69%.

paper.title: 844 Evaluating the Accuracy of CT Reported Uncomplicated Appendicitis Versus Intraoperative Findings: A Single Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the accuracy of CT reports in correctly identifying and classifying complicated versus uncomplicated appendicitis through comparison with intraoperative findings. Method A single-centre retrospective audit was conducted over a 3-month period (14/08/25–15/11/25). All adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent contrast-enhanced CT abdomen and pelvis for suspected appendicitis and proceeded to appendicectomy were included. Complicated appendicitis was defined intraoperatively as perforation, abscess, phlegmon, or gangrenous change. Data extracted included CT classification, reporting radiologist grade, timing of consultant radiologist addenda, pre-operative inflammatory markers, operative findings, histology if applicable and time from CT to theatre. Diagnostic accuracy metrics were calculated. Results A total of 33 patients were included. CT correctly identified four of 13 cases with complicated appendicitis and 16 of 18 cases with uncomplicated appendicitis. We noted two patients labelled as uncomplicated appendicitis on CT had no appendicitis at surgery and two patients with a normal appendix on CT had uncomplicated appendicitis intraoperatively. For detection of complicated appendicitis, CT yielded a sensitivity of 31%, specificity 100%, positive-predictive value of 100%, negative-predictive value of 69%, and a false-negative rate of 69%, indicating substantial under-detection of complicated disease. Conclusions A substantial proportion of complicated appendicitis was not recognised on CT interpretation, with nearly 70% of complicated cases misclassified as uncomplicated. These findings highlight the need to improve reporting precision, strengthen radiology–surgical communication, and review local pathways to reduce diagnostic delay and optimise patient outcomes.

paper.title: 854 An Audit of Perioperative Diabetes Management Against GIRFT Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim GIRFT guidance for perioperative diabetes management was developed to reduce perioperative infection, length of stay and readmission for surgical patients with diabetes. In this double-cycle audit, we evaluate perioperative diabetes care at a tertiary centre against GIRFT guidance, aiming to identify safety-critical gaps and inform targeted improvements before cycle-2 re-audit. Method A retrospective audit was conducted on 145 National Confidential Enquiry into Patient Outcome and Death (NCEPOD) Category 3 surgical inpatients in August 2025 at University Hospital Southampton. 19 patients had diabetes. Data were extracted from anaesthetic charts, perioperative documentation, inpatient paper records, and biochemical results. Standards were defined using GIRFT guidance. Domains assessed included pre-operative investigations, withholding SGLT-2 on admission, intra-operative and recovery glucose monitoring, variable rate insulin (VRI) initiation and transition, anaesthetic-to-ward handover, and postoperative glycaemic outcomes. Results Among the 19 patients, metabolic optimisation before surgery was incomplete, with only 53% receiving HbA1c and ketones checks. Intra-operative and recovery CBG monitoring were 59% and 63% respectively. VRI management showed variability, with only 45% receiving the appropriate long-acting insulin dose while on VRI. Anaesthetic to ward handover occurred in only 42% cases. Glycaemic outcomes showed clinically significant dysglycaemia, with 42% of patients experiencing hyperglycaemia and 21% with hypoglycaemia. Conclusions Cycle-1 demonstrates important shortfalls in perioperative diabetes documentation, monitoring, and handover. Findings highlight the need for multidisciplinary interventions, including targeted education for surgical and anaesthetic teams and clearer handover processes. These actions will be implemented before cycle-2 re-audit to improve compliance with GIRFT standards.

audits.standard: National guidance on early frailty assessment, recognition of high-risk patients and specialist geriatric involvement

paper.title: 855 Management of Frail Patients in Acute Surgical Wards: A First-Cycle Audit of Compliance With National Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Frailty is associated with increased postoperative complications, mortality, and prolonged hospital stay. National guidance recommends early frailty assessment, recognition of high-risk patients, and involvement of specialist geriatric services. This audit evaluates compliance with these standards for older adults admitted under general surgery at Hull University Teaching Hospitals. Method A retrospective snapshot audit was conducted for patients aged ≥65 years admitted to acute surgical wards between April and July 2024. Frailty was assessed using the Clinical Frailty Scale. Data were collected on frailty documentation, frailty team involvement, ReSPECT and DNACPR completion, length of stay, management, and 30-day outcomes. Results Eighty-three patients were included; 29 (34.9%) were frail with a Clinical Frailty Scale score ≥5. Frailty status was documented in all cases. Despite this, none were referred to or reviewed by the frailty team. Among frail patients, DNACPR status was recorded as “Not for CPR” in 51.7%, “For CPR” in 24.1%, and was undocumented in 24.1%. Mean length of stay for frail patients was 24.7 days (range 2–86). Surgical intervention was required in 55.2%. Thirty-day readmission was 24.1%, and mortality was 17.2%. Conclusions Although frailty assessment was completed for all patients, frail individuals received no specialist geriatric input and experienced high readmission, mortality, and prolonged hospital stay. These findings demonstrate the need for a structured frailty pathway within general surgery, including routine specialist referral, geriatric review, and multidisciplinary involvement. The results will guide the second audit cycle and support development of a dedicated frailty service to improve outcomes for older surgical patients.

paper.title: 887 Enhancing Frailty Assessment in Emergency Surgical Admissions: Two-Cycle Audit of Screening Practices
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Frailty is a strong predictor of adverse outcomes in emergency general surgery (EGS), yet assessment remains inconsistently documented. Guidance from GIRFT and the British Geriatrics Society’s “Six Steps to Better Care for Older People in Acute Hospitals”, recommend frailty screening at admission for all ≥65 year old patients. This closed-loop audit evaluated frailty screening using four measures - Clinical Frailty Score (CFS), baseline mobility, 4AT delirium screening, and Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), aiming to develop a frailty assessment bundle for routine clerking. Method Two retrospective audit cycles were undertaken. The first reviewed 50 consecutive EGS admissions ≥65 years between 27/08/2025–08/09/2025. Following this, a targeted intervention was introduced, including - raising awareness, education of clerking teams, and promoting a frailty screening bundle comprising CFS, baseline mobility, 4AT and MUST. The second cycle reviewed 52 EGS admissions between 03/11/2025–17/11/2025. Documentation rates were compared across cycles and benchmarked against GIRFT and BGS standards. Results Documentation improved across several domains. CFS completion increased from 8% to 28%, baseline mobility from 44% to 48%, and 4AT remained high (100% → 92.3%). Nutritional screening showed a modest decline (82% → 67.3%). The intervention improved awareness and uptake of CFS, though variation persisted across supporting assessments. Conclusions Targeted intervention improved compliance with frailty assessment, though it still remains below recommended levels. Continued reinforcement of the frailty assessment bundle is likely to sustain progress. Improved CFS documentation will help identify patients with CFS >6, providing essential data to support a business case for dedicated comprehensive geriatric assessment within the surgical pathway.

paper.title: 895 Improving Ward Round Documentation Through Implementation of a Structured Template: An Audit Cycle
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Ward round documentation is an important communication tool in healthcare. The recent implementation of electronic patient records (EPR) in our trust raised concerns regarding ward round documentation. We conducted an audit on the endocrine ward in October 2024, and the main observation was that there is great variability between ward round entries, between doctors, and between entries from the same doctor. Aim This re-audit aimed to evaluate whether the implementation of a ward round template improved the documentation of essential components. Method Data were collected by analysing ward round notes from the EPR on the endocrine ward. The data was collected as a snapshot in time. 1-3 ward round entries were analysed per patient. The data was collected using a 16-point checklist developed by the audit team based on the guidelines and standards used for this audit Results There was improvement in documentation across all categories. The average number of fields completed per ward round entry out of a 16-point checklist ranged between 43.75% fields to 100% with the average of 82.1% completeness per ward round entry. Improved from 71.38% in the initial audit. Bleep number documentation increased to 57% from 37%. Medication reviews documentation improved: VTE prophylaxis 69.5% (26.5%), Antibiotics 58.5% (30.1 %), Analgesia 58.5% (19.28%). Conclusions Using a structured ward round template helped improve ward round documentation. Given the rotational aspect of resident doctors’ training leading to working across different specialties, the use of a structured template can prompt review and documentation of essential elements during daily ward rounds and improve patient safety.

audits.finding: Tokyo Grade II/III indication 56%; decision within 48 hours 52%; antibiotics 100%; post-procedure documentation 96%; tubogram 40%; definitive plan within 8 weeks 80%.

paper.title: 927 Cholecystostomy Audit of Practice in a District General Hospital: Time for a Standardised Pathway
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Percutaneous cholecystostomy is a recognised option for high-risk patients with acute cholecystitis who are unsuitable for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Our Trust currently lacks a standardised clinical pathway for its use, which has contributed to variation in decision-making and post-procedure management. This audit’s aim was to evaluate adherence to best-practice standards and identify areas for improvement. Method A retrospective review was undertaken of all patients undergoing cholecystostomy between January 2022 and August 2025. Data extracted from electronic records included indication, timing of decision and intervention, procedural details, post-procedure management, tubogram completion, and documentation of definitive plans. Fifty cases met inclusion criteria. Results Only 56% of procedures were performed in patients with Tokyo Grade II/III cholecystitis (standard >90%). Decision-making within 48 hours of admission was achieved in 52% of cases (standard >80%). Antibiotic administration met standards (100%), and immediate post-procedure documentation was completed in 96% of patients. Tubogram completion was low at 40% (standard >80%). A definitive management plan within 8 weeks was documented in 80% of cases, with many patients managed with long-term drains. Only 22% ultimately underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Conclusions There is significant variability in the indications, timing, and follow-up of cholecystostomy within our Trust. Key deficiencies include non-adherence to severity criteria, low tubogram utilisation, and inconsistent definitive planning. These findings highlight the need for a unified, evidence-based pathway to improve patient selection, ensure consistent practice, and reduce prolonged dependence on cholecystostomy drains. The pathway we have devised will be introduced in early 2026, with plan for re-audit one year after establishment.

audits.change: Planned: standardised TURBT operative template and targeted education, with re-audit to follow.

paper.title: 973 Assessing the Quality of TURBT: A Comprehensive 18-Month Audit from a UK District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the quality of transurethral resection of bladder tumour at a district general hospital, focusing on detrusor muscle sampling, documentation standards, Mitomycin C instillation, adherence to EAU indications for re-resection, and early recurrence patterns. Method A retrospective review was conducted of all first TURBTs performed between January 2023 and July 2024 (n=101). Data collected included tumour stage and grade, presence of detrusor muscle, operative documentation, MMC use, operator grade, re-TURBT indications and findings, and recurrence at 3 and 12 months. Results were compared with BAUS and EAU guideline standards. Operator case volume was considered when interpreting individual performance, including procedures carried out during a period of locum consultant cover. Results Detrusor muscle was present in 55.4% of specimens, below the BAUS standard of 70%. Documentation was variable, with tumour number recorded in 86%, tumour size in 84%, and completeness of resection in 78% of cases. MMC was administered in 53.5% of all cases and 58.8% of eligible NMIBC cases. Forty-three patients underwent re-TURBT; 39 met EAU indications, while four had no clear indication. Residual tumour was identified in seven patients, and one case was upstaged from T1 to T2. Recurrences were documented in nine patients at 3 months and eight at 12 months, mainly within the high-risk cohort. Conclusions The audit demonstrates reasonable adherence to BAUS re-TURBT criteria and MMC usage, but highlights areas for improvement, particularly muscle sampling and documentation. A standardised TURBT operative template and targeted education are being introduced, with plans to re-audit following these interventions.

paper.title: 1016 A 2 Cycle Audit Evaluating the Impact of an RCS-Aligned Proforma on Surgical Handover Compliance in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Effective surgical handovers are essential for patient safety, continuity of care and minimising clinical errors. The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) outline core criteria for safe handover. This audit evaluated local compliance with RCS standards in a district general hospital and assessed whether a structured proforma could improve handover quality. Method A two-cycle audit was conducted. In Cycle 1, a questionnaire based on 13 RCS criteria was distributed to surgical staff (n=27). Data were collected on the quality of information handed over, handover structure, and staff perception of safety. A structured RCS-aligned proforma was subsequently introduced. Cycle 2 repeated the questionnaire to assess its impact (n=20). Following cycle 2, the proforma was incorporated into the electronic system to enhance compliance. Mean adherence scores were compared using Student’s t-test. Results Cycle 1 compliance revealed shortcomings in key areas including operational issues and resuscitation status. Following intervention, adherence improved across all criteria, with notable gains in the documentation of admission date, existing management plans and outstanding tasks. The mean total compliance score improved significantly from 44.6% to 70.2% between cycle 1 and cycle 2 (p<0.001). Staff rated the proforma positively as a guide for safe handover. Conclusions This audit demonstrated the value of a structured proforma in enhancing the quality and consistency of surgical handovers with minimal resource investment. Following cycle 2, an electronic proforma was developed to improve adherence. Further re-audit is recommended to evaluate long-term uptake and patient-centred outcomes as well as embedding staff induction training.
