audits.title: 1029 Time to Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) in Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Two Cycle Audit at a Rural District General Hospital
audits.standard: NICE: OGD within 24 hours of admission for acute upper GI bleeding
audits.finding: 32% (n=19) received OGD within 24 hours.
audits.change: Formal inclusion of the AUGIB OGD caseload in the on-call handover.

paper.title: 1029 Time to Oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) in Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: A Two Cycle Audit at a Rural District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim At Dumfries & Galloway Royal Infirmary, a rural district general hospital, referrals for the management of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (AUGIB) with oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) are the responsibility of the on-call general surgeons. This audit assessed local compliance with NICE guidance, which recommends OGD within 24 hours of admission. Method A retrospective cohort study of all AUGIB OGD referrals over 10 months was conducted. It was agreed that formally including the AUGIB caseload in the on-call handover could improve timely access to OGD, and this change was implemented. A second 10-month audit cycle was undertaken one month after implementation. Results In cycle one, 60 patients underwent OGD, and 32% (n=19) received it within 24 hours. In cycle two, 89 patients underwent OGD, but only 16% (n=14) met the 24-hour target. Intervention rates were similar (11.7% [n=7] vs. 11.1% [n=11]). Conclusions Implementing formal discussion of the AUGIB OGD caseload at handover did not improve compliance with NICE guidance on the timing of OGD after AUGIB. The increase in AUGIB OGD caseload during the second cycle likely had a significant impact on this outcome, and, coupled with a similar intervention rate, supports the case for a dedicated emergency OGD list to meet this clinical need.

audits.change: Educational posters, daily reminders at morning handover, and results shared at the monthly audit meeting.

paper.title: 1250 Improving Documentation of the Clinical Frailty Scale and Social History in ICU Admissions: A Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Accurate documentation of social history and the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) is vital for holistic assessment, care escalation decisions, and discharge planning. Incomplete information can overlook key psychosocial and frailty factors. This audit assessed the completeness of social history and CFS documentation in ICU clerking proformas and evaluated the impact of targeted educational interventions. Method A prospective review of clerking proformas was conducted for 30 ICU admissions (≥18 years) between 13–27 January 2025. Two PDSA cycles were completed. Data collection focused on CFS and social history subsections. A pre-audit survey was distributed to resident doctors and consultants. Following analysis, Interventions included educational posters and daily reminders during the morning handover. Results were shared at the monthly audit meeting. The second cycle, using the same methodology, reviewed 19 ICU admissions between 24 October and 7 November, 2025. Results Survey results showed that 67% of resident doctors recognised the importance of the CFS, while 87% of consultants felt CFS and social histories were often 'incomplete' despite being 'heavily relied upon' for decision-making. After the intervention, CFS completion improved from 52% to 68%, and social history completion from 54% to 84%, reflecting improvement across family history, mobility, carer status, alcohol use, and smoking. Mental health history (11%) and recreational drug use (42%) remained poorly documented. Conclusions The QIP improved completion of both the CFS and social history documentation. Although CFS documentation increased, further work is needed to raise completion rates above 80%. Regular audits, targeted teaching, and consistent reminders appear key to sustaining good documentation.

audits.standard: ESTS and BTS intraoperative lymph node staging guidelines for NSCLC resection

audits.change: Presentation of results and dissemination of guideline summaries.

paper.title: 1264 Audit: Compliance With ESTS and BTS Guidelines for Intraoperative Lymph Node Staging in NSCLC Surgery
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This audit assesses variations in surgical practice and evaluates compliance with European Society of Thoracic Surgeons (ESTS) and British Thoracic Society (BTS) intraoperative lymph node (LN) staging guidelines in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) surgery, aiming to improve staging accuracy and optimise oncological treatment pathways. Method A retrospective closed-loop audit of NSCLC resections (lobectomy and wedge with LN dissection) was undertaken at a tertiary thoracic centre. Cycle 1 included 92 cases (10/2024–02/2025), followed by 76 re-audited cases after presentation of results and dissemination of guideline summaries (03/2025–07/2025). LN yield was stratified, and “potential compliance” was assessed where N1 nodes may have been incorporated within the specimen. Operative notes and histopathology were reviewed for N1/N2 involvement. Percentage compliance was compared across thoracotomy, VATS and RATS. Results Across both audit cycles, modest improvement in guideline compliance was observed. Overall compliance rose from 16.3% to 17.1%, with slight increases in thoracotomy (8.7% to 12.5%) and VATS (6.5% to 8.0%), while RATS remained the highest-performing approach. The average LN stations dissected were similar across cycles, with a cohort median of 5 stations (range 1-9; IQR 4-6). RATS consistently yielded the greatest nodal clearance and highest compliance. Although station 7 was consistently dissected, overall clearance remained below ESTS standards, partly due to hilar nodes being included within the specimen. Conclusions This closed-loop audit showed persistent variability and overall low compliance, highlighting a continued gap in nodal staging that may risk under-staging. Continued education and regular audit cycles are needed to standardise practice and improve staging accuracy.

audits.finding: Mean overall turnaround 37.7 mins (SD 15.4), above the 15-minute target; cleaning 8.11 mins, extubation 5.11 mins, scrub 4.7 mins.

paper.title: 1374 Theatre Turn-Around Times in Northern Ireland (NI) – a Baseline Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To establish a contemporary baseline for theatre turn-around times across Northern Ireland (NI) and identify areas to improve efficiency within gynaecological and general surgery theatres. Method A prospective multicentre audit was conducted across nine NI hospital sites. Only general surgery and gynaecology lists were included. Data collection was carried out over six consecutive weeks. Forty-six variables were collected for each case, capturing key components of the turn-around process. Descriptive statistics were generated, normality was confirmed using the Shapiro–Wilk test, and t-tests were performed for inter-trust comparisons. Results A total of 116 cases were analysed (Belfast n=17, Northern n=56, Southern n=20, Western n=23). Mean component times included: scrub time 4.7 mins (SD 2.2), induction of anaesthesia 4.59 mins (SD 4.19), transfer onto table 1.27 mins (SD 1.18), operation duration 70.59 mins (SD 47.85), transfer back to bed 3.03 mins (SD 3.17), extubation 5.11 mins (SD 4.87), cleaning 8.11 mins (SD 5.51), and ready time 3.3 mins (SD 9.33). The mean overall theatre turn-around time was 37.7 mins (SD 15.4), exceeding the accepted gold standard. Median turn-around times were longer in general surgery than in gynaecology. No significant differences were observed between trusts in relation to delayed list starts (p=0.2703). Specific causes of delay could not be determined. Conclusions This audit provides the first contemporary baseline of theatre turn-around times in NI, demonstrating times well above the national benchmarking targets(15 minutes). Targeted local reviews are required to identify actionable areas for improvement.

paper.title: 1378 Adherence to Guidelines on Smoking Cessation and Weight Optimisation in Elective Umbilical and Epigastric Hernia Repair: A Multi-Centre Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess compliance with European and American Hernia Society guidelines on preoperative smoking cessation and weight optimisation in patients undergoing elective umbilical and epigastric hernia repair. Method A retrospective multi-centre audit was conducted across three hospitals (FPH, WPH and HWH). All adult patients undergoing elective umbilical or epigastric hernia repair between November 2024 and January 2025 were included. Emergency cases and patients under 18 years were excluded. Data collected included age, sex, BMI, smoking status, and documentation of lifestyle modification advice or referral for patients with BMI ≥35 kg/m² or who were active smokers. Results Fifty-nine patients were included (41 males, 18 females) with a median age of 54 years (range 22–86). Nineteen patients (32.2%) had a BMI ≥35 kg/m², and 10 patients (16.9%) were active smokers. Of the obese cohort, only one patient had surgery postponed and was referred for weight loss, while 17 (89.5%) proceeded without documented intervention. Among smokers, only two received documented cessation advice, while eight had no evidence of intervention. Six patients were both smokers and had a BMI ≥35 kg/m². Conclusions This audit demonstrates poor compliance with guideline-recommended preoperative risk optimisation in elective umbilical and epigastric hernia repair. Standardised documentation, routine counselling, and structured referral pathways are required to improve modifiable risk factor management and surgical outcomes.

paper.title: 1386 Are We Recording What We Should? a Closed-Loop Audit of Surgical Operation Notes
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess the quality of general surgery operation note documentation at our hospital against RCSEng Good Surgical Practice standards, evaluate the impact of targeted interventions introduced after the first audit cycle, and identify areas requiring further improvement. Method A closed-loop, retrospective audit was completed over two cycles. 50 randomly selected elective and emergency cases were reviewed in Cycle 1 (August-September 2025). Following this, interventions were introduced, including presenting findings at the departmental audit meeting and displaying posters in the theatre office. Cycle 2 reviewed a further 50 cases from November 2025. Documentation was assessed against the 2025 RCSEng Good Surgical Practice standards. Results Cycle 1 demonstrated high compliance for surgeon details, procedure, date, and operative findings (>98%), but several key fields were poorly documented, including time of operation, elective/emergency status, complications, prosthesis details, estimated blood loss (EBL) and antibiotic/DVT prophylaxis. Following interventions, Cycle 2 demonstrated improvement in: time of operation (2% to 28%), elective/emergency status (10% to 28%), complications (22% to 40%), prosthesis documentation (18% to 55%), EBL (2% to 20%), antibiotic prophylaxis (50% to 66%) and DVT prophylaxis (48% to 56%). Core elements remained consistently well recorded. However, several fields continued to fall below expected standards. Conclusions Operation notes are essential medico-legal documents that contribute to the safe continuity of care of surgical patients post-operatively. Targeted interventions improved overall documentation quality, though many remain below the expected standard. Continued reinforcement of documentation requirements, ongoing availability of guideline reminders, and repeat audit within 6-12 months are recommended for sustained improvement.

paper.title: 1475 Advancing Rib Fracture Care: Two-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate departmental compliance with local Trust guidelines for the management of multiple rib fractures, and to assess improvement following implementation of recommendations from the first audit cycle. Method A two-cycle retrospective audit was undertaken at Peterborough City Hospital. The first cycle reviewed patients admitted with multiple rib fractures between March 2023 and February 2024. The re-audit assessed practice between November 2024 and April 2025 after targeted interventions. Data were obtained from eTrack, ICE, EVOLVE, Symphony and Xero Viewer. Compliance with analgesia standards, imaging, chest injury scoring, pain team and regional anaesthesia referral, ABG performance, CCU referral and complication rates were evaluated. Length of stay (LOS) and patient comorbidities were also analysed. Results The first cycle included 101 patients and the second 62 patients. Across both cycles, elderly patients formed a substantial proportion and showed higher complication rates. Improvements observed in appropriate analgesia prescription and documentation of chest injury scoring. In the second cycle, regional analgesia was associated with reduced LOS (9.8 vs 12.6 days). However, persistent deficiencies remained: over 75% of patients meeting criteria were not referred to Critical Care, and compliance with ABG performance in hypoxic patients deteriorated. Pneumonia continued to significantly prolong LOS, increasing mean stay from 10.4 to 18.3 days. Patients with ≥16 fractures had markedly higher complication rates (27% vs 9%). Conclusions Despite targeted interventions, compliance with rib fracture management guidelines remains suboptimal. Key safety issues include inadequate CCU referral and inconsistent use of ABGs. Standardised pathways, mandatory proformas and improved education are required to enhance patient outcomes.

paper.title: 1108 Improving Patient Flow in a 2 Week Wait One-Stop Breast Clinic: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate the time patients spend in the Breast Outpatient Clinic during triple assessment, identify factors contributing to prolonged total clinic duration, and assess the impact of introducing a new breast clinic proforma on reducing waiting times and improving patient experience. This quality-improvement project was guided by the Royal College of Surgeons’ Outpatient Clinics: A Guide to Good Practice and the GIRFT Clinically-Led Specialty Outpatient Guidance (2023), both of which promote efficient one-stop outpatient pathways. Method A prospective audit (n=38) was conducted analysing key time intervals: patient arrival-to-clinical review, clinical review-to-imaging, imaging-to-results, and total clinic duration. A new breast clinic proforma was developed to improve documentation, optimise workflow, and facilitate earlier discharge for patients with normal clinical and radiological findings. A prospective re-audit was performed following implementation (n=56). Results The initial audit demonstrated prolonged waits, with a mean 2 hours 20 minutes from imaging to results. Only 20% required core biopsy, additional imaging or further assessment, indicating potential to reduce unnecessary waiting by over one hour for the majority of patients. Following introduction of the proforma, the re-audit showed a 36-minute reduction in total clinic duration. Time saved was redirected to patients requiring more complex assessment, while overall clinic flow and patient experience improved. Conclusions A standardised breast clinic proforma and pathway redesign significantly reduced patient waiting times and improved efficiency and patient experience within the one-stop 2 Week Wait breast clinic.

paper.title: 333 Rates and Outcomes of Renal Replacement Therapy in Post-Cardiac Surgery Patients: A Single-Centre Audit Against National Recommendations
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute renal failure is a recognised complication after cardiac surgery and is associated with increased mortality and prolonged length of stay (LOS). National guidance recommends benchmarking rates of renal replacement therapy (RRT). This study aims to describe the rates, preoperative factors, outcomes associated with RRT in post-cardiac surgery patients at a single institution. Method This is a retrospective audit of all adult cardiac surgery between January 2019 and October 2024 at Northern General Hospital, Sheffield. Demographics, comorbidities, operative variables, postoperative outcomes were compared between patients requiring RRT and others. Results were benchmarked against GIRFT and NICOR data. Results Of 3,261 patients, 90 required RRT (1.14%), below the GIRFT 2018 benchmark (1.56%). However, isolated CABG had a higher RRT rate (2.76%) than NICOR reports (0.98–1.45%). Mortality was significantly higher in RRT cohort (33.3% vs 2.2%, p < 0.0001). Lower pre-operative eGFR (50 vs 73 ml/min/1.73m², p < 0.0001). EuroSCORE was an independent predictor, with 16.4% increase (OR 1.164, 95% CI 1.101–1.232). Complex procedures and prolonged aortic cross-clamp time were strongly associated with RRT (p < 0.0001 and p = 0.0469, respectively). Patients requiring RRT had longer hospital stays (38.41 vs. 15.91 days, p < 0.0001) and higher reoperation rates (6.7% vs. 1.6%, p = 0.0014). Median RRT duration was 6 days; early RRT (1–3 days) was associated with the highest mortality. Conclusions RRT after cardiac surgery remains infrequent but carries increased mortality and LOS. Pre-existing renal dysfunction, CVA, higher EuroSCORE and complex surgery significantly predict postoperative RRT.

audits.title: EP 591 Follow-Up Colonoscopy in Acute Diverticulitis: A Retrospective Audit of Guideline Adherence
audits.standard: WSES and ESCP guidelines: colonoscopy 6-8 weeks after complicated diverticulitis

paper.title: EP 591 Follow-Up Colonoscopy in Acute Diverticulitis: A Retrospective Audit of Guideline Adherence
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim This retrospective audit evaluated compliance with follow-up colonoscopy guidelines in patients with acute diverticulitis, specifically adherence to the recommended 6-8 week follow-up for complicated cases. Current guidelines from the World Society of Emergency Surgery and European Society of Coloproctology advise colonoscopy 6-8 weeks after resolution of complicated diverticulitis to rule out malignancy. Colonoscopy is not routinely recommended for uncomplicated cases unless malignancy is suspected. Method The audit was conducted in two cycles. The first cycle (September 2023–March 2024) included 51 patients: 23 with complicated and 28 with uncomplicated diverticulitis. The second cycle (September 2024–March 2025) included 46 patients: 24 complicated and 22 uncomplicated cases. Colonoscopy rates, timing, and findings were recorded and compared. Malignancy rates and the need for emergency surgery were also assessed. Results In the first cycle, only 1 of 21 colonoscopies was performed within the 6-8 week period, and 1 malignancy was detected. After staff training and awareness initiatives, 6 of 18 complicated cases in the second cycle received timely colonoscopy, representing a significant improvement. No malignancies were detected in the second cycle. Overall, 46% of complicated cases had timely colonoscopy, compared to 5% in the first cycle. Conclusions The audit shows significant improvement in colonoscopy compliance for complicated diverticulitis. Given the low malignancy risk, routine colonoscopy for uncomplicated cases should be reconsidered. Future recommendations include enhancing discharge procedures and prioritizing colonoscopy for complicated cases.

paper.title: 468 Post-Thyroidectomy Voice and Vocal Cord Function Outcomes and Management: A Two-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Voice changes and recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) injury remain key complications following thyroid surgery. Although national guidelines (BAETS/ENT UK) recommended; structured documentation, early flexible nasendoscopy (FNE), timely SLT referrals, practice varies. This audit assessed adherence to these standard in a high-volume tertiary centre and identified opportunities to optimised postoperative voice outcomes. Method A retrospective audit of adult thyroidectomies performed between September 2024 and June 2025 evaluated compliance with BAETS/ENT UK postoperative standards: (1)voice documentation within 24 hours, (2)FNE for symptomatic/asymptomatic patients, (3)SLT/Laryngology referral when indicated, (4)use of validated PROMs. Secondary measures included incidence of VC dysfunction and comparing outcomes between benign and malignant disease. Minimum follow-up being three months. Results 100 patients were included (mean age 50; 75% female). Malignancy confirmed in 66%. Postoperative voice changes occurred in 20%, with 18% resolving and 2% persisting at three months. RLN injury occurred in 4%; two patients were referred to SLT and two developed bilateral vocal cord palsy. Among symptomatic patients, 35% underwent FNE within 24 hours, 55% confirmed malignancy. PROMs (VHI-10, EAT-10) were not routinely used. Voice documentation within 24 hours was achieved in 89%, but longer-term monitoring was inconsistent. Following implementation of targeted interventions (structured proforma, SLT referral, PROM integration), early second-cycle data indicated improved documentation and referral rates. Conclusions This audit highlights variability in adherence to national voice-care standards post-thyroidectomy. Implementing structured documentation, mandatory SLT referral pathways and routine PROM use can enhance MDT care, support early detection of complications and improve patient-reported outcomes.

audits.standard: not reported
audits.finding: 44 of 149 tonsillectomies were for histology, 29 for asymmetry; only 16 histology reports gave tonsil weight, 60% with weight difference of 0.5g or less; visual asymmetry did not predict weight difference (p=0.0561); no malignancy; postoperative bleeding 10.3%.

paper.title: 1195 Asymmetrical Tonsils - Audit of Clinical Practice
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Diagnostic tonsillectomy is commonly performed to exclude malignancy. We aimed to audit local diagnostic tonsillectomy practices to determine if tonsillar asymmetry is predictive of significant weight difference of the tonsils. Method Retrospective audit of diagnostic tonsillectomy cases performed at Salford Royal Hospital between September 2022-September 2024. Clinical notes were reviewed for primary indication for procedure, Brodsky grading on clinical examination, histological results, post-tonsillectomy bleeding and detection of malignancy. Results Data from 149 tonsillectomies were reviewed, with 44 performed for histological analysis. Asymmetrical tonsils were the most common and primary indication in 29 cases. Only 16 histology reports contained the required data on tonsil weight, with 60% showing a weight difference of 0.5g or less. In 20% of cases, the clinically “enlarged” tonsil was the lighter of the two. The tonsillar asymmetry on visual inspection was not predictive of significant weight difference of the two tonsils on histology (t-test p= 0.0561 P<0.05). No malignant cases were detected, and the rate of postoperative bleeding was 10.3%. Conclusions Based on our data, pre-operative detection of tonsillar asymmetry and visual grading system do not correlate with significant weight difference on histology. The high risk of post-tonsillectomy bleeding and absence of any malignant cases suggests that asymmetrical tonsils in isolation, with no red flag symptoms, should be carefully considered for tonsillectomy. Other approaches such as a period of observation, or additional imagining may be safer, this however may increase the risk of missing neoplasia. Further studies with bigger sample size may be helpful to draw further conclusions.

paper.title: 117 Initial Severity Assessment in Patients with Acute Pancreatitis in a UK District General Hospital: A Closed Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The existing Inernational Association of Pancreatology guidelines provide the standard framework for assessing the aetiology and severity of acute pancreatitis, with the Modified Atlanta Classification being the most widely adopted severity scoring system. This study aimed to audit compliance with IAP guidance regarding initial severity assessment in acute pancreatitis and to evaluate the impact of implementing a Pancreatitis Severity Scoring proforma incorporating the Modified Atlanta system. Method A retrospective audit was conducted of all acute pancreatitis admissions to a large UK district general hospital between October and December 2023 (Group 1). A Pancreatitis Severity Scoring proforma, including the Modified Atlanta criteria, was subsequently introduced, supported by education sessions during morbidity and mortality meetings, junior doctor inductions, and multidisciplinary awareness campaigns. Prospective data were then collected between February and March 2025 (Group 2). Data were obtained from hospital e-care records and discharge summaries. Results Fifty-one patients were included in Group 1 and twenty-seven in Group 2. In Group 2, 66.6% (18/27) had a proforma completed in e-care, of which 38.8% (7/18) were fully completed. In comparison, none of the Group 1 patients had a formal severity assessment recorded. Introduction of the proforma improved documentation of severity assessment by 66.6%. Conclusions Implementation of a structured Pancreatitis Severity Scoring proforma significantly improved compliance with IAP severity assessment standards. Regular reassessment facilitated monitoring of clinical progress and escalation needs. Ongoing education, re-auditing, and hospital-wide dissemination are planned to sustain and enhance adherence.

audits.standard: Local guideline: postoperative outpatient colonoscopy or CT colonography for patients aged ≥40 after appendicectomy
audits.finding: 25 patients (37.3%) referred for postoperative colonic evaluation.
audits.change: Educational email with supporting evidence sent to surgical teams.

paper.title: 1186 Outpatient Colonoscopy After Appendicectomy in Patients Over the Age of 40: Clinical Audit of Compliance in Practice
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute appendicitis is commonly triggered by obstruction of the appendiceal lumen or orifice. Multiple studies have highlighted increased risk of underlying colonic malignancy in older adults presenting with acute appendicitis. This audit aimed to evaluate compliance with recommending postoperative outpatient colonoscopy or CT colonography in patients aged ≥40 undergoing appendicectomy, and to assess the effectiveness of an intervention designed to improve adherence to this local guideline. Method An audit was conducted in two cycles at a district general hospital. The first cycle included patients aged ≥40 who underwent emergency appendicectomy between February and October 2024. The second cycle followed implementation of an action plan, consisting of educational email with supporting evidence sent to surgical teams, and included patients from March to July 2025. Electronic clinical records were reviewed for demographics, imaging, operative findings, histology and documentation of postoperative colonic evaluation. Exclusion criteria were primary appendiceal tumours, conversion to right hemicolectomy, recent prior colonic imaging, or other intraoperative findings. Results Cycle 1 included 67 patients. Only 25 patients (37.3%) were referred for postoperative colonic evaluation, and no malignant/premalignant lesions were identified. Cycle 2 included 45 patients. Following the intervention, referral rates improved substantially, with 28 patients (62.2%) receiving appropriate postoperative colonic evaluation—almost doubling compliance. Notably, two patients were found to have proximal ascending colon polyps, one demonstrating high-grade dysplasia. Conclusions This audit demonstrates significantly improving compliance with postoperative colonic evaluation in patients aged ≥40 following appendicectomy. Ongoing reinforcement and further re-audit are planned, aiming for early detection of caecal and colorectal pathology.

audits.standard: BOMSS annual nutritional monitoring (five blood tests), 80% standard; mean BMI reduction audit standard 20%
audits.finding: Mean BMI reduction 23.07% (standard 20%); 14.29% had all five recommended annual blood tests; FBC 63.74% highest, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 25.27% lowest.

paper.title: 473 Primary Care Perspectives on Bariatric Surgery: An Audit of Outcomes and Monitoring of Patients Discharged to Primary Care
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate long-term outcomes of bariatric surgery in primary care by determining (1) changes in BMI, comparing pre-operative, post-discharge and current values, and (2) the GP practice’s compliance with BOMSS recommended nutritional monitoring following bariatric surgery, which was not commissioned or resourced. Method A retrospective audit was conducted, identifying adults who had undergone gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy more than 2 years before the search date, indicating discharge from specialist care. 91 patients met the inclusion criteria: correct procedure type, and sufficient BMI data documented. Mean percentage BMI reduction was calculated using pre-operative, 2-years post-operative and latest BMI values. Compliance with monitoring was assessed by identifying whether patients had received all five recommended blood tests (FBC, ferritin, B12 and folate, bone profile, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D) within the past 12 months. Results Mean BMI reduction from pre-operative to current measurement was 23.07%, exceeding the audit standard of 20%. Further analysis of a 10-patient sub-sample revealed mean BMI reduction of 32.85% within the 2-year post-operative period. 14.29% of patients had received all five recommended annual blood tests; adherence varied by test, with FBC highest (63.74%) and 25-hydroxyvitamin D lowest (25.27%). Conclusions Bariatric surgery produced sustained BMI reduction, meeting expected long-term efficacy, although BMI increased after discharge from Tier 4 Weight Management. Annual nutritional monitoring in primary care fell below the 80% standard, highlighting the need for dedicated commissioning, improved systems in GP practices, such as proactive follow-up for non-responders and dedicated post-bariatric monitoring clinics, and suggesting benefit in extending specialist hospital follow-up beyond two years.

paper.title: 856 Gallbladder Polyp Surveillance at MFT Hospitals: Audit of Current Practice Against Latest Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Gallbladder polyps are a common incidental finding on ultrasound imaging. The majority are benign; however, studies report 4% are neoplastic with malignant potential. Appropriate surveillance is warranted to optimise early detection of these high-risk lesions. Although local guidelines direct surveillance to primary care, recent service pressures have redirected responsibilities to secondary settings. The latest guidelines provide updated evidence-based surveillance pathways. This study aims to evaluate the adherence of current gallbladder polyp surveillance against the latest 2021 joint European guidelines across Manchester NHS Foundation Trust (MFT) hospitals and identify factors influencing adherence. Method A retrospective audit across 8 MFT hospitals reviewed 448 ultrasound reports between 2023-2025. 100 patients with gallbladder polyps meeting the inclusion criteria were audited against the 2021 joint European guidelines. Data on demographics, polyp characteristics, radiological reports, clinician acknowledgement, follow-up intervals and outcomes were retrieved from electronic records. Results Adherence for polyps sized 5.1-5.9mm and 9.1-9.9mm was not assessable due to a lack of guideline acknowledgement. Only 17% of patient pathways adhered to the 2021 guidelines. 58 unnecessary scans were performed, and 35 referrals for cholecystectomy were missed. For patients with risk factors, only 14% of surveillance plans were adherent. 63% of ultrasound reports had no documentation of gallstones, 35% had no documentation of gallbladder wall thickness, and 0% documented polyp sessility. Conclusions Adherence to the guidelines was suboptimal. Poor clinician awareness of risk factors and inconsistent radiological reporting may have contributed to poor adherence. Revisions to include unacknowledged size thresholds, single guideline distribution, and standardised radiological reporting template are recommended.

paper.title: 1088 Evaluating the Impact of an Advanced Nurse Practitioner on Surgical Referral-to-Review Times in General Surgery: A Closed-Loop Quality Improvement Cycle
paper.abstract: Abstract Background East Suffolk & North Essex Foundation Trust (ESNEFT) intends to achieve the four-hour emergency department (ED) standard, by reviewing surgical referrals within 30 minutes. Cycle One revealed that 33% of referrals were reviewed within this guideline, with administrative burden identified as a major barrier. Aim Evaluate the impact of an Advanced Nurse Practitioner (ANP) on referral-to-review times (RTR) within General Surgery. Method Direct observation of on-call resident surgeons took place during 8am-8pm shifts and referral times, and activity data were recorded using pro-formas. Cycle one included General Surgery, Vascular and Urology. The ANP was introduced in Cycle Two to General Surgery only, as the poorest performing department. Results There was an improvement in RTR performance following the intervention. The mean RTR decreased from 1h 52m (Cycle One) to 1h 2m (Cycle Two) and median RTR dropped from 1h 8m to 40m. The proportion of patients reviewed within 30 minutes increased from 27% to 34%. Time spent on administrative tasks decreased from 33.2% to 24.4% (p = 0.045), and medical scan waiting times also decreased (p = 0.026). Addtionally, SHOs saw fewer patients within the trust guideline in Cycle Two (100% to 25%) . Conclusions The introduction of the ANP within General Surgery was associated with improved RTR performance and reduced administrative burden. While the 30-minute target was still not consistently met, the intervention showed promise improving patient triage and senior clinical review. Further audits with a longer data collection period and direct observation of the ANP are recommended.

paper.title: 792 IR-Guided Cerebral Angiograms: A Local Audit of RCR Compliance
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim IR-guided cerebral angiography is central to the diagnosis and management of cerebrovascular disease. This audit evaluated local practice against Royal College of Radiologists (RCR) standards with particular attention to complication rates and documentation quality. Method Data collected between April and October 2025, obtained from WebICE, PACS (angiogram reports), the departmental angiogram log and collated in Excel. Practice was assessed against key RCR standards, including documented written consent (100%), accurate procedural documentation (100%), and complication benchmarks: pseudoaneurysm/AV fistula ≤1%, access-site haematoma requiring intervention ≤3%, arterial dissection ≤1%, reversible neurological deficit ≤2%, permanent neurological deficit ≤1% and major contrast reactions ≤5%. Results A total of 206 procedures were performed, comprising mainly diagnostic DSA (n=175) and embolization (n=60). Common indications included subarachnoid hemorrhage, incidental aneurysm and follow-up imaging. Complications recorded were: groin hematoma with pseudoaneurysm (n=2), pseudoaneurysm with groin hematoma (n=6; managed with 2 surgical repairs, 3 thrombin injections, and 1 conservatively), procedure-related bleeding (n=4;two required craniotomy) and procedure-related stroke (n=4). Thirteen deaths occurred within the cohort, predominantly reflecting underlying pathology rather than procedure-related harm. Conclusions Complication rates were broadly in line with RCR thresholds, although the frequency of pseudoaneurysm formation exceeded the ≤1% target, highlighting a need to strengthen ultrasound-guided access and post-procedure monitoring. Documentation standards and consent recording were consistent but further streamlining is planned. Recommendations have been implemented and a re-audit will reassess compliance.

paper.title: 96 Enhancing Referrals to Our Surgical Ambulatory Unit: A Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The surgical ambulatory unit (SAU) is a vital aspect of our general surgical department within the Southern Health & Social Care Trust. It reduces unnecessary admissions and facilitates early discharge. It is imperative that accurate clinical information is available for the ambulatory team to perform effective and efficient reviews. The aim of this quality improvement project is to enhance referrals to our SAU in line with National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) QS174 and Royal College of Surgeons England (RCSEng) safe handover guidelines. Method A standard was set with regards to adequate referral information (diagnosis, background & plan) with referral data collected retrospectively in the first cycle through our electronic health record and SAU calendar. Departmental intervention was made through team education and reminder prompts across the department. Post-intervention re-audit was then undertaken. Statistical analysis was performed using chi-square using graph pad, a p value <0.05 was deemed significant. Results 57 appointments were analysed in the first audit cycle and 67 appointments post-intervention in the second cycle. Improvement was seen across all referral information domains including diagnosis (p<0.0001), background (p<0.0001) and plan (p=0.0007). Referrals with no information was significantly reduced (p=0.0063). Conclusions Enhancing SAU referrals by including diagnosis, background and plan is a straightforward and easy means to provide adequate referral information to the SAU team. This can improve efficiency, effective patient reviews as well as adherence to NICE and RCSEng guidelines re clinical handover and governance.

paper.title: 347 Implementing SINBAD Classification for Improved Documentation of Diabetic Foot Ulcers: A Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Proper documentation of diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) is essential for assessing severity, planning treatment, and tracking outcomes. NICE guidelines recommend using a standardised system like SINBAD or the University of Texas classification. In our unit, structured documentation was rarely used. Aim To improve DFU documentation by introducing the SINBAD classification in line with NICE recommendations. Method We conducted a retrospective audit of all patients with DFUs admitted under the General Surgery team at Prince Digna Hospital, Port Sudan, Sudan. Baseline records were checked for the six SINBAD components: Site, Ischaemia, Neuropathy, Bacterial infection, Area, and Depth. Staff were then trained, and a SINBAD-based documentation template was introduced. Records were re-audited after the intervention. Results Before the intervention, compliance was low: Site 65%, Ischaemia 41%, Neuropathy 0%, Bacterial infection 35%, Area 58%, Depth 35%. None of the notes used a standardised system. After the intervention, all criteria were documented at 100% except neuropathy, which was documented in 62%. Assessment of neuropathy was limited by the lack of monofilament testing in Port Sudan, and clinical examination findings were not consistently reliable. Conclusions Using a structured SINBAD-based template significantly improved the completeness and consistency of DFU documentation, supporting adherence to NICE guidelines. Limited resources affected neuropathy assessment, highlighting the need for proper diagnostic tools. Routine use of the template and ongoing staff training are key to maintaining these improvements.

paper.title: 430 A Two Cycle Closed-Loop Audit Evaluating MSU Compliance for New Urology Admissions at Royal Bolton Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Mid-stream urine (MSU) sampling is used to investigate urinary tract infections (UTI). An initial audit at Royal Bolton Hospital (RBH) in November 2024 revealed a 60% compliance, with only 16.7% of patients having an MSU sample sent before antibiotics were started. The SMART aim was to improve MSU adherence for suspected UTIs in all new RBH admissions to 100% by July 2025. Interventions were implemented, followed by a second audit in July 2025 to evaluate the impact and identify improvements. Method A retrospective analysis of electronic records identified 30 patients in the first cycle and 21 in the second who met the inclusion criteria: new urology admissions via Emergency Department with indications for MSU based on national and local guidance, admission exceeding one day. Data included patient demographics, admission reason, timing and location of MSU sampling, and timing of antibiotics. PDSA cycles focused first on raising awareness amongst doctors, then nursing and HCA staff. The second cycle also included time between triage to MSU collection. Results The second cycle showed improved MSU sampling from 60% to 67%. Number of patients receiving antibiotics following MSU collection improved from 16.7% to 50% and the median time between MSU and administration of the first antibiotic dose decreased from 22.25 hours to 5. Conclusions This closed-loop audit demonstrated improvements in MSU compliance, antibiotic timing and reduction in treatment delays at RBH. Although complete adherence has not been achieved yet, further PDSA cycles-such as introducing yellow wristbands to identify patients in ED-may strengthen compliance and improve patient care.

audits.title: 542 Assessment of Inflammatory Markers and Antibiotic Prescribing Practices in Acute Diverticulitis: Insights from a District General Hospital Audit
audits.standard: National guidelines (NICE NG147, ACPGBI, GIRFT) recommending selective antibiotic use in uncomplicated diverticulitis
audits.finding: Among immunocompetent patients with CT-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis (modified Hinchey ≤1A), 95.3% received antibiotics; 97% in the whole cohort.

paper.title: 542 Assessment of Inflammatory Markers and Antibiotic Prescribing Practices in Acute Diverticulitis: Insights from a District General Hospital Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute diverticulitis accounts for a substantial proportion of emergency presentations in the UK. Current national guidelines recommend selective antibiotic use in uncomplicated diverticulitis and emphasize the role of inflammatory markers and CT findings in stratifying severity. We evaluated real-world practice and explored clinical factors associated with complicated diverticulitis in a district general hospital. Method A retrospective analysis of 143 patients with CT-confirmed acute diverticulitis over 6 months was performed. Data collected included demographics, inflammatory markers (CRP, WCC), CT severity, modified Hinchey classification, antibiotic use, immunocompetence and 30-day reattendance. Associations between inflammatory markers, age, time-to-presentation and complicated disease were analysed using t-tests and chi-square tests. Results are reported using descriptive statistics following analysis. Results Uncomplicated diverticulitis accounted for 74.9% of cases. Among immunocompetent patients with CT-confirmed uncomplicated diverticulitis (modified Hinchey </=1A), antibiotic prescribing remained almost universal at 95.3%, rising to 97% in the entire cohort. CRP was significantly higher in complicated cases (148.1 vs 71.2 mg/L, p=0.0035), as was WCC (12.55 vs 10.70×10⁹/L, p=0.049). Complicated patients were older (66.2 vs 60.0 years, p=0.035) and less often immunocompetent (30.6% vs 59.8%, p=0.0044). Time-to-presentation was not significantly different. The 30-day reattendance rate was 8.4%, primarily due to recurrent symptoms. Conclusions CRP, WCC, age and immunocompetence are significantly associated with disease severity. However, antibiotic prescribing was almost widespread, irrespective of clinical risk indicators. These results highlight importance of consideration of these factors in patient assessment and support the adoption of severity-guided prescribing pathways in line with NICE NG147, ACPGBI and GIRFT recommendations.

paper.title: 550 A Closed Loop Audit of Ultrasound Use in Paediatric Patients Presenting with Abdominal Pain in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Ultrasound is the gold standard imaging modality recommended in paediatric patients presenting with suspected acute appendicitis. Ultrasound is highly specific and moderately sensitive for assessment of appendicitis in children. An audit of paediatric appendicectomy outcomes from 2022 showed that ultrasound use was limited to 30% of patients diagnosed with appendicitis. MRI was the most common index modality in 42% of patients. Subsequent interventions included increasing slot availability and access to sonographer training and providing a standardised ultrasound reporting format for suspected appendicitis to aid surgical decision making. Cycle two aims were to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention. Method Retrospective case study analysis of 220 patients up to age 16 admitted to general surgery with abdominal pain from 01/10/2023-30/09/2024. Results Ultrasound was used as an index imaging modality in 77% patients presenting with suspected appendicitis. Specificity of appendicitis was 93% (n=80) and sensitivity 27% (n=11). Clinical suspicion was the most sensitive indictor for appendicitis. Analysis of ultrasound reports compared to the standardised format found only 5% commented on all markers of inflammation. 25% of patients initially imaged with ultrasound required re-imaging. Outcome was changed in 25%. Conclusions Ultrasound is highly valuable tool in assessing children presenting with suspected appendicitis. A standardised reporting format can prove extremely helpful in guiding the need for further imaging or clinical intervention by describing the presence of inflammatory changes in cases where the appendix was not identified. Integrating this model into practice can help improve communication between the surgical and radiology department and ultimately reduce time to diagnosis.

paper.title: 112 Empowering Surgical Trainees in ENT Emergencies: Lessons From a Dual-Cycle ED Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate and strengthen clinicians’ competence in managing ENT emergencies (epistaxis and vertigo) within the emergency-general-surgical (EGS) framework, using structured teaching, simulation, and pathway-based quality improvement in a district general hospital. Method Two sequential audits assessed emergency clinicians’ knowledge and management of epistaxis and vertigo against NICE and RCEM standards. Domains included anatomy, first aid, procedural skills (nasal cautery, packing, Dix-Hallpike, Epley, HINTS), escalation, and documentation. Interventions comprised:Joint ED–EGS teaching sessions with simulation and practical workshops.Introduction of ENT management proformas and algorithmic flowcharts accessible via the intranet.Visual learning resources and QR-linked videos for procedural refreshers. Cycle-2 data captured post-intervention improvement and qualitative feedback on applicability to surgical training. Results Knowledge and confidence improved across both domains: first-aid and procedural steps (Epistaxis: 33 → 84 %; Vertigo: 69 → 80 %) and recognition of central-cause red flags (Vertigo: 32 → 85 %). Respondents reported better procedural confidence, more consistent escalation, and reduced inappropriate ENT referrals. Simulation sessions were rated highly useful for embedding skills transferable to other surgical emergencies such as airway and bleeding control. Conclusion Integrating ENT emergency management into surgical education through structured teaching, visual tools, and re-audit enhances diagnostic accuracy, procedural skill, and interdepartmental collaboration. The project demonstrates a reproducible, low-cost model linking quality improvement with surgical-training objectives. Sustained incorporation into induction and re-audit cycles can improve workforce readiness, promote safer patient care, and help develop confident, adaptable surgeons prepared for cross-specialty acute scenarios.

paper.title: 676 So What Is NEWS? an Audit of Near to Peer Surgical Teaching With Qualitative and Quantitative Analyses
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To analyse and improve the effectiveness of an existent surgical teaching programme by incorporating formal assessment. Method Southport Hospital (MWL Teaching Hospitals) operates a teaching programme for Y5 medical students from the University of Liverpool, which includes a hybrid session on NEWS2 utilising didactic and bedside teaching techniques. Advancing the feedback process used in a previous cycle, the authors developed a compound questionnaire to assess confidence and formatively test knowledge before and after each session, allowing qualitative and quantitative analysis. Results Previous analysis found that following the session, confidence responding to NEWS rose 62.2%, confidence taking histories rose 7.09%, and confidence examining a patient rose 25.3%. This repeat cycle demonstrated consistency with confidence responding to NEWS rising 87%, using ABCDE rising 51%, and new tenets of the teaching -escalating concerns (38%), and delivering emergency treatments (86%). The authors demonstrated efficacy in addressing students’ self-reported pre-session aims with feedback highlighting the benefits of exposure to a real patient scoring high NEWS and the hybrid approach built confidence and forced critical thinking. Students improved in formative assessment from scoring initially 61% to 72% (after the session) on average – underperforming mainly on questions about septic screening. Conclusions This project demonstrated that the teaching methods are effective in addressing students’ aims, concerns, and built confidence. The addition of formative assessment revealed gaps in the teaching that were not covered by text-based feedback. Further adaptation to the didactic component would cover the gap in knowledge of septic screening and be amenable to re-audit.

audits.title: 828 Improving Access to Lymph Node FNA: An Audit of Diagnostic Timelines, Inconclusive Rates, and Outcomes in Cutaneous Malignancy
audits.standard: Faster Diagnosis Standard: diagnosis within 28 days; Cheshire and Merseyside guidelines and GIRFT standards
audits.finding: 22 (38%) underwent FNA; median time from detection to FNA result exceeded the 28-day target by 8 days; inconclusive FNAs averaged 62.5 days to final diagnosis.

paper.title: 828 Improving Access to Lymph Node FNA: An Audit of Diagnostic Timelines, Inconclusive Rates, and Outcomes in Cutaneous Malignancy
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Fine needle aspiration (FNA) under ultrasound (USS) guidance is the first-line investigation for lymphadenopathy in cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) and melanoma according to Cheshire and Merseyside guidelines. The Faster Diagnosis Standard (FDS) requires diagnosis or exclusion within 28 days. This audit evaluated diagnostic delays, inconclusive rates, and inefficiencies in the pathway for melanoma and cSCC patients undergoing USS-guided FNA. Method A retrospective analysis was performed for patients referred for USS-guided lymph node assessment between 1st August 2024 and 28th August 2025. Electronic notes, histology, USS reports, and FNA outcomes were reviewed. Fifty-eight diagnostic cases were included. Primary outcomes included median times from lymph node detection to FNA, from FNA to histology, and overall time to diagnostic confirmation. Secondary outcomes included inconclusive FNA rates, repeat sampling, and subsequent management decisions, compared with GIRFT standards. Results Of the 58 diagnostic nodal scans performed on radiology consultant lists, 22 patients (38%) underwent FNA, while 36 did not require biopsy. Over half of FNAs confirmed metastatic disease requiring surgical or systemic treatment. The median time from detection to FNA result exceeded the 28-day target by 8 days. Inconclusive FNAs nearly doubled diagnostic timelines, with an average of 62.5 days to final diagnosis after repeat sampling. Conclusions The major delay occurred between lymph node detection and USS/FNA, largely due to limited radiology consultant capacity and the absence of two-week-wait prioritisation. Evidence supports surgeon-performed USS/FNA to improve access and reduce delays. Expanding surgical-led USS and integrating USS/FNA training into surgical curricula would streamline diagnostic pathways.

audits.standard: BAUS recommendation for urgent CT KUB; EAU guidelines on metabolic tests (calcium, uric acid) in confirmed urolithiasis
audits.finding: CT KUB positive in 60/136 (44.1%); calcium checked in 38.3% (23/60); urate in 20.0% (12/60)
audits.change: Email reminder to urology middle grades and consultants

paper.title: 37 From Stones to Standards: A Two-Cycle Audit on Optimising Urolithiasis Management
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Acute ureteric colic is a common presentation, with an annual incidence of 1–2 cases per 1,000 people (1). The British Association of Urological Surgeons (BAUS) recommends urgent CT KUB in standard, non-pregnant adults to diagnose urolithiasis and guide management (2). We aimed to evaluate the positive yield of CT KUB in patients presenting with suspected ureteric colic in NHS Lanarkshire and assess whether patients with confirmed urolithiasis had appropriate metabolic tests in accordance with EAU guidelines. Method In February 2025, 136 patients with suspected ureteric colic underwent CT KUB. Data collected included age, past history of urolithiasis, CT KUB results, and calcium and uric acid blood levels. An email reminder was sent to urology middle grades and consultants after the first cycle. A second cycle assessed whether calcium levels were checked, two months post-intervention. Results CT KUB was positive in 60 patients (44.1%). Of these, 38.3% (23/60) had calcium levels checked in the first cycle, improving to 71.1% (32/45) post-intervention. Urate levels were assessed in 20.0% (12/60) of patients. 48.3% (29/60) had a previous history of urolithiasis. Abnormal calcium levels were identified in 4.3% (1/23) in the first cycle and 6.25% (2/32) in the second. Conclusions CT KUB demonstrates good diagnostic yield for urolithiasis, consistent with a study at Newham University Hospital (40.5%) (3). However, metabolic investigations remain underutilized. Targeted interventions, such as reminders, improve compliance with guideline-recommended metabolic testing. Further strategies are required to ensure all patients with confirmed urolithiasis undergo appropriate metabolic assessment.

audits.standard: Timely surgery for suspected testicular torsion with TWIST score risk stratification
audits.finding: Mean time to theatre 276 minutes from ED presentation and 200 minutes from decision-to-operate; TWIST score calculated in 3.6% of cases.
audits.change: New torsion pathway in 2023: expedited referral from triage, electronic TWIST-based risk stratification tool, and targeted ED and urology education.

paper.title: 154 Recovering From Multiple Missed Torsions: A Service Improvement in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Testicular torsion (TT) is a time-critical urological emergency in which delayed recognition can lead to testicular loss and medicolegal risk. Following five cases of ‘missed torsion’ at Wexham Park Hospital (2021-2022), this project aimed to evaluate a dedicated TT pathway designed to reduce diagnostic delay, standardise risk assessment and improve patient safety. Method Serious incidents were thematically analysed to identify contributory factors. Patient journey was audited for delays; TWIST scores were calculated retrospectively and compared with operative findings. A new TT pathway was implemented in 2023, incorporating: (1) expedited referral from triage, (2) an electronic TWIST-based risk stratification tool, and (3) targeted education for ED and urology teams. Outcomes were re-audited in 2025. Results Before pathway implementation, mean times from ED presentation and decision-to-operate to theatre were 276 and 200 minutes respectively, with TWIST scores calculated in just 3.6% of cases. Retrospective calculation showed a correlation between TWIST score and confirmed TT. From implementation to re-audit no missed torsions were reported. Re-audit (June - September 2025) demonstrated reduced mean times to theatre (162 minutes from presentation; 100 minutes from decision-to-operate) and TWIST score documentation in 75% of patients. High-risk TWIST scores (≥5) accurately predicted TT in all cases. Conclusion This QIP demonstrates how serious incident analysis can drive system-level change. A structured pathway, incorporating risk stratification and staff education, has reduced ‘missed torsions’ locally and reduced delays to theatre. Our findings support the role of TWIST scoring as a valuable adjunct to clinical assessment in safeguarding patients and providing high quality urological care.

audits.title: 327 Improving Compliance with a Ureteric Stent Database: A Two-Year Retrospective Audit
audits.standard: Trust stent database documenting insertion and removal dates
audits.finding: 173 (42.5%) had no documented stent outcome; 16 overdue stents, 12 already listed; two patients missed completely.

paper.title: 327 Improving Compliance with a Ureteric Stent Database: A Two-Year Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Timely removal of ureteric stents is essential to prevent complications such as infection, encrustation, blockage, and complex removals. Our trust maintains a stent database to track insertion and removal dates; however, concerns were raised about incomplete documentation and overdue stents. This audit assessed compliance with the existing database and identified patients requiring further action. Method A retrospective review of the stent database was performed for all entries between June 2023 and June 2025. Data were cross-referenced with clinical systems to establish insertion dates, expected removal dates, documented outcomes, and reasons for delays. A total of 407 patients were analysed. Results A total of 407 patients were recorded on the database. 173 patients (42.5%) had no documented stent outcome, largely related to removals performed in flexible cystoscopy lists or outpatient clinics without subsequent database updates. Of 16 patients with overdue stents, 12 were already listed for removal or exchange; 4 required further follow-up due to DNAs, pending investigations, or difficulty contacting the patient. Among 5 additional patients, stents were removed privately, at other centres, or fell out spontaneously. Importantly, only two patients were found to have been missed completely by the service. Conclusions Compliance with documenting stent insertions was good; however, outcome documentation after stent removal was inconsistent, leading to risk of overdue or missed stents. Most overdue cases were already actioned once identified. Improving accountability—such as allocating responsibility to a designated SHO or healthcare professional for routine database maintenance—may enhance completeness, reduce overdue stents, and improve patient safety.

audits.title: 328 Is It Our Culture to Culture? a Second-Loop Audit of Preoperative MSU Screening Prior to Endourological Procedures
audits.standard: EUA 2024 and GIRFT 2025 guidance on preoperative urine testing and treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria; 100% standard
audits.finding: MSU uptake 3.8%; suboptimal management of positive cultures.
audits.change: New screening pathways in the pre-operative assessment clinic and microbiology team.

paper.title: 328 Is It Our Culture to Culture? a Second-Loop Audit of Preoperative MSU Screening Prior to Endourological Procedures
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) remains a significant contributor to peri-operative delays and complications in urological surgery. Whilst EUA (2024) recommends treating ASB, GIRFT (2025) emphasises tailored urine testing prior to procedures that breach the mucosa. Local practice in the first audit loop demonstrated poor MSU uptake and suboptimal management of positive cultures. This second-loop audit evaluates the impact of implemented changes within the Pre-Operative Assessment Clinic (POAC) and Microbiology team. Method A retrospective review of 73 patients undergoing endourological procedures (TURP, TURBT, FURS, URS) between July–August 2025 was conducted, three months after new screening pathways were introduced. Data were collected from theatre lists, operation notes, discharge summaries, and microbiology results. Primary outcomes were MSU submission rates and actioning of positive cultures; secondary outcomes included postoperative infections. Results MSU uptake improved from 3.8% in the first loop to 47.9% (35/73). Of the samples submitted, 13 (37.1%) were culture-positive; however, only 3 patients received documented antibiotic treatment. No postoperative infections or infection-related admissions were recorded. Despite improvement, compliance remains below the expected 100% standard, with several positive results demonstrating no evidence of clinical action. Limitations Challenges included incomplete documentation of antibiotics issued outside hospital systems, patient compliance with sampling instructions, and capturing individuals assessed prior to policy changes. Conclusions Enhanced POAC and microbiology processes substantially improved MSU submission rates; however, management of positive cultures remains inconsistent. Further refinement of patient information, documentation practices, and microbiology processing pathways is required. A re-audit is planned following refinement of the local protocol.

audits.title: 730 Are We Over-Stenting? a Single-Centre Audit of Ureteric Stent Use After Uncomplicated Ureteroscopy
audits.standard: Guidelines advise against routine ureteric stenting after uncomplicated ureteroscopy for stones
audits.finding: 91/143 (63.6%) were stented and 52 (36.4%) were not stented.

paper.title: 730 Are We Over-Stenting? a Single-Centre Audit of Ureteric Stent Use After Uncomplicated Ureteroscopy
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Guidelines advise against routine ureteric stenting after uncomplicated ureteroscopy (URS) for stones, yet practice varies considerably. The aim of this audit was to evaluate local stent use following uncomplicated rigid or flexible URS and compare post-operative outcomes between stented and non-stented patients. Method All uncomplicated RURS/FURS procedures with presumed complete stone clearance performed between January and December 2024 at a single centre were reviewed. Exclusions included planned second-stage URS, PCNL/ECIRS, concomitant procedures, and non-stone indications. Outcomes assessed were stent insertion rate, day-case vs inpatient stay, 30-day emergency re-presentations, and complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥2). Results A total of 143 URS procedures met inclusion criteria: 91 stented (63.6%) and 52 non-stented (36.4%). Among stented patients, 56 (61.5%) were day cases and 35 (38.5%) required overnight admission (mean stay 1.2 days, range 1-5). In the non-stented cohort, 39 (75%) were day cases and 13 (25%) were admitted (mean stay 1.2 days, range 1-3). Emergency re-presentations occurred in 7 stented patients (7.7%; 2 pain, 5 UTI) and 2 non-stented patients (3.8%; 1 pain, 1 UTI). One stented patient developed a ureteric stricture; one non-stented patient had a calyceal perforation requiring nephrostomy. Overall complication rates were low and comparable between groups. Conclusions Routine stenting after uncomplicated URS did not reduce re-presentation or complication rates. These findings support more selective stent use and improved adherence to guideline recommendations to reduce avoidable morbidity.

audits.title: 1000 Improving Ureteric Stent Follow-Up: A Retrospective Audit of Delayed and Retained Stents in a District General Hospital
audits.standard: Stent removal within 6 weeks or by target date
audits.finding: Removal plan documented in 95.7% (93.5% of discharge summaries); timely removal 59.1%; delayed 35.5% (33/93), 4.3% in situ over six months; possible retained 3.2%; unknown 2.1%.

paper.title: 1000 Improving Ureteric Stent Follow-Up: A Retrospective Audit of Delayed and Retained Stents in a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To evaluate documentation, follow-up planning and timeliness of ureteric stent removal in a district general hospital without an electronic stent-tracking system, and to quantify delayed or retained stents to support adoption of a registry. Method A retrospective review of all ureteric stents inserted between 1 March 2024 and 30 April 2025 was performed. Operation notes, discharge summaries and clinic letters were examined for removal plans and final outcomes. Long-term stents were excluded. Stents were classified as Not Delayed (≤6 weeks or by target), Delayed (>6 weeks without justification), Possible Retained (in situ at audit close), or Not Known (status unclear). Complications and device-related patterns were recorded. Results Ninety-three short-term stents were analysed. A documented removal plan appeared in 95.7% of cases and in 93.5% of discharge summaries. Timely removal occurred in 59.1%. Delayed removal occurred in 35.5% (33/93), including 4.3% that had remained in situ for more than six months. A further 3.2% had no evidence of removal at audit close (possible retained), and 2.1% could not be classified due to incomplete documentation. In 88% of delayed cases, no reason was recorded. The Cook UFI-600-R accounted for nearly half of insertions but 73% of delays and 93% of encrustations. The overall complication rate was 22.6%, predominantly encrustation. Conclusions Most delays lacked a recorded reason, and the Cook UFI-600-R accounted for the majority of prolonged dwell times and encrustations. These findings demonstrate significant gaps in follow-up processes and support the introduction of an electronic stent-tracking registry together with review of device choice.

paper.title: 1068 Identifying gaps in the transition to benign LUTS Care Following Negative 2WW Prostate Cancer Referral: A NICE and EAU Guideline-Based Outpatient Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Men referred via the two-week-wait (2WW) suspected prostate cancer (PCa) pathway frequently report lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), the majority of which are benign rather than malignant. NICE CG97 and EAU 2024 guidelines emphasize structured LUTS assessment, lifestyle advice, and appropriate transition into benign LUTS pathways once malignancy has been excluded. Failures in this transition can contribute to persistent symptoms and avoidable pressure on outpatient services. This audit assessed local adherence to guideline-recommended LUTS care following a negative cancer work-up. Method A retrospective audit was conducted in a district general hospital urology service. All men referred via the 2WW suspected PCa pathway between January–June 2024 who were subsequently confirmed cancer-negative were included (N = 268). Standards assessed were: (1) documentation of LUTS assessment at the initial 2ww appointment, and (2) evidence of lifestyle counselling, structured follow-up, or activation of a formal LUTS pathway. Data were analysed descriptively. Results LUTS assessment was documented in 203/268 patients (76%). LUTS were present in 143 men (53%). Of these, 54 (38%) had formal LUTS pathway activated, 4 (3%) received general lifestyle advice and 1 (1%) declined referral. Consequently, 84 symptomatic men (59% of those with LUTS; 31% of the total cohort) had no documented lifestyle advice, pathway activation, or follow-up plan, representing a gap in benign symptom management. Conclusions Significant deficiencies exist in both LUTS assessment and onward transition into benign LUTS care following negative PCa investigation. Embedding routine LUTS evaluation and automatic pathway referral are required to deliver guideline-aligned, continuous care.

paper.title: 1421 Epididymitis and Orchitis Management: An Audit of Compliance With GIRFT and Local Antimicrobial Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess local performance in the management of epididymitis and orchitis against GIRFT guidelines and local antimicrobial guidelines. Method A retrospective audit of patients presenting with testicular pain to the Surgical Same Day Emergency Centre (SSDEC) and Surgical Assessment Unit (SAU) was conducted. The first cycle of the audit reviewed compliance with age-based antimicrobial prescribing, sexual health assessment and compliance with the GIRFT pathway. Following this, an intervention was implemented consisting of QR code links to GIRFT pathways and antimicrobial guidelines. These were in poster format throughout SSDEC and SAU. A second audit with the same parameters was conducted after intervention. Results Across both cycles, 88 patients were included in the audit: 58 in cycle 1 and 30 in cycle 2. Antibiotics compliance improved from 50% to 70% following the intervention. Uptake of sexual health history and assessment increased by 34%. However, the main barrier for compliance was the non-compliance of IM ceftriaxone due to a lack of familiarity with reconstituting with 1% lidocaine. Conclusions Following 2 audit cycles, there was demonstrable improved adherence to GIRFT and antimicrobial guidelines and sexual health assessment as part of epididymitis/orchitis management. Patients with LUTS and symptomatic hydroceles were given outpatient follow-up. The above findings were discussed in a local meeting which yielded a collaboration with the antimicrobial team and prompted a change from IM to IV administration for ceftriaxone to increase compliance. This will be further re-audited to ensure the achieved improvements are sustained.

paper.title: 742 Improving Cardiovascular Risk Optimisation in Vascular Surgery Patients: A Two-Cycle Audit of Adherence to VSGBI Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Peripheral arterial disease carries high cardiovascular morbidity, yet best medical therapy (BMT) prescribing and relevant risk assessments remain variable. The Vascular Society of Great Britain and Ireland (VSGBI) framework provides guidance on BMT, glycaemia and lipid assessments. This quality improvement project aimed to improve adherence to VSGBI cardiovascular risk reduction standards through targeted education and visual reminders. Method Cycle one (C1): Retrospective analysis of vascular inpatients over a three-month period, assessing:BMT (antithrombotic, statin) prescribing;Gastro-protection;HbA1c testing;Lipid profiles. Intervention Surgical team teaching sessions, supported by departmental posters. Cycle Two (C2): Post-intervention snapshot audit of vascular inpatients, one-month duration. Results C1 included 153 patients (mean age 68; 117, 76.5% male) and C2 included 60 patients (mean age 66; 45, 75% male). Most admissions across C1/C2 were for chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and diabetic foot infections. Modest improvement occurred across prescribing domains: antiplatelet therapy (124/153, 81.1% to 50/60, 83.3%); anticoagulation (60/153, 39.2% to 30/60, 50.0%); statin (122/153, 79.7% to 48/60, 80.0%) and gastroprotection (54/153, 35.3% to 40/60, 66.7%). Metabolic evaluation increased considerably: HbA1c (17.7%, 27/153 to 30.0%, 18/60) and lipid profiles (12.4%, 19/153 to 65.0%, 39/60). Conclusions Targeted teaching and visual interventions moderately improved BMT prescribing, diabetic screening/monitoring and lipid assessment. However, substantial work is still required to optimise this fundamental cornerstone of cardiovascular medicine in this uniquely high-risk population. Developing these educational strategies with team empowerment to apply basic cardiovascular risk reduction principles and regular re-auditing may benefit long-term cardiovascular outcomes in vascular inpatients.

paper.title: 780 Assessment of Alignment with National ReSPECT and Cardiac Arrest Decision-Making Standards: A Quality Improvement Audit of Escalation of Care Planning for Frail and Older Vascular Inpatients
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Timely escalation-of-care planning is critical to delivering safe, patient-centred care for frail and elderly inpatients. National guidance from the British Medical Association (BMA), Royal College of Nursing (RCN), and Resuscitation Council (UK) recommends early senior-led discussions, shared decision-making, and structured documentation using the ReSPECT (Recommended Summary Plan for Emergency Care and Treatment) form. This audit evaluated adherence to these standards in a vascular inpatient cohort. Method A retrospective audit was conducted over 2 months, including vascular inpatients aged ≥75 or clinically frail. The audit standard, based on national recommendations, was 100% completion of a ReSPECT form for eligible patients. Documentation rates were assessed using electronic health records and analysed descriptively. Results A total of 47 patients met inclusion criteria. ReSPECT forms were completed in 11 cases (23.4%), significantly below the expected standard. Most missing documentation occurred in patients with urgent admissions—contexts where early escalation planning would be most valuable. Timing of form completion was inconsistently recorded, and no additional escalation-related domains met guideline expectations. Conclusions Compliance with national standards for escalation-of-care planning was low, highlighting systemic gaps in the application of ReSPECT and CPR decision-making frameworks in frail vascular patients. Integrating ReSPECT initiation into admission workflows, incorporating escalation discussions into multidisciplinary team (MDT) rounds, and introducing electronic prompts may improve uptake. Targeted education for junior clinicians could further strengthen documentation. Re-audit following implementation of these interventions is warranted.

paper.title: 1414 Improving the Detection and Initial Management of Phantom Limb Pain Post-Amputation: A Close-Looped Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Phantom Limb Pain (PLP) is a common, distressing neuropathic syndrome affecting up to 80% of post-amputation patients. If untreated, PLP often rapidly progresses into debilitating chronic pain syndrome that severely impedes rehabilitation, prosthesis use, and overall quality of life. Despite NICE guidelines advocating for early neuropathic treatment, acute surgical care frequently fails to meet this standard, contributing to significant patient morbidity and increased healthcare costs. Method A two-cycle closed loop audit was performed at a major trauma centre, on all major limb amputation patients (Pre: N=48, Post: N=27). The initial intervention included targeted educational sessions and informational posters for junior ward doctors. We measured PLP assessment, Pain Team referral, neuropathic medication initiation within 48 hours, and discharge documentation. Results The intervention successfully improved referral of PLP to the pain team, which increased by 15 percentage points (from 52% to 67%. Conversely, documentation of PLP assessment within 48 hours post-operatively paradoxically reduced from 44% to 33% The initiation of new neuropathic medication within 48 hours also dropped slightly from 42% to 37%, while discharge plan documentation saw a minimal rise from 21% to 22%. Conclusions Junior doctor education was insufficient to overcome entrenched systemic barriers to care. The failure to improve assessment and prescribing highlights a need to error-proof the clinical process rather than just improving awareness. The next QI cycle will address this by implementing an Electronic Prescribing System (EPS) Amputation Order Set and a Standardised Discharge Documentation Template to compel immediate and correct treatment initiation and ensure a comprehensive, patient-centred discharge plan.

audits.standard: BSG standards (rectal diclofenac prophylaxis); published PEP incidence benchmark 3–8%
audits.finding: PEP in 9/157 (5.7%); rectal diclofenac compliance ≈99%; pre-ERCP amylase documented in 6.3%; pre-operative IV fluids 29%; post-operative IV fluids 41.4%.

paper.title: 12 Post-ERCP Pancreatitis in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit of Incidence, Peri-Procedural Practice, and Clinical Outcomes in 157 Consecutive Procedures
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Post-ERCP pancreatitis (PEP) is the most clinically significant complication of ERCP, with a reported incidence of 3–8%. Evidence from district general hospital (DGH) settings, where operator volume and resources differ from tertiary centres, remains limited. This audit evaluated PEP incidence, peri-procedural management compliance, and outcomes at a single DGH endoscopy unit. Method This was a retrospective audit of all ERCPs performed between September 2024 and August 2025. Variables included demographics, procedural indication, operator, cannulation technique, pharmacological prophylaxis, intravenous fluid administration, amylase documentation, and clinical outcomes. PEP was defined according to consensus criteria as abdominal pain with serum amylase ≥3× the upper limit of normal at 24 hours, requiring unplanned admission or prolonged stay. Results A total of 157 procedures were analysed (58% female; mean age 70 years). The commonest indication for ERCP was choledocholithiasis (120/157; 76%). PEP occurred in 9/157 cases (5.7%). All 9 PEP cases arose at the index procedure. Rectal diclofenac compliance was ≈99%, meeting BSG standards. Significant deficiencies identified included pre-ERCP amylase documentation in only 6.3% of cases, pre-operative IV fluids in 29%, and post-operative IV fluids in 41.4%. Younger age and female sex were identified as risk factors. Severe PEP occurred in 1/9 cases (11%), including one ITU admission leading to one procedure-related death. Conclusions PEP incidence is within published benchmarks; however, remediable deficiencies in pre-procedural amylase documentation, hydration protocols, and pancreatic duct cannulation management were identified. Implementation of a standardised ERCP peri-procedural pathway aligned with current guidelines is recommended to optimise patient safety.
