paper.title: 11 A Closed-Loop Audit of Operative Note Quality in HPB Surgery: Adherence to RCS Good Surgical Practice 2025 Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess and improve operative note quality in HPB surgery through a closed-loop audit of compliance with RCS Good Surgical Practice 2025 standards. Method Elective HPB procedures at a tertiary centre were audited across two cycles: Cycle 1 (May–June 2025, n=71) and Cycle 2 (August–September 2025, n=75). Emergency cases were excluded. Parameters included RCS core fields and HPB-specific adjuncts: Pringle’s time, intraoperative ultrasound (IOUS), indocyanine green (ICG) fluorescence, and frozen section. Following Cycle 1, interventions included integration of a structured EPIC SmartPhrase template (hpbopnote), departmental presentations, theatre visual reminders, and targeted education. Results Overall compliance improved from 67% to 94%. The greatest gains were observed in operative diagnosis (18.3%→93.9%), estimated blood loss (23.9%→95.5%), and intraoperative complications (1.4%→69.7%). HPB-specific adjunct documentation improved markedly: IOUS (40.9%→100%), Pringle’s time (88.2%→100%), frozen section (21.4%→69.2%), and ICG usage (28.6%→58.3%). Improvements were observed across all remaining audited parameters. Conclusions Structured, prompt-driven documentation tools significantly improved operative note quality and adherence to RCS standards in HPB surgery. Embedding a SmartPhrase template within the electronic health record standardised documentation of both RCS-mandated fields and HPB-specific adjuncts. Well-documented operative notes are fundamental to continuity of care, trainee education, and medico-legal protection. This project demonstrates that closed-loop audits drive sustainable, meaningful improvements and provide a transferable model for documentation quality initiatives across surgical specialties.

audits.standard: SAGES 2025 guideline standards; 12-point checklist for IOC reading
audits.finding: IOC successful in 93.2%; CBD filling defects in 6.2%; 4/279 (1.5%) needed further imaging; no post-cholangiography pancreatitis.

paper.title: 13 Routine Intraoperative Cholangiography (IOC) in Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: A Single-Centre Audit of 279 Consecutive Cases
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Bile duct injury (BDI) remains a serious complication of laparoscopic cholecystectomy (LC), with reported rates of 0.3–0.6%. Intraoperative cholangiography (IOC) offers real-time biliary anatomy delineation reducing the rate of BDI and allowing common bile duct (CBD) stone detection. Despite endorsement in SAGES 2025 guidelines, NICE CG188, and EAES consensus statements, IOC uptake remains inconsistent across UK surgical centres. Aim To evaluate IOC performance rates, diagnostic yield, and impact on post-operative biliary imaging and clinical outcomes in a consecutive LC + routine IOC cohort. Method A retrospective single-centre audit of 279 patients undergoing LC with routine IOC. Successful IOC performance rate, mutually agreed quality metrics (12-point checklist) by three independent surgeons for reading IOC in a standard manner, BDI rates, CBD filling defect detection, post-operative imaging requirements, and length of stay (LOS) were assessed. Guideline compliance against SAGES 2025 standards was evaluated. Results IOC was successful in 93.2% of cases. CBD filling defects indicating choledocholithiasis were identified in 6.2% of IOC patients. Only 4/279 (1.5%) required further imaging. Zero patients had pancreatitis after routine cholangiography. Demographic and comorbidity profiles were consistent across subgroups. Conclusions Routine IOC in LC is achievable, diagnostically valuable, and associated with reduced post-operative imaging, shorter LOS, and less costly. These findings support routine IOC as standard practice. Sustained implementation requires IOC training and theatre infrastructure. However, for validation in the UK a multicenter study is recommended.

audits.standard: NELA process standards (critical care admission, CT imaging, data completeness, elderly assessment)

paper.title: Learning from Regional Excellence: Geographic Analysis of the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) Mortality Improvement
paper.abstract: Abstract Background NELA demonstrates mortality improvement from 11.36% (2016) to 8.15% (2025), representing a 28% relative reduction across 145,163 verified patients. Understanding the geographic distribution of this improvement offers opportunities for knowledge transfer and targeted quality enhancement. Methods Longitudinal analysis of NELA data (2016-2025) examined mortality trends across 15 geographic regions. Cross-sectional 2018 analysis of 23,929 patients across 190 hospitals characterised regional variation. Subsequent datasets confirmed patterns: 2022 (65,561 patients, 193 hospitals), 2025 (55,673 patients, 167 hospitals). Process standards, including critical care admission, CT imaging, data completeness, and elderly assessment, were analysed alongside outcomes. Results Geographic analysis revealed substantial regional variation, ranging from 5.4% (London-South-West) to 11.3% (Yorkshire & Humber). Excellence concentrated geographically: 60% of London-South-East hospitals achieved <8% mortality, compared with 13.3% in Yorkshire. In 2018, 6,439 patients (26.9%) received care in consistently low-mortality regions, whilst 7,700 patients (32.2%) underwent surgery in higher-mortality regions. North West (3,362 patients, 27 hospitals) achieved 8.4%, demonstrating scalable excellence at volume. Within-region variation suggested individual hospital practices merit investigation. Critical care admissions remained stable (78% to 77.5%), reflecting capacity constraints. CT imaging declined (65% to 54%) before standard redefinition. Data capture decreased (91% to 83%). These patterns suggest mortality improvement mechanisms differ from traditionally measured processes. Conclusions Analysis identifies high-performing regions: North-West demonstrates low mortality at scale (8.4%), London South West achieves exceptional outcomes (5.4%). Future initiatives should establish peer-learning networks, conduct site visits to identify transferable practices in surgical technique and perioperative management, and address infrastructure constraints, particularly in critical care capacity.

paper.title: SP 2.07 A National Prospective Audit of Acute Pancreatitis in the era of GLP-1 agonists (PANDORA): Breaking Results
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Acute pancreatitis (AP) occurs in 56 per 100,000 people each year in the UK. The use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) is increasing and may be linked to the development of AP. The PANDORA audit aimed to describe the diagnosis, management, and outcomes of patients presenting with AP with concurrent use of GLP-1RA. Methods A national, observational, snapshot audit of practice was undertaken between Sept-Dec 2025. Consecutive patients presenting with proven AP and concurrent GLP-1RA were included. Endpoints of interest comprised diagnostic (biochemical & radiological) modality, incidence of ICU admission and complications, and compliance to MHRA Yellow Card reporting. The data presented are early breaking results based on an interim analysis. Results The audit took place across 105 UK hospitals. A small majority of patients were female (53.4%) with median age 45-55. The most common aetiology of AP was gall stones (54%). Some 8% of patients with proven AP were taking a GLP-1RA, most commonly for the indication of weight loss (90%) and mostly sourced from private pharmacies (42%). Few instances of AP with GLP-1RA were reported to the MHRA (<5%). Admission to critical care occurred in 4.8% (GLP-1RA) and 4.2% (non-GLP-1RA) patients in this interim analysis. Conclusion Early breaking results of the national PANDORA audit are presented. Almost 1-in-10 patients presenting to UK hospitals with AP are taking a GLP-1RA. The full data will inform our understanding of diagnosis, management, and outcomes of this important group.

paper.title: SP 3.17 A Multicentre Audit Comparing Decision-Making Across Welsh Multidisciplinary Teams for Newly Diagnosed Rectal Cancer
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Rectal cancer management is increasingly complex due to expanding neoadjuvant and adjuvant options, including total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT), organ preservation, and immunotherapy. While these advances may improve outcomes, they risk introducing inter-centre variation between, raising concerns about equity. This audit evaluated rectal cancer management across Welsh multidisciplinary teams (MDTs), explored inter-centre variation, and aimed to inform future pathway alignment. Methods Prospective data were collected during MDT meetings over one month using a standardised electronic form. Data captured the first definitive MDT discussion for rectal cancer patients, including tumour stage, anatomical level, circumferential resection margin (CRM) and extramural venous invasion (EMVI) status, MSI status, performance status, and planned management. Decisions regarding neoadjuvant therapy, radiotherapy, surgical intent, and organ preservation were recorded. Patient outcomes were not assessed. Results Fifty-seven cases were recorded across seven centres. TNT was recommended in 21 cases, mainly for T3/4 tumours with nodal disease, EMVI positivity, or threatened CRM. Use of short-course radiotherapy varied markedly between centres, while long-course radiotherapy was more commonly used in frail patients with mid or low rectal tumours. Eleven patients were managed with organ preservation intent. MSI status was frequently pending at decision-making, with inconsistent documentation of its influence. Management of high-risk T3 tumours varied between TNT and upfront surgery. Conclusion Welsh MDT decision-making was broadly guideline-aligned but demonstrated variation in radiotherapy strategy, TNT use, organ preservation, and low rectal tumour management. These findings support further pathway alignment across the network, particularly in anticipation of AI-supported MDTs and emerging colorectal cancer biomarkers.

paper.title: SP 6.03 Improving Surgical Handover Report Documentation: A Three-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To evaluate the completeness and timeliness of general surgery handover report documentation used for weekend on-call cover. To assess whether an induction-embedded intervention improved compliance with national handover standards. Methods A prospective three-cycle audit assessed handover reports for all general surgery inpatients across three wards prior to weekend on-call cover. Variables assessed included patient inclusion on the handover list, whether entries were updated prior to handover, and documentation completeness in line with Royal College of Surgeons of England guidance on safe handover. Following the initial audit cycle, results were disseminated departmentally, after which a structured handover tutorial was embedded into resident doctor induction. Compliance with audit standards was then compared across cycles. Results Across 304 patients, patient inclusion in the handover list rose from 42% at baseline to 89%, and the proportion of entries updated prior to handover rose from 27% to 77%. Documentation completeness in line with guidance increased from 23% to 50%; however, omissions in patient status and outstanding investigations persisted. These gains were most marked in the acute admission ward and among on-call teams and were sustained despite resident doctor turnover. Conclusions Embedding handover expectations into resident doctor induction was associated with sustained improvements in handover list inclusion and update frequency, despite staff turnover. Documentation completeness plateaued at 50%, indicating that while human-factor interventions improve consistency of handover report updates, further gains are likely to require system-level solutions such as electronic handover templates.

Using those characteristics with NELA data, drew up a pathway and audited two separate 7-day periods to assess pathway validity and utility. audits.finding: Emergency vs elective: R0 96.97% vs 100%; lymph node yield >15 94.74% vs 98.99% (p = 0.2973); no conversion 89.47% vs 97.98% (p = 0.1211); overall compliance 84.21% vs 94.95%.

paper.title: SP 10.14 Oncological Outcomes of Emergency Versus Elective Colonic Resection for Colon Cancer: A Retrospective Audit Based on Guideline Compliance
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Emergency colonic resection for cancer is often associated with concerns regarding oncological adequacy compared with elective surgery. National and international guidelines, including ESMO and RCPATH, define standards for optimal surgical and histopathological outcomes, including R0 resection, adequate lymph node yield, and avoidance of conversion. Aim This study assessed whether emergency colonic resections for locally infiltrative colon cancer achieve satisfactory oncological outcomes in line with established guidelines and compared these outcomes with elective resections. Methods A retrospective audit compared emergency and elective colonic resections for cancer. Key outcome measures included R0 resection status, lymph node yield greater than 15, and absence of conversion. Compliance with guideline-recommended standards was assessed, and statistical comparisons were performed between groups. Results Emergency cases achieved an R0 resection rate of 96.97% compared with 100% in elective cases. Lymph node yield greater than 15 was achieved in 94.74% of emergency cases and 98.99% of elective cases (p = 0.2973). No conversion occurred in 89.47% of emergency cases versus 97.98% of elective cases (p = 0.1211). Overall compliance was lower in emergency resections (84.21%) than elective resections (94.95%). No statistically significant differences were identified between groups for R0 clearance, lymph node yield, or conversion rates. Conclusion Emergency resections for colon cancer can achieve oncological outcomes comparable to elective surgery when measured against established guidelines. Although compliance was lower in emergency cases, differences in key parameters were not statistically significant. Limitations include the retrospective design and small cohort size. Larger studies are needed to confirm these findings.

paper.title: TPT 1.12 Closing The ERAS Compliance Gap in Colorectal Surgery: A Completed Audit Cycle Highlighting Persistent Intra-Operative Variation
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims ERAS reduces length of stay (LOS) after colorectal surgery, but effectiveness depends on compliance. We completed an ERAS audit cycle to measure adherence, implement an action plan, and assess improvement. Methods Two retrospective cohorts of elective colorectal resections were reviewed (Audit: Dec 2024–Jan 2025, n=16; Re-audit: Aug–Oct 2025, n=20). Compliance was recorded for pre-operative counselling/documentation, fasting, carbohydrate loading, regional anaesthesia, normothermia; intra-operative use of NG/OG tubes and drains; and post-operative mobilisation, oral intake and opioid use. Results In the audit cohort (n=16), counselling documentation was low (6.25%), while pre-operative documentation was high (93.75%); fasting (87.5%), carbohydrate drink (75%), regional anaesthesia (100%) and normothermia (100%) were achieved. NG tubes were used in 25% and drains in 14/16, with opioids used in 100%. Mobilisation occurred on POD1 in 75% and was associated with shorter LOS (4–7 days). In the re-audit cohort (n=20), all pre-operative measures improved to 100%, mobilisation within 24 hours increased to 85% (POD0/1), liquids by POD1 reached 95%, and solids by POD3 were 85%, with median LOS 5 days. However, drains remained high (85%), NG tube use was 80%, and opioids remained 100%. Conclusions Completing the ERAS cycle improved pre-operative compliance and early recovery metrics, with shorter LOS. Persistent intra-operative variation (drains/NG tubes) and universal opioid use remain high-yield targets for the next intervention cycle using standardised criteria and opioid-sparing protocols.

paper.title: TPT 1.13 Assessment of Compliance with ACPGI Guidelines for Patients Undergoing Endoscopy Post Diverticulitis: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background The incidence of colonic neoplasia in uncomplicated diverticulitis remains low (1.6–1.9%); however, in complicated diverticulitis, it increases to 7.8–10.9%, underscoring the need for selective interval endoscopy in this group. In 2021, the ACPGBI introduced guidelines advocating a selective approach to post-diverticulitis endoscopy. Endoscopy is recommended at 6 weeks in patients with complicated diverticulitis, age >50 years, rectal bleeding, and/or concerning features on imaging, if not previously performed. Methods We performed a closed-loop audit of patients presenting with diverticulitis to assess adherence to ACPGBI guidelines. Patients who underwent surgical management were excluded. Results In the first cycle (n = 29), 25 patients met criteria for endoscopic evaluation, of whom 15 (60%) had endoscopy booked. In the second cycle (n=29), 24 patients met criteria, of whom 17 (71%) had endoscopy booked, demonstrating improved compliance. Indications related to complicated diverticulitis showed the highest adherence to guidelines. Overall, compliance improved following targeted teaching after the first cycle and the introduction of departmental posters. Conclusion In conclusion, our audit improved compliance with ACPGBI guidelines, significantly reducing the number of missed indicated endoscopies.

paper.title: TPT 2.02 The Right Tool for the Job: A Completed Audit Cycle of Trainee Surgical Equipment Knowledge with A Novel Educational Intervention
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Early career introduction to the operating theatre can be an intimidating prospect. Resident doctors (RDs) at our institution reported low confidence and anxiety using surgical instrumentation and drapes. We hypothesised this reflected a lack of practical teaching and sought to audit competence and knowledge in this area with a view to addressing these concerns. Methods Junior surgical RDs underwent a 14-item multiple choice questionnaire (MCQ) on surgical equipment, adapted from the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons (RACS) membership examinations. A digital survey captured demographics, experience, prior teaching, and subjective confidence using Likert scales. The audit standard was the RACS MCQ pass grade of 60%. Following first-cycle results, a practical multidisciplinary teaching session was delivered in collaboration with scrub nurse educators, incorporating demonstration of a general surgical set and patient draping. Re-audit was conducted four weeks post-intervention using the same MCQ and survey. Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used to compare pre- and post-intervention MCQ scores. Results Sixteen surgical RDs participated. 81% felt the topic was overlooked. First-cycle MCQ results did not meet the audit standard (mean 46.4%, median 35.7%, range 28.6–85.7%). Following the intervention, second-cycle MCQ results reached the standard (mean 80.4%, median 71.4%, range 71.4–100%), with a highly significant improvement in scores (p < 0.001). Conclusion This completed audit cycle identified a gap in education and demonstrated that a focused multidisciplinary intervention can improve both objective knowledge and subjective confidence. Our novel intervention has been incorporated biannually into the RD teaching programme and expanded to other hospital sites.

paper.title: TPT 3.04 Acute Diverticulitis: An Audit of Management Against NICE Guidelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Acute diverticulitis is a common presentation to the emergency general surgical take. This audit aimed to assess clinical practice at a single District General Hospital against NICE guidelines (NG147) for antibiotic prescribing and surgical management. Methods Clinical records of patients presenting with acute diverticular disease (diverticulitis, abscess, perforation, fistula or stricture) (N=26) over a two-month period (29/10/25-31/12/25) were reviewed to assess compliance with NICE guidelines. Results All patients had appropriate blood tests and CT imaging performed (100%). Complications were present in 35% (9/26) of whom 89% (8/9) were conservatively managed. All patients received antibiotics, of which prescribing was compliant with NICE guidelines in 38% (10/26). Duration of antibiotic prescribing ranged from 3-42 days, with a median duration of 8 days. No patients with a diverticular abscess underwent IR-guided drainage. In all cases (n=3) this was discussed with the radiology team and decided not technically feasible. One of the two patients with a diverticular fistula underwent expedited surgery. Conclusions The vast majority of patients with diverticular disease were conservatively managed. Variation in antibiotic prescribing despite the same clinical presentation was seen. Compliance with NICE guidelines on duration of antibiotics in uncomplicated diverticulitis was low. Educational intervention and re-audit are planned for February-March 2026.

paper.title: TPT 3.11 Evaluating Emergency Appendicectomy Practice in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Emergency appendicectomy is a common urgent surgical procedure, with national guidance emphasising timely surgery, appropriate use of diagnostic imaging, and rational postoperative antibiotic prescribing. This audit evaluated emergency appendicectomy practice in a district general hospital reviewing these principles. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted of emergency appendicectomies performed between January and June 2025. Data was collected from theatre logbooks and electronic records, including time from decision to operate to surgery, documented reasons for delay, use and findings of preoperative imaging, histopathology results, postoperative antibiotic prescribing, and 30-day readmission rates. Results 186 emergency appendicectomies were included. Surgery was performed within 24 hours of decision to operate in 73.4% of cases. Of delayed procedures, 45.0% had documented justification, with lack of emergency theatre capacity accounting for 41.0% of recorded delays. Histopathology confirmed acute appendiceal pathology in 79.0% of cases. Preoperative imaging was performed in 61.3% of patients. Of CT scans reported as acute appendicitis, 27.3% showed no histological evidence of appendicitis, while 25.0% of ultrasound-diagnosed cases were histologically negative, contributing to a notable negative appendicectomy rate. Postoperative antibiotics were prescribed in 67.2% of cases, with substantial variation in choice and duration. No clear association was identified between antibiotic prescribing and postoperative recovery or 30-day readmission. Conclusion This audit identified delays to surgery primarily related to theatre capacity, inconsistencies in diagnostic pathways, and variation in postoperative antimicrobial prescribing. Standardised imaging protocols, improved theatre prioritisation and evidence-based antibiotic guidelines may reduce negative appendicectomy rates and improve patient care. Re-audit following implementation is planned.

paper.title: TPT 5.03 Closed-Loop Audit of Failed Day-Case Discharges following Inguinal Hernia Repair
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Day-case surgery for inguinal hernia repair is widely practiced in UK; however, failure to discharge these patients on the same day causes significant strain on hospital system. Identifying and addressing preventable causes is essential to improve the service. Aim To identify factors contributing to failed day-case discharges following inguinal hernia repair and to evaluate the impact of targeted interventions through a closed-loop audit. Methods A closed-loop audit was conducted. The first cycle involved a one-year retrospective review of data of patients admitted for elective day-case inguinal hernia repair. Based on the first cycle result, a standardized day-case discharge checklist was developed following BADS and GIRFT guidelines. Doctors, nursing staff and ward managers were briefed on its use. The second cycle consisted of a one-year prospective data collection following implementation of the discharge checklist. Results In the first audit cycle, 44% of patients failed same-day discharge. The most common contributing factor identified was failure to discharge by nursing staff (42%) despite patients being medically fit for discharge. Other factors included urinary retention and post-operative complications. Following implementation of the discharge checklist, the overall failed discharge rate improved significantly from 44% to 12.7%. However, 32.7% of these patients in the second cycle experienced prolonged hospital stay despite being medically fit for discharge. Identified contributing factors in second cycle includes advanced patient age and operations scheduled on Friday afternoon lists. Conclusion Implementation of a standardized discharge checklist significantly reduced failed day-case discharge rates, hence improved service.

paper.title: TPT 5.07 Improving Postoperative Discharge Documentation for Inguinal Hernia Repair: An Audit of Compliance with British Hernia Society Guidelines and the Impact of Standardised Patient Leaflets
paper.abstract: Abstract Background Clear postoperative discharge advice is vital for patient recovery, understanding, and reducing avoidable healthcare use. The British Hernia Society outlines essential components of postoperative information for inguinal hernia repair, yet documentation consistency varies across institutions. Objective To assess compliance of discharge summaries with British Hernia Society guidelines for postoperative inguinal hernia repair and evaluate the impact of introducing structured patient-information leaflets. Methods A retrospective audit of 25 postoperative inguinal hernia repair patients was undertaken. Discharge summaries were reviewed against guideline domains, including analgesia advice, wound care, activity restrictions, suture or staple documentation, postoperative complications and safety-netting. In the second audit cycle, all patients received a standardised information leaflet detailing analgesia self-administration, exercise and lifting guidance, wound care, closure type, and red-flag symptoms. Results Documentation compliance varied significantly: analgesia 0%, bruising/swelling 45%, heavy lifting 75%, DVT/mobility 63%, numbness/pain 0%, closure type 36%, safety-netting 45%, exercise 45%, dressing changes 16%, mesh documentation 90%, postoperative bleeding 50%, showering/bathing advice 50%. Following the introduction of standardised postoperative leaflets, general practitioner and emergency department attendances related to postoperative concerns decreased substantially, and 98% of patients reported improved understanding of their postoperative instructions. Conclusion Baseline postoperative documentation was inconsistent and frequently incomplete. Standardised patient-information leaflets significantly improved patient comprehension and reduced unplanned healthcare usage. Routine incorporation of structured, guideline-based discharge materials is recommended, particularly within high-volume surgical centres.

paper.title: TPT 6.05 Breaking Routine Practice: Eliminating Unnecessary Pus Swabs and Antibiotic Use in Perianal Abscess Drainage — A Closed-Loop Audit Promoting Guideline Adherence
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim ACPGBI consensus guidance on emergency surgery recommends against routine pus swabs and antibiotics in uncomplicated cases of perianal abscess. Despite the guidance, these practices remain common, increasing cost, workload, and antimicrobial resistance. In this audit, we aim to evaluate the impact of team-based interventions and targeted education on improving guideline adherence. Methods A retrospective closed-loop audit was conducted at a District General Hospital. In first cycle, 50 patients who had the procedure (October 2024–March 2025) were evaluated for pus swab and antibiotic use. Interventions included targeted education to the surgical team, theatre staff engagement, and guideline distribution. A re-audit was conducted (n=21, July–December 2025) to assess the changes in practice following the interventions. Results In the first cycle, pus swabs were taken in 70% (n=35/50) of cases, antibiotics were given in 54% (n=27/50) cases, with no effect on recurrence reduction. Only 6% (n=2/35) of cultures sent were reviewed. Therefore, the first cycle audit showed a lack of adherence to the current recommended guidelines. Following interventions, in second cycle, the use of pus swabs was reduced to 23% (n=5/21). Antibiotic use without a clear indication remained unchanged in both cycles. Conclusion This study demonstrates that routine pus swabs and antibiotics in uncomplicated cases of perianal abscess did not alter patient outcomes. Team-based interventions, including targeted teaching, improved adherence to guidance regarding pus swab use, enhancing patient safety and reducing unnecessary costs. Further emphasis on reducing antibiotic use is required to improve antibiotic stewardship.

paper.title: TPT 6.07 Treatment Escalation Plan Documentation in Emergency Surgical Admissions: A Multi-Site Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Treatment Escalation Plans (TEPs) facilitate timely and patient-centred decision-making during episodes of clinical deterioration, extending beyond cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) status. This audit examined the prevalence, timeliness, and quality of TEP documentation at two hospital sites. Methods A retrospective review was conducted on 200 consecutive adult acute surgical admissions across two district general hospitals. Variables assessed included patient age, presence of a TEP, time to TEP completion, CPR status documentation, capacity assessment, and discussion of patient preferences. Data were analysed using descriptive methods. Results The mean age of the cohort was 62 years (range: 18–99). TEPs were documented for 39 patients (19.5%), with those patients generally older than those without TEPs (mean age 80 versus 56.6 years). Of these 39 TEPs, 21 (53.8%) were completed within 24 hours, 6 (15.4%) within 72 hours, and 12 (30.8%) after 72 hours. CPR status was consistently recorded for all admissions, whereas capacity assessments were noted in 34 cases (17%) and patient preferences in 14%. Conclusion While CPR decisions were uniformly documented, comprehensive use of TEPs in acute surgical admissions remains limited, often delayed, and frequently lacks documentation regarding patient capacity and preferences. Enhancing early completion and improving documentation quality may promote safer and more consistent escalation decisions, especially during off-hours and clinical handover. These findings were comparable between both sites, indicating widespread workflow and documentation challenges within General Surgery.

paper.title: TPT 6.09 Enhancing Patient Safety through Standardised Operative Note Documentation- A Closed-Loop Audit on Laparoscopic Appendicectomy Operative Note
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim Accurate operative note documentation is essential for patient safety, effective postoperative care, and medico-legal protection. National guidance from GIRFT and the Royal College of Surgeons of England emphasises the importance of comprehensive operative documentation. This closed-loop audit aims to evaluate the impact of a procedure-specific operative note for laparoscopic appendicectomy and education following the first-cycle audit, which identified significant deficiencies in the documentation. Methods A retrospective closed-loop audit was conducted at a District General Hospital. In first cycle, laparoscopic appendicectomy operative notes (n=56; February–April 2025) were assessed against GIRFT standards. Interventions included distribution of a standardised procedure-specific operative note template, targeted teaching, and workflow reinforcement. A re-audit was performed (n=46; July–October 2025) to compare compliance across standardised templates, handwritten/self-designed notes, and first-cycle results. Results Following the intervention, significant improvement was noted in the documentation of laparoscopic appendicectomy operative notes. 27 criteria were assessed in operative notes, and comprehensive documentation of all 27 measured criteria (100% in 22 and >95% in 5 criteria) was achieved using a standard operative note template. In second cycle, 85% (n=23/27) of standardised template operative notes achieved 100% compliance, compared with 7% (4/56) of operative notes in the first cycle. None of handwritten or self-made operative notes in the second cycle achieved full compliance. Conclusion This study demonstrated that implementing a standardised, procedure-specific operative note template with targeted teaching significantly improved documentation quality, enhancing patient safety. These interventions, grounded in human factors principles, are easily reproducible and applicable to other surgical procedures.

paper.title: TPT 7.01 An Audit of Awareness and Education of Surgical Staff Regarding the Green Theatre Checklist: A Tertiary Care NHS Trust Experience
paper.abstract: Abstract Background The Green Theatre Checklist (GTC) promotes environmentally sustainable surgical practice within the NHS. This audit assessed baseline awareness and knowledge of the GTC and sustainable surgical practices in a tertiary care NHS trust and evaluated the impact of targeted educational interventions. Methods A two-cycle audit was conducted using a structured questionnaire distributed to theatre-based surgical staff, including consultants, trainees, nurses, operating department practitioners, and anaesthetic staff. Cycle one assessed awareness of the GTC and knowledge of measures to reduce the environmental impact of anaesthesia, surgery, intra-operative, and post-operative practice. Results were presented at a clinical governance meeting, followed by a brief educational session. Interventions included posters and QR codes placed in theatre areas and hospital notice boards, alongside dissemination via mobile communication platforms. The same questionnaire was used for cycle two, and results were again presented at clinical governance. Results Awareness of the GTC increased from 37.5% to 64.5%. Knowledge of methods to reduce the environmental impact of anaesthesia improved from 57.5% to 77.4%, and awareness of sustainable surgical practices increased from 67.5% to 93.5%. Recognition of intra-operative measures rose from 40% to 93.5%, while awareness of post-operative sustainability measures increased from 22.5% to 87.9%. Knowledge of theatre waste management and the principles of the ‘R’s’ of sustainability also improved. Conclusion This closed-loop audit demonstrates that governance-led education significantly improves awareness and knowledge of the Green Theatre Checklist. This work is now progressing towards implementation of GTC learning into routine theatre practice.

paper.title: TPT 7.17 Standardising Docking Time in Robotic General Surgery: A Closed-Loop Audit Using Phase-Based Workflow Analysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To standardise docking time in robotic general surgery by implementing a structured, phase-based workflow analysis, enabling reproducible benchmarking and identification of workflow inefficiencies. Methods A closed-loop audit was conducted across two cycles in a robotic general surgery programme. Cycle 1 (n=43) measured docking time from knife-to-skin until the surgeon sat at the console. Procedures included cholecystectomies (n=9), inguinal hernia repairs (n=14), and major colorectal resections (n=17). Cycle 2 (n=30) introduced a phase-based approach, dividing docking into five sequential steps: (1) knife-to-port placement, (2) drive-in, (3) drive-in to dock, (4) dock-to-target, and (5) target-to-console. Times were prospectively recorded and analysed to identify workflow delays, procedure-specific variation, and learning curve effects. Results Mean docking time decreased from 34 minutes in Cycle 1 to 32 minutes in Cycle 2. Inguinal hernia docking improved from ∼28 to 20 minutes, and major resections from 58 to 42 minutes. Cholecystectomy times increased slightly due to a small sample size and the inclusion of a new surgeon. Phase-based timing allowed precise identification of workflow bottlenecks and facilitated targeted optimisation. The structured approach enabled consistent benchmarking and assessment of team performance across different procedures. Conclusions Breaking‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌ down robotic docking into discrete, quantifiable stages provides a consistent way to standardise docking time and pinpoint inefficiencies in the workflow. The use of phase-based docking as a tool to understand the surgical team’s workflow is thus a strong, widely applicable method to not only enhance operative workflows but also to set up significant performance metrics in robotic general ‍‌‍‍‌‍‌‍‍‌surgery.

paper.title: TPW 2.08 Post-Colonoscopy Colorectal Cancer (PCCRC): Two-Year Audit Using the WEO Framework to Target Preventable Harm
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Post-colonoscopy colorectal cancer (PCCRC) is a key quality marker reflecting missed lesions, incomplete therapy, or pathway delays. We audited PCCRC rates across two annual cohorts and applied the World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) framework to identify avoidable factors and improvement actions. Methods All colorectal cancers diagnosed between March 2023 and March 2025 were retrospectively reviewed. Cases preceded by lower GI-endoscopy within 36 months were classified as PCCRC using WEO criteria. Index endoscopy records were assessed for bowel preparation, lesion recognition, completeness, resection planning, coding, and time to definitive-therapy. Results Two PCCRC cases were identified across two cycles with low rates. Cycle 1 (03/2023–03/2024) recorded one PCCRC (0.6%), WEO Category C (detected but not resected), following poor bowel-preparation and delayed-definitive management. Learning themes included missed appointments, missed surveillance, cancers after flexible sigmoidoscopy, colonoscopy >3 years prior, and cancers diagnosed within 6 months. Improvements strengthened bowel prep/rebooking, surveillance tracking, and pathway awareness. Cycle 2 (03/2024–03/2025) recorded one PCCRC (0.7%) in an 81-year-old male with distal sigmoid cancer diagnosed 28 months after an index colonoscopy reporting small-benign-polyps and diverticulosis; further learning points related to investigation choice and referral delays. Conclusions The incidence of PCCRC at DGH remains below the threshold of 5%, suggested by JAG. Contributing factors included structured follow-up for patients ensuring optimal surveillance in tune with ACPGBI guidelines, improved awareness of PCCRC, enhanced techniques such as double walk on the right colon with white light and Narrow Band Imaging, standardised withdrawal times and regular emphasis on Key performance indicators.

paper.title: TPW 4.11 Audit of Knowledge and Utilization of Oakland Scores for Lower GI Bleeds in Ulster Hospital Dundonald (UHD)
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB) is a common reason for emergency surgical referral. The British Society of Gastroenterology 2019 guidelines recommend use of the Oakland score to risk-stratify patients and identify those suitable for discharge. This audit aimed to assess knowledge and utilisation of the Oakland score among Emergency Department (ED) and surgical residents and to improve adherence to guideline-based management. Methods A pre-intervention survey assessed knowledge and self-reported use of the Oakland score among ED and general surgical trainees. Surgical handover lists were reviewed to identify patients referred from ED with LGIB between July–August 2025, and clinical notes were assessed for Oakland score documentation. Interventions included posters in ED and seminar rooms, and a departmental teaching session. Re-audit was conducted over October–November 2025. Inpatients with per-rectal bleeding were excluded. Results Thirty-four clinicians completed the baseline survey – 61.8% of respondents were unaware of the Oakland score. In cycle 1, 21 patients were identified; only one patient (4.8%) had an Oakland score documented. Following intervention, 43 patients were identified in cycle 2, with Oakland scores documented in 48.8% of cases. Seven patients (33.3%) had scores ≤8; five were appropriately discharged and two admitted for alternative medical diagnoses. Fourteen patients (66.7%) had scores >8; ten were admitted and four discharged following senior review, all with appropriate follow-up or recent endoscopic assessment. Conclusions Targeted education significantly improved use of the Oakland score in LGIB assessment. Routine incorporation of the Oakland score may further enhance patient safety and optimise resource utilisation.

paper.title: TPW 5.02 Improving Outcomes in No-Lap Reporting: A NELA Quality Improvement Project
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) captures outcomes for patients undergoing emergency laparotomy; however, patients in whom surgery is indicated but not performed (NoLap) are frequently under-reported. These patients tend to be HIGH-RISK: older, frailer, and have more co-morbidities which is essential in identifying Care Gaps, Understanding variations in decision-making and improving future patient management. Method A quality improvement project using two PDSA cycles was undertaken between March 2024 and October 2025. Baseline review demonstrated no recorded NoLap cases and limited awareness of the criteria amongst surgeons. Initial interventions included education at M&M meetings, monthly reminders to surgical colleagues and retrospective review of previous cases. A second PDSA cycle introduced more structured measures, including involvement of junior doctors in data collection, creation of a shared NELA folder, regular review of M&M cases and on-call lists, and engagement with anaesthetic colleagues to improve case identification. Results Prior to intervention, no NoLap cases were captured. Following the first cycle, three cases were identified retrospectively. After implementation of the second cycle, ten additional NoLap patients were identified over a seven-month period. Awareness of NoLap criteria improved across the multidisciplinary teams and reporting became more consistent and reliable. Conclusion This project demonstrates that simple, low-cost interventions significantly improved recognition and reporting of NoLap patients. Regular education, shared responsibility, and clear systems for data capture were key to success. Furthermore, ongoing engagement and designated ownership are fundamental in sustaining improvements and ensuring accurate national reporting.

paper.title: TPW 5.04 Introduction of Post-Operative Antibiotic Guidelines Leads to Reduced Length of Post-Operative Stay and Improved Antimicrobial Stewardship in Uncomplicated Appendicectomy: A Single Centre Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Although appendicitis is one of the most common emergency surgical presentations, there is no clear national guidance regarding post-appendicectomy antibiotic prescription. Evidence suggests antibiotics are unnecessary for uncomplicated appendicitis, as reflected in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery Jerusalem guidelines. We conducted a closed-loop, single centre audit of appendicectomies, aiming to reduce unnecessary antibiotic prescriptions and assess the impact on postoperative length of stay and complications. Methods A retrospective audit of 100 patients with appendicitis was undertaken at a single UK centre, excluding paediatric and conservatively managed cases, and compared against Jerusalem guideline standards. Data collected included demographics, postoperative antibiotic administration, length of post-operative stay, complications and antibiotic-related sequelae such as C. difficile infection. The guidelines were subsequently implemented, followed by a second cycle. Data were analysed using RStudio. Results Of the 100 patients per cycle, 77 in cycle 1 and 71 in cycle 2 were included. Demographics were similar, with comparable sex distribution and a mean age of 41.1 years in both cycles. Each cycle included 46 cases of uncomplicated appendicitis. The proportion of patients not receiving postoperative antibiotics increased from 54.3% in cycle 1 to 78.3% in cycle 2 (p = 0.0024). Mean postoperative inpatient stay decreased from 23.3 hours to 14.5 hours (p = 0.0002). No significant difference complications rate was observed, and no C. difficile cases occurred in either cycle. Conclusion Guideline implementation reduced unnecessary antibiotic prescribing and shortened postoperative inpatient stay without increasing complications, demonstrating improved antimicrobial stewardship, patient experience, and bed costs.

paper.title: TPW 5.06 Emergency Appendicectomy Outcomes: A Benchmark Audit Against National Standards
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction Emergency appendicectomy is one of the most common emergency general surgical procedures. National bodies including GIRFT and the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) have defined benchmarks for operative approach, length of stay, complications, and readmission. This audit assessed local outcomes following emergency appendicectomy and benchmarked them against national standards. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted of all patients undergoing emergency appendicectomy at a district general hospital over the study period. Data collected included demographics, operative approach, post-operative length of stay (LOS), complications, and 30-day readmission. Outcomes were benchmarked against GIRFT and RCS standards. Secondary analysis explored factors associated with prolonged LOS. Results One hundred and twenty patients were included (mean age 34.8 years; 52.5% male). Laparoscopic appendicectomy was performed in 95.0% of cases, with a conversion rate of 0.8%. Median post-operative LOS was 1 day (IQR 1–2), with a mean of 2.0 days. Thirty-day readmission occurred in 6.7% of patients. Post-operative surgical site infection occurred in 4.2%, and unplanned re-operation was rare. Patients with complicated appendicitis and those experiencing post-operative complications had longer LOS. Conclusion Outcomes following emergency appendicectomy demonstrated strong compliance with national benchmarks, particularly for laparoscopic utilisation, length of stay, and readmission. Targeted strategies for higher-risk patients may further optimise bed utilisation and service efficiency.

paper.title: TPW 5.08 Improving Outcomes in Emergency Laparoscopic Appendicectomy: A Two-Cycle Audit in a UK Tertiary Centre
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To audit laparoscopic appendicectomy practice against national and WSES recommendations at a tertiary hospital, identifying areas for clinical improvement. Methods A two-cycle audit of adult (≥17 years) emergency laparoscopic appendicectomies was conducted at Royal Sussex County Hospital. Cycle 1 (n=101) was retrospective (July–October 2024); Cycle 2 (n=90) was prospective (April–July 2025). Exclusions: elective, pediatric, and diagnostic-only cases. Data on demographics, imaging, operative findings, drain use, antibiotics, and complications were extracted via Bamboo, Careflow Connect, and BlueSpier software. Results Across 191 cases (mean age 39.6 vs 41.4 years), time to diagnosis decreased from 16.8 to 8.27 hours, and time from diagnosis to surgery fell from 28.1 to 20.54 hours. CT utilization decreased (80% to 77.8%). Scoring system usage remained low (0% to 3.3%). The negative appendicectomy rate fell from 8.9% to 7.7%. Significant reductions were noted in drain usage (44% to 31%) and postoperative antibiotic administration (92.1% to 75.6%). The complication rate improved markedly from 17.8% to 3.3% (Cycle 2 complications were exclusively postoperative ileus). Conclusions The audit demonstrates successful reductions in diagnostic/surgical delays, drain and antibiotic use, and postoperative complications while maintaining low negative appendicectomy rates. Future focus should prioritize the adoption of validated scoring systems and continued antimicrobial stewardship. References Di Saverio et al. (2020) WSES Jerusalem guidelines; Gomes et al. (2015) WJES grading system; Li et al. (2021) Cochrane Database; UK National Surgical Research Collaborative (2014) Ann Surg; NICE Appendicitis Scenario (2024).

paper.title: TPW 6.13 Timing of Cholecystectomy for Gallstone Disease in a District General Hospital: A Retrospective Audit of Guideline Compliance, Readmissions and Service Burden
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims To assess compliance with guideline-recommended timing of cholecystectomy for patients admitted with acute cholecystitis and gallstone pancreatitis, and to evaluate the associated burden of gallstone disease, including readmissions, length of stay, and operative outcomes. Methods A retrospective audit was conducted of adult patients admitted with gallstone-related disease between January and April 2025. Patients with acute cholecystitis or gallstone pancreatitis were included. An initial cohort was identified via a data extract, with individual case review performed using electronic patient records. Data collected included admission diagnosis, timing and type of cholecystectomy (emergency or elective), drain usage, length of stay, and readmissions. Time to surgery was calculated from admission to cholecystectomy. Results A total of 136 patients were included. Although 73 patients were deemed fit for surgery, only 11% underwent cholecystectomy within 10 days. Among patients awaiting elective surgery beyond 10 days, 13 of 28 (46%) experienced at least one readmission. Emergency surgery was associated with higher drain usage (approximately 75%) but favourable recovery, with a mean length of stay of 3 days (median 2 days) which is in line with the benchmark average for the trust of 3 days. Elective surgery had lower drain usage (approximately 25%) but was frequently preceded by recurrent admissions. Conclusions Compliance with guideline-recommended early cholecystectomy was low. This led to preventable readmissions and increased healthcare utilisation. Emergency cholecystectomy appears safe and resource-efficient. Optimising acute gallbladder pathways and access to early surgery may improve outcomes and reduce service burden.

audits.finding: Options-based SDM documented in 73/356 (20.5%) ERCP episodes: low risk 19/78 (24.4%), medium 21/141 (14.9%), high 33/137 (24.1%) (p=0.105). Increased from 12.5% (2023Q4) to 31.8% (2024Q4) (p=0.160). LCBDE 38/38 (100%).

paper.title: TPW 7.03 Shared Decision-Making and Documentation before ERCP for Choledocholithiasis: A GMC-Aligned Audit Using Prespecified Operative-Risk Strata
paper.abstract: Abstract Background ERCP is widely used for duct clearance in choledocholithiasis but carries material risks (including pancreatitis, bleeding, and perforation); alternatives include single-stage LCBDE and intraoperative (“rendezvous”) ERCP. UK legal and professional standards require discussion and documentation of material risks and reasonable alternatives. We aimed to quantify documented options-based discussions before ERCP and benchmark against contemporaneous LCBDE practice. Methods Retrospective documentation audit of prospectively maintained biliary stone pathway database across two acute hospitals in one UK health board. Included index ERCP for choledocholithiasis and contemporaneous LCBDE cases (January 2023–December 2024). Non-stone indications and repeat ERCPs were excluded; each patient counted once. The primary outcome was explicit pre-procedure documentation of an options-based shared decision-making (SDM). Risk strata were prespecified as low/medium/high (ASA grade and Charlson comorbidity index); variation assessed by calendar quarter. Results 394 index duct-clearance procedures were analysed: 356 ERCP and 38 LCBDE. ERCP SDM was auditable in 356/356 and documented in 73/356 (20.5%). Rates by risk were: low 19/78 (24.4%), medium 21/141 (14.9%), high 33/137 (24.1%) (p=0.105). Documentation increased from 12.5% (2023Q4) to 31.8% (2024Q4) (OR 1.09 per quarter, 95% CI 0.96–1.24; p=0.160). Among ERCP episodes with a recorded procedure date (355/356), 30- and 90-day all-cause mortality were 1.4% (5/355) and 2.5% (9/355). LCBDE: no deaths; SDM 38/38 (100%). Conclusion Only one in five ERCP episodes had contemporaneous documentation of options and alternatives. Complete documentation in LCBDE indicates feasibility; an options-led consent template prompting locally available alternatives and patient priorities could standardise recording and strengthen governance.

paper.title: TPW 7.13 Audit into the Management of Gallstone Pancreatitis at A Tertiary Care NHS Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Background NICE guidelines recommend early cholecystectomy for patients with gallstone pancreatitis (unless severe), either during the index admission or within two weeks of discharge, to prevent recurrent biliary events. This audit assessed compliance with NICE guidance at a teaching hospital. Methods All patients admitted between 1 June 2025 and 15 September 2025 with biochemical and/or radiological evidence of acute pancreatitis and radiological confirmation of gallstones were included. Data collected included patient demographics, severity of pancreatitis, timing of cholecystectomy, and documented reasons for delay when surgery was not performed during the index admission. Results Thirty-one patients were identified; 18 (58%) were female. Twenty-seven patients (87%) had mild pancreatitis, three (9.6%) had moderate pancreatitis, and one (3%) had severe pancreatitis. Among patients with mild or moderate pancreatitis (n=30), only two (6.6%) underwent cholecystectomy during the index admission. Fourteen patients (45%) underwent elective cholecystectomy within five months of discharge; however, only two (14%) received surgery within the NICE-recommended two-week period. Common reasons for delay included uncertainty regarding surgical fitness (n=4), awaiting MRCP results (n=6), and awaiting ERCP (n=3). Three patients (10.7%) were readmitted with recurrent biliary pathology following their index admission. Conclusion Compliance with NICE-recommended early cholecystectomy following gallstone pancreatitis was poor, exposing patients to avoidable risk of recurrent biliary events and readmission. We aim to improve compliance by introducing a dedicated hot cholecystectomy pathway with protected theatre capacity and re-audit to assess the impact on adherence to NICE guidance and readmission rates.

paper.title: TPW 7.16 Improving Compliance with Severity Scoring in Acute Pancreatitis: A Two-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims The British Society of Gastroenterology recommends that all patients admitted with acute pancreatitis undergo severity scoring within 48 hours, as this facilitates early risk stratification, guides management, and improves prognostication. Failure to implement this standard may contribute to avoidable morbidity and mortality. Methods Medical records of patients admitted with acute pancreatitis at a District General Hospital were audited. The first cycle reviewed admissions between 23/11/2024 and 09/12/2024 for documentation of severity scoring using the Glasgow Imrie score. Following targeted teaching for resident doctors and the introduction of a process whereby the on-call team ensured scoring for all new admissions, a second cycle was conducted between 23/12/2024 and 10/01/2025. Results In the first cycle, only 2 of 12 patients (16.7%) had a Glasgow Imrie score recorded. Retrospective scoring revealed two patients had a score of ≥3 within 48 hours; one was not escalated until day five, requiring ICU admission for ARDS. After interventions, compliance improved markedly: 9 of 11 patients (81.8%) in the second cycle received severity scoring, and no ICU admissions occurred. Conclusions This audit demonstrates that simple, targeted educational and procedural interventions can substantially improve compliance with national guidelines on severity scoring in acute pancreatitis. Improved adherence ensures earlier identification of severe cases and timely escalation of care, with the potential to reduce complications and improve patient outcomes.

paper.title: TPW 7.20 Closed Loop Audit: Assessing Parenteral Nutrition in General Surgical Patients in A Busy Teaching Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Early consideration for Parenteral Nutrition (PN) in general surgical patients can reduce poor surgical outcomes and hospital length of stay (HLOS). This quality improvement project and audit assessed the quality of referrals for PN and the on impact timely delivery. The first cycle was presented at ASGBI 2025 (EP513). Methods A retrospective review was undertaken of patients referred for PN from General Surgery wards between 01/11/23–01/12/23 and re-audited in 2024. Data were compared against local nutrition standards and analysed using Microsoft Excel. Results Fourteen patients were referred in 2023 and eighteen in 2024. 20232024Median Age (range)75 years (28-89)67.5 years (24-80)Median BMI (range)20.1 (13.7-31.2)31.4 (17.3-54.3)Median HLOS (range)30 days (6-44)17 days (7-38) All cases across both cycles had a documented reason for gut failure (nil by mouth, poor intake, or vomiting) and appropriate baseline blood tests. Documentation improved by 4% in recorded height and weight (from 11/14 to 15/18) and by 30% in documented MUST scores (from 9/14 to 17/18). Median time from referral to venous access was 1 day, and all patients were reviewed by the PN nurse within 1 day, compared to a median of 1 day (0–2) previously. Rejected referrals decreased by 53%, PN commencement improved by 19% (from 9/14 to 15/18) and median duration increasing from 4 to 6 days. Conclusions Referral quality has significantly improved, allowing earlier and more appropriate nutrition, with an associated reduction in hospital length of stay.

paper.title: TPW 9.02 Routine Preoperative Investigations in Low-Risk Elective Inguinal Hernia Patients: A Closed-Loop Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Background NICE recommends specific preoperative investigations which should or should not be performed routinely in adult patients undergoing elective inguinal hernia repair, depending on their ASA grades and comorbidities. This two-cycle audit aimed to evaluate the routine investigations performed in ASA 1 and 2 adult patients prior to their elective inguinal hernia repair at a large tertiary centre. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 200 elective inguinal hernia patients between September 2023 and March 2024. The results were presented at a local meeting, and interventions were subsequently implemented including updated trust guidance and a digital decision-aid tool. To evaluate the impact of these changes, 96 patients were retrospectively analysed between December 2024 and June 2025. This was limited to one of the two hospitals within the trust, where interventions were first implemented. Results The first cycle showed poor overall compliance with NICE guidelines, but the second cycle demonstrated a marked improvement. Among ASA 1 patients, unnecessary preoperative tests decreased by 20.5% for FBC, 21.4% for haemostasis, 22.6% for U&E and 33.0% for ECG. In ASA 2, reductions were 75.0% for FBC, 16.7% for haemostasis, 11.9% for U&E and 9.4% for ECG. No lung function tests or ABG were performed in either cycle. Conclusion The updated trust guidance and digital decision-aid tool were effective in improving compliance with national standards. Further improvements can be achieved by wider implementation across the trust and continued re-auditing. Additionally, the audit can be expanded to assess financial and environmental impact.

paper.title: TPW 9.08 Establishing and Evaluating a Laparoscopic Peritoneal Dialysis Catheter Insertion Service in NHS Lanarkshire: A Two-Cohort Comparative Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Renal transplantation remains the gold-standard treatment for end-stage renal disease, but peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a valuable alternative. A laparoscopic PD catheter insertion service was reintroduced in NHS Lanarkshire and has matured. This audit retrospectively compares outcomes from the initial reimplementation phase with a recent cohort to assess ongoing performance against International Society for Peritoneal Dialysis (ISPD) guidelines. Methods Two cohorts were compared: - Cohort 1 (initial reintroduction): 19 consecutive patients undergoing laparoscopic PD catheter insertion from 17/12/2019 to 06/01/2021, followed up for 6 months. - Cohort 2 (recent audit): 34 patients from 24/04/2023 to 13/11/2024, followed up for up to 6 months. Demographics, complications, day-case success rates, and catheter survival were evaluated. ISPD guidelines were followed in both groups. Results Both cohorts had 0% 30-day peritonitis and surgical site infection rates. At 6 months, PD peritonitis was 22% (4/18) in Cohort 1, improving to 5.8% (2/34) in Cohort 2. Postoperative urinary retention fell from 11% (2/18) to 2.9% (1/34). Day-case feasibility improved, with overnight stays required for 83% (15/18) initially versus 44.1% (15/34) recently. Only one case of PD peritonitis had a positive PD fluid culture (Stenotrophomonas maltophilia). Conclusion The laparoscopic PD catheter insertion service in NHS Lanarkshire has matured, with reduced early complication rates in the recent cohort. Day-case procedures are feasible, supporting the long-term safety and viability of the service.

paper.title: TPW 9.16 Comparative Re-Audit of Unplanned Delays in Emergency General Surgery Theatre Lists
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Prompt theatre start times can maximise theatre usage. This may reduce cancellations, length of stay and staff overtime. Our audit aimed to identify late theatre starts, review reasons for them, and conduct an intervention to reduce them. Methodology Late start was defined as any session where the time into operating room is after the scheduled session start time, according to the Operating Theatre Efficiency Guideline. This re-audit compared the rate of late starts and reasons for late starts in the scheduled Monday-Friday emergency theatre lists, between two 3-month periods, with an initial data collection period between 01/11/2024-11/02/2025 (n=71) and follow-up period between 01/04/2025-12/07/2025 (n=60). An educational intervention was delivered to the surgical and anaesthetic teams, and the registrar role was updated between the two periods. Results There was modest improvement in number of delayed morning lists, improving from 81% to 66% delayed. Mondays and Thursdays showed the best reduction in number of lists delayed, improving from 77% to 56% delayed, and from 69% to 43% delayed, respectively. Afternoon lists were slightly more delayed in the second cycle, increasing from 50% to 55% delayed. No reasons were given for any delayed starts to morning lists. Afternoon lists were most commonly delayed due to overrunning elective lists, but this was poorly documented. Conclusion Increased focus on emergency list planning helps to reduce late starts, improving efficiency. Most lists are still starting later than the required standard; improved documentation of reasons for theatre start delays could advise additional targeted interventions in future.

paper.title: TPTh 1.09 Improving Prescribing of Regular Medications in Nil-by-Mouth Surgical Patients: A Closed-Loop Audit at a District General Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims Omission of essential regular medications in ‘nil by mouth’ (NBM) surgical patients is a recognised patient safety issue despite national guidance advising continuation of most regular medications. This audit assessed adherence to national standards and the impact of an intervention at a district general hospital in London. Methods A retrospective audit of electronic healthcare records was conducted across two audit cycles. Adult general surgical inpatients prescribed at least one regular medication were included. Day-case procedures, patients on no regular medications, and medications withheld for documented clinical reasons were excluded. Outcomes measured were prescribing of regular medications while NBM on the day of surgery, duration of omission, and documented reasons for withholding. Following the first cycle, graphical reminders were placed in clinical workspaces and a departmental audit presentation delivered. Pre- and post-intervention outcomes were compared using Fisher’s exact test. Results Regular medication prescribing while NBM on the day of surgery increased from 13.7% pre-intervention (n=51) to 28.6% post-intervention (n=42), p=0.12. In emergency surgery patients, prescription rates improved from 15.0% (n=20) to 43.5% (n=23), p=0.054. Failure to prescribe was the most common reason for medication omission in both cycles. The proportion of patients with medications omitted for four or more days did not differ significantly between groups (19.6% vs 11.9%, p=0.40). Conclusions Prescribing of regular medications for NBM surgical inpatients improved following low-cost interventions but remained suboptimal. Planned electronic prescribing prompts to document reasons for withholding may support further improvement.

paper.title: TPTh 2.12 Regional Adherence to National GIRFT Surgical Guidelines on Post-Operative Antibiotic Prescribing in Paediatric Appendicitis: Multi-Centre Multi-Cycle Audit of Clinical Practice
paper.abstract: Abstract Introduction National guidelines for paediatric appendicitis stipulate a pathway for post-operative antibiotic management based intraoperative findings. Despite this, significant variation in practice persists between surgeons and departments. Unnecessary post-operative antibiotics contribute to antimicrobial resistance, C. difficile infection and prolonged inpatient stay. We assessed compliance with GIRFT guidelines on post-operative antibiotic prescribing in uncomplicated and complicated paediatric appendicitis and aimed to standardise practice in line with GIRFT guidelines. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of paediatric appendicectomies performed at four central London hospitals over a 3-month period. Findings were presented at department and site-wide governance events. This was followed by a second prospective cycle after targeted education-based interventions at each site, focusing on junior doctors most commonly responsible for prescribing. Results The average number of cases across four sites was 20.5 (range=13-34) and compliance with GIRFT guidelines ranged from 46-75% between hospitals. Compliance did not significantly vary between sites (p=0.08). Non-compliant practice seen was the continuation of antibiotics following an uncomplicated appendicectomy, with a median duration of 4.5 days antibiotics post-op. Following education-based interventions, rates of compliance improved in subsequent cycles to 53-73%. (p=0.045). Conclusions Post-operative antibiotic prescribing for uncomplicated appendicitis were grossly discordant with national guidance. Clear documentation of antibiotic plans in operation notes and empowering junior doctors to challenge prescriptions with seniors helped improve compliance. Ongoing education supports appropriate cessation of antibiotics, reducing harm and healthcare costs.

audits.standard: BSG risk stratification guidance for lower gastrointestinal bleeding (Shock Index and Oakland score)
audits.finding: Shock Index calculated in 27% (18/66), Oakland score in 36% (24/66); admission rate 53% (35/66); 44% (15/35) of admitted patients had Oakland scores consistent with safe discharge.

paper.title: TPTh 2.14 Enhancing Guideline Adherence in Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding Through Structured Risk Stratification: A Two-Cycle Audit
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim The aim of the audit was to assess local adherence to BSG risk stratification guidance in lower GI bleeding and evaluate the impact of a targeted educational intervention on clinical documentation and risk scoring practices. Methods A retrospective two-cycle audit was conducted over twelve-month periods in an acute tertiary hospital. Adult patients presenting with lower gastrointestinal bleeding were included (Cycle 1: n=66; Cycle 2: n=57). Data collected included Shock Index documentation, Oakland score calculation, admission status, and discharge suitability. A targeted educational intervention was introduced between cycles, and outcomes were re-audited to assess changes in risk stratification, admission practice, and resource utilisation. Results In Cycle 1, Shock Index was calculated in 27% of patients (18/66), and Oakland score in 36% (24/66). Overall admission rate was 53% (35/66). Among admitted patients, 44% (15/35) had Oakland scores consistent with safe discharge, indicating potentially avoidable admissions and associated financial cost to the hospital. In Cycle 2, SI calculation increased to 82% (47/57), and Oakland score use to 79% (45/57). Admission rate reduced to 38% (22/57). Among admitted patients, only 18% (4/22) had Oakland scores consistent with safe discharge, demonstrating improved patient selection, more appropriate admission decision-making, and better utilisation of inpatient resources. Conclusion Targeted, low-resource educational interventions improved compliance with national LGI bleeding risk stratification guidance. Routine use of Shock Index and Oakland scoring supported safer clinical decisions, enabling early escalation, appropriate discharge, reduced avoidable admissions, and meaningful cost savings while maintaining patient safety.

paper.title: TPTh 3.08 Multi-Centre Audit of Abdominal Pain CT Pathways to Identify Emergency Laparotomy Patients Shows an Innovative “Straight to Test” Pathway from ED Triage is Possible Without Senior Surgeon Input in More than just One Hospital
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims National Guidelines from RCS and RCEM suggest assessment of patients who might require emergency laparotomy by senior doctors. NHSE guidelines for abdominal cancer include “Straight to test pathways” for diagnostic tests not involving doctors. We have previously shown that a “straight to test” CT pathway approach for emergencies is practical and potentially reduces mortality (ASGBI EGS 2024). We have also shown in a single unit that the information given at triage could initiate the CT pathway (ASGBI EGS 2025). We aimed to see whether identification of potential patients who might benefit from “straight to test CT pathway” at triage was possible in more than one unit. Methods 70 patients from 3 different hospitals undertaking emergency laparotomy audited consecutive non-IBD NELA laparotomy patients to see whether the information given at ED triage was sufficient to trigger CT scan. Mean time to CT request from ED triage was also recorded. Results 67 out of 70 (96%) patients met hospital abdominal pain CT pathway criteria at triage. Only 10 out of 70 (14%) met RCEM criteria for CT at triage. The average time to CT from arrival in ED was 11hr 36 min for all 70 patients. Conclusions We conclude that information given at triage could trigger a validated CT pathway for abdominal pain, potentially leading to faster diagnosis of patients requiring emergency laparotomy. Adoption of targeted abdominal pain “straight to test CT pathways” might give a greater chance of meeting NELA care standards surrounding this vulnerable emergency group.

paper.title: TPTh 3.09 Audit of Diagnosis and Management of Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Tract Bleeding (LGIB) in a Rural General Hospital, can we reduce hospital admissions?
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims This audit was conducted to compare our practice of management of LGIB to British Society of Gastroenterology 2019 guidelines, and to evaluate the benefits of applying Oakland Score in assessing safe discharges. Methods Adult patients who presented with acute LGIB were included. Data were collected from hospital information systems and physical notes. An excel sheet was developed to collect: patient demographics, data to calculate shock index and Oakland score on admission, investigations, blood transfusion, length of stay (LOS), cause of LGIB and in-hospital mortality. Analysis of the data was undertaken using excel. Results Between February 2019 and September 2023, 73 patients fit the criteria to be included (39 females, 34 males) with median age of 76 years (19-102 years). Using Oakland Score, 13 patients were deemed minor and 60 patients major. Out of 73 patients, 4 were discharged same day, 2 with Oakland score of 9 & 10 while the other two scored below 8. The median LOS was 3 days (1-38 days) 3 patients required surgery and 18 patients required blood transfusion, all other patients were treated conservatively (72%) with observations. Commonest cause of LGIB was diverticular disease (45%), followed by haemorrhoids (17%). Conclusions Oakland score appears insufficiently accurate for identifying patients who can be discharged. As 72% patients were managed by observations only, admission decisions may be better guided by other criteria as shock index, blood transfusion or surgical requirement. Patients not meeting these criteria could be safely managed outside hospital, for example through outreach or ambulatory service.

paper.title: TPTh 4.02 A Retrospective Audit of Routine Preoperative Blood Grouping and Saving in Laparoscopic Appendicectomy
paper.abstract: Abstract Aims This audit aimed to assess the necessity of routine preoperative blood grouping and saving (G&S) tests for patients undergoing laparoscopic appendicectomy. Specifically, we evaluated the frequency of perioperative blood transfusions and conducted a cost analysis of G&S samples. The secondary aim was to determine if routine G&S testing could be optimized to reduce unnecessary resource use. Methods The audit was conducted in two cycles: the first (October–December 2024) included 150 patients, and the second (January–May 2025) included 100 patients. Retrospective analysis of case notes was performed, collecting data on demographics, ASA (American Society of Anesthesiologists) grades, number of G&S samples, and blood transfusion requirements. Inclusion criteria were laparoscopic appendicectomy patients, excluding high-risk individuals, those on anticoagulants, or with preoperative anemia. Results In the first cycle, no patients required blood transfusions. Of 150 patients, 75% had two G&S samples, and 21% had one. A similar pattern was observed in the second cycle, with no transfusions required. Demographics, including ASA grades, were consistent across both cycles, with 53% of patients being ASA Grade 1 in cycle one and 80% in cycle two. Conclusions Routine preoperative G&S testing for laparoscopic appendicectomy is unnecessary, as no transfusions were required in either cycle. We recommend a more selective approach to G&S testing, based on patient risk factors such as comorbidities, anticoagulant use, and anemia, improving cost-efficiency without compromising safety.

paper.title: TPTh 4.03 Improving Antimicrobial Stewardship in Acute Appendicitis Through Education and System-Level Documentation Redesign: A Closed-Loop Audit at Wirral University Teaching Hospital NHS Trust
paper.abstract: Abstract Aim To assess adherence to World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) 2020 guidelines in the management of acute appendicitis, focusing on post-operative antibiotic prescribing and intra-operative documentation, and to evaluate the impact of targeted educational and system-level interventions Methods A closed-loop audit was conducted across two cycles. The first cycle included patients undergoing laparoscopic appendicectomy over a six-month period. Compliance with WSES-recommendations regarding post-operative antibiotic use and duration, intra-operative documentation of disease severity and contamination, and microbiological sampling was assessed. Findings were presented locally and informed consultant-led education and the development of a revised electronic laparoscopic appendicectomy theatre note designed to embed guideline-based prompts within the documentation workflow. A second audit cycle evaluated early changes in prescribing behaviour and documentation practices following these interventions, prior to full system-wide implementation. Results Eighty-one patients were included in cycle one and 31 in cycle two. The re-audit demonstrated early changes in antibiotic prescribing, with reduced duration in complicated appendicitis (9.2 to 8.4 days). Ongoing variation in prescribing for uncomplicated appendicitis was identified. Selective fluid culture sampling in high-risk cases yielded positive microbiology in all samples. Improved data capture supported refinement of discharge planning and antimicrobial stewardship. Negative appendicectomy rates remained low-6.5% Conclusions This audit demonstrates that combining education with early system development can support improved antimicrobial stewardship in acute appendicitis. The development of an electronic documentation tool embedding guideline-based prompts represents a sustainable strategy to reduce practice variation. Ongoing evaluation will assess the impact of full implementation on guideline adherence and patient outcomes.
